# About the Author

**Chris J. Mitchell** received his BSc (1975) and PhD (1979) degrees in mathematics from Westfield College, University of London. Prior to his appointment as Professor of Computer Science at Royal Holloway in March 1990, he worked at Hewlett-Packard Labs in Bristol, UK, and before that at Racal-Comsec in Salisbury, UK. At Royal Holloway, he co-founded the internationally renowned Information Security Group with his PhD supervisor, Professor Fred Piper, along with Professors Dieter Gollmann and Peter Wild, and he continues to play a role in its ongoing development. His research interests lie at the intersection of discrete mathematics, computer science and digital engineering, focusing in particular on cryptography and its applications as well as on combinatorial mathematics. He has successfully supervised around 40 PhD students to completion. He has been an active participant in the international standardisation of cryptography and information security for over 30 years. He was born near the South Downs in Sussex and today lives in an old cottage in Wiltshire with his wife and Pluto, a rather eccentric Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, where he spends much of his time in a shed at the bottom of the garden.

 

 

# Preface: Why This Book?

> The good Christian should beware of mathematicians.^()
> 
> > Mathematics is what mathematicians do.^()
> > 
> > > Some are mathematicians; Some are carpenters’ wives. Don’t know how it all got started; I don’t know what they’re doin’ with their lives.^()
> > > 
> > > There are a vast number of books on mathematics, so why should you read this one? That is, of course, the million dollar question, which I will now try to answer. I should first say that I doubt that anything I say in this book has not been said many times before, and often in much greater detail. Indeed, in sketching historical and philosophical ideas relating to mathematics, I am very much aware that a huge amount could, and indeed has been, said already. If you find yourself interested in these topics, there are many excellent books on the history of mathematics, and also a host of discussions of a more philosophical nature on what mathematics is.
> > > 
> > > The main aim of this book is to provide a straightforward introduction to topics such as groups and finite fields to engineers and computer scientists who find themselves working with—and possibly implementing—some of the strange types of arithmetic involved. These arithmetics are fundamental to much modern information and communications technology.
> > > 
> > > Why is this book necessary? After all, there are plenty of excellent books that provide a grounding in mathematics for engineers and computer scientists. However, existing books cover what is commonly known as ‘traditional’ applied mathematics, that is very different to the topics that I cover in this book. While applied mathematics in the traditional sense is still of huge importance, modern digital systems increasingly build on very different types of mathematics, and these very different types of mathematics form the focus of this book.
> > > 
> > > I have attempted to make the book accessible to as large an audience as possible. I will provide some proofs (it wouldn’t be a mathematics book without proofs) but if you like you can skip them, although I think it would be a shame to avoid them altogether since they are such an integral part of mathematics. More importantly, in all the main chapters after the introductory material I provide case studies of how the mathematics I introduce underlies key modern digital technologies, in particular focussing on those relating to secure and reliable communications.
> > > 
> > > A somewhat subsidiary aim of the book is to introduce the general reader to some of the fascinating mathematics underlying the modern digital and information-centric world. In doing so, I am hoping to give non-mathematicians a taste of what mathematics is really about, at least as mathematicians see it. I should say that I first wanted to write this book at least ten years ago, but finding the time has been the main obstacle.^()
> > > 
> > > It seems rather ironic, to me at least, that much of the mathematics I will attempt to describe in this book was not developed with applications in mind. Instead it was developed, and is still largely taught, very much under the banner of *Pure*, as opposed to *Applied*, mathematics where—historically at least—pure mathematics means mathematics done without worrying about applications. The key area I will explore comes under the heading of what might be called ‘Abstract Algebra’ (or ‘Modern Algebra’).
> > > 
> > > So why do I say that this seems ironic? Well, traditionally, and perhaps surprisingly, some pure mathematicians have been a little sniffy about applied mathematics, regarding it as a lower form. Pure mathematics, at least as some see it, is somehow superior precisely because it isn’t related to applications but has been developed purely for its own sake. To some extent such a view seems nonsensical, since I suspect that the original roots of all of mathematics lie in applications, although in some cases mathematics has progressed a very long way from its origins. Of course mathematics is not unique; I suspect such views pervade other areas of human activity—for example, perhaps the art world is a little like this, where I get the impression that commercial art is sometimes thought of as being less worthy than fine art, or ‘art for art’s sake’.
> > > 
> > > Of course when I mention applied mathematics I mean mathematics applied to the physical sciences or to mechanical or electrical engineering. The term *applied mathematics* is often taken to mean just this, where other areas of mathematics which find real-world applications are not given the label. Anyway, while I’m sure not everyone would agree with this rather simple discussion of terminology, I hope it gives you a flavour of the rather strange way in which the terms pure and applied are used when referring to mathematics. My emphasis in this book is on mathematics which finds application in real-world systems relating to computing and communications, but is nonetheless often thought of as pure.
> > > 
> > > Anyway, back to algebra. The word algebra comes from the Arabic word al-jabr meaning ‘the reunion of broken parts’, used by the Persian mathematician and astronomer Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (in the 9th century CE) for naming a method of transforming equations. Interestingly, al-Khwarizmi also gives his name to the term algorithm, but that’s a story for another book.
> > > 
> > > I suspect most readers will think of algebra as relating to manipulating and solving equations involving symbols which represent numbers. Of course, using symbols in equations to solve problems is a hugely powerful technique that you were very probably taught at school. So we all know what algebra is; but what about ‘abstract’ algebra? Abstract algebra, as I will discuss in a little more detail in the first chapter, seeks to look at what happens when we think about some of the rules underpinning addition and multiplication of numbers, and look at what happens when we apply these rules to operations on more general objects—which might be thought of as new types of numbers. The implications turn out to be profoundly important for the modern world.
> > > 
> > > At this point I should also mention another branch of mathematics known as *Number theory.*^()
> > > 
> > > Until the second half of the twentieth century, number theory was thought of as the purest of pure mathematics. After all, what possible application could exist for investigating prime numbers, a subject of study by mathematicians for its own sake for at least two thousand years? Well, as I explore in this book, a hugely important method for encrypting data, which has been widely used in securing everyday financial transactions, is built on key results from number theory. So even number theory is not really ‘pure’ any more.
> > > 
> > > Another area of mathematics that forms a theme of this book is known as *Discrete Mathematics*. Discrete mathematics is the mathematics of discrete objects, such as the numbers 1, 2, 3, etc., as opposed to the world of continuous functions (such as the trigonometric functions *sine* or *cosine*). Why is discrete mathematics important here? Well, the numbers and objects processed by digital computers, including all the phones, tablets, PCs and servers we use on an everyday basis, are by definition discrete. These devices store and interchange information as zeros and ones, not as continuous values, and so it is inevitable that discrete mathematics is of key importance to the modern information age.
> > > 
> > > I have tried to give credit throughout this book to some of the great mathematicians of the past two or three thousand years who have developed the ideas I describe. However, I am a little ashamed to have to confess that the vast majority of the mathematicians I mention are men. There are many and varied reasons for this, not least because in many cultures women have been, and continue to be, denied access to mathematical education. More sinisterly, it seems that, as in many other walks of life, efforts have been made to hide contributions made by women, perhaps to try to maintain the fiction that women and mathematics do not go together.^()
> > > 
> > > Finally, given my claim about the importance of the mathematical ideas introduced here to the digital world, I will provide examples of how they are used throughout the book. I have to confess I haven’t chosen the applications I mention systematically—they simply happen to be the ones I know best. However, rest assured that there are many more that I don’t discuss here.
> > > 
> > > Chris J. Mitchell
> > > 
> > > Wiltshire
> > > 
> > > August 2025

> > > 5.  [5](#f08.xhtml#rfn_5) Number theory is exalted by some as the pinnacle of pure mathematics. For example, the great early 19th century mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss is quoted as having said ‘Mathematics is the queen of the sciences—and number theory is the queen of mathematics’. Gauss, of course, gave his name to the unit (with symbol G) of magnetic flux density. This unit is part of the cgs (centimetre-gram-second) system of units, superseded by the SI unit system in which the unit of magnetic flux density is the Tesla (with symbol T), where 1T=104G. This is, in my view, rather a shame, since in terms of their mathematical contributions at least I think Gauss is worth 104 Teslas, and not the other way round.
> > > 6.  [6](#f08.xhtml#rfn_6) A well-known example of the difficulties encountered by women mathematicians in the past is provided by the French mathematician Sophie Germain.

 

# Acknowledgements

I would first like to thank all my mathematics teachers, both at school and university. From school a special mention is due to Mr ‘Snowy’ Winter, whose teaching I found inspiring—indeed he was just about the only teacher throughout school for whom I made sure I sat at the front in a classroom. At university I had the privilege to be taught algebra by Professor Fred Piper and Dr Chris Norman, both of whose lectures I hugely enjoyed. Fred Piper was particularly inspiring, and I am forever grateful that he agreed to be my PhD supervisor and continued to be my mentor and friend until his death after a long illness in 2024.

I would also thank all those who read preliminary versions of this book, and whose valuable advice and encouragement enabled me to get it over the line. Of course any remaining errors are my fault! I would particularly like to thank Haitham Al Sinani, Duncan Drysdale, Siaw-Lynn Ng and Po-Wah Yau, as well as a number of anonymous reviewers, for many valuable comments and corrections.

Finally I must thank the team at Wiley, including in particular Aileen Storry and Christina Spinks for their help and encouragement throughout the publication process. Wiley also kindly provided the index, prepared by specialists. I have taken the definitive advice of Claire Minton, who said, ‘Never index your own book’ and that indexing is ‘a thing that only the most amateurish author undertook to do for his own book’.^()

# Chapter 1  
A Gentle Introduction

> Mathematics is the language with which God wrote the universe.^()
> 
> > Logic is the foundation of the certainty of all the knowledge we acquire.^()
> > 
> > > Mathematicians are like Frenchmen: whatever you say to them they translate into their own language, and forthwith it is something entirely different.^()
> > > 
> > > ## 1.1 What Is This Book About?
> > > 
> > > As I mentioned in the introduction, this is a book about numbers, but not just the numbers we are familiar with and use every day (such as 1, 2, 3, and fractions like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by two](images/c001_dequ1.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![three divided by four](images/c001_dequ2.png)). I want to introduce you to some rather less familiar types of numbers, which, whilst not something we as individuals use every day, nonetheless underlie much of the information and communications technology we take for granted. At the same time I hope to introduce you to mathematics as seen by mathematicians—which may be rather different, and perhaps more abstract, than what you thought of as mathematics at school. I am, of course, assuming that you would not call yourself a professional mathematician, but are nonetheless curious about the subject. If, for example, you have a degree in mathematics, you may find pretty much everything I have to say is routine, but I have nonetheless tried to stay on the right side of rigour; that is, I am hoping there are not too many errors!
> > > 
> > > Why is the title of this book *Mathematics for the digital systems engineer?* Well, as I just mentioned, although the numbers introduced in later chapters are not numbers as we are used to them, they are key to today’s information-centric world. I find the whole subject fascinating, as I have since I was introduced to them over 50 years ago as an undergraduate, and I hope to share some of that fascination with you, and give you the tools to engage with the mathematics involved when working with and developing new systems.
> > > 
> > > This is perhaps not a typical textbook. I have been rather self-indulgent and allowing myself to go down all sorts of rabbit holes. It has made writing this book more fun for me, and I hope you enjoy some of these diversions. Apart from its intended role as an introduction to the mathematics of many modern digital systems, I would also hope that it might be something of interest to anyone thinking of studying mathematics at university, as it attempts to give an introduction to one of the subjects forming a key part of any mathematics degree.
> > > 
> > > ## 1.2 Mathematics as Mathematicians See It
> > > 
> > > I would like to start by saying that what professional mathematicians do, i.e. inventing (or perhaps *discovering*) new mathematics, is a creative activity. That is, a goal of mathematical research is to state and prove new theorems or conjectures, or to find examples which disprove conjectures or show that some set of conditions can actually be met. The hope of every working mathematician is always that in some way they can extend the body of mathematics.
> > > 
> > > At this point, I would like to have a quick gripe about the use of the word ‘creative’ in relation to certain endeavours, as if no other activities are creative. Indeed, the term creative is often used in connection with the so-called ‘creative arts’, as if to deliberately exclude any other pursuits, including science and mathematics. I would like to make the case that while undoubtedly painting a picture or composing a piece of music are creative acts, so is the development of a new piece of mathematics.
> > > 
> > > However, at this point I want to slightly contradict myself! Whilst mathematics is clearly something completely created by humanity, it is important to observe that many—if not most—mathematicians, consciously or unconsciously, talk about mathematics as if it has always existed. For example, they (and that includes me) will talk about ‘discovering’ a theorem rather than creating a theorem. Indeed, there is a widespread—often unarticulated—feeling that the ideas we develop and the theorems we prove always existed, and it was just up to us to *discover* them. This has been discussed at length by many previous authors, and *platonism* is the name usually given to this belief (although this is not the same as Platonism, the philosophy of Plato). Of course, when questioned about this seemingly bizarre belief, many mathematicians will row back somewhat and avow that mathematics is something created, but this doesn’t quite explain why talk of *discovering* a theorem or proof is so widespread in the mathematics community.
> > > 
> > > The fact that mathematics *works*, i.e. that it is not self-contradictory and is so effective when applied to a very wide range of activities, adds to the feeling that it is universal and has an existence beyond its human creators.^()
> > > 
> > > One of the great powers of mathematics comes from abstraction and generalisation. By abstraction I mean taking something concrete, for example addition over the whole numbers (the *integers*^()
> > > 
> > > This leads us to what I regard as the core of mathematics: theorems and proofs. Theorems and lemmas are simply statements about the properties of certain mathematical structures. To be a theorem, and not simply a conjecture, there must be an accompanying proof. The proof will establish the truth of the theorem in a logical way. Until a theorem has a complete proof, it will not be accepted as true by the mathematical community.
> > > 
> > > So why do we need proofs? Many of the theorems and lemmas I will state and prove in this book will seem obvious or intuitively true. However, while mathematical intuition is hugely important, it is also very unreliable, and ‘obvious’ results can turn out to be false. This is the main reason so much effort was made by mathematicians during the 18th and 19th centuries to put the mathematics of real and complex numbers on a firm foundation.
> > > 
> > > Of course, at this point I have to concede that we are all fallible; indeed, in the words of Alexander Pope ‘To err is human’.^()
> > > 
> > > The Four Colour Theorem (the ‘4CT’) is a famous case in point.^()
> > > 
> > > A ‘proof’ of this theorem was published by Alfred Kempe in 1879, which was accepted at the time. However, in 1890, a flaw was found by Percy Heawood. So, at that point, it became the ‘Four Colour Conjecture’, and it didn’t become the 4CT again until 1976, when Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken announced their computer-assisted proof. They needed the assistance of a computer to complete their proof to check through 1482 individual cases.
> > > 
> > > Generally speaking, we rely on other mathematicians checking proofs during the refereeing process for a paper when submitted for publication, although this is clearly not infallible. More generally, any major results are likely to be looked at and checked by many mathematicians. Interestingly, the fact that the 1976 proof of the 4CT was computer-assisted made human checking almost impossible, and this gave rise to a lot of controversy at the time, although the result is today well-accepted. Indeed, a second proof has since been published (or should I say discovered?)—requiring a substantially smaller number of cases to be checked by computer.
> > > 
> > > ## 1.3 Theorems and Proofs
> > > 
> > > So if theorems are the bread and butter of mathematics, what do they look like? The statement of a theorem will typically start by saying what mathematical object (or objects) it applies to, such as the integers. It may also say what additional restrictions are in place—for example, a theorem about integers might only apply to certain specific integers, for example, prime numbers. The theorem will then list one or more statements which are true about the objects under consideration. This is all rather abstract, but the details of the statement of a theorem will vary a great deal depending on the subject matter.
> > > 
> > > A simple example is what is known as *Pythagoras’ Theorem*, although, as is often the case for named theorems, Pythagoras was not the first to know about it. Apparently, the Pythagorean rule was well-known over a 1000 years before Pythagoras was born. The theorem goes as follows.
> > > 
> > > The little box at the end of the previous line (the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#9633;</mo></math>![white square](images/c001_dequ20.png)symbol) marks the end of the proof,^()
> > > 
> > > So now we know what a theorem looks like, I should also try to explain the difference between a theorem and a lemma. At the most fundamental level there is no difference, since they both involve the statement of the truth of something and must both be accompanied by a proof. It is often a matter of authorial taste as to what gets labelled a lemma and what gets called a theorem. In general, a theorem is something that is worth stating for its own sake, whereas a lemma is typically something whose only purpose is to help prove other lemmas or theorems.
> > > 
> > > When stating a theorem, or indeed within a proof of a theorem, it is common practice to use the phrase ‘if and only if’ (sometimes abbreviated to ‘iff’) for a two-way implication. The usual context is something like ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c001_dequ21.png)is true if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c001_dequ22.png)is true’. The meaning is simply that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c001_dequ23.png)is true, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c001_dequ24.png)is true *and also* that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c001_dequ25.png)is true, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c001_dequ26.png)is true.
> > > 
> > > There are a number of ways a theorem can be proved; indeed, logicians interested in the underlying rules of mathematics have identified a range of different *types* of proof. Probably the most obvious method of proof is to give a logical progression of arguments starting from the assumptions of the theorem that lead to the desired result. The proof I gave of Pythagoras theorem is of this type.
> > > 
> > > Another very common type of argument is the *reductio ad absurdum*. This involves assuming the opposite of the result that is to be proved, and then following a series of logical deductions to result in something that cannot possibly be true—typically something that contradicts one of the assumptions underlying the theorem. As a result, the statement must be true (since, if it cannot be false, it must be true^()
> > > 
> > > A third form of argument, known as *induction*, only applies to theorems which assert the truth of a statement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c001_dequ27.png)that is a function of the positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c001_dequ28.png). This method of proof is explained in [Chapter 3](#c003.xhtml#c003).
> > > 
> > > Finally, for theorems that state that a certain mathematical object exists, for example, a theorem stating that there exist Pythagorean triples, i.e. sets of three integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c001_dequ29.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c001_dequ30.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c001_dequ31.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![a squared plus b squared equals h squared](images/c001_dequ32.png), a proof need only exhibit an example. For the case of the Pythagorean triples theorem, it is simply necessary to give an example of a suitable triple <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a comma b comma h right parenthesis](images/c001_dequ33.png), e.g. (3, 4, 5).
> > > 
> > > There are other methods of proving theorems, for example, giving counterexamples to show that a claim is untrue, but the preceding list is good enough for this book.
> > > 
> > > Before moving on, I feel I should explain a little about how one might come up with a proof for a theorem. Often, when trying to prove a result, I might wrestle with the problem in my head until I think I have something—perhaps not a full proof, but maybe a step in the right direction. The acid test then comes when I try to write it down; sadly, often when I come to write down an idea, I find it doesn’t actually work because I missed some point that only came to light when I worked through the details. So writing things down is an absolutely key step; actually, I believe this principle applies in many areas of study, not just in mathematics.
> > > 
> > > When I have actually proved something, the first proof I come up with may be rather long and inelegant—indeed, it may still be wrong, as even writing things down doesn’t always catch subtle errors! The final proof that gets included in an academic paper or book is typically not the first proof that was found but a polished version, i.e. a version which is as succinct and neat as possible. Indeed, for well-known theorems, such as those included in this book, the mathematical community has often had hundreds, if not thousands, of years to come up with the cleverest, most elegant proof.
> > > 
> > > This is not something that is always discussed as much as it should be; you could even call it a slightly dirty secret of mathematicians. When you are presented with a proof as a student of mathematics, they always look so much better than any proof you might come up with when asked to devise one for ‘homework’ or as an exercise. But, of course, you shouldn’t feel bad about this—the same is true for most of us! So, when at various points in this book I ask you to try to prove a result, don’t be disheartened if your proof is rather less elegant or simple than the one I present at the end of the book; remember that I’ve cheated and used a wide variety of established sources to find the proof I like best. Also, don’t worry if your proof is different to mine; there are many different and equally valid ways to establish the same result.
> > > 
> > > In fact, finding a proof is often much simpler than working out what the theorem is that one should try to prove.^()
> > > 
> > > ## 1.4 Abstract Algebra
> > > 
> > > I already briefly talked about the ideas of abstraction and generalisation. Abstract algebra, as its name suggests, is about investigating what happens when you throw away your preconceptions about what adding or multiplying together two objects means. The objects involved can be drawn from a finite or an infinite set, and the objects could be the familiar numbers, geometric objects, or more complex entities such as polynomials. As you proceed through the book, you will encounter a wide range of examples.
> > > 
> > > At the end of the next chapter, I will give some examples of abstract properties we might expect for our generalised notions of addition or multiplication (or *operations* as I call them). The list given there is by no means complete, and again later in the book, I will introduce other examples, notably one governing how two operations interact.
> > > 
> > > ## 1.5 What Do You Need to Know to Make Sense of This Book?
> > > 
> > > This is, of course, a question of key importance. I am assuming a very basic familiarity with mathematics that you may have learnt at school, in particular elementary ideas about whole numbers, addition, multiplication, subtraction, and exponentiation (i.e. raising one number to the power of another).
> > > 
> > > However, in other respects, I have tried to make the book self-contained, and where I introduce new ideas I give examples which I hope you will find helpful. At times I suspect you may need to take a little time to play with a concept before proceeding, and I would recommend working out your own examples using pen and paper if you have trouble understanding something. Don’t worry, every mathematician (except perhaps those with planetary-sized intelligences) needs to scribble on a piece of paper every now and then to try to grasp a concept or check that something really does work.
> > > 
> > > ## 1.6 Case Studies of Applications
> > > 
> > > I already mentioned in the preface that the main goal of this book is to provide an accessible introduction to topics such as groups and finite fields for the benefit of engineers and computer scientists who find themselves working on applications of these mathematical notions. Of course, I am hoping that the book will also be of interest to anyone interested in how key modern digital technologies actually work. The main emphasis is on the mathematics itself; however, in every chapter after the opening three introductory chapters, I provide case studies of applications of the mathematics that has been introduced. The main focus is on topics I am personally familiar with, in particular relating to the protection of digital communications, but I have tried to cover a range of application domains. The main case study topics are summarised as follows.
> > > 
> > > *   In [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004), I introduce two quite different applications, both resting on modular arithmetic. The first is the notion of check digits, as used to protect the integrity of numerical data against accidental errors. Second, I introduce both the idea of public key cryptography and the RSA public key cryptosystem, whose security rests on the difficulty of finding the prime factors of very large numbers; RSA has been very widely used in many domains, notably in the protection of credit card transactions.
> > > *   [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005), which introduces groups, contains a description of a different type of public key cryptosystem, namely Diffie–Hellman key exchange, which has been widely implemented using a range of underlying groups.
> > > *   In [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006), where I introduce rings, I return to the problem of protecting data integrity and introduce a technology of huge practical importance over the last 60 years or so, namely block codes. I also introduce one key example of a class of block code, namely the Hamming codes.
> > > *   [Chapter 7](#c007.xhtml#c007) introduces the idea of polynomials as mathematical objects in their own right. The key application explored here is the linear feedback shift register and the sequences such registers generate. Shift register sequences have been widely used in a range of digital communication domains, including in cryptography and spread spectrum communications.
> > > *   The summit of the mathematical mountain is reached in [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008), where I introduce finite fields. The case study application described here again relates to cryptography, and in particular to what is known as elliptic curve cryptography.
> > > *   The last main chapter, [Chapter 9](#c009.xhtml#c009), is a little different from the rest of the book in that it consists of a compendium of topics I could not bear to leave out. Whilst some of the topics do not have immediate application, the introduction to difference sets and finite geometry touches on a range of topics of practical interest, including cryptography, although the applications are not explored here.
> > >

# Chapter 2  
Sets, Functions and Relations

> A set is a Many that allows itself to be thought of as One.^()
> 
> ## 2.1 Why Are Sets Important?
> 
> In this chapter, I will explore ideas that are fundamental for the mathematics in the rest of this book. I will use all these simple, but sometimes quite subtle, concepts throughout.
> 
> First I will introduce the idea of a *set*, which you can think of as a collection of objects of some kind; in principle these objects could be anything: people, animals, houses, planets or anything else, but here I will mainly be concerned with mathematical objects such as numbers. You may find the discussions in this chapter a little abstract in tone, but I will try to provide some examples to make the ideas more concrete.
> 
> So why am I going to the trouble of bothering you with all this? It turns out that sets are an absolutely fundamental tool for mathematics. This is perhaps surprising given that the notion of a set didn’t emerge until the late 19th century, notably in the work of Georg Cantor whose quote starts this chapter, but the idea of a set is so useful that today it pervades almost any discussion of mathematics. It gives us a convenient way of describing the objects we are dealing with.
> 
> I will also introduce the notion of a *relation*, where a relation is something that either holds or does not hold between any pair of elements in a set. For example, if a set consists of all the people living in a village, the relation ‘is married to’ probably applies to certain pairs of individuals in the village, but almost certainly not to every pair of individuals!
> 
> Following on from the introduction to relations, I will describe a particularly important type of relation known as an *equivalence relation*. Equivalence relations generalise the idea of equality, which is itself a special type of relation.
> 
> An equally important notion is that of a *function*. A function maps elements from one set (the *domain* of a function) to a second set (the function’s *codomain*). Of course the domain and codomain may be the same, but that is certainly not necessary. Examples of functions you will likely have already encountered are the trigonometric functions: sine, cosine and tangent (commonly known as sin, cos and tan), as well as numerical functions such as logarithm (usually abbreviated to log).
> 
> The chapter concludes with an introduction to *operations*, namely defined ways of combining pairs of elements from a set to give another element of the same set, just as addition or multiplication can be used to combine two numbers to give another number. Certain special types of operation will be key to just about all the rest of this book.
> 
> Indeed, one could say that all of mathematics is about investigating and proving properties of certain special types of sets, along with particular relations, functions and operations defined on elements of these sets. So in this chapter I am laying out the fundamental tools for just about all of mathematics. These fundamental tools of mathematics are simple and easy to state, but there seems to be no limit to what can be achieved using them—much as the few tens of thousands of words in the English language can be used to build an apparently unlimited number of pieces of literature, great and not so great.
> 
> ## 2.2 Sets
> 
> So what is a set? As I already mentioned, a set can be thought of as a collection of things of some kind. There are no restrictions on what can be contained in a set; the key thing when defining a set is to ensure that there is an unambiguous rule enabling anyone to decide whether or not a particular object is a *member* of the set.
> 
> I will use some special notation to describe sets. First, I will always use curly brackets, {…}, to delimit the contents of a set. A simple example of a set might be
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ1.png)
> 
> This set contains three objects, which happen to be the colours pink, blue and green. The members of the set are called its *elements*. I also use the special symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8712;</mo></math>![element of](images/c002_dequ2.png)to say that an object is a member of a set. Thus I could write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![pink prefix element of of left curly bracket pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ3.png)
> 
> I could also write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mtext>yellow</mtext><mo>&#8713;</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![yellow prefix not an element of of left curly bracket pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket comma](images/c002_dequ4.png)
> 
> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8713;</mo></math>![not an element of](images/c002_dequ5.png)can be read as ‘not a member of’ or ‘not an element of’.
> 
> One important property of a set is its size, or *cardinality*, i.e. the number of elements in the set. For our simple example, the cardinality of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>Pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket Pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket](images/c002_dequ6.png)is clearly 3. If I called this set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ7.png), i.e.
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![cap c equals left curly bracket pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket comma](images/c002_dequ8.png)
> 
> then I use vertical bars to denote cardinality, that is, I can write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![absolute value of cap c equals three full stop](images/c002_dequ9.png)
> 
> Two very important examples of sets are the *Natural Numbers* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ10.png)and the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ11.png). The special symbols <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ12.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ13.png)are used very widely in mathematics. The natural numbers, as the name implies, consist of the everyday whole numbers we are all familiar with, i.e.
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![double-struck cap n equals left curly bracket one comma two comma three comma ellipsis right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ14.png)
> 
> The set of integers contains all the natural numbers, and consists of all the whole numbers, positive and negative, as well as zero. That is
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![double-struck cap z equals left curly bracket ellipsis comma negative three comma negative two comma negative one comma zero comma one comma two comma three comma ellipsis right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ15.png)
> 
> These two examples of sets contain an unbounded number of elements, so what is their cardinality? Well, informally they are said to have infinite cardinality, without necessarily wanting to define what infinity means. In fact, it is possible to formally define what infinite cardinality means—this is a subject I return to in the final main chapter of this book (see [Section 9.2](#c009.xhtml#c009-sec-0002)).
> 
> Often it is interesting to look at cases where one set is contained in another, meaning that all the elements in one set are contained in the other set. This is clearly the case for the examples I just gave, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ16.png)is contained in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ17.png). I say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ18.png)is a *subset* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ19.png), and write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![double-struck cap n subset of or equals double-struck cap z full stop](images/c002_dequ20.png)
> 
> You should read the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8838;</mo></math>![subset of or equals](images/c002_dequ21.png)as meaning ‘is contained in’ or ‘is a subset of’. [Figure 2.1](#c002.xhtml#c02-fig-1) depicts the subset relationship between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ22.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ23.png).
> 
> ![Figure 2.1 Showing how double-struck cap n relates to double-struck cap z.](images/c02f001.png)
> 
> [Figure 2.1](#c002.xhtml#rc02-fig-1) Showing how <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ22.png)relates to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mo mathvariant="double-struck">.</mo></mrow></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ23.png).
> 
> I also need one more piece of notation relating to sets. There is a (unique) set containing no elements at all. This is called the *empty set* and is written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8709;</mi></math>![normal empty set](images/c002_dequ26.png).
> 
> I promised you proofs, so it is about time I gave you one apart from the example in [Chapter 1](#c001.xhtml#c001). In formal mathematics we give statements that we want to show are true, and as I mentioned in [Chapter 1](#c001.xhtml#c001), we label them theorems or lemmas (or lemmata if you’re being pedantic). For my first example of a proof (apart from that of Pythagoras’ theorem), I’ll start with a very simple result; I’ll call it a lemma rather than a theorem, as it is only a minor, albeit useful, result.
> 
> Note that in the proof I could equally well have supposed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![x element of cap b](images/c002_dequ40.png)but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8713;</mo><mi>A</mi></math>![x not an element of cap a](images/c002_dequ41.png)and used precisely the same argument—this is an example of an assumption made in a proof which is commonly said to apply ‘without loss of generality’.
> 
> I suspect you are a little puzzled (a) as to why I bothered to state this result, and (b) why I took the trouble to give a proof, since it seems as if it is blindingly obvious. The answer to (a) is simple: it gives us a simple way of proving two sets are equal—that is, if I can prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![cap a subset of or equals cap b](images/c002_dequ42.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi>A</mi></math>![cap b subset of or equals cap a](images/c002_dequ43.png), then I immediately know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![cap a equals cap b](images/c002_dequ44.png)from [Lemma 2.1](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0003). Indeed, that is often how we build mathematics: we develop a series of lemmas which we can then use together to prove whatever main result we wish to establish.
> 
> The answer to (b) is more complex. First and foremost I wanted to give you an example of a very simple proof, just to get you in the mood. Second, just because something seems obvious doesn’t mean it is true. Sadly the history of mathematics is littered with errors caused by blind acceptance of obvious claims which turn out to be false.^()
> 
> Third, I wanted to demonstrate the so-called *reductio ad absurdum* proof technique, in which I suppose that the result I am trying to prove is false, and then show that this results in a contradiction of something I assumed to be true—and hence the result must be true! Reductio ad absurdum is a hugely useful technique; indeed, as the great 20th-century British mathematician Godfrey Harold Hardy said^()
> 
> > Reductio ad absurdum, which Euclid loved so much, is one of a mathematician’s finest weapons. It is a far finer gambit than any chess play: a chess player may offer the sacrifice of a pawn or even a piece, but a mathematician offers the game.
> 
> It is common to be dealing with cases where two sets have elements in common, and sometimes these common elements are of interest. To take a simple example, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ45.png)is the set of colours conventionally associated with the rainbow, that is
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>red</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>orange</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>yellow</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>indigo</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>violet</mtext><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![cap b equals left curly bracket red comma orange comma yellow comma green comma blue comma indigo comma violet right curly bracket comma](images/c002_dequ46.png)
> 
> and, as previously, suppose that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![cap c equals left curly bracket pink comma blue comma green right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ47.png)
> 
> Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ48.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ49.png)have two elements in common: blue and green. I say that the *intersection* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ50.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ51.png), i.e. the set of elements that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ52.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ53.png)have in common, is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket blue comma green right curly bracket](images/c002_dequ54.png), and I write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8745;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![cap b intersection cap c equals left curly bracket blue comma green right curly bracket comma](images/c002_dequ55.png)
> 
> i.e. the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8745;</mo></math>![intersection](images/c002_dequ56.png)denotes set intersection. The relationship between the sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ57.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ58.png)is shown in [Figure 2.2](#c002.xhtml#c02-fig-2), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8745;</mo><mi>C</mi></math>![cap b intersection cap c](images/c002_dequ59.png)is the area where the two circles overlap. If the intersection of two sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ60.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ61.png)is empty, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#8745;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8709;</mi></math>![cap a intersection cap b equals normal empty set](images/c002_dequ62.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ63.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ64.png)are said to be *disjoint*.
> 
> ![Figure 2.2 Relationship between bold-italic cap b and bold-italic cap c.](images/c02f002.png)
> 
> [Figure 2.2](#c002.xhtml#rc02-fig-2) Relationship between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">B</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic cap b](images/c002_dequ65.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic cap c](images/c002_dequ66.png).
> 
> In a similar way, I am also sometimes interested in the set of all elements which are contained in at least one of two sets. For two sets, the set of all elements in either one set or the other is called the *union* of the sets, and we use the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8746;</mo></math>![union](images/c002_dequ67.png)to indicate this. So I could write
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8746;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>pink</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>red</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>orange</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>yellow</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>green</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>blue</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>indigo</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>violet</mtext><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![cap b union cap c equals left curly bracket pink comma red comma orange comma yellow comma green comma blue comma indigo comma violet right curly bracket comma](images/c002_dequ68.png)
> 
> meaning that the union of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ69.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ70.png)is a set containing all the eight colours occurring as elements of either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ71.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c002_dequ72.png). Looking again at [Figure 2.2](#c002.xhtml#c02-fig-2), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi><mo>&#8746;</mo><mi>C</mi></math>![cap b union cap c](images/c002_dequ73.png)is represented by the area inside one (or both) of the two circles. The figure is a simple example of a widely used way of depicting sets and their intersections, namely *Venn diagrams*, named after British mathematician, logician and philosopher John Venn, who was an advocate of their use back in the late 19th century. In a Venn diagram, a set is typically shown as a circle or ellipse, with the elements of the set placed inside the boundary.
> 
> Whilst the notion of a set is a relatively recent one compared to the long history of mathematics, during the 20th century sets came to be used as a fundamental and everyday tool by almost all mathematicians. However, those interested in the fundamentals of mathematics will tell you that sets need to be used with a little care, as became clear when Russell’s paradox was first formulated in 1901 by British logician and philosopher Bertrand Russell.^()
> 
> ## 2.3 Cartesian Products of Sets
> 
> Before looking at what we can do with sets, I need to briefly introduce a way of combining sets to make larger sets. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ74.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ75.png)are sets. Then the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![cap a multiplication cap b](images/c002_dequ76.png)is the set of all pairs of elements, the first of the pair being from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ77.png)and the second of the pair from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ78.png). This is known as the Cartesian Product of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ79.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ80.png). The name derives from the 17th-century French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes.^()
> 
> More formally,
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![cap a multiplication cap b equals left curly bracket left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis colon a element of cap a comma b element of cap b right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ81.png)
> 
> I can extend this definition to three or more sets, so that, for example, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi></math>![cap a comma cap b comma cap c comma cap d](images/c002_dequ82.png)are four sets, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>D</mi></math>![cap a multiplication cap b multiplication cap c multiplication cap d](images/c002_dequ83.png)consists of all ordered quadruples where the first element is from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ84.png), the second from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ85.png), and so on.
> 
> As is standard practice, I will refer to ordered pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis](images/c002_dequ86.png)as 2-tuples, ordered triples <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a comma b comma c right parenthesis](images/c002_dequ87.png)as 3-tuples, and so on.
> 
> As a simple example, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap a equals left curly bracket one comma two right curly bracket](images/c002_dequ88.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap b equals left curly bracket a comma b comma c right curly bracket](images/c002_dequ89.png). Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![cap a multiplication cap b](images/c002_dequ90.png)contains a total of six elements:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis one comma a right parenthesis comma left parenthesis one comma b right parenthesis comma left parenthesis one comma c right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma a right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma b right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma c right parenthesis full stop](images/c002_dequ91.png)
> 
> More generally, it is simple to see that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ92.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ93.png)are finite, the cardinality of (i.e. the number of elements in) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi></math>![cap a multiplication cap b](images/c002_dequ94.png)is simply the product of the cardinalities of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c002_dequ95.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c002_dequ96.png). In the above example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![absolute value of cap a equals two](images/c002_dequ97.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![absolute value of cap b equals three](images/c002_dequ98.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 absolute value of cap a multiplication cap b equals part 2 absolute value of cap a multiplication absolute value of cap b equals part 3 six](images/c002_dequ99.png).
> 
> ## 2.4 Relations
> 
> Sets on their own are not much use. I need to be able to say things about how elements of a set relate, or can be combined. As a first step in this direction I will define the notion of a *relation* on the members of a set. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ100.png)is a set, then a relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ101.png)holds for certain pairs of elements from the set. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![a element of cap s](images/c002_dequ102.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![b element of cap s](images/c002_dequ103.png)then I write ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>b</mi></math>![a times cap r times b](images/c002_dequ104.png)’ if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c002_dequ105.png)is related to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c002_dequ106.png). (An alternative way of thinking about a relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ107.png)is that it is a subset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>U</mi></math>![cap u](images/c002_dequ108.png)of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s multiplication cap s](images/c002_dequ109.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>b</mi></math>![a times cap r times b](images/c002_dequ110.png)if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>U</mi></math>![left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis element of cap u](images/c002_dequ111.png).)
> 
> Consider the following simple example. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ112.png)is the set of numbers {1, 2, 3, 4}, and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ114.png)be the relation ‘is less than or equals to’—normally written as ≤. Then 1 ≤ 1, 1 ≤ 2, 1 ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ 4, but the only number 4 is related to is itself (i.e. 4 ≤ 4). A complete listing of the relation is given in [Table 2.1](#c002.xhtml#c02-tbl-1).
> 
> ![Table 2.1 The less-than-or-equals relation defined on {1, 2, 3, 4}.](images/c002_dequ121.png)
> 
> [Table 2.1](#c002.xhtml#rc02-tbl-1) The less-than-or-equals relation defined on {1, 2, 3, 4}.
> 
> More strictly, I have defined a *binary* relation, since it applies to pairs of elements of a set. It is, of course, possible to define operations on groups of three or more elements, but that is outside the scope of what I am interested in here.
> 
> The example I have just given is a special type of relation called an *ordering*, and orderings have a theory of their own—I will give some basic properties of orderings in [Chapter 3](#c003.xhtml#c003). However, next I want to define and give examples of another type of relation of key importance both in this book and for mathematics generally.
> 
> ## 2.5 Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes
> 
> The notion of an *equivalence relation* is simple yet powerful. The idea behind the definition of an equivalence relation is to generalise the notion of equality, which is, after all, a special type of relation. To understand the motivation for the definition of an equivalence relation, it is important to think about the properties of equality.
> 
> The first key property of equality is that it is *reflexive*, that is, for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ137.png)(whatever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ138.png)might be), it is always true that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![x equals x](images/c002_dequ139.png). The second important property of equality is that of *symmetry*, namely that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c002_dequ140.png)then it always follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y equals x](images/c002_dequ141.png). The third fundamental property of equality is that it is *transitive*, that is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c002_dequ142.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![y equals z](images/c002_dequ143.png), then it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![x equals z](images/c002_dequ144.png). These are, of course, trivial observations, but they motivate a very important idea.
> 
> Suppose a relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ145.png)is defined on a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ146.png). Also suppose that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ147.png)has the following three properties:
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![x times cap r times x](images/c002_dequ148.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x element of cap s](images/c002_dequ149.png)(reflexivity),
> *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ150.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x comma y element of cap s](images/c002_dequ151.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![y times cap r times x](images/c002_dequ152.png)(symmetry), and
> *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ153.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>z</mi></math>![y times cap r times z](images/c002_dequ154.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x comma y comma z element of cap s](images/c002_dequ155.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>z</mi></math>![x times cap r times z](images/c002_dequ156.png)(transitivity).
> 
> Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ157.png)is said to be an equivalence relation, meaning that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ158.png)is a relation that has some of the key properties of equality. It turns out that equivalence relations crop up in many branches of mathematics.
> 
> In particular, because equivalence relations have important properties, whenever I encounter an example of such a relation, I immediately know it has all these properties. This is an important idea in mathematics, namely that of proving properties of a general class of objects, and then applying it to specific examples. It shows the power of abstraction.
> 
> A simple, non-mathematical example involves people. Let the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ159.png)be all the people in the United Kingdom, and suppose the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ160.png)is ‘living on the same street as’. It is not hard to see that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ161.png)is an equivalence relation. Every individual lives on the same street as themselves (reflexivity). If Jane lives on the same street as Mary, then Mary lives on the same street as Jane (symmetry). Finally, if John lives on the same street as Jim, and Jim lives on the same street as Mike, then clearly John lives on the same street as Mike (transitivity).^()
> 
> Of course, I’ve glossed over two issues with this example. First, there are people who don’t have a fixed street address, for whatever reason, so in such cases the relation is not defined. I could fix this by restricting the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ162.png)to people with fixed street addresses—of course, this is often what governments do when wishing to ignore the problem of homelessness. Second, people are being born, moving house and also dying, all the time, and so the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ163.png)and the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ164.png)are not fixed; nonetheless, the result holds as long as we consider <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ165.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ166.png)for a fixed point in time. Of course, that’s the trouble with real life—it is not as easy to deal with as the abstract world of mathematics!
> 
> I am particularly interested in one key property, namely that an equivalence relation partitions the set it is defined on, that is, it divides the set into discrete (non-overlapping) parts. To establish this important result, we first need another piece of notation. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ167.png)is an equivalence relation defined on a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ168.png), then for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x element of cap s](images/c002_dequ169.png)let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>R</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket x right curly bracket sub cap r](images/c002_dequ170.png)denote the set of all elements that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ171.png)is related to; that is, in formal language:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket x right curly bracket sub cap r equals left curly bracket y element of cap s colon x times cap r times y right curly bracket full stop](images/c002_dequ172.png)
> 
> The above can be read as ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>R</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket x right curly bracket sub cap r](images/c002_dequ173.png)equals the set of all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ174.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ175.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ176.png)’, i.e. when defining sets we use the colon as shorthand for ‘such that’ or ‘with the property that’.
