We call <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>R</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket x right curly bracket sub cap r](images/c002_dequ177.png)an *equivalence class*.
> 
> Armed with this notation we can now give (and prove) our key result. The theorem immediately below is expressed rather formally, but its implications are explained more informally below.
> 
> So what does this theorem mean? If you think about it a little, it means that the equivalence classes partition the set on which the relation is defined, and all the members of an equivalence class are related to each other. Returning to our simple example where the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ213.png)means ‘living on the same street as’, then the equivalence classes are the sets of people living on a particular street—each street has its own equivalence class of people. So this relation partitions all the people in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ214.png)into street-subsets.
> 
> A simple equivalence relation defined on the set of words in English is ‘starts with the same letter as’. Some of the equivalence classes for this equivalence relation are shown in [Figure 2.3](#c002.xhtml#c02-fig-3).
> 
> ![Figure 2.3 Equivalence classes for ‘starts with the same letter as’.](images/c02f003.png)
> 
> [Figure 2.3](#c002.xhtml#rc02-fig-3) Equivalence classes for ‘starts with the same letter as’.
> 
> In [Section 2.6](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0008), I give a more detailed example of how this theorem works. However, before moving on to this example, I would like—as a bit of fun—to share a plausible (but false) argument with you. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ215.png)is a relation on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ216.png)which is symmetric and transitive. Choose any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ217.png), and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ218.png)be any other element in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ219.png)for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ220.png). By symmetry we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![y times cap r times x](images/c002_dequ221.png). Moreover, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ222.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![y times cap r times x](images/c002_dequ223.png), by transitivity we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![x times cap r times x](images/c002_dequ224.png), that is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ225.png)must be reflexive. So it seems as if we can simplify our definition of an equivalence relation to be a relation which is just symmetric and transitive (and we don’t need to assume reflexivity).
> 
> So what is wrong with this argument? Please think about it. I discuss this further in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 222).
> 
> Of course, spotting errors in proofs is something mathematicians worry about a lot. It is sometimes easy to miss an implicit assumption, which is what has happened here.
> 
> ## 2.6 Relations: A Detailed Example
> 
> I next want to give a rather more subtle example of a relation. The relation is again defined on people from a particular set. This time the set includes living and dead people—for the sake of argument I will define the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ226.png)to be all the people alive in the United Kingdom since the beginning of 1800, but the arguments below would apply to any other defined set of people. The relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ227.png)is then ‘is a blood relative of’. This is a rather woolly notion so, to make it more precise, I will say that two individuals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ228.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ229.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ230.png)are blood-related (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ231.png)) if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ232.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ233.png)have a common ancestor in the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ234.png). So, for example, if Bob’s great-grandmother is Doris’s grandmother, then Bob and Doris are blood relatives (in fact they are first cousins once removed).
> 
> So what properties does this relation have? Well, it is clearly reflexive since any individual has two common ancestors with themselves, namely their mother and father.^()
> 
> So, this is not an equivalence relation, and it does not partition humanity into blood-related groups. Perhaps this is a good thing, as we hardly need another way for people to divide themselves into ‘us’ and ‘them’; after all, in recent years it seems to be increasingly popular for populist politicians to whip up prejudices against individuals who can be identified as ‘them’, with clearly highly undesirable results; after all, ‘us versus them’ is a well-established meme used by dictators. Nonetheless, is there any way we can restrict our definition to enable us to define an equivalence relation of this type? Well, it turns out that we can by looking only at one sex.
> 
> Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub f](images/c002_dequ235.png)be the subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ236.png)containing all the women alive in the United Kingdom since 1800. Of course, without loss of generality we could do the same analysis for men. Then the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub f](images/c002_dequ237.png), defined to be ‘have a common ancestor in the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub f](images/c002_dequ238.png)’, *is* an equivalence relation on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub f](images/c002_dequ239.png). Why is this?
> 
> Well, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub f](images/c002_dequ240.png)is clearly reflexive and symmetric, just like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ241.png). Why is it transitive as well? Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ242.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ243.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ244.png)are all in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub f](images/c002_dequ245.png), and that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/c002_dequ246.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>z</mi></math>![y times cap r times z](images/c002_dequ247.png), that is suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ248.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ249.png)have a common female ancestor (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ250.png)say), as do <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ251.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ252.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ253.png)say). We need to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>z</mi></math>![x times cap r times z](images/c002_dequ254.png), i.e. that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ255.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ256.png)have a common (female) ancestor. It is straightforward to verify that the female ancestors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ257.png)form a chain, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ258.png)had one mother, who had one mother (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ259.png)’s maternal grandmother), who had one mother, and so on. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ260.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ261.png)must both lie somewhere in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ262.png)’s ancestor chain of mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, etc., since they are both ancestors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ263.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y equals c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ264.png)then we are done since this means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ265.png)is a common ancestor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ266.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ267.png). So suppose that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ268.png)is lower down (more recent) in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ269.png)’s ancestor chain than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ270.png). Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ271.png)is an ancestor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ272.png)(which is an ancestor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ273.png)); that is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ274.png)is an ancestor of both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ275.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ276.png)and we are done since we could use exactly the same argument if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub y times z](images/c002_dequ277.png)is lower down (more recent) in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ278.png)’s ancestor chain than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub></math>![c sub x times y](images/c002_dequ279.png).
> 
> So what does this mean when we look at the equivalence classes this family-based relation defines? Interestingly, all women in an equivalence class share the same mitochondrial DNA, since this is always inherited from an individual’s mother. Also, if we look at the corresponding relation for men (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub m](images/c002_dequ280.png)say), then all men in the same equivalence class have the same Y chromosome, since this is always inherited from an individual’s father. Moreover, if I make the simplifying assumptions that men never change their surname and male children always take the surname of their father, then all men in an equivalence class will share the same surname.
> 
> This suggests two things to me. First that, unlike common practice in the United Kingdom and many other countries, perhaps women should take their surname from their mother not their father, so that females in the same equivalence class under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub f](images/c002_dequ281.png)would share the same surname,^()
> 
> Of course, there are certain problematic edge cases with our analysis of this relation. If the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ283.png)was extended to all of humanity, living or dead, then all living humans would have a common ancestor, given that evolutionary biologists tell us that all of (today’s) humanity is descended from a single woman living in Africa two or three hundred thousand years ago—the so called Mitochondrial Eve. That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c002_dequ284.png)would be rather uninteresting since everyone would be related to everyone else. This is one case where modern science agrees with the accounts in the Torah, the Quran and the Christian Old Testament, although the timescales are rather different!
> 
> More fundamentally, modern medical science enables babies to incorporate genetic material from more than two parents, which complicates matters. Also, DNA mutates over time, so it may not always be true that women in an equivalence class under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub f](images/c002_dequ285.png)will always share the same mitochondrial DNA, and similarly not all men in the same equivalence class under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub m](images/c002_dequ286.png)will share the same Y chromosome, although in both cases the differences within a class will almost certainly be very small. Indeed, if mutations didn’t happen, then we would all have the same mitochondrial DNA, given the (past) existence of Mitochondrial Eve.
> 
> To wrap things up, the above analysis suggests that proving that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub f](images/c002_dequ287.png)(or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>![cap r sub m](images/c002_dequ288.png)) is an equivalence relation reveals some non-obvious facts about familial relationships. It turns out that equivalence relations crop up in most unexpected places, and [Theorem 2.1](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0007) is therefore a very useful tool which tells us interesting things in many different contexts.
> 
>  
> 
> ## 2.7 Functions
> 
> I suspect you already have an informal idea of what a function is, but I want to briefly put the idea into the more formal context of sets. For example, I’m sure you will have encountered examples of functions, such as the trigonometric functions sin and cos, but perhaps you have never seen a formal definition in terms of sets.
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ289.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ290.png)are sets, then a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ291.png)that maps from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ292.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ293.png)(written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![f colon cap x right arrow cap y](images/c002_dequ294.png)) is a rule which, given any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ295.png), specifies a unique element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![y element of cap y](images/c002_dequ296.png), and we write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![y equals f of x](images/c002_dequ297.png). We call <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ298.png)the *image* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ299.png)under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ300.png); conversely, we call <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ301.png)the *pre-image* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ302.png)under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ303.png). Also, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![f colon cap x right arrow cap y](images/c002_dequ304.png)then we call <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ305.png)the *domain* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ306.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ307.png)the *codomain* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ308.png). The *range* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ309.png)is a subset of the codomain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ310.png), defined to be all the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ311.png)for which there is an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ312.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f of x equals y](images/c002_dequ313.png). That is, the range is the set of elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ314.png)which are mapped to by at least one element in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ315.png).
> 
> We can represent a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ316.png)pictorially as shown in [Figure 2.4](#c002.xhtml#c02-fig-4).
> 
> ![Figure 2.4 A function mapping from bold-italic cap x to bold-italic cap y.](images/c02f004.png)
> 
> [Figure 2.4](#c002.xhtml#rc02-fig-4) A function mapping from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic cap x](images/c002_dequ317.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic cap y](images/c002_dequ318.png).
> 
> A simple example of a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ319.png)which maps from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ320.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ321.png)is specified by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of x equals x plus one](images/c002_dequ322.png)(or we could equally write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f colon x right arrow x plus one](images/c002_dequ323.png)). In this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of negative two equals negative one](images/c002_dequ324.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![f of negative one equals zero](images/c002_dequ325.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of zero equals one](images/c002_dequ326.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![f of one equals two](images/c002_dequ327.png), and so on.
> 
> There are two particularly important properties that a function can possess.
> 
> *   **One-to-one**. A function is said to be *one-to-one* (or simply 1-to-1 or *injective*) if each input to the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ328.png)gives a different output <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ329.png). More formally we say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ330.png)is one-to-one if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x equals f of y](images/c002_dequ331.png)implies that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c002_dequ332.png). Alternatively, and equally validly, I could define one-to-one as meaning that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x not equals y](images/c002_dequ333.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x not equals f of y](images/c002_dequ334.png).
> *   **Onto**. A function is *onto* (or *surjective*) if the outputs of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ335.png)cover the whole of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ336.png), i.e. for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![y element of cap y](images/c002_dequ337.png)there is an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ338.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f of x equals y](images/c002_dequ339.png). In such a case we say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ340.png)maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ341.png)*onto* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Y</mi></math>![cap y](images/c002_dequ342.png). We could equivalently define a function to be onto if and only if the range is the same as the codomain.
> 
> I suspect a few examples will help:
> 
> *   If we start with the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of x equals x plus one](images/c002_dequ343.png), as mentioned above, then this maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ344.png)*onto* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ345.png). To see this, observe that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ346.png)is any integer then its pre-image under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ347.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![y minus one](images/c002_dequ348.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f times left parenthesis y minus one right parenthesis equals y](images/c002_dequ349.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![y minus one element of double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ350.png). That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ351.png)covers the whole of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ352.png). It is also clearly one-to-one, since if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x equals f of z](images/c002_dequ353.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x plus one equals z plus one](images/c002_dequ354.png)and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![x equals z](images/c002_dequ355.png).
>     
>     The same function, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of x equals x plus one](images/c002_dequ356.png), also maps from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ357.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ358.png). In this case it is again one-to-one, but it is not onto, since there is no <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![x element of double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ359.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of x equals one](images/c002_dequ360.png)(recalling that zero is not in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ361.png)).
>     
> *   The next example is the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>![g colon x right arrow two times x](images/c002_dequ362.png). It maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ363.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ364.png). It is clearly one-to-one, but it is not onto, since an odd number cannot be an image of an integer under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c002_dequ365.png).
> *   The final example is the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![h colon x right arrow absolute value of x](images/c002_dequ366.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of x](images/c002_dequ367.png)denotes the *absolute value* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ368.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ369.png)is positive or zero then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![absolute value of x equals x](images/c002_dequ370.png), and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ371.png)is negative then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![absolute value of x equals negative x](images/c002_dequ372.png); this ensures that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of x](images/c002_dequ373.png)is always positive. The function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c002_dequ374.png)maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ375.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ376.png). It is not onto since no negative number can be an image under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c002_dequ377.png), and it is not one-to-one either, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of x equals f of negative x](images/c002_dequ378.png).
>     
>     However, if we consider the same function mapping from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ379.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ380.png)then it is both one-to-one and onto. Indeed, in this case it is what is known as the *identity function* for the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c002_dequ381.png). More generally, the identity function, sometimes denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>I</mi></math>![cap i](images/c002_dequ382.png), is the function that maps from a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ383.png)to itself and for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![cap i of x equals x](images/c002_dequ384.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ385.png); <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>I</mi></math>![cap i](images/c002_dequ386.png)is clearly always both one-to-one and onto.
>     
> 
> Two functions can be *composed*, by first applying one function and then applying the second function to the result. That is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![f colon cap x right arrow cap y](images/c002_dequ387.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Z</mi></math>![g colon cap y right arrow cap z](images/c002_dequ388.png), then we can define the *composition* of the functions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ389.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c002_dequ390.png)to be the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Z</mi></math>![left parenthesis f ring operator g right parenthesis colon cap x right arrow cap z](images/c002_dequ391.png)defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f ring operator g of x equals g of f of x](images/c002_dequ392.png). Obviously, it is only possible to compose two functions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ393.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c002_dequ394.png)if the domain of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c002_dequ395.png)contains the range of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ396.png).
> 
> We can immediately state the following simple result.
> 
> I leave the proof as a simple exercise for you. If you start with the definitions the proof is almost immediate. It is interesting to observe that the other possible results don’t hold; that is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/c002_dequ405.png)is one-to-one then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c002_dequ406.png)need not be, and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/c002_dequ407.png)is onto then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ408.png)need not be. I provide a proof of the lemma and also counterexamples^()
> 
> I already mentioned the *identity function*. For any set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ409.png), the identity function is a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>![cap i sub cap x](images/c002_dequ410.png)that maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ411.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>X</mi></math>![cap x](images/c002_dequ412.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![cap i sub cap x of x equals x](images/c002_dequ413.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ414.png). This then enables me to introduce the notion of an *inverse function*.
> 
> Suppose the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![f colon cap x right arrow cap y](images/c002_dequ415.png)is both one-to-one and onto. Then I define its inverse function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>:</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![f super negative one colon cap y right arrow cap x](images/c002_dequ416.png)as follows. Choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Y</mi></math>![y element of cap y](images/c002_dequ417.png). Then there exists an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ418.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f of x equals y](images/c002_dequ419.png), since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ420.png)is onto, and moreover this <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ421.png)is unique since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c002_dequ422.png)is one-to-one. So define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![f super negative one of y equals x](images/c002_dequ423.png). It is straightforward to see that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></math>![f ring operator f super negative one equals cap i sub cap x](images/c002_dequ424.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![f super negative one of f of x equals x](images/c002_dequ425.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>X</mi></math>![x element of cap x](images/c002_dequ426.png).
> 
> I conclude this quick discussion of functions by giving the following useful result.
> 
> ## 2.8 Operations
> 
> I will conclude this rather abstract chapter by introducing the key notion of an *operation* on pairs of elements of a set. In fact, we are all very familiar with some important operations on numbers, such as addition and multiplication. The abstract notion of an operation generalises these ideas.
> 
> Formally, I define an operation to be a process that takes any pair of elements of a set (not necessarily distinct) and gives as output an element of the set. So if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo></math>![ring operator](images/c002_dequ437.png)is an operation on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ438.png)then, for any pair of elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ439.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ440.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ441.png)(where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ442.png)may be the same as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ443.png)), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x ring operator y](images/c002_dequ444.png)is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ445.png).
> 
> So what might be examples of operations, apart from addition and multiplication of course? The not so helpful answer is—almost anything! Two obvious examples applying to numbers are subtraction and division, and another is exponentiation, where the first number is raised to the power of the second number.
> 
> As I will discuss in later chapters, there are some key properties I would like an operation to satisfy in order for it to be ‘interesting’. These key properties are typically properties that some (or all) well-known operations have. We can then start to establish results about operations which satisfy certain key sets of properties, and these results will then apply no matter what the operation is, as long as it possesses the necessary set of properties. This is another example of the power of abstraction and generalisation.
> 
> Throughout the discussion below, I assume that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo></math>![ring operator](images/c002_dequ446.png)is an operation on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ447.png), that is, for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x comma y element of cap s](images/c002_dequ448.png), there is a defined <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x ring operator y element of cap s](images/c002_dequ449.png).
> 
> 1.  The first example of a key property is that there is an element in the set called an *identity element*, often written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c002_dequ450.png). An identity element has the property that if it is combined with any element of the set then the output is that element (i.e. it has no effect). Formally, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c002_dequ451.png)is an identity element if and only if: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>for every</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 x ring operator e equals part 2 e ring operator x equals part 3 x for every x element of cap s full stop](images/c002_dequ452.png)
>     
>     Zero (0) is an obvious example of an identity element when the set is the integers, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></mrow></math>![cap s equals double-struck cap z](images/c002_dequ453.png), and the operation is addition (+). Zero is an identity element in this case because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 x plus zero equals part 2 zero plus x equals part 3 x](images/c002_dequ454.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ455.png). Another obvious example for the integers would be when the operation is multiplication; in this case 1 (one) is an identity element, because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 x multiplication one equals part 2 one multiplication x equals part 3 x](images/c002_dequ456.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ457.png).
>     
>     If you think for a moment about the subtraction operation on the integers, then 0 only partly fits the definition of identity element. This is because while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![x minus zero equals x](images/c002_dequ458.png)for every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ459.png), as we would hope, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![zero minus x equals negative x](images/c002_dequ460.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![negative x not equals x](images/c002_dequ461.png)unless <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x equals zero](images/c002_dequ462.png). That is, for the subtraction operation on the integers, 0 is an example of a *right identity*, and an element is only a true identity element if it is a right identity *and* a left identity, where left identity is defined in the obvious way.
>     
>     What about division? Well, division is not an operation on the integers according to the definition we have given, because dividing an integer by any integer other than +1 or −1 does not result in an integer, so it doesn’t work (in this case the operation is said to be ‘not well-defined’). Remember that an operation must always give a result *within the set it is defined on*. Indeed there is another problem with division since, even when we work with fractions, dividing by 0 is undefined.
>     
>     Finally, it is important to note that an identity element, if it exists, will always be unique. This can be shown using the following simple argument. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c002_dequ465.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![e super prime](images/c002_dequ466.png)are identity elements for an operation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8727;</mo></math>![asterisk operator](images/c002_dequ467.png)on a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ468.png). I need to show that this means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![e equals e super prime](images/c002_dequ469.png). Now since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c002_dequ470.png)is an identity element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![e asterisk operator e super prime equals e super prime](images/c002_dequ471.png). But since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![e super prime](images/c002_dequ472.png)is also an identity element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![e asterisk operator e super prime equals e](images/c002_dequ473.png). So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![equation sequence part 1 e equals part 2 e asterisk operator e super prime equals part 3 e super prime](images/c002_dequ474.png), and I have established uniqueness.
>     
> 2.  A related property is the *existence of an inverse* for every element. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c002_dequ475.png)is an identity element for the operation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo></math>![ring operator](images/c002_dequ476.png)on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ477.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ478.png)is any element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ479.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![x ring operator y equals e](images/c002_dequ480.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ481.png)is called a *right inverse* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ482.png). Similarly, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![y ring operator x equals e](images/c002_dequ483.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ484.png)is called a *left inverse* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ485.png). We are typically interested in the case where every element has both a right and a left inverse and they are equal. 
>     
>     An obvious example again involves addition and the integers. Every integer has an inverse under addition, namely the negative of the integer (recalling that the negative of a negative number is positive). So 3 + (− 3) = 0 and (−7) + (− (−7)) = (−7) + 7 = 0. However, when we look at the integers with the operation multiplication, no element has an inverse except for +1 and −1. Of course, if we allow fractions then the situation is different, but we are getting ahead of ourselves.
>     
> 3.  The third important property is a little less obvious and is known as *associativity*. In essence, associativity means we can move or remove brackets without affecting the result. Formally, an operation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo></math>![ring operator](images/c002_dequ490.png)on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ491.png)is said to be associative if and only if, for any elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ492.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ493.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c002_dequ494.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ495.png)(not necessarily distinct): <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis x ring operator y right parenthesis ring operator z equals x ring operator left parenthesis y ring operator z right parenthesis full stop](images/c002_dequ496.png)
>     
>     Yet again addition and multiplication over the integers have this property. However, subtraction does not, as (6 − 3) − 2 = 3 − 2 = 1 is not equal to 6 − (3 − 2) = 6 − 1 = 5.
>     
> 4.  The final property we introduce here is known as *commutativity*. An operation is commutative if the order of the elements does not matter. That is, put formally, an operation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo></math>![ring operator](images/c002_dequ499.png)on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ500.png)is said to be commutative if and only if, for any elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c002_dequ501.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c002_dequ502.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c002_dequ503.png)(not necessarily distinct): <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8201;&#8728;&#8201;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![x ring operator y equals y ring operator x full stop](images/c002_dequ504.png)
>     
>     Unsurprisingly, addition and multiplication over the integers have this property, but again subtraction does not, as 3 − 2 = 1, which is not equal to 2 − 3 = − 1.
>     
>     You might be tempted to speculate that, since associativity and commutativity both deal with the ordering of operations, one might imply the other. However, this is most definitely not the case; that is, it is possible to define an operation that is associative but not commutative and also to define one that is commutative but not associative.^()
>     
>     There are many other possible properties of operations that I could have described, but the ones I have just introduced are some of the most important for the discussions in later chapters of this book. I will be particularly interested in the case where an operation has the first three of the four properties above, which will give an example of what is known as a *group*. Indeed, groups are so important that they are a topic for a chapter of their own ([Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005)).
>     
> 
> ## Notes
> 
> 1.  [1](#c002.xhtml#rfn_1) Georg Cantor, 1845–1918.
> 2.  [2](#c002.xhtml#rfn_2) A reader of an early draft of this book challenged me to come up with an example of something obvious which turns out to be wrong. Of course, one problem with coming up with an example is that what is obvious to one person may not be obvious to another. Anyway, after some thought I decided that ‘obvious’ calculations of simple probabilities can often be wrong. One well-known example is provided by the following scenario. An opaque bag contains two balls, which may be white or black—each with a probability of 1/2 (or 50%). That is, there are three possibilities for the contents of the bag: both balls are black (probability 1/4), both balls are white (probability 1/4) and there is one black ball and one white ball (probability 1/2). You put your hand in the bag (without looking in) and draw out a black ball. What is the probability that the remaining ball is white? I suggest that the ‘obvious’ answer is 2/3 (67%), since the ball you have drawn out tells you that the bag does not contain two white balls, and the bag is twice as likely to contain one white and one black ball as it is to contain two black balls. However, the obvious answer is wrong—the probability that the other ball is white is 1/2, i.e. 50%. I explain why this apparently counter-intuitive answer is correct in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book—see page 221.

# Chapter 3  
Numbers as We Know and Love Them

> Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk (God made the integers, all else is the work of man).^()
> 
> ## 3.1 Where Does Mathematics Start?
> 
> The quote from Kronecker that starts this chapter is a surprisingly accurate summary of where mathematics starts. Over the last 200 years or so, and particularly during the 19th century, mathematicians have sought to rebuild all known mathematics from simple foundations in a rigorous way. That is, all of the mathematics you might remember from school, including the trigonometric functions like sine and cosine, logarithms, vectors, matrices, etc., have been rigorously developed from first principles. This means, in every case, starting from the fundamentals and proving that the functions exist and have the expected properties, without resorting to geometric arguments. This monumental effort gave a much firmer foundation to mathematics.
> 
> However, this rigorous development started from the integers. That is, the integers themselves form a fundamental building block on which rigorous mathematics has been built. Mathematicians would typically regard the definition of the integers as being part of the *Foundations of Mathematics* and not ‘regular mathematics’. Of course, there have also been efforts to build the integers from rigorous first principles, but such work is generally regarded by mathematicians as something that, while clearly important, constitutes a subject separate from ‘regular’ mathematics. Indeed, such work on the foundations of mathematics includes trying to analyse the very rules we use to build proofs and the various types of logic. By and large mathematicians take these concepts for granted. Of course, much more could be said about the nature of logic and mathematics, but doing so here would mean getting away from the main purpose of this book. I propose to follow the lead of other mathematicians and assume the integers are well-defined, as well as taking for granted certain fundamental properties of the integers.
> 
> At this point, you might reasonably ask, exactly what are the properties that I assume the integers possess? Well, to start, we assume that the integers have two associated operations: addition (+) and multiplication (×). Moreover, we assume that:
> 
> *   the addition operation satisfies all four of the properties listed in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012) (i.e. the existence of an identity (namely zero) and additive inverses, as well as the associative and commutative properties);
> *   the multiplication operation satisfies three of the four properties listed in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012) (i.e. the existence of an identity (namely one), as well as the associative and commutative properties, but it does not possess multiplicative inverses except for +1 and −1);
> *   multiplication distributes over addition, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![a multiplication left parenthesis b plus c right parenthesis equals a multiplication b plus a multiplication c](images/c003_dequ4.png)for any integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ5.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ6.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c003_dequ7.png).
> 
> Of course, these are all properties we assume when doing any arithmetic on integers. We also assume that the integers are ordered, a topic we revisit in [Section 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0004).
> 
> While the integers are not the main subject of this book, I nevertheless feel we need to start at the beginning and consider some of their key properties. The integers are also the basis of everything covered here, so it is worth spending a little while thinking about them. Given their importance as examples, at the end of the chapter I will also briefly introduce how we can build the rationals from the integers.
> 
> ## 3.2 The Natural Numbers and the Integers
> 
> I really need to start with the natural numbers, that is, the whole numbers 1, 2, 3, …. The integers are simply the natural numbers extended to include negative numbers and zero, i.e. …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …. I already used the natural numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap n right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ10.png)and the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ11.png)as examples in [Chapter 2](#c002.xhtml#c002). I should say at this point that some authors include zero in the natural numbers, but for the purposes of this book, I exclude zero from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c003_dequ12.png). Whilst discussing notation, I should also mention the sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap z super plus](images/c003_dequ13.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap z super minus](images/c003_dequ14.png), the positive and negative integers, respectively. I’m sure you will immediately observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap z super plus](images/c003_dequ15.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c003_dequ16.png)are the same set, at least as I have defined <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c003_dequ17.png). Indeed, given the possible ambiguity regarding whether <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c003_dequ18.png)contains zero or not, I will mostly use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap z super plus](images/c003_dequ19.png)from here on.
> 
> The idea of the natural numbers (or *counting numbers*) has been around for a very long time. At some point in prehistory, humans detached the idea of a number (three, say) from the existence of three objects of a particular kind. This involved recognising the idea of ‘three-ness’, so that three rabbits and three trees share this abstract notion of the number three. This fundamental idea was almost certainly reinvented many times, and no doubt it is something many of us rediscover for ourselves as infants. In any event, while much has been written about the development of the idea of counting numbers, in this book, I want to take them as something fundamental and immutable.
> 
> So what about the integers? Well, the idea that zero is a *number* (just like one, two, three, etc.), as opposed to simply being the absence of anything, is much more recent. Of course, using *positional* or *place notation* for numbers, i.e. writing 123 to mean one hundred plus two tens plus three, clearly requires some form of notation for zero, so that we can write 103 to mean one hundred, no tens and three; positional notation is discussed in a little more detail in [Section 3.3](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0003). So does this mean that the invention of positional notation must have come *after* the idea of zero as a number?
> 
> Well, this is far from clear. Whilst various types of positional notation were invented in antiquity, it seems that the base 10 notation we use today originated in India, although other such systems were invented elsewhere, including in China. The positional notation came to Europe via the Arab world, who adopted position notation in Arabic numerals from around the 10th century c.e. This explains why—in English at least—the numerals we use today are known as Arabic numerals, even though they differ from the numerals used in Arabic!
> 
> So does this mean that zero was well-recognised as a number by the 10th century c.e.? Well, not necessarily, as early positional systems used a space or some other marker instead of the zero we would use today. I think it is fair to say that the adoption of zero as a number on an equal footing with 1, 2, 3, etc., is something that happened gradually.
> 
> Something similar appears to be true for the concept of negative numbers, i.e. −1, −2, −3, etc. That is, it is not unrealistic to say that in many cultures the natural numbers came first, then zero, and then the negative numbers. Of course, today we treat them all as part of the integers, and we call them all ‘numbers’, even though negative numbers can’t be used for counting things (despite the word number clearly originating in the notion of counting, as in the word ‘enumeration’).
> 
> Indeed, today we automatically use the word ‘number’ to cover many quantities which don’t directly relate to counting objects. For example, while I would call the fraction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by four](images/c003_dequ23.png)a number, it clearly isn’t useful for counting sheep—except perhaps in a butcher’s shop or in the meat section of a supermarket—but it is very useful for measuring things, for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by four](images/c003_dequ24.png)kg of butter. I intend to use the word ‘number’ in an even more general way to cover less familiar quantities, but nonetheless quantities which can be added or multiplied together and which may have an interpretation in real life. Indeed, this is the main purpose of this book.
> 
> Going back to the properties of operations we introduced in [Chapter 2](#c002.xhtml#c002), zero has the benefit of providing an identity element for addition, and negative numbers provide inverses for the positive numbers under addition. That is to say that the operation of addition over the integers has all four of the properties we introduced, namely the existence of an identity element, the existence of inverses for all elements, associativity and commutativity.
> 
> ## 3.3 Writing Down Numbers
> 
> In [Section 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0002), I referred to the idea of positional or place notation. The version of place notation we all use is referred to as *base 10* or *decimal*, since, working left from the rightmost digit of a number, the digits represent the number of ones, the number of tens, the number of hundreds, and so on. That is, successive digits represent multiples of successive powers of 10. So, for example, the number 4567 is equal to
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![seven multiplication one times zero super zero plus six multiplication one times zero super one plus five multiplication one times zero squared plus four multiplication one times zero cubed full stop](images/c003_dequ25.png)
> 
> Obviously the idea could be extended to work with any base, and not just 10. A particularly important alternative representation is base 2, or ‘binary’.
