In a binary representation of a number, successive digits represent multiples of 1, 2, 4, 8, …, i.e. successive powers of 2. The digits in a binary representation are either 0 or 1—and are referred to as *bits* as an abbreviation of binary digits. For example, the number 10110 in a binary representation is equal to 22 in the more familiar decimal representation. This follows since
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 zero multiplication two super zero plus one multiplication two super one plus one multiplication two squared plus zero multiplication two cubed plus one multiplication two super four equals part 2 sum with 5 summands zero plus two plus four plus zero plus 16 equals part 3 22 full stop](images/c003_dequ26.png)
> 
> Binary representations are fundamentally important in computing and digital electronics, since computer memory is made up of individual memory elements, each capable of storing a single bit, i.e. a single 0 or 1. As a result, computers store numbers using a binary representation. Analogously, digital communications typically involves sending sequences of zeros and ones.
> 
> Other widely used number bases include 8, where base 8 is referred to as *octal*, and 16, known as *hexadecimal*. In the latter case, we need six more digits to represent the numbers 10–15, and for this the letters a, b, c, d, e, f are almost always used, sometimes in upper case, where a = 10, b = 11, and so on. So, for example, the hexadecimal number fe equals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>14</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>254</mn></math>![14 multiplication one plus 15 multiplication 16 equals 254](images/c003_dequ27.png)in decimal. To avoid confusion, when using multiple bases, it is common practice to write the base as a subscript, so we could write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mtext>fe</mtext><mn>16</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><msub><mn>4</mn><mn>10</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1111111</mn><msub><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![equation sequence part 1 fe sub 16 equals part 2 25 times four sub 10 equals part 3 1111111 times zero sub two](images/c003_dequ28.png).
> 
> ## 3.4 Ordering the Integers
> 
> As I mentioned in [Section 3.1](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0001), there are a number of properties of the integers that mathematicians take for granted in building mathematics. One is, of course, the fact discussed earlier that the addition operation has the four properties introduced in [Chapter 2](#c002.xhtml#c002). Another key property is that the integers are *totally ordered*, i.e. given any two integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ29.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ30.png), then either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x less than or equals y](images/c003_dequ31.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y less than or equals x](images/c003_dequ32.png)(or both, in which case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c003_dequ33.png)). Moreover, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x less than or equals y](images/c003_dequ34.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![y less than or equals z](images/c003_dequ35.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![x less than or equals z](images/c003_dequ36.png). The ordering property also separates the integers into positive and negative values—the positive integers are those for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x greater than zero](images/c003_dequ37.png), and the negative integers are those for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x less than zero](images/c003_dequ38.png)(where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x greater than y](images/c003_dequ39.png)simply means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x greater than or equals y](images/c003_dequ40.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x not equals y](images/c003_dequ41.png)). This ordering property is something we all take for granted; otherwise, how would we know which team was winning a football match?
> 
> The fact that the integers satisfy this ordering property underlies a widely used depiction of the integers on a ‘number line’, as shown in [Figure 3.1](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-1). All the integers to the left of an integer are smaller than it, and all the integers to its right are larger.
> 
> ![Figure 3.1 The number line with small integers.](images/c03f001.png)
> 
> [Figure 3.1](#c003.xhtml#rc03-fig-1) The number line with small integers.
> 
> A further assumed property of the integers is that both the sum and the product of two positive integers is also positive.
> 
> In fact, the ordering relationship between pairs of integers is just one example of a special type of relation called a *partial ordering*. If a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ42.png)has a relation (usually written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8804;</mo></math>![less than or equals](images/c003_dequ43.png)) with the following three properties, then the pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis cap s comma less than or equals right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ44.png)is called a *partially ordered set* and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8804;</mo></math>![less than or equals](images/c003_dequ45.png)is referred to as a *partial ordering* (on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ46.png)):
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![x less than or equals x](images/c003_dequ47.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x element of cap s](images/c003_dequ48.png)(reflexivity);
> *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x less than or equals y](images/c003_dequ49.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y less than or equals x](images/c003_dequ50.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x comma y element of cap s](images/c003_dequ51.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c003_dequ52.png)(antisymmetry); and
> *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x less than or equals y](images/c003_dequ53.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![y less than or equals z](images/c003_dequ54.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![x comma y comma z element of cap s](images/c003_dequ55.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![x less than or equals z](images/c003_dequ56.png)(transitivity).
> 
> If you check back, you’ll see that the first and third properties are exactly the same as the first and third properties required of an equivalence relation. However, the second property has changed from symmetry to antisymmetry.
> 
> It should be clear that the integers and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8804;</mo></math>![less than or equals](images/c003_dequ57.png)relation, i.e. the pair (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c003_dequ58.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8804;</mo></math>![less than or equals](images/c003_dequ59.png)), form a partially ordered set. In fact, as I already mentioned, (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c003_dequ60.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8804;</mo></math>![less than or equals](images/c003_dequ61.png)) is an example of a *totally ordered set*, since for any two integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ62.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ63.png), either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x less than or equals y](images/c003_dequ64.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y less than or equals x](images/c003_dequ65.png)(or both, in which case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![x equals y](images/c003_dequ66.png)).
> 
> There are, of course, partial orderings which are not total orderings. A simple example is provided by the ordering on subsets of a set defined by the ‘subset’ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mo>&#8838;</mo></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis subset of or equals right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ67.png)relationship. It is not hard to see that this gives a partially ordered set. An example for the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap s equals left curly bracket a comma b comma c right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ68.png)is shown in [Figure 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-2).
> 
> ![Figure 3.2 The ordering relationship for the subsets of a set.](images/c03f002.png)
> 
> [Figure 3.2](#c003.xhtml#rc03-fig-2) The ordering relationship for the subsets of a set.
> 
> In this figure, all the subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ69.png)are shown, and arrows are drawn to show the subset relationship. That is, there is an arrow from the subset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ70.png)to the subset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket a comma b right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ71.png)to indicate that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>&#8838;</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket subset of or equals left curly bracket a comma b right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ72.png). Of course, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ73.png)is also a subset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket a comma b comma c right curly bracket](images/c003_dequ74.png), but there is no need to provide an arrow, in this case, because the subset-ordering relation is transitive.
> 
> Another key property of the integers is that any subset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ75.png)of positive integers, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>![cap s subset of or equals double-struck cap z super plus](images/c003_dequ76.png), has a least element.^()
> 
> As an example, consider the, hopefully familiar, set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ80.png)of all fractions, i.e. the set
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math>![double-struck cap q equals left curly bracket x divided by y colon x comma y element of double-struck cap z comma y not equals zero right curly bracket full stop](images/c003_dequ81.png)
> 
> Note that we need to ensure that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![y not equals zero](images/c003_dequ82.png), since dividing by zero is not meaningful. I will explore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ83.png)in a little more detail later in this chapter.
> 
> Now, let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ84.png)be the set of all fractions of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by y](images/c003_dequ85.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![y equals one comma two comma three comma ellipsis](images/c003_dequ86.png). That is,
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math>![cap a equals left curly bracket one divided by one times left parenthesis equals one right parenthesis comma one divided by two comma one divided by three comma one divided by four comma ellipsis right curly bracket full stop](images/c003_dequ87.png)
> 
> Formally, we can write:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="{" close="}"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![cap a equals left curly bracket one divided by y colon y element of double-struck cap z super plus right curly bracket subset of or equals double-struck cap q full stop](images/c003_dequ88.png)
> 
> Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ89.png)does not contain a least element. Clearly zero is less than any element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ90.png), and we can find an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ91.png)as close as we like to zero, but zero is not in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ92.png)(in this case, zero is known as the *infimum* of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ93.png)). Proving that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c003_dequ94.png)does not have a least element can be achieved with a simple application of a reductio ad absurdum argument. Have a think about it. If you want to see why, I give a simple proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of the book (see page 243).
> 
> So, the property that every set of integers has a least element is perhaps not so obvious …. I should also say that I have glossed over one important point in these discussions. I have been careful to refer to ‘a least element’ rather than ‘the least element’, since I have not shown that a least element is unique. Of course, I expect you already *knew* that any least element must be unique, but it is not something we can simply assume—we need to prove it. In fact, as we next show, we can prove a more general result for any partially ordered set.
> 
> This shows that if a partially ordered set contains a least element, then it is unique, and so I can safely refer to the least element.
> 
> There is very much more than could be written about orderings, and in particular about partially ordered sets. However, as with so many other topics touched on in this book, I’ll next move on to explaining an important consequence of the property that any set of positive integers has a least element.
> 
> ## 3.5 Induction
> 
> This may seem like a digression from the topic of integers, but *induction* is a vital part of mathematics that depends on the least element property. Induction is a method for proving theorems. The principle of induction is simple to state.
> 
> Sometimes the induction principle is stated in a slightly different way. That is, the statement of the second requirement is changed to:
> 
> > if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of i](images/c003_dequ146.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c003_dequ147.png)satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![m less than or equals i less than or equals k](images/c003_dequ148.png), then this implies that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p times left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ149.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![k greater than or equals m full stop](images/c003_dequ150.png)
> 
> The proof of the modified theorem works in exactly the same way.
> 
> For a very simple example of the use of induction, suppose the statement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c003_dequ151.png)is:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands one plus three plus ellipsis plus left parenthesis two times n minus one right parenthesis equals n squared full stop](images/c003_dequ152.png)
> 
> We want to prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c003_dequ153.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than or equals one](images/c003_dequ154.png).
> 
> From the principle of induction (i.e. [Theorem 3.1](#c003.xhtml#c003-secc-0007)), I need to show two things: (a) that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/c003_dequ155.png)is true and (b) that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/c003_dequ156.png)is true, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p times left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ157.png)is also true. To show (a), observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/c003_dequ158.png)is simply asserting that 1 = 1², and hence is clearly true. Now suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/c003_dequ160.png)is true, i.e. we know that:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands one plus three plus ellipsis plus left parenthesis two times k minus one right parenthesis equals k squared full stop](images/c003_dequ161.png)
> 
> So, we know that:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis sum with variable number of summands one plus three plus ellipsis plus left parenthesis two times k minus one right parenthesis right parenthesis plus left parenthesis two times k plus one right parenthesis equals k squared plus left parenthesis two times k plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c003_dequ162.png)
> 
> But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi/><mn>2</mn></msup></msup><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="-0.167em"/></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![k squared plus left parenthesis two times k plus one right parenthesis equals left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis super squared comma](images/c003_dequ163.png)and so we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p times left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ164.png)is true. So, from [Theorem 3.1,](#c003.xhtml#c003-secc-0007) we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c003_dequ165.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than or equals one](images/c003_dequ166.png).
> 
> This is a rather trivial example, but induction can be used to prove much less obvious results, and it is an extremely useful tool in the mathematician’s locker. However, it must be used with care, as it is easy to go wrong. I will show this by giving a false proof of an obviously erroneous proposition.
> 
> Before doing so, I can’t resist mentioning that I don’t believe I am alone in feeling that proofs by induction are somehow aesthetically less pleasing than other types of proof. Why might this be? After all, isn’t a proof a proof, regardless of how it works? I am certainly not suggesting that proofs by induction are less valid than other types of proof; it is just that, in some cases at least, they do not shed much light on *why* the theorem is true. It is hard to justify this claim, and no doubt some mathematicians will think I am slightly crazy. However, I would certainly always prefer to prove something directly rather than by induction, I guess primarily for aesthetic reasons.^()
> 
> Anyway, back to the false proof. Suppose the statement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c003_dequ167.png)is ‘Every group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ168.png)people have the same name’. We want to prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/c003_dequ169.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than or equals one](images/c003_dequ170.png). We need to show that (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/c003_dequ171.png)is true, and (b) if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/c003_dequ172.png)is true, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p times left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ173.png)is true. Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/c003_dequ174.png)is clearly true since one person clearly has the same name as themself. Now suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/c003_dequ175.png)is true, i.e. we know that any group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c003_dequ176.png)people always have the same name. Now consider any group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k plus one](images/c003_dequ177.png)people, and suppose they line up in some order. We know that the first <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c003_dequ178.png)people have the same name (since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/c003_dequ179.png)is true) and also that the last <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c003_dequ180.png)people have the same name. Thus, all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k plus one](images/c003_dequ181.png)people must have the same name.
> 
> This is clearly a rather surprising result, and so there must be something wrong with the argument! See if you can spot the error. I have provided a short discussion of this in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of the book (see page 223).
> 
> I want to conclude this discussion of induction with a rather frivolous example—one that is well-known, at least in mathematical circles. But first, I want to mention an interesting piece of mathematical history. The number 1729 is sometimes known as the Ramanujan number (or the Hardy-Ramanujan number) because of a famous anecdote due to Godfrey Harold Hardy.^()
> 
> > I remember once going to see him \[Ramanujan\] when he was ill at Putney. I had ridden in taxi cab No. 1729 and remarked that the number seemed to me rather a dull one, and that I hoped it was not an unfavourable omen. ‘No’, he replied, ‘it is a very interesting number; it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways’.
> 
> This is often used as an example of the brilliance of Ramanujan. Whilst Ramanujan is not the subject of this chapter, I nevertheless want to explore the notion of a number being ‘interesting’, and contrariwise ‘not interesting’, a little further. I offer the following (somewhat tongue-in-cheek) proof that, in fact, all numbers are interesting, where by numbers I mean the positive integers. The proof relies on the fact that every set of positive integers has a least element, which is equivalent to the induction principle.
> 
> Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ182.png)be the set of uninteresting numbers—we wish to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ183.png)is empty. Suppose the claim is not true, i.e. suppose there are some uninteresting numbers and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ184.png)is non-empty. By the well-ordering principle, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ185.png)will contain a least element, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ186.png)say. That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ187.png)is the smallest uninteresting number. But this makes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ188.png)rather interesting, which is clearly a contradiction, and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ189.png)must be empty.
> 
> Make of this what you will. Perhaps the most obvious problem with this argument is that I have not provided a rigorous definition of what ‘interesting’ means—without this the whole thing is rather meaningless. Nonetheless, this old chestnut has provoked much discussion over the last few decades—there is even a Wikipedia page devoted to it,^()
> 
> Before concluding, I can’t resist mentioning the Online Encyclopaedia of Integer Sequences^()
> 
> Why have I raised this here? Well, one way of deciding whether a number is interesting is whether it appears in an entry in the OEIS, and so we could define the smallest uninteresting number as the smallest integer *not* appearing in the OEIS. Of course, this is a moving target; as new sequences are added, so uninteresting numbers become interesting. Wikipedia^()
> 
> ## 3.6 The Division Theorem
> 
> I now want to introduce an important theorem which I suspect you will think is obvious. It turns out to be key to understanding the behaviour of the integers, and I will need this theorem to help develop ideas later in this chapter and the next.
> 
> Before stating the result, I need to mention an important point about notation. In this book, I often write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![a multiplication b](images/c003_dequ190.png)to mean <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ191.png)multiplied by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ192.png), i.e. what is often called <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ193.png)‘times’ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ194.png). However, in places, and where the context is clear, I will just write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></math>![a times b](images/c003_dequ195.png). To be honest with you, I only added this remark after writing this chapter, as it is automatic for me to leave out the × sign. Of course, this is a very standard way of proceeding—you will no doubt have come across the famous equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![cap e equals m times c squared](images/c003_dequ197.png), and of course you could more formally write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![cap e equals m multiplication c squared](images/c003_dequ198.png)but no one does.^()
> 
> As a simple example, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>![a equals nine](images/c003_dequ268.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![b equals four](images/c003_dequ269.png). Then we know that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![nine equals two multiplication four plus one comma](images/c003_dequ270.png)
> 
> i.e. in this case, the unique quotient <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>q</mi></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ271.png)is 2 and the remainder <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>r</mi></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis r right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ272.png)is 1.
> 
> ## 3.7 Prime Numbers and Common Factors
> 
> I now want to spend a little time visiting a subject I hope you are all familiar with—the prime numbers (or just the *primes*). The prime numbers have been studied for thousands of years, as far as I am aware purely for reasons of curiosity, although mysticism and religion may also have been involved. However, before trying to define what a prime is, I need to introduce the notion of divisibility.
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ273.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ274.png)are positive integers and there is a positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ275.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![m multiplication a equals n](images/c003_dequ276.png), then we say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ277.png)is a *divisor* or *factor* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ278.png)(and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ279.png)is a *multiple* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ280.png)). We also sometimes write ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ281.png)divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ282.png)’ and use the shorthand notation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![m bar n](images/c003_dequ283.png)to mean that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ284.png)is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ285.png). So, for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![two multiplication three equals six](images/c003_dequ286.png), so both 2 and 3 are divisors of 6, and we can write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8739;</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![two bar six](images/c003_dequ287.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8739;</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![three bar six](images/c003_dequ288.png).
> 
> We can now define what a prime number is. A prime number is a positive integer greater than one with the property that its only divisors are one and itself. Obviously, every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ289.png)has divisors 1 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ291.png)since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![one multiplication n equals n](images/c003_dequ292.png), and a prime number has no factors apart from these. The first few primes are:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![two comma three comma five comma seven comma 11 comma 13 comma ellipsis](images/c003_dequ293.png)
> 
> You might be slightly surprised to see that I have excluded one from the list of primes. In the past, it was not uncommon to include one as a prime number but, because of its very special properties, the consensus over the last 100 years or so has been to exclude one from the list of primes. It is common practice to refer to any positive integer greater than 1 that is not prime as a *composite*.
> 
> Over the last 3000 years the study of prime numbers has given rise to a vast amount of new mathematics. However, it was not until the second half of the 20th century that prime numbers and their properties began to have an impact on the real world—apart, perhaps, via mysticism. I won’t spend a lot of time discussing the properties of prime numbers here, but I can’t resist mentioning one key fact known to the ancient Greeks (and written about by Euclid), namely that there are infinitely many primes. Proving this is actually quite straightforward, and I include a proof in [Chapter 9](#c009.xhtml#c009).
> 
> A related concept is that of a *common factor* or *common divisor*. Given any two positive integers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ294.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ295.png)say, a common divisor is any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/c003_dequ296.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/c003_dequ297.png)is a divisor of both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ298.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ299.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>m</mi></math>![r bar m](images/c003_dequ300.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![r bar n](images/c003_dequ301.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ302.png)is the set of all common divisors of a pair of integers, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ303.png)must be finite, and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ304.png)must have a greatest element; this greatest element is known as the *highest common factor* or *greatest common divisor*. As a convenient shorthand, I will write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![gcd left parenthesis m comma n right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ306.png)) for the greatest common divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ307.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ308.png).
> 
> As a simple example, consider the numbers 12 and 18. They have four common divisors; the complete set of common divisors is:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma three comma six right curly bracket full stop](images/c003_dequ309.png)
> 
> The greatest common divisor is 6, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis 12 comma 18 right parenthesis equals six](images/c003_dequ310.png).
> 
> We next establish a slightly surprising but very useful result.
> 
> In case you find this lemma hard to believe, here is a simple example for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![a equals seven](images/c003_dequ385.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![b equals 11](images/c003_dequ386.png). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ387.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ388.png)are distinct primes, it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis equals one](images/c003_dequ389.png). Hence, we need to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/c003_dequ390.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c003_dequ391.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>7</mn><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![seven times s plus 11 times t equals one](images/c003_dequ392.png). I claim that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![t equals two](images/c003_dequ393.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![s equals negative three](images/c003_dequ394.png)will work, since
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>21</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 seven multiplication left parenthesis negative three right parenthesis plus 11 multiplication two equals part 2 left parenthesis negative 21 right parenthesis plus 22 equals part 3 one full stop](images/c003_dequ395.png)
> 
> The following set of three basic results are all simple to prove using Bézout’s identity.
> 
> If two positive integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ415.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ416.png)have greatest common divisor 1, i.e. if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis m comma n right parenthesis equals one](images/c003_dequ417.png), then we say <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c003_dequ418.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ419.png)are *coprime*. That is, a pair of coprime positive integers have no common divisor apart from 1. This notion is key when we look at modular arithmetic in [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004).
> 
> The following somewhat similar result also follows from Bézout.
> 
> The proof is a straightforward application of Bézout’s identity ([Lemma 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0011)), and I suggest you try to prove it. I have provided a short proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section (see page 224).
> 
> Lastly, I need to give the following result on divisibility.
> 
> One thing I haven’t discussed so far is how to find the greatest common divisor of two integers. Of course, you could work through all the integers less than the smaller of the two and check whether they are a divisor or not. However, this could become extremely time-consuming for relatively modest-sized integers, and even a fast computer would take a considerable period of time to complete such a calculation if the numbers have, say, 20 decimal digits. A better way is needed, and that is precisely what I will demonstrate later in this chapter.
> 
> ## 3.8 Unique Factorisation
> 
> Having introduced prime numbers in [Section 3.7](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0010), I feel obliged to introduce a result I suspect many of you know already, namely that any integer can be represented uniquely as a product of prime numbers, although the order of the prime numbers can vary. This result goes back to Euclid and is implicit in a result stated in Euclid’s ‘Elements’, written in the 3rd century B.C.E.
> 
> It can be stated as follows.
> 
> ## 3.9 The Euclidean Algorithm
> 
> I now want to introduce the first algorithm in this book. Before going into detail, I need to explain what an algorithm is. For my purposes, an algorithm can be thought of as a precisely defined sequence of steps to be followed to perform a particular calculation or to solve a problem. An entire major branch of Computer Science is dedicated to finding efficient algorithms to solve commonly occurring computational problems so that these algorithms can be coded up in computer software.
> 
> The Euclidean algorithm is, as its name suggests, an algorithm dating back to the ancient Greeks and was described by Euclid. It can be used to compute the greatest common divisor of any pair of positive integers in a very efficient way.
> 
> As an example of how the algorithm operates, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>260</mn></math>![a equals 260](images/c003_dequ554.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![b equals 184](images/c003_dequ555.png).
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>260</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>76</mn></math>![260 equals one multiplication 184 plus 76](images/c003_dequ556.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>184</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![184 equals two multiplication 76 plus 32](images/c003_dequ557.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>76</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![76 equals two multiplication 32 plus 12](images/c003_dequ558.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>32</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![32 equals two multiplication 12 plus eight](images/c003_dequ559.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![12 equals one multiplication eight plus four](images/c003_dequ560.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![eight equals two multiplication four plus zero](images/c003_dequ561.png).
> 
> So, gcd(260,184)=4.
> 
> For practical purposes (as discussed in [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004)), it may be necessary to compute the greatest common divisor of two very large integers (with hundreds if not thousands of decimal digits). Fortunately, the Euclidean Algorithm is very efficient, and the number of iterations is bounded above by a constant factor times the number of digits in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ562.png). This result was established independently in 1969/1970 by German mathematician Hans Arnold Heilbronn and Canadian mathematician John D Dixon. More recently, in 1998, French mathematician and computer scientist Brigitte Vallée formally established a comparable result for an efficient version of the algorithm known as the binary Euclidean algorithm. Just because an algorithm is ‘old’ doesn’t mean that there aren’t new things to discover about it!
> 
> ## 3.10 The Rationals
> 
> In this section, I briefly introduce the *rationals* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ563.png). As you might expect, the rationals are derived from the fractions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ564.png)for integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ565.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ566.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis b not equals zero right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ567.png). I am not absolutely sure where the name ‘rational’ comes from, but it probably relates to the word ‘ratio’, since a fraction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ568.png)can be thought of as the ratio between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ569.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ570.png).
> 
> It is possible to define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ571.png)from first principles, starting with the known properties of the integers. To get started, define addition and multiplication of fractions in the following ways.
> 
> To define addition, put:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![a divided by b plus c divided by d equals a times d plus b times c divided by b times d comma](images/c003_dequ572.png)
> 
> and to define multiplication, let
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>&#215;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>.</mo></math>![a divided by b multiplication c divided by d equals a times c divided by b times d full stop](images/c003_dequ573.png)
> 
> It is straightforward to verify that all the expected properties hold.
> 
> For example, for addition:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 one divided by two plus two divided by three equals part 2 one multiplication three plus two multiplication two divided by two multiplication three equals part 3 seven divided by six comma](images/c003_dequ574.png)
> 
> and for multiplication:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>&#215;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 one divided by two multiplication two divided by three equals part 2 one multiplication two divided by two multiplication three equals part 3 two divided by six full stop](images/c003_dequ575.png)
> 
> The integers are a subset of the fractions consisting of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by one](images/c003_dequ576.png)for integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ577.png). It is simple to verify that this works since, using the rules stated earlier:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 a divided by one plus b divided by one equals part 2 a multiplication one plus b multiplication one divided by one multiplication one equals part 3 a plus b divided by one comma](images/c003_dequ578.png)
> 
> and
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>&#215;</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 a divided by one multiplication b divided by one equals part 2 a multiplication b divided by one multiplication one equals part 3 a multiplication b divided by one comma](images/c003_dequ579.png)
> 
> as expected.
> 
> However, you will no doubt have seen a problem here. If I simply defined the rationals to be equivalent to the set of all the fractions, I would end up with lots of repetitions. As I expect you know, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![two divided by three](images/c003_dequ580.png)is the ‘same’ as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![four divided by six](images/c003_dequ581.png); more generally, it is the same as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![two times n divided by three times n](images/c003_dequ582.png)for all integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ583.png). This problem can be avoided by first defining an equivalence relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8764;</mo></math>![tilde operator](images/c003_dequ584.png)on the set of fractions.
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ585.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![c divided by d](images/c003_dequ586.png)are two fractions, then say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator c divided by d](images/c003_dequ587.png)if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times d equals b times c](images/c003_dequ588.png). Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![three divided by five tilde operator six divided by 10](images/c003_dequ589.png)since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>6</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![three multiplication 10 equals five multiplication six left parenthesis equals 30 right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ590.png). I leave it to you to check that the three properties of an equivalence relation (reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity) hold for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8764;</mo></math>![tilde operator](images/c003_dequ591.png). If you don’t believe me, I include a brief proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of the book (see page 224).
> 
> I can then formally define the rationals to be the set of equivalence classes of fractions, and an equivalence class can be represented by any fraction in that class; put another way, each equivalence class contains all the fractions representing the same value (the same ratio). You can then check whether two fractions (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ592.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![c divided by d](images/c003_dequ593.png), say) represent the same value by seeing whether they are in the same equivalence class, i.e. by checking that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times d equals b times c](images/c003_dequ594.png). In such a case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b equals c divided by d](images/c003_dequ595.png).
> 
> As I already observed, there are many ways of representing the same value as a fraction. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ596.png)is a fraction, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c003_dequ597.png)is a common divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ598.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ599.png). Then, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a equals x times c](images/c003_dequ600.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![b equals y times c](images/c003_dequ601.png)for some integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ602.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ603.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![x divided by y equals a divided by b](images/c003_dequ604.png). This is easy to check:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>x</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 x times b minus y times a equals part 2 x of y times c minus y of x times c equals part 3 left parenthesis x times y right parenthesis times c minus left parenthesis x times y right parenthesis times c equals part 4 zero comma](images/c003_dequ605.png)
> 
> as required. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c003_dequ606.png)is the greatest common divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ607.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ608.png), then this gives a fraction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![x divided by y](images/c003_dequ609.png)in its *lowest terms*, i.e. so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis equals one](images/c003_dequ610.png)or, to put it another way, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ611.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ612.png)are coprime.
> 
> Whilst they are not one of the main subjects of the book, one reason for discussing the rationals is that they are a very useful example of some of the algebraic structures I will introduce in later chapters. They are also a ‘natural’ extension of the integers. What do I mean by that?
> 
> As I have discussed, the integers under the addition operation satisfy all four of the properties introduced in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012), namely the existence of an identity element (zero), the existence of an inverse for every element (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![negative x](images/c003_dequ613.png)is the inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ614.png)), associativity (moving brackets does not change the result), and commutativity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></mfenced></math>![left parenthesis x plus y equals y plus x right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ615.png). However, what about multiplication? It too has an identity element (1, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![x multiplication one equals x](images/c003_dequ616.png)for every non-zero <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ617.png)), is associative (since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x multiplication y right parenthesis multiplication z equals x multiplication left parenthesis y multiplication z right parenthesis](images/c003_dequ618.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ619.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ620.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c003_dequ621.png)) and is commutative (since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![x multiplication y equals y multiplication x](images/c003_dequ622.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ623.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ624.png)). However, apart from +1 and −1, no integers have an inverse under multiplication.
> 
> If I want to add multiplicative inverses to the integers, then I will end up with all the rationals. To see this, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ627.png)is a set containing the integers, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ628.png)is closed under multiplication (i.e. the product of two elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ629.png)is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ630.png)), and every element apart from zero has an inverse. Of course I cannot require zero to have an inverse under multiplication, as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![zero multiplication x equals zero](images/c003_dequ631.png)for every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ632.png). Then, since every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x not equals zero](images/c003_dequ633.png)must have an inverse, the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ634.png)must contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by x](images/c003_dequ635.png)for every non-zero <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ636.png), since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x multiplication one divided by x equals one](images/c003_dequ637.png), as desired.
