But I required <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ638.png)to be closed under multiplication, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></math>![one divided by x multiplication y equals y divided by x](images/c003_dequ639.png)must be an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ640.png)for every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c003_dequ641.png)and every non-zero integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ642.png). That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c003_dequ643.png)must contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ644.png).
> 
> So, the rationals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ645.png)have the nice property that the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c003_dequ646.png)have all four of the properties listed in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012) for both the addition and the multiplication operations.
> 
> It is sometimes helpful to think about the *number line*, a straight line on which all the integers and rationals are located. [Figure 3.3](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-3) gives a very simple picture of the number line with the integers on it.
> 
> ![Figure 3.3 The number line with small integers.](images/c03f003.png)
> 
> [Figure 3.3](#c003.xhtml#rc03-fig-3) The number line with small integers.
> 
> I can add rationals to this picture—[Figure 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-4) zooms in to the piece of the number line between 0 and 1 and shows a small selection of fractions in that part of the line.
> 
> ![Figure 3.4 Zooming in: the number line between 0 and 1.](images/c03f004.png)
> 
> [Figure 3.4](#c003.xhtml#rc03-fig-4) Zooming in: the number line between 0 and 1.
> 
> [Figure 3.5](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-5) zooms in again to the piece of the number line between 0 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by eight](images/c003_dequ647.png), the first fraction shown in [Figure 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c03-fig-4). I have again shown a small selection of fractions in that part of the line.
> 
> ![Figure 3.5 Zooming in further: the number line between 0 and 1/8.](images/c03f005.png)
> 
> [Figure 3.5](#c003.xhtml#rc03-fig-5) Zooming in further: the number line between 0 and 1/8.
> 
> I could carry on indefinitely, showing figures like this for ever-decreasing sections of the number line, and in every case, I could still find as many fractions as I like to show in the figure. That is, the rationals are *dense* on the number line. If I choose any two fractions, no matter how close together, I can find another fraction, in fact, an infinite number of them, to fit between these two fractions.
> 
> So, given that the number line is densely packed with rationals, surely that’s it? Surely we can’t find any more numbers to fit in? This leads neatly to a discussion of the *real numbers* ….
> 
>  
> 
> ## 3.11 The Real and Complex Numbers
> 
> If I try to assume that the rationals complete the number line, then I will quickly encounter major problems. These problems were first observed in antiquity.
> 
> To see this, let’s start with trying to solve a simple quadratic equation. Consider the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![x squared equals two](images/c003_dequ648.png); this is equivalent to saying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![x equals Square root of two](images/c003_dequ649.png). It seems reasonable that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ650.png)should be a number of some kind, and so let’s suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c003_dequ651.png)is a rational, i.e. let
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![x equals a divided by b comma](images/c003_dequ652.png)
> 
> where we assume that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ653.png)is in its lowest terms, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis equals one](images/c003_dequ654.png). Then it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![left parenthesis a divided by b right parenthesis squared equals two](images/c003_dequ655.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![left parenthesis a squared divided by b squared right parenthesis equals two](images/c003_dequ656.png). This means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![a squared equals two times b squared](images/c003_dequ657.png). So 2 is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![a squared](images/c003_dequ658.png), and so, since 2 is a prime, this means that 2 is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ660.png)(this follows from [Lemma 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0013)). So, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi></math>![a equals two times d](images/c003_dequ661.png)for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c003_dequ662.png). Then, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![a squared equals two times b squared](images/c003_dequ663.png), we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![left parenthesis two times d right parenthesis squared equals two times b squared](images/c003_dequ664.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![four times d squared equals two times b squared](images/c003_dequ665.png)and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![b squared equals two times d squared](images/c003_dequ666.png). That is, 2 is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![b squared](images/c003_dequ667.png), and so, since 2 is a prime, this means that 2 is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ669.png).
> 
> So, 2 is a divisor of both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ670.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c003_dequ671.png). But I assumed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c003_dequ672.png)was in its lowest terms, and this is a contradiction. So, I have shown that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![Square root of two](images/c003_dequ673.png)is not a rational. In fact, the same is true for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt><mo>,</mo></math>![Square root of n comma](images/c003_dequ674.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c003_dequ675.png)that is not a square. But it seems reasonable that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![Square root of two](images/c003_dequ676.png)lies on the number line, because you can quickly work out roughly where it lies; it is approximately 1.4142, so it clearly lies between the fractions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1414</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![1414 divided by 100](images/c003_dequ677.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1415</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![1415 divided by 100](images/c003_dequ678.png)—and it would be straightforward to continue to get better approximations. However, no matter how hard I try, and I can get as close as I like, I can never find a fraction that actually *equals* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![Square root of two](images/c003_dequ679.png). As a result, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![Square root of two](images/c003_dequ680.png)is said to be *irrational* because it is not a rational.
> 
> Finding solutions to equations like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![x squared equals two](images/c003_dequ681.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![x super four equals three](images/c003_dequ682.png)is not the only problem. You are probably familiar with the value known as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi></math>![pi](images/c003_dequ683.png), which equals the ratio between the length of the circumference and the diameter of a circle. The value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi></math>![pi](images/c003_dequ684.png)is also irrational, although this was only shown in the 18th century by Swiss-French mathematician Johann Lambert. Indeed, finding a ratio equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi></math>![pi](images/c003_dequ685.png)was a problem known to ancient Greek mathematicians, and it closely relates to the geometric problem of *squaring the circle*. To ‘square the circle’ would involve constructing a square with the same area as a particular circle, using only a finite number of steps involving a compass and a straight edge. Squaring the circle is impossible, although this hasn’t stopped people from trying!
> 
> The problem posed by the irrationals is solved by the so-called *real numbers*, commonly written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![double-struck cap r](images/c003_dequ686.png), which can best be thought of as including every possible value on the number line—including, of course, the rationals. Whilst the real numbers had been widely used for a long time, it wasn’t until the 19th century that mathematicians were able to formally define the reals using the rationals. This was a huge achievement, but sadly I would need the rest of this book to explain in full detail how it can be done. I can only refer you to a book on *real analysis* for an explanation—although, be warned, it is not at all straightforward.
> 
> The sets of integers, rationals and real numbers are clearly all infinite in cardinality (or size). However, it can be shown that the cardinality of the set of reals is somehow larger than the cardinality of the set of integers, so there is more than one kind of infinity. This surprising result is way beyond the main scope of this book, but I briefly explore it in [Section 9.2](#c009.xhtml#c009-sec-0002).
> 
> Before concluding the chapter, I want to very briefly mention the complex numbers. I already mentioned that an obvious omission from the rationals are the solutions to quadratic equations such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x squared minus two equals zero](images/c003_dequ687.png), and this gap is solved by creating the reals which *do* contain solutions to this equation (there are actually two solutions, one positive and one negative). However, there remain equations of this type which do not have solutions in the reals. An obvious simple example is the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x squared plus one equals zero](images/c003_dequ688.png). This clearly cannot have a solution in the reals since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![r squared greater than or equals zero](images/c003_dequ689.png)for any real number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/c003_dequ690.png). The complex numbers are created by adding a new number to the reals, namely the solution to this equation. This number, usually labelled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c003_dequ691.png), has the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![i squared equals negative one](images/c003_dequ692.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c003_dequ693.png)is added to the reals, along with all the other numbers necessary to ensure that the result is closed under addition and multiplication, then this results in the complex numbers, usually written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8450;</mi></math>![normal double struck cap c](images/c003_dequ694.png), and these complex numbers open up a whole new world of mathematical possibilities. However, I will leave it there, as I have other things to discuss!
> 
> Ultimately there is a lot more to ‘regular’ numbers than meets the eye! For the rest of this book, I want to look at different types of numbers which are in many ways much easier to handle than rationals, real and complex numbers, but have rather different properties. It also turns out that they have a host of important applications in the world of digital information communications and processing.
> 
> ## 3.12 Applying Complex Numbers—An Everyday Example
> 
> Before moving on, I will briefly introduce an important application of complex numbers in electrical engineering. This sort of application very much falls into the category of ‘traditional applied mathematics’ and hence is not typical of the applications in the rest of this book. Nonetheless, it helps to illustrate why somewhat bizarre concepts, that seem only of interest to mathematicians, turn out to be vitally important for the real world.
> 
> Electrical circuits are very commonly built to make use of Alternating Current (AC); indeed, domestic electrical supplies all use AC. In an AC system, the polarity of the electrical current changes regularly; for example, in the United Kingdom and most of Europe, the electrical current switches polarity at 50 cycles per second. When analysing the behaviour of electrical systems using AC, it is most convenient to model current using complex numbers.
> 
> In particular, voltages and currents can be expressed as functions of complex numbers. If the voltage is written as a function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap v of t](images/c003_dequ695.png)of the time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c003_dequ696.png), then we have:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mi>cos</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![cap v of t equals cap v sub m times cosine of omega times t plus theta comma](images/c003_dequ697.png)
> 
> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>![cap v sub m](images/c003_dequ698.png)is the amplitude, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#969;</mi></math>![omega](images/c003_dequ699.png)is the angular frequency and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#952;</mi></math>![theta](images/c003_dequ700.png)is the phase angle. We can rewrite this formula using complex numbers as:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![cap v of t equals cap v sub m times e super i times left parenthesis omega times t plus theta right parenthesis full stop](images/c003_dequ701.png)
> 
> This representation can make circuit-related calculations much simpler.
> 
> More generally, complex numbers have applications in signal processing and control systems analysis, making a range of computational tasks simpler and more efficient.
>

[12](#c003.xhtml#rfn_12) The cancellation law says that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times b equals a times c](images/c003_dequ711.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ712.png)is non-zero, then it is possible to *cancel* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c003_dequ713.png)to deduce that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![b equals c](images/c003_dequ714.png). This law holds for the integers because the product of two non-zero integers is always non-zero (see [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006), where the cancellation law is discussed in the context of general structures called rings). The fact that the product of two non-zero integers is non-zero can in turn be derived from the assumption that the product of two positive integers is always positive.

# Chapter 4  
Modular Arithmetic on the Integers

> Mathematics is the queen of the sciences.^()
> 
> ## 4.1 Working Relative to a Modulus
> 
> The idea of modular arithmetic was first developed by Gauss, one of the all-time greats of mathematics, whose quote starts this chapter. I will start by giving a rather informal introduction to modular arithmetic, before giving a more formal version.
> 
> Modular arithmetic works on a subset of the integers, relative to a specific positive integer known as the *modulus*. When numbers reach the modulus they go back to the beginning. It is like the numbers on a clock—on a typical clock face you will find the numbers 1 up to 12. One hour after 12 o’clock is not 13 o’clock—instead it is one o’clock. That is, the hours on a clock face work modulo 12. Indeed, modular arithmetic is sometimes informally known as *clock arithmetic*. In modular arithmetic, instead of a number line there is a number circle, just like the face of a clock. The number circle when working modulo 6 is shown in [Figure 4.1](#c004.xhtml#c04-fig-1).
> 
> ![Figure 4.1 The number circle modulo 6.](images/c04f001.png)
> 
> [Figure 4.1](#c004.xhtml#rc04-fig-1) The number circle modulo 6.
> 
> Apart from the hours in a (half) day, the other ways we measure time also use modular arithmetic (apart from years). Seconds and minutes run from 0 to 59, and then go back to 0, that is, they work modulo 60. Days of the week work modulo 7, although we use seven different names rather than numbers. Time is not the only example where we use modular arithmetic.
> 
> For example, degrees on a compass work modulo 360.
> 
> So if we are, for example, working modulo 6, we would count as follows:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![zero comma one comma two comma three comma four comma five comma zero comma one comma two comma three comma four comma five comma zero comma ellipsis](images/c004_dequ1.png)
> 
> Again working modulo 6, if we add 3 and 5 we get 2, and not 8 as we would if working in the integers!
> 
> It turns out that modular arithmetic has a very wide range of applications, as well as being interesting mathematically, as we will see.
> 
> ## 4.2 Congruences: Making It More Mathematical
> 
> So far everything I have said is informal. I now want to make it all rather more formal so I can start to establish some important properties of modular arithmetic (or what are known as ‘the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ2.png)’). I first need to define a simple relation on the integers.
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ3.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ4.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ5.png)are integers, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![n greater than zero](images/c004_dequ6.png), then we write:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>a</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![a identical to b left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ7.png)
> 
> if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![n bar left parenthesis b minus a right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ8.png). You should read the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo></math>![identical to](images/c004_dequ9.png)as meaning *congruent*. In other words, the theorem says that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ10.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ11.png)are congruent modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ12.png)if and only if the difference between them is an integer multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ13.png). Relating this back to our more informal notion of modular arithmetic, we can say that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a identical to b left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ14.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ15.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ16.png)are ‘the same’ modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ17.png).
> 
> Going back to our example of working modulo 6, i.e. where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![n equals six](images/c004_dequ18.png), it should be clear that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>3</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>15</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![three identical to 15 left parenthesis mod six right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ19.png)
> 
> since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>15</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![15 minus three equals 12](images/c004_dequ20.png)is an integer multiple of 6, so informally we can say that 3 and 15 are the same modulo 6. Similarly
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>18</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![18 identical to zero left parenthesis mod six right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ21.png)
> 
> since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>18</mn></math>![zero minus 18 equals negative 18](images/c004_dequ22.png)is also an integer multiple of 6.
> 
> Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![identical to left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ23.png)is a relation defined on the integers, it is natural to ask what properties it has. The following result is of key importance.
> 
> This means that, for any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ67.png), we can divide all the integers into equivalence classes. When working modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ68.png), we denote the equivalence class containing the integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ69.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket sub n](images/c004_dequ70.png). Every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ71.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket sub n](images/c004_dequ72.png)satisfies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a identical to b left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ73.png). So, for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![n equals six](images/c004_dequ74.png), there are six equivalence classes: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ75.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ76.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket two right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ77.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket three right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ78.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>4</mn><msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket four right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ79.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket five right curly bracket sub six](images/c004_dequ80.png), where, for example,
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket two right curly bracket sub six equals left curly bracket ellipsis comma negative 16 comma negative 10 comma negative four comma two comma eight comma 14 comma ellipsis right curly bracket full stop](images/c004_dequ81.png)
> 
> The set of equivalence classes modulo 6 are shown in [Figure 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c04-fig-2).
> 
> ![Figure 4.2 The equivalence classes modulo 6.](images/c04f002.png)
> 
> [Figure 4.2](#c004.xhtml#rc04-fig-2) The equivalence classes modulo 6.
> 
> We can then define addition on equivalence classes, based on integer addition, where
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket sub n plus left curly bracket b right curly bracket sub n equals left curly bracket a plus b right curly bracket sub n full stop](images/c004_dequ82.png)
> 
> It is not hard to see that, for addition, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub n](images/c004_dequ83.png)is an identity element, for every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket sub n](images/c004_dequ84.png)there is an inverse element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket negative a right curly bracket sub n](images/c004_dequ85.png), and addition is associative because integer addition is associative. We use the symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c004_dequ86.png)for the set of equivalence classes modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ87.png).
> 
> As I have just described, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![identical to left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ88.png)is a relation defined on the integers. Slightly confusingly, the ‘mod’ notation is also used for an operation (closely related to the mod relation), defined below. The dual use of the term is regrettable, but I am simply following established practice and it is almost certainly too late to change the terminology now. Fortunately, the terms are used in different ways, so it should be clear from the context whether a relation or an operation is meant.
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ89.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ90.png)are integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x003E;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis n greater than zero right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0001.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi></math>![r equals a mod n](images/c004_dequ92.png)is defined to be the unique integer with the property that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![a equals q times n plus r comma](images/c004_dequ93.png)
> 
> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ94.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/c004_dequ95.png)are integers and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![multirelation zero less than or equals r less than n](images/c004_dequ96.png). We know <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi></math>![r](images/c004_dequ97.png)is unique from the division theorem ([Theorem 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-secc-0009)). It follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r identical to a left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ98.png)(since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mi>n</mi></math>![r minus a equals q times n](images/c004_dequ99.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![n bar left parenthesis r minus a right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ100.png)).
> 
> To see how this works, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![a equals 12](images/c004_dequ101.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n equals five](images/c004_dequ102.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![12 mod five equals two](images/c004_dequ103.png), so that 2 is the unique value in the range 0, 1, …, 4 that is congruent to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![12 left parenthesis mod five right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ104.png).
> 
> This all seems very nice, but is modular arithmetic just a game? Can we do something serious with this? Well, unsurprisingly, the answer is very much so. This is true not only in terms of the mathematics we can derive, but also in terms of real world applications, as I will next describe.
> 
> ## 4.3 Parity Checks: Using Modulo 2 Arithmetic
> 
> The first and perhaps simplest example of the application of modular arithmetic is in calculating check digits. What is a check digit, I hear you ask?
> 
> Check digits are used in many contexts, but in all cases it amounts to protecting against accidental errors when entering or managing numbers which have a special meaning. For example, I imagine that all of us, no matter where we are from, have a wide range of numbers that identify us, our possessions or other objects in some way. Obvious examples include credit card numbers, phone numbers, membership numbers, serial numbers, model numbers, postal codes or (in the United Kingdom) National Insurance numbers. Such *identification numbers*^()
> 
> When entering such numbers there is always the possibility of making an error, e.g. by entering an incorrect digit, and the consequences can potentially be very serious. The idea is to add one or more *check digits* to a number to enable the recipient of the number to check whether or not it is valid, and thereby reduce the chance of an incorrect number being accepted. If, for example, the number specifies a bank account that is to receive a large deposit, I’m sure you can see the importance of trying to ensure the number is right.
> 
> Perhaps the simplest example of a check digit applies to numbers consisting of purely zeros and ones, when we are working in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c004_dequ105.png). In <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c004_dequ106.png), addition is simple:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two plus left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two equals left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two semicolon equation sequence part 1 left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two plus left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub two equals part 2 left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub two plus left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two equals part 3 left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub two semicolon and left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub two plus left curly bracket one right curly bracket sub two equals left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub two full stop](images/c004_dequ107.png)
> 
> For convenience we often simplify the notation and leave out the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![left curly bracket ellipsis right curly bracket sub two](images/c004_dequ108.png)and write^()
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![zero plus zero equals zero semicolon zero plus one equals one semicolon one plus zero equals one semicolon and one plus one equals zero full stop](images/c004_dequ109.png)
> 
> Computers store data as sequences of zeros and ones (or *bits*), arranged in bytes (8-bit blocks) and words; the length of a word will vary depending on the computer, but is typically 64 bits. A modern computer can store vast numbers of words of data, and there is always the possibility of a bit being changed in error.
> 
> To enable such accidental errors to be detected, it has been common practice to add an extra *parity check bit* to a byte or word, the presence of which is purely to detect errors. That is, instead of allocating 8 bits to store a byte, 9 bits will be used. The parity check bit for a byte (or word) can be computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the bits in the byte (or word). So, for example, if the bits of a byte are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis a sub zero comma a sub one comma ellipsis comma a sub seven right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0002.png), then the parity bit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>8</mn></msub></math>![a sub eight](images/c004_dequ113.png)is defined as:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![a sub eight identical to sum with variable number of summands a sub zero plus a sub one plus ellipsis plus a sub seven left parenthesis mod two right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ114.png)
> 
> As a result, it will always be the case that the modulo 2 sum of all the nine bits making up a byte and its associated parity check bit will be zero. This is known as *even parity*. This means that if a single-bit error occurs anywhere in the byte, including in the parity bit, i.e. if a one is changed to a zero or vice versa, the modulo 2 sum of the nine bits will give a one, indicating that an error has occurred. Of course, if two errors occur then the parity check will not detect this, but in most cases this is much less likely than a single-bit error. This means we can greatly reduce the probability of an undetected error in calculations.
> 
> Clearly, to make this work, every time a byte is changed then the parity bit will need to be changed as well, and every time the value of a byte is used the parity bit should be checked. However, this should be simple to arrange and can be built into the memory hardware.
> 
> As a simple example, consider the byte (11011100). Summing the bits we have:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 sum with 8 summands one plus one plus zero plus one plus one plus one plus zero plus zero identical to part 2 five identical to part 3 one left parenthesis mod two right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ115.png)
> 
> So the check bit is 1, and so the byte with its added check bit now looks like (11011100 1). If we add the bits together again we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>6</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![six identical to zero left parenthesis mod two right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ116.png), i.e. the byte with added check bit has even parity, as desired.
> 
> Observe that the system would work equally well if the default parity is *odd parity*, i.e. if
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>7</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![a sub eight identical to sum with variable number of summands a sub zero plus a sub one plus ellipsis plus a sub seven plus one left parenthesis mod two right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ117.png)
> 
> In such a case the modulo 2 sum of all nine bits will always be one, and if the sum is ever zero then an error must have occurred.
> 
> ## 4.4 Check Digits: A More Complex Example
> 
> The parity check example is a very simple one, and much more complex check digit systems can be devised, typically using modular arithmetic. Indeed, there is an international standard for the calculation of check digits: ISO/IEC 7064, entitled *Check character systems.*^()
> 
> The method, known as MOD 11-2, is (not surprisingly given the name) based on arithmetic modulo 11. MOD 11-2 is a technique for computing a single check digit for numeric strings, i.e. where the value to be protected against errors consists of a sequence of digits between 0 and 9. More formally, if the sequence of digits to be protected against error is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#x2212;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis a sub n comma a sub n minus one comma ellipsis comma a sub two right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0003.png)then the check digit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![a sub one](images/c004_dequ121.png)is computed so that the following equation holds:
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub one plus two times a sub two plus two squared times a sub three plus ellipsis plus two super n minus one times a sub n identical to one left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ122.png)
> 
> Observe that the value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ123.png)is equal to one more than the length of the string of digits to be protected, and the digits are numbered in reverse order. These slightly odd choices were made by the original authors of the standard, and so I have stuck with them here to avoid confusion.
> 
> This apparently rather complicated formula is actually easy to compute in practice by processing one digit at a time in the following way. Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap s equals a sub n](images/c004_dequ124.png), and then perform the following sequence of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![n minus two](images/c004_dequ125.png)steps (in each step the left arrow symbol <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mo>&#x2190;</mo><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis left arrow right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0004.png)means that the variable on the left is given the value of the expression on the right):
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>;</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub n minus one right parenthesis mod 11 semicolon](images/c004_dequ127.png)
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>;</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub n minus two right parenthesis mod 11 semicolon](images/c004_dequ128.png)
> *   …
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub two right parenthesis mod 11 full stop](images/c004_dequ129.png)
> 
> Finally set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></math>![a sub one equals left parenthesis one minus two times cap s right parenthesis mod 11](images/c004_dequ130.png).
> 
> You may have noticed that while, by definition, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![a sub n](images/c004_dequ131.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![a sub n minus one](images/c004_dequ132.png), …, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![a sub two](images/c004_dequ133.png)are all digits in the range 0–9, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![a sub one](images/c004_dequ134.png)is computed modulo 11 and hence may be any one of 0, 1, …, 9, 10. So what if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>![a sub one equals 10](images/c004_dequ135.png)? This is solved by replacing 10 by X (the Roman numeral for 10), so the check digit at the end may be any one of 0, 1, …, 9, X.
> 
> I’ll next work through a simple example to show how it works. Suppose we need to calculate the check digit for the number ‘0749’, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a sub five equals zero](images/c004_dequ136.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![a sub four equals seven](images/c004_dequ137.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![a sub three equals four](images/c004_dequ138.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>![a sub two equals nine](images/c004_dequ139.png); we need to calculate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![a sub one](images/c004_dequ140.png). Following the recipe above, we first put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap s equals part 2 a sub n equals part 3 a sub five equals part 4 zero](images/c004_dequ141.png). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n equals five](images/c004_dequ142.png), we then need to perform the following <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![n minus two equals three](images/c004_dequ143.png)steps.
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub four right parenthesis mod 11](images/c004_dequ144.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>;</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two multiplication zero plus seven right parenthesis mod 11 equals seven mod 11 equals seven semicolon](images/c004_dequ145.png)
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub three right parenthesis mod 11](images/c004_dequ146.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>;</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two multiplication seven plus four right parenthesis mod 11 equals 18 mod 11 equals seven semicolon](images/c004_dequ147.png)
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two times cap s plus a sub two right parenthesis mod 11](images/c004_dequ148.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![cap s left arrow left parenthesis two multiplication seven plus nine right parenthesis mod 11 equals 23 mod 11 equals one full stop](images/c004_dequ149.png)
> 
> Finally set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>![a sub one equals left parenthesis one minus two times cap s right parenthesis mod 11 equals left parenthesis one minus two multiplication one right parenthesis mod 11 equals negative one mod 11 equals 10](images/c004_dequ150.png). So the check digit is X. That is the four digit number with its check digit is 0749-X.
> 
> So why do we go to all this trouble to compute the check digit? After all, analogously to the parity check, we could simply have added all the digits working modulo 10 to obtain a check digit, and this would have enabled us to detect any single error. However, doing this would not enable us to detect if we had written the digits in the wrong order, since they would add up to exactly the same value. Performing this slightly more complex calculation means that any single numerical error, as well as any transposition of adjacent digits (as well as transposition of digits separated by a small number of other digits) will be detected by the check digit. That is, if any of these types of error occur then the check digit calculation will give the wrong result, and hence the error will be detected. This is especially useful, as—at least from personal experience—accidentally getting digits the wrong way round is a common error when writing or typing a long number.
> 
> You might reasonably ask why the particular calculations involved in the MOD 11-2 check digit calculation give these desirable properties. Well, I can assure you that this is no accident. Please see if you can think of why the calculation works the way it does. I have included a discussion of the properties of the MOD 11-2 system in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 225).
> 
> Because of its relative simplicity and effectiveness in catching errors, a slight variant of this method was used in the original 10-digit version of the International Standard Book Number (ISBN), known as ISBN-10, that was in use until 2007.^()
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>13</mn></msub><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub one plus three times a sub two plus a sub three plus three times a sub four plus ellipsis plus three times a sub 12 plus a sub 13 identical to zero left parenthesis mod 10 right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ155.png)
> 
> ISBN-13 check digits are slightly less effective at detecting errors than their ISBN-10 counterparts, and can miss a pair of transposed digits if the two digits differ by 5.
> 
> Many other numbering systems use modular arithmetic to calculate check digits. For example, the International Bank Account Number (IBAN) contains two check digits calculated working modulo 97. The method is one of these specified in ISO 7064. Indeed, I would strongly recommend any new numbering system to incorporate at least one check digit using an appropriate method from ISO 7064.
> 
> ## 4.5 Elementary Properties of ℤ[*n*]
> 
> Before moving on to the final, and what I think is the most interesting real world example application, I need to introduce two more important properties of modular arithmetic. If you want to skip this rather theoretical section for the time being then that’s fine, although you will probably need to refer back to the results later on.
> 
> ### 4.5.1 Solving Simultaneous Congruences
> 
> The first result, known as the *Chinese Remainder Theorem* provides a computationally efficient method for solving simultaneous equations in modular arithmetic. The name apparently derives from the fact that the earliest known statement of the theorem was made by the Chinese mathematician Sun Tzu^()
> 
> As an example, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x identical to three left parenthesis mod 17 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ201.png)(i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![t sub one equals three](images/c004_dequ202.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></math>![n sub one equals 17](images/c004_dequ203.png)) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x identical to four left parenthesis mod 23 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ204.png)(i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![t sub two equals four](images/c004_dequ205.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></math>![n sub two equals 23](images/c004_dequ206.png)). Since 17 and 23 are coprime—indeed they are both primes—there must exist a solution, and all solutions will be congruent modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>17</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>391</mn></math>![17 multiplication 23 equals 391](images/c004_dequ207.png). But how can a solution be found?
> 
> Following the proof of [Theorem 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0008), Bézout’s identity implies that there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ208.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ209.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>17</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>23</mn><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![17 times a plus 23 times b equals one](images/c004_dequ210.png). The values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ211.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ212.png)can be found using the Euclidean Algorithm, as follows.
> 
> *   First of all, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>23</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![23 equals 17 plus six](images/c004_dequ213.png)(and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn></math>![six equals 23 minus 17](images/c004_dequ214.png)).
> *   Next, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![17 equals two multiplication six plus five](images/c004_dequ215.png)(and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 five equals part 2 17 minus two multiplication six equals part 3 17 minus two multiplication left parenthesis 23 minus 17 right parenthesis equals part 4 three multiplication 17 minus two multiplication 23](images/c004_dequ216.png)).
> *   Finally, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![six equals five plus one](images/c004_dequ217.png)(and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 one equals part 2 six minus five equals part 3 left parenthesis 23 minus 17 right parenthesis minus left parenthesis three multiplication 17 minus two multiplication 23 right parenthesis equals part 4 three multiplication 23 minus four multiplication 17](images/c004_dequ218.png)).
> 
> Thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![three multiplication 23 minus four multiplication 17 equals one](images/c004_dequ219.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![a equals negative four](images/c004_dequ220.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![b equals three](images/c004_dequ221.png). Again following the proof of the theorem,
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 x equals part 2 left parenthesis t sub two minus t sub one right parenthesis times a times n sub one plus t sub one equals part 3 left parenthesis four minus three right parenthesis multiplication left parenthesis negative four right parenthesis multiplication 17 plus three equals part 4 negative 68 plus three equals part 5 negative 65 full stop](images/c004_dequ222.png)
> 
> It is then a simple matter to check that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>65</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>17</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![negative 65 identical to three left parenthesis mod 17 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ223.png)(which follows since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![negative 65 equals left parenthesis negative four right parenthesis multiplication 17 plus three](images/c004_dequ224.png)) and also that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>65</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![negative 65 identical to four left parenthesis mod 23 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ225.png)(which follows since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![negative 65 equals left parenthesis negative three right parenthesis multiplication 23 plus four](images/c004_dequ226.png)).
> 
> All the above calculations were done in a few minutes without even using a calculator, which I hope convinces you that this is an effective approach. It also works very efficiently for large numbers.
> 
> ### 4.5.2 The Euler Totient Function
> 
> The second result involves something called the *Euler phi function*, otherwise known as *Euler’s totient function*. Unsurprisingly this function was first introduced by Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler in 1763, although he did not use the Greek letter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi></math>![phi](images/c004_dequ227.png)for it. The use of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi></math>![phi](images/c004_dequ228.png)dates back to the beginning of the 19th century and is due to Johann Carl Friedrich Gauss. This very important function is highly honoured to be associated with two such great mathematicians!
> 
> The function can be defined in the following way. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ229.png)is a positive integer.
