Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![phi of n](images/c004_dequ230.png)is the number of integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ231.png)(with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![multirelation zero less than m less than or equals n](images/c004_dequ232.png)) that are coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ233.png), i.e. for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis m comma n right parenthesis equals one](images/c004_dequ234.png). So, for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![phi of three equals two](images/c004_dequ235.png)as, 1 and 2 are coprime to 3. We also have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![phi of four equals two](images/c004_dequ236.png), since 1 and 3 are coprime to 4, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![phi of five equals four](images/c004_dequ237.png), since 1, 2, 3 and 4 are all coprime to 5.
> 
> Importantly, it should be clear that for any prime number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ238.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![phi of p equals p minus one](images/c004_dequ239.png), since every number between 1 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p minus one](images/c004_dequ240.png)is coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ241.png). We can now state the following result, which is variously known as Euler’s theorem, the Euler–Fermat theorem, or Euler’s Totient theorem.
> 
> I will break with normal practice here and not provide a proof immediately. The simplest way to prove this theorem involves the theory of groups, which I will introduce in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005). I provide a proof in [Section 5.5](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0008).
> 
> As an example of how it works, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>![n equals 10](images/c004_dequ246.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![phi of 10 equals four](images/c004_dequ247.png), since 1, 3, 7 and 9 are the four positive integers less than 10 that are coprime to 10. So
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mn>3</mn><mrow><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>81</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![multirelation three super phi of 10 equals three super four equals three multiplication three multiplication three multiplication three equals 81 identical to one left parenthesis mod 10 right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ248.png)
> 
> as required by the theorem. I leave you to check that the formula also works for 7 and 9, the other two integers (other than 1) that are coprime to 10.
> 
> One key, and slightly surprising, property of the Euler phi function is that it is *multiplicative*. That is, the following result holds.
> 
>  
> 
> I leave the proof as an exercise for the reader. I have provided a proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of the book (see page 226).
> 
> This lemma has one immediate consequence of importance to the application described in [Section 4.6](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0013). If we suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></math>![n equals p times q](images/c004_dequ253.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ254.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ255.png)are primes, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![phi of n equals left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ256.png). So, for example, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 n equals part 2 15 equals part 3 three multiplication five](images/c004_dequ257.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>15</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 phi of 15 equals part 2 phi of three multiplication phi of five equals part 3 two multiplication four equals part 4 eight](images/c004_dequ258.png). You can check this immediately by observing that the set of positive integers less than 15 that are coprime to 15 is {1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14} which has cardinality 8, as expected.
> 
> I want to conclude this discussion by giving what can be thought of as a special case of Euler’s theorem ([Theorem 4.3](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0010)) but which is a century or so older and which has a very simple proof. This result is known as *Fermat’s Little Theorem*. It has this name because it was first stated, albeit without proof, by Pierre de Fermat in 1640 in private correspondence, although the name only seems to date back to the early 20th century. Proofs were subsequently formulated by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and Leonhard Euler. I will use this result in [Section 4.10.1](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0019).
> 
> There are many proofs of this nice result, which (at least to me), seems quite unexpected. I suggest you try to prove the result. There is a very nice elementary proof due to Solomon Wolf Golomb (who is mentioned again in [Chapter 7](#c007.xhtml#c007)) which involves considering all possible vectors of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ263.png)with elements from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero comma one comma ellipsis comma a minus one right curly bracket](images/c004_dequ264.png). First observe that there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>![a super p](images/c004_dequ265.png)such vectors (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ266.png)choices for the first element of the vector, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ267.png)choices for the second element, and so on). There are also <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ268.png)vectors of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma x comma ellipsis comma x right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ269.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c004_dequ270.png). The other <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![a super p minus a](images/c004_dequ271.png)vectors can be divided into sets containing cyclic shifts of the same sequence of values. I leave it to you to use these observations to complete the proof. I have provided a proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ at the end of the book (see page 227).
> 
> ## 4.6 The Extended Euclidean Algorithm
> 
> In [Section 3.9](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0017), I described the Euclidean algorithm, which can be used to determine the greatest common divisor of any two integers. However, the algorithm can be extended in a simple way to enable a second very useful computation.
> 
> Recall that in [Section 3.7](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0010), I introduced Bézout’s identity ([Lemma 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0011)). This states that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ272.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ273.png)are any two integers, not both zero, then there exist integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/c004_dequ274.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c004_dequ275.png)such that
> 
>  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![g times c times d of a comma b equals a times s plus b times t full stop](images/c004_dequ276.png)
> 
> This slightly surprising result turns out to be extremely useful in all sorts of ways. However, it is what one might call an *existence* result—i.e. it proves something exists but doesn’t tell you how to find it. In general, when proving something exists, it is far more helpful to actually show how to construct an example. Indeed, if you can show how to construct an example of something, then you have clearly shown that such a something (whatever it might be) exists!
> 
> We can bridge this gap with the *Extended Euclidean Algorithm* (EEA); that is, for any integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ277.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ278.png)this algorithm will enable us to find integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/c004_dequ279.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c004_dequ280.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>t</mi></math>![g times c times d of a comma b equals a times s plus b times t](images/c004_dequ281.png). The EEA involves running the Euclidean algorithm in reverse. It is probably easiest to explain how it works using an example.
> 
> Back in [Section 3.9](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0017), I gave the following example of how to compute the greatest common divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>260</mn></math>![a equals 260](images/c004_dequ282.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![b equals 184](images/c004_dequ283.png)using the Euclidean algorithm.
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>260</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>76</mn></math>![260 equals one multiplication 184 plus 76](images/c004_dequ284.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>184</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![184 equals two multiplication 76 plus 32](images/c004_dequ285.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>76</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![76 equals two multiplication 32 plus 12](images/c004_dequ286.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>32</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![32 equals two multiplication 12 plus eight](images/c004_dequ287.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![12 equals one multiplication eight plus four](images/c004_dequ288.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![eight equals two multiplication four plus zero](images/c004_dequ289.png).
> 
> So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>184</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![g times c times d of 260 comma 184 equals four](images/c004_dequ290.png).
> 
> The EEA simply involves starting at the penultimate step and working back, in the following way.
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![12 equals one multiplication eight plus four](images/c004_dequ291.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![four equals 12 minus one multiplication eight](images/c004_dequ292.png);
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>32</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![32 equals two multiplication 12 plus eight](images/c004_dequ293.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![eight equals 32 minus two multiplication 12](images/c004_dequ294.png). Substituting into the equation from the previous step we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 four equals part 2 12 minus one multiplication left parenthesis 32 minus two multiplication 12 right parenthesis equals part 3 three multiplication 12 minus 32](images/c004_dequ295.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>76</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![76 equals two multiplication 32 plus 12](images/c004_dequ296.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![12 equals 76 minus two multiplication 32](images/c004_dequ297.png). Substituting in we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#x2009;</mtext><mo>&#x00D7;</mo><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>&#x2212;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#x00D7;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo><mo>&#x2212;</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#x00D7;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>&#x2212;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#x00D7;</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></math>![four equals three prefix multiplication of left parenthesis 76 minus two multiplication 32 right parenthesis minus 32 equals three multiplication 76 minus seven multiplication 32](images/MMit1EQ_0001.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>184</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![184 equals two multiplication 76 plus 32](images/c004_dequ300.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>32</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn></math>![32 equals 184 minus two multiplication 76](images/c004_dequ301.png). Substituting in we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>76</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 four equals part 2 three multiplication 76 minus seven multiplication left parenthesis 184 minus two multiplication 76 right parenthesis equals part 3 17 multiplication 76 minus seven multiplication 184](images/c004_dequ302.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>260</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>76</mn></math>![260 equals one multiplication 184 plus 76](images/c004_dequ303.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>76</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![76 equals 260 minus 184](images/c004_dequ304.png). Substituting in we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>184</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 four equals part 2 17 multiplication left parenthesis 260 minus 184 right parenthesis minus seven multiplication 184 equals part 3 17 multiplication 260 minus 24 multiplication 184](images/c004_dequ305.png).
> 
> So we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>184</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>260</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>184</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 g times c times d of 260 comma 184 equals part 2 four equals part 3 17 multiplication 260 minus 24 multiplication 184](images/c004_dequ306.png).
> 
> In fact, the two series of steps can be combined, to avoid the need to go backwards as well as forwards. The EEA may seem quite complicated, but the ‘extended’ part does not involve a single multiplication, just some additions and subtractions. It is very straightforward to mechanise, and is very efficient even for very large numbers.
> 
> Before concluding I need to mention another result that is not only key for the operation of the RSA algorithm (described later in this chapter) but is also of wider importance. We will refer to it again in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005).
> 
> It is important to observe that, given any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ321.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ322.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![g times c times d of c comma n equals one](images/c004_dequ323.png), the EEA can be used to find an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ324.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a times b identical to one left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ325.png). This follows since the proof of [Lemma 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0014) uses Bézout’s identity, and the EEA provides solutions to Bézout’s identity.
> 
> We now have the machinery we need to look at our next real world example, namely the RSA cryptosystem.
> 
> ## 4.7 Cryptography Ancient and Modern
> 
> Before giving this example I need to explain a little about modern cryptography and its use of *keys*. The history of cryptography goes back over 2000 years, and until the 20th century cryptography was synonymous with the study of designing (and breaking) ciphers, i.e. methods for concealing the content of a message, so that a message could be sent via an untrusted channel without fear that its content would be divulged. The sender of a message (or *plaintext*) encrypts it using a procedure known only to the intended recipient to obtain the *ciphertext*; the recipient then decrypts the ciphertext to reveal the original plaintext. The encrypted message, i.e. the ciphertext, should not reveal anything about the plaintext message except, perhaps, its length.
> 
> In practice this meant, and still means, that although the underlying method of encryption might be well known—perhaps instantiated in a mechanical device—the sender and receiver share a secret value which is used with the method of encryption to define how the encryption procedure works. This secret value is known as a *key*. In today’s very widespread commercial use of cryptography, the methods of encryption, known as *encryption algorithms*, are public—indeed, they are typically standardised. So the security of the encryption process rests on just two things: the robustness of the encryption algorithm against *cryptanalysis*, and the secrecy of the key. By cryptanalysis I mean ways of trying to decrypt the data without knowing the key in advance—typically cryptanalysis works by analysing the ciphertext to find the key, and then using this key to decrypt all the encrypted data.
> 
> One rather trivial method of cryptanalysis involves trying every possible key, a bit like trying to unlock a combination lock by trying every possible sequence of digits. To resist this method it is sufficient to ensure that there are enough keys so this approach cannot succeed in a feasible amount of time—modern encryption methods typically involve keys that are at least 128 bits long, i.e. so that there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>128</mn></msup><mo>&#8771;</mo><mn>3.4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>38</mn></msup></math>![two super 128 asymptotically equals 3.4 multiplication one times zero super 38](images/c004_dequ326.png)keys, i.e. 34 followed by 37 zeros; a very large number indeed! Of course, there are many more sophisticated methods of cryptanalysis, depending on the nature of the encryption algorithm. However, my main interest here is in the keys.
> 
> The encryption scenario I have just described remained essentially unchanged for 2000 years or more until the 1970s. All that changed during that very long period of time were the methods of encryption, which became increasingly sophisticated (and eventually mechanised) to resist increasingly clever methods of cryptanalysis. Before proceeding note that every method of encryption also needs an associated method of decryption. Typically they work in a very similar way; moreover, conventionally, the same secret key is used for both encryption and decryption.
> 
> So what changed in the 1970s? In 1976, American cryptographers Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the truly ground-breaking paper ‘New Directions in Cryptography’.^()
> 
> Of course, so far there is nothing revolutionary in the idea. After all, this model works for conventional encryption (also known as *symmetric encryption*), where the decryption key happens to be the same as the encryption key. However, they then hypothesised that a system could be designed where (a) generating new key pairs is easy, and (b) finding the decryption key even if you know the corresponding encryption key is very difficult. If we could design such a system then everyone could choose their own key pair and could publish their encryption key (hence the term *public key* encryption). So if I want to send you a secret message, I first look up your public encryption key (e.g. on the Internet) and then use it to encrypt this message. I can then send you the encrypted message through an insecure channel (e.g. I could just post it on a social media page) and you would be the only one who could decrypt it, since only you know your personal decryption key.
> 
> Diffie and Hellman also described a linked idea, which is today known as Diffie–Hellman key exchange. This is a method designed to enable two parties to agree on a shared secret value, e.g. for use as a secret key with a conventional encryption scheme. This is described in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005).
> 
> While the Diffie–Hellman paper described the properties of a public key encryption algorithm, they did not have an example to give.^()
> 
> However, one proposed method not only survived careful scrutiny but became very widely used. This method, known as RSA after the names of its inventors American cryptographer and computer scientist Ronald Linn Rivest, Israeli cryptographer Adi Shamir and American computer scientist Leonard M. Adleman, was published in 1978,^()
> 
> It was revealed some years later that the idea of public key cryptography (also known as asymmetric cryptography), as well as the RSA algorithm, had been developed independently and in secret in the early 1970s by cryptographers working at the the UK’s Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ). James Ellis came up with the idea of public key cryptography, and his colleague Clifford Cocks later came up with the RSA algorithm (although of course it was not called that then). However, it seems that the GCHQ cryptographers had no conception of how their discovery could have such a major impact on the commercial world of security, perhaps because their role was to protect government secrets and not to make the wider commercial world secure. This is just one case of where a great idea is developed quite independently by different individuals, or groups of individuals, at roughly the same time. Sometimes the world is ready for an idea, and it gets invented independently multiple times.
> 
> The reason I am giving all this preamble is because RSA is based on modular arithmetic. Indeed, the fact that it works is based on theorems from number theory dating back hundreds of years. In the remainder of this chapter, I will explore how it works, how it is used and how implementation issues it presents can be overcome.
> 
> ## 4.8 RSA: How Does It Work?
> 
> RSA works in the following way. Anyone wishing to receive encrypted messages must first generate their key pair, made up of an encrypting key (to be made public) and a decrypting key (to be kept secret). They proceed in the following way, noting that part of the key is the *modulus*, i.e. a positive integer used in modular arithmetic calculations.
> 
> 1.  They first need to decide on the length of the modulus—the longer the modulus the greater the security, but also the more difficult the calculations involved in encryption and decryption. A typical length for the modulus might be 700–800 decimal digits. We are dealing with very large numbers here!
> 2.  Next, two large prime numbers, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ327.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ328.png), must be chosen, where they have a roughly similar number of decimal digits and where this number is equal to half the chosen modulus length.
> 3.  The modulus for the key pair is then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>q</mi></math>![cap n equals p multiplication q](images/c004_dequ329.png).
> 4.  They must next choose a pair of positive integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis d comma e right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0007.png)with the property that
>     
>     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![d multiplication e identical to one left parenthesis mod phi of cap n right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ332.png)
>     
>     observing that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![phi of cap n equals left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ333.png)from [Lemma 4.1](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0011). Such a pair exists by [Lemma 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0014) (observing that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ334.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ335.png)must be coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![phi of cap n](images/c004_dequ336.png)). There are a variety of ways to choose such a pair—one possibility is simply to choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ337.png)at random subject to the constraint that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis e comma left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis right parenthesis equals one](images/c004_dequ338.png), and then work out what the corresponding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ339.png)must be. Note that, however we choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ340.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ341.png), they must both be coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis equals phi of cap n](images/c004_dequ342.png), and hence they must both be odd.
>     
> 5.  Finally, set the encryption key to be the pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis e comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0008.png), and set the decryption key to be the pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis d comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0009.png). The encryption key can now be published. However, the decryption key and the primes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ347.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ348.png)must be kept secret.
> 
> The idea underlying RSA is that, even if you know the public key, i.e. the pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis e comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0010.png), then finding the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ351.png)is computationally infeasible as long as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ352.png)is sufficiently large. This difficulty is, in turn, based on the difficulty of finding the prime factors of a very large composite number.
> 
> To illustrate the process, a simple example may help. This example uses very small primes, just to show how keys are generated. Suppose that the primes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![p equals 11](images/c004_dequ353.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></math>![q equals 17](images/c004_dequ354.png)are chosen, so the modulus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>187</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap n equals part 2 p multiplication q equals part 3 11 multiplication 17 equals part 4 187](images/c004_dequ355.png). It also follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 phi of cap n equals part 2 left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis equals part 3 10 multiplication 16 equals part 4 160](images/c004_dequ356.png).
> 
> Suppose, as is common practice, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ357.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ358.png)are generated by first choosing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ359.png)so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis e comma phi of cap n right parenthesis equals one](images/c004_dequ360.png), and then calculating the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ361.png), using knowledge of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ362.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ363.png). So, for the sake of this example, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![e equals three](images/c004_dequ364.png)is chosen, observing that 3 and 160 have greatest common divisor equal to 1.
> 
> We now need to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ365.png)so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![e multiplication d identical to one left parenthesis mod phi of cap n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ366.png), i.e. so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mi>d</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>160</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![three times d identical to one left parenthesis mod 160 right parenthesis](images/MMit1EQ_0002.png). A solution is to set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>107</mn></math>![d equals 107](images/c004_dequ369.png), since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>107</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>321</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>160</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![multirelation three multiplication 107 equals 321 identical to one left parenthesis mod 160 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ370.png). That is, the public encryption key is (3, 187), and the corresponding decryption key is (107, 187). Of course, this example would be hopelessly insecure, since it is trivially easy to factorise 187 (just by trying all possible prime factors until 11 is found); it is then straightforward to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis d comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0011.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis e comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0012.png). Very much larger numbers are required in practice to make factorisation infeasible.
> 
> It is important to explain why it is not easy to work out the decryption key from the encryption key. The piece of information the generator of the key pair has that a potential third party doesn’t, is knowledge of the primes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ375.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ376.png). If you know <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ377.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ378.png), then calculating <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ379.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ380.png)is relatively straightforward, as I discuss in [Section 4.9](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0017). Without knowledge of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ381.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ382.png), this is computationally infeasible as long as the primes are large enough.
> 
> Why is this? Well, it turns out that, although it is not difficult to multiply two numbers together, even when they have something like 400 decimal digits each, trying to find the prime divisors of a very large number (the *integer factorisation problem*) is a very difficult problem. Indeed, with current computers and the best available methods, trying to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ383.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ384.png)from an 800-decimal-digit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ385.png)is something that would take hundreds of years—at least using currently available techniques. The current record for factorising the largest number of RSA type (i.e. a number that is the product of two large primes) is around 250 decimal digits.
> 
> So learning <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ386.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ387.png)by first finding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c004_dequ388.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c004_dequ389.png)is not a viable route. Suppose it was possible to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ390.png)by some other means? Well, it is not hard to show that if you can find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ391.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ392.png)(other than the trivial solution where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ393.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ394.png)are both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#177;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![prefix plus minus of one](images/c004_dequ395.png)) such that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![d multiplication e identical to one left parenthesis mod left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ396.png)
> 
> then it is possible^()
> 
> So, how are these keys used? That is, how does message encryption and decryption work?
> 
> A message <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ400.png)to be encrypted must be in the form of a number satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>N</mi></math>![zero less than m less than cap n](images/c004_dequ401.png). If, for example, the message is a string of bits, then the number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ402.png)could be the integer having that string of bits as its binary representation. Encryption simply involves calculating
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![c equals m super e mod cap n comma](images/c004_dequ403.png)
> 
> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ404.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ405.png)make up the public encryption key. So the encrypted version of a message will simply be another number between 0 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ406.png).
> 
> Decryption is very similar. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ407.png)is a received encrypted message, then the plaintext <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ408.png)can be recovered by calculating
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![m equals c super d mod cap n full stop](images/c004_dequ409.png)
> 
> So why does it work? Well, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![m super prime equals c super d mod cap n](images/c004_dequ410.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![c equals m super e mod cap n](images/c004_dequ411.png). We need to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![m equals m super prime](images/c004_dequ412.png). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![m super prime equals c super d mod cap n](images/c004_dequ413.png), we can substitute in for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ414.png)to get
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![m super prime identical to left parenthesis m super e right parenthesis super d left parenthesis mod cap n right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ415.png)
> 
> But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></math>![left parenthesis m super e right parenthesis super d equals m super e times d](images/c004_dequ416.png), and so
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![m super prime identical to m super e times d left parenthesis mod cap n right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ417.png)
> 
> We also know that
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![e times d identical to one left parenthesis mod phi of cap n right parenthesis comma](images/c004_dequ418.png)
> 
> i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e times d equals s times phi of cap n plus one](images/c004_dequ419.png)for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/c004_dequ420.png). Hence
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 m super prime identical to part 2 m super s times phi of cap n plus one identical to part 3 m multiplication m super s times phi of cap n left parenthesis mod cap n right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ421.png)
> 
> But from Euler’s theorem ([Theorem 4.3](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0010))
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m super s times phi of cap n identical to one left parenthesis mod cap n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ422.png)
> 
> and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>m</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m super prime identical to m left parenthesis mod cap n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ423.png), as required.
> 
> I will next show how this works using the example keys described above, namely where the public encryption key is (3, 187), and the corresponding decryption key is (107, 187). Suppose the message to be encrypted is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![m equals 12](images/c004_dequ424.png). Then
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>c</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![c identical to one times two cubed left parenthesis mod 187 right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ425.png)
> 
> Because the numbers are small, this is simple to calculate: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1728</mn></math>![one times two cubed equals 1728](images/c004_dequ426.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1728</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn></math>![1728 mod 187 equals 45](images/c004_dequ427.png)(since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1728</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>45</mn></math>![1728 equals nine multiplication 187 plus 45](images/c004_dequ428.png)), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn></math>![c equals 45](images/c004_dequ429.png).
> 
> We now need to show that decryption works. To decrypt <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn></math>![c equals 45](images/c004_dequ430.png), we raise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ431.png)to the power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>107</mn></math>![d equals 107](images/c004_dequ432.png), i.e. we calculate
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>107</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![m super prime identical to four times five super 107 left parenthesis mod 187 right parenthesis full stop](images/c004_dequ433.png)
> 
> This is not so simple! If you simply try to calculate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>107</mn></msup></math>![four times five super 107](images/c004_dequ434.png)using an ordinary calculator application, the result will be far too large to be given accurately since it contains 177 decimal digits. This means that, instead of computing the complete exponential and only then reducing modulo 187, we need to perform single multiplications and reduce modulo 187 every time. There is a simple way of doing this called ‘square and multiply’ (discussed further later in this chapter) which enables you to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>107</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![four times five super 107 mod 187](images/c004_dequ435.png)using just four multiplications and six squaring operations, reducing modulo 187 every time. I will show how you can do this calculation easily just using a calculator (or pencil and paper) in [Section 4.10](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0018). In the meantime you can check that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>107</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![four times five super 107 mod 187 equals 12](images/c004_dequ436.png)using one of the online multi-precision calculators.^()
> 
> Clearly the security of RSA rests on the difficulty of factoring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ437.png). That is, if it is possible to factorise the modulus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ438.png)making up part of a public key, then it is possible to determine the private key corresponding to that public key, and hence decrypt any intercepted encrypted messages. I also pointed out that learning <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ439.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ440.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ441.png)is just as difficult as factorising <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ442.png). So does this mean that breaking RSA has the same difficulty as factoring large numbers? The simple answer is: no one knows.
> 
> The problem comes because it might conceivably be possible to decrypt an encrypted message without knowing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ443.png). This may seem unlikely, but no one has been able to show that decryption is impossible without knowing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ444.png). As other authors have observed, today this question seems rather less important than it used to given that, if a suitably large scale general purpose quantum computer is ever built, then factorising large integers becomes straightforward and RSA will be immediately rendered insecure. This issue is discussed further in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005).
> 
> ## 4.9 Using RSA
> 
> So far I have described RSA purely in the context of encryption. Indeed, under the heading of cryptography I have only discussed encryption. However, today cryptography embraces a larger collection of important security-related functions.
> 
> Encryption provides one very important security service, namely the protection of sensitive information against disclosure to unauthorised parties. However, there are other very important security services relating to data, namely protecting *data integrity* and *data origin authentication*. Data integrity protects data against unauthorised modifications, and origin authentication enables the recipient of data to verify where it comes from. For example, if you send a message to a bank asking for a sum of money to be transferred to a specific recipient, you are relying on the integrity of the message being preserved, so that the bank doesn’t transfer the wrong amount or perhaps the right amount to the wrong recipient. The bank is also relying on origin authentication, since it wants to be sure that it is a genuine instruction from you and not from an impostor.
> 
> These services can be provided using cryptographic methods. Indeed, in many cases it would seem that protecting integrity and verifying origin are even more important than confidentiality. In today’s Internet, these services are provided automatically using cryptography-based protocols such as Transport Layer Security (TLS).
> 
> One way of providing integrity protection is by using something called a *digital signature*. A digital signature scheme is another type of public key cryptographic method, that enables the sender of a message to compute a value called a digital signature; this digital signature is computed as a function of a message, and if sent with a message can be used to verify its origin and integrity. The idea is that every party wishing to generate digital signatures creates a special pair of keys: a key that can be made public used for checking signatures, and a key used for creating signatures that needs to be kept secret.
> 
> As Rivest, Shamir and Adleman described in their 1978 paper, the RSA algorithm can be used as a way of creating and verifying digital signatures. This makes RSA especially valuable, as it can be used for both encryption and creating digital signatures. Anyone wishing to create digital signatures using RSA generates an RSA key pair, just as I have already described. However, in this case the key pair is made up of a signing key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis d comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0013.png)(which is kept secret) and a verification key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis e comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0014.png)which can be made public, so that everyone can verify generated signatures.
> 
> In order to create and verify digital signatures, a special type of function called a *cryptographic hash function* is needed. These functions are designed using cryptographic principles, but do not use a key. A cryptographic hash function takes as input a string of bits of arbitrary length and outputs a fixed length string of bits (e.g. a block of 256 bits). It must satisfy the following properties:
> 
> *   it must be simple and fast to calculate the output, even for long inputs;
> *   given a possible output, i.e. a string of bits of the appropriate length, it must be computationally infeasible^()
> *   for a given input, it must be computationally infeasible to find a second input which maps to the same output;
> *   it shall be computationally infeasible to find two inputs which give the same output (this is known as the ‘collision-resistance property’).
> 
> There are a number of well-known, well-accepted and internationally standardised hash functions, including a very widely used function known as SHA-256, part of the SHA family of hash functions^()
> 
> Creating a digital signature for a message <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ449.png), which is assumed to be a sequence of bits, then involves the following steps:
> 
> *   Apply an agreed cryptographic hash function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c004_dequ450.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ451.png)to obtain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![h of m](images/c004_dequ452.png).
> *   If the RSA signing key for the sender is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis d comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0015.png), compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![cap s equals left parenthesis h of m right parenthesis super d mod cap n](images/c004_dequ455.png), where the string of bits <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![h of m](images/c004_dequ456.png)is converted to an integer, e.g. by regarding it as the binary representation of a number.
> *   The signature on the message <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ457.png)is then simply <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c004_dequ458.png), and the originator sends the pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis m comma cap s right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0016.png)as the signed message.
> 
> Verifying a signed message works in the following way.
> 
> *   If the RSA verification key for the sender is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis e comma cap n right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0017.png), compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![h super prime equals cap s super e mod cap n](images/c004_dequ463.png).
> *   Apply the agreed cryptographic hash function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c004_dequ464.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ465.png)to obtain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![h of m](images/c004_dequ466.png).
> *   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![h super prime equals h of m](images/c004_dequ467.png)then the signature should be accepted; otherwise it should be rejected as invalid.
> 
> The descriptions I have given of using RSA for encryption and for digital signatures have been a little naive. In both cases, some data formatting is required before computing the exponential. In the case of encryption, this formatting needs to include the addition of some random bits, which can be discarded after decryption. This formatting and use of randomness is necessary to address certain possible attacks.
> 
> Over the last 30 years, RSA has been very widely used, although we are almost certainly now past ‘peak RSA’ (a topic we address at the end of this chapter). For example, RSA has been used to underlie security for chipcard-based credit and debit card transactions, as well as being commonly used to help set up secure TLS sessions between web browsers and web servers. RSA is used both for encryption and for creating digital signatures.
> 
> RSA encryption is primarily used for encrypting keys for more conventional encryption algorithms. This is because performing an RSA encryption is computationally complex, and RSA encryption is several orders of magnitude slower than encryption using a modern conventional algorithm. So, instead of encrypting a message directly with RSA, a one-time key for a conventional encryption algorithm is randomly generated and used to encrypt the message. This one-time key is then encrypted using RSA with the public key of the intended recipient, and the encrypted one-time key is sent with the encrypted message. The recipient can first decrypt the RSA-encrypted one-time key, and then use the one-time key to decrypt the message.
> 
> The complete set of operations needed to encrypt a key, including the formatting and adding of randomness, forms what is known as a *Key Encapsulation Mechanism* or KEM. There are a variety of well-established and standardised KEMs involving the use of RSA.^()
> 
> There is, unsurprisingly, much more that could be said about the use of RSA, but I hope I have given you enough to whet your appetite and convince you that number theory and modular arithmetic are actually useful—as well as a source of mathematical interest for the last two or three thousand years.
> 
> ## 4.10 Implementing RSA
> 
> There are a number of steps in the process of generating keys and using RSA which I have stated without any hint of how they might actually be implemented, and I suspect you have already been questioning the feasibility of certain calculations. The following three functions are necessary to use RSA, but it is perhaps less obvious how to implement them. I will round off this chapter by briefly explaining that the apparently infeasible is actually feasible after all.
> 
> ### 4.10.1 Choosing the Primes *p* and *q*
> 
> This might appear to be the most challenging part of all. I suspect that for many readers, the only way of determining whether a number is prime is by finding its prime factors, and we are assuming that the numbers involved are so large that this is infeasible! So how do we decide whether a number is prime? We use what is known as a *primality test*. We know that primes have certain special properties, so if we have a ‘candidate prime’, i.e. a number which we hope might be prime, we can check whether it possesses this property. If it doesn’t, it is not prime, and so we can choose another candidate. If, on the other hand, it does have the property then it *may* be prime, ideally with high probability. If we repeat this process a sufficient number of times, and the candidate passes every test, then we know the candidate is prime with very high probability—which is good enough for our purposes.
> 
> So what might we test? Well, from Fermat’s little theorem ([Theorem 4.4](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0012)) we know that, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ470.png)is a prime, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a super n identical to a left parenthesis mod n right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ471.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ472.png). So, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ473.png)is a candidate prime, we can choose a random <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ474.png)and compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![a super n](images/c004_dequ475.png)—if the result is not congruent to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ476.png)modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ477.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ478.png)is definitely not prime—otherwise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ479.png)is prime with probability greater than 1/2, i.e. the probability it is composite is less than 1/2. So if this test is repeated with random values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ480.png)and it passes, say, 20 times, then the probability it is not prime is less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>20</mn></msup></math>![left parenthesis one solidus two right parenthesis super 20](images/c004_dequ481.png)which is less than 1 in a million.
> 
> In practice, we can use other more efficient tests which weed out non-primes with a much higher probability, so far fewer tests are needed to be almost certain the candidate is a prime. Also, there is a small flaw in the use of Fermat’s little theorem as a primality test. Some composite numbers (the so-called *Carmichael Numbers*^()
> 
> ### 4.10.2 Finding the Pair (*d*, *e*)
> 
> As I mentioned previously, there are many ways to choose such a pair. A commonly used approach is first to choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ487.png)—perhaps to have convenient properties or simply at random. A candidate for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ488.png)must satisfy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![g times c times d of e comma left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis equals one](images/c004_dequ489.png).
