Then it is a simple matter of using the EEA (explained in [Section 4.6](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0013)) to find integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ490.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ491.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![c times left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis plus d times e equals one](images/c004_dequ492.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c004_dequ493.png)is exactly what we need to complete key generation.
> 
> Fortunately, as mentioned in [Section 4.6](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0013), the EEA is highly efficient, meaning this part of key generation can be completed very quickly.
> 
> ### 4.10.3 Computing *m*^(*e*) mod *N* and *c*^(*d*) mod *N*
> 
> The final piece of the implementation jigsaw involves finding a way to compute a very large number raised to the power of another very large number, all modulo a third very large number. Obviously it won’t be possible to first perform the exponentiation step and then reduce modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ496.png), since if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c004_dequ497.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ498.png)both have 1000 decimal digits, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup></math>![m super e](images/c004_dequ499.png)will have around 10^(1000) decimal digits; given that there are only of the order of 10^(80) atoms in the universe, we couldn’t store such a number even if we could calculate it! So we need to perform the calculation in stages, and at every opportunity reduce the number we are dealing with modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/c004_dequ502.png).
> 
> The answer is to use a process called *square and multiply.*^()
> 
> Suppose we wish to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![m super e mod cap n](images/c004_dequ507.png). First suppose that the binary representation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c004_dequ508.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![e sub s minus one times e sub s minus two times ellipsis times e sub zero](images/c004_dequ509.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub s minus one equals one](images/c004_dequ510.png). Then do the following:
> 
> Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>m</mi></math>![a left arrow m](images/c004_dequ511.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![i left arrow s minus one](images/c004_dequ512.png).
> 
> 1.  Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![a left arrow a squared mod cap n](images/c004_dequ513.png).
> 2.  Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![i left arrow i minus one](images/c004_dequ514.png).
> 3.  If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub i equals one](images/c004_dequ515.png)then set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![a left arrow a multiplication m mod cap n](images/c004_dequ516.png).
> 4.  If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![i equals zero](images/c004_dequ517.png)then stop, else go to step 1.
> 
> To show how this works, I will look again at the example from [Section 4.8](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0016). I claimed there, without proof, that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>107</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![four times five super 107 mod 187 equals 12](images/c004_dequ518.png). I will now show how this apparently problematic calculation can be done very easily using the square and multiply method.
> 
> First note that in this case the exponent 107 has binary representation 1101011, so, using the notation above, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![s equals seven](images/c004_dequ519.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1101011</mn></math>![e sub six times e sub five times e sub four times e sub three times e sub two times e sub one times e sub zero equals 1101011](images/c004_dequ520.png).
> 
> We start by putting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a equals part 2 m equals part 3 45](images/c004_dequ521.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 i equals part 2 s minus one equals part 3 six](images/c004_dequ522.png). We then work through the loop <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![s minus one equals six](images/c004_dequ523.png)times, as follows:
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![a left arrow a squared mod cap n](images/c004_dequ524.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow four times five squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ525.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2025</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>155</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 four times five squared equals part 2 2025 equals part 3 10 multiplication 187 plus 155](images/c004_dequ526.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>155</mn></math>![a left arrow 155](images/c004_dequ527.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals five](images/c004_dequ528.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub five equals one](images/c004_dequ529.png)so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>m</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![a left arrow a multiplication m mod cap n](images/c004_dequ530.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>155</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 155 multiplication 45 mod 187](images/c004_dequ531.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>155</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6975</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>37</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>56</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 155 multiplication 45 equals part 2 6975 equals part 3 37 multiplication 187 plus 56](images/c004_dequ532.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>56</mn></math>![a left arrow 56](images/c004_dequ533.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow five times six squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ534.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>5</mn><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3136</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>144</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 five times six squared equals part 2 3136 equals part 3 16 multiplication 187 plus 144](images/c004_dequ535.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>144</mn></math>![a left arrow 144](images/c004_dequ536.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals four](images/c004_dequ537.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![e sub four equals zero](images/c004_dequ538.png), so we do nothing.
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>14</mn><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 14 times four squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ539.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>14</mn><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>20736</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>110</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>166</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 14 times four squared equals part 2 20736 equals part 3 110 multiplication 187 plus 166](images/c004_dequ540.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>166</mn></math>![a left arrow 166](images/c004_dequ541.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals three](images/c004_dequ542.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub three equals one](images/c004_dequ543.png), so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>166</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 166 multiplication 45 mod 187](images/c004_dequ544.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>166</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7470</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>39</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>107</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>177</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 166 multiplication 45 equals part 2 7470 equals part 3 39 multiplication 107 plus 177](images/c004_dequ545.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>177</mn></math>![a left arrow 177](images/c004_dequ546.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>17</mn><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 17 times seven squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ547.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>17</mn><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>31329</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>167</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 17 times seven squared equals part 2 31329 equals part 3 167 multiplication 187 plus 100](images/c004_dequ548.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>100</mn></math>![a left arrow 100](images/c004_dequ549.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals two](images/c004_dequ550.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![e sub two equals zero](images/c004_dequ551.png), so we do nothing.
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>10</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 10 times zero squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ552.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>10</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>10000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>53</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>89</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 10 times zero squared equals part 2 10000 equals part 3 53 multiplication 187 plus 89](images/c004_dequ553.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>89</mn></math>![a left arrow 89](images/c004_dequ554.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals one](images/c004_dequ555.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub one equals one](images/c004_dequ556.png), so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>89</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 89 multiplication 45 mod 187](images/c004_dequ557.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>89</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4005</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>78</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 89 multiplication 45 equals part 2 4005 equals part 3 21 multiplication 187 plus 78](images/c004_dequ558.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>78</mn></math>![a left arrow 78](images/c004_dequ559.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow seven times eight squared mod 187](images/c004_dequ560.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>7</mn><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>6084</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 seven times eight squared equals part 2 6084 equals part 3 32 multiplication 187 plus 100](images/c004_dequ561.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>100</mn></math>![a left arrow 100](images/c004_dequ562.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![multirelation i left arrow i minus one equals zero](images/c004_dequ563.png).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![e sub zero equals one](images/c004_dequ564.png), so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>187</mn></math>![a left arrow 100 multiplication 45 mod 187](images/c004_dequ565.png). Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>100</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4500</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>187</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 100 multiplication 45 equals part 2 4500 equals part 3 24 multiplication 187 plus 12](images/c004_dequ566.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><mn>12</mn></math>![a left arrow 12](images/c004_dequ567.png).
> 
> That is, we get 12, as expected!
> 
> If the binary representation of the exponent has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/c004_dequ568.png)digits, the above routine involves <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![s minus one](images/c004_dequ569.png)rounds, so computing the exponentiation requires just <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![s minus one](images/c004_dequ570.png)squaring operations, and roughly half that number of multiplications—the precise number of multiplications will depend on the number of ones in the binary representation of the exponent. Of course, all these calculations involve very large numbers, so they are not cheap in computational terms. Nonetheless, performing an RSA computation can be done in much less than a second on a modern computer.
> 
> ## 4.11 RSA and the Future
> 
> I previously mentioned that we are probably beyond ‘peak RSA’. Why is this? There are two main reasons.
> 
> First, and perhaps most important, there are other schemes for both digital signatures and for encryption that are more efficient, i.e. that require less complex computations. In particular, schemes based on discrete logarithms in finite groups (a topic for [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005)) have rather taken over. With a careful choice of group, not only can operations be made more efficient, but keys can be made smaller.
> 
> Second, I think we can expect to see RSA and discrete logarithm based schemes gradually being phased out over the next 10–20 years, because of the threat posed by quantum computing. As far as RSA is concerned, if a sufficiently large-scale quantum computer is built, it could be used to factorise numbers much larger than can be factorised with today’s computers; this would mean that RSA would be insecure for any practical choices of modulus lengths. This issue is discussed in greater detail in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005).
> 
> Of course, improving methods of factorisation have always posed a threat to the security of RSA. Indeed, the advent of RSA suddenly meant that finding computationally efficient methods for factorisation, previously a rather niche area of computational number theory, suddenly became a mainstream topic. This meant many more academics working on the problem, as well as greatly increased funding!
> 
> Since the late 1970s, the lengths of numbers that can be readily factorised have increased very significantly. In the early days, it was deemed secure to use an RSA modulus containing 100 decimal digits. However, during the 1990s and 2000s a series of ‘challenge numbers’ of increasing sizes, i.e. RSA moduli promulgated to test the ability of research workers to factorise numbers, were gradually factorised. A 110-digit number was factorised in 1992, a 120-digit number in 1993, a 140-digit number in 1999, a 150-digit number in 2004 and so on. A history of this work up to around 2010 can be found in a short paper by American cryptographer Burt Kaliski^()
> 
> Progress has been achieved for three main reasons: improved algorithms, more powerful and greater numbers of computers and more effective implementations. It is difficult to untangle the precise contributions made by each of these advances, but my personal impression is that more efficient implementation has been the most effective tool. Certainly the fastest algorithm for integers not having a special form, known as the *number field sieve*, has been known for decades.
> 
> ## 4.12 Other Applications of Modular Arithmetic
> 
> I already mentioned that computers store data as binary digits or bits (zeros and ones) arranged in words, where a typical word length is 64 bits. These words can be used to store a variety of types of information. If they are used to store whole numbers then, when two words are added together and the result stored in another word, this result will typically be computed modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>64</mn></msup></math>![two super 64](images/c004_dequ571.png). This is necessary as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>64</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super 64 minus one](images/c004_dequ572.png)is the largest number whose binary representation can be stored in 64 bits. That is, computers do not really do integer arithmetic—instead they do modular arithmetic. If you need to process numbers larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>64</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super 64 minus one](images/c004_dequ573.png), then special software will need to be employed so that multiple words can be used to store the numbers you are working with.
> 
> Further applications of modular arithmetic are discussed in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005). However, before concluding this chapter, I want to mention one simple application you may already be familiar with, but that you may not have realised relates to modular arithmetic. I already talked in [Chapter 3](#c003.xhtml#c003) about divisibility of integers; on occasion it is of interest to know whether a given number is a multiple of a small value, such as 2, 3 or 5. The key principle here is that a number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c004_dequ574.png)is divisible by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ575.png)if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![n identical to zero left parenthesis mod a right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ576.png). This is the basis of all the following simple checking methods.
> 
> Checking divisibility by 2 is simple, since a number is divisible by 2 only if it is even, i.e. if it ends with 2, 4, 6, 8 or 0. The fact that we only need to check the final digit follows because 10 is a multiple of 2, i.e. because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>10</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![10 mod two equals zero](images/c004_dequ577.png). If, for example, a three-digit number has the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times b times c](images/c004_dequ578.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c004_dequ579.png)is the number of hundreds, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c004_dequ580.png)is the number of tens and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ581.png)is the final digit, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>c</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a times b times c identical to c left parenthesis mod two right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ582.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times b times c](images/c004_dequ583.png)is divisible by 2 if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c004_dequ584.png)is divisible by 2. The same would be true for a value with an arbitrarily large number of digits.
> 
> Checking divisibility by 5 works in exactly the same way. We only need to check whether the final digit is divisible by 5 since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>10</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![10 mod five equals zero](images/c004_dequ585.png).
> 
> Extending this idea, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>100</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![100 identical to zero left parenthesis mod four right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ586.png), it is possible to check a number for divisibility by 4 simply by checking the last two digits. So, for example, 12364 is divisible by 4 because 64 is divisible by 4. Moreover, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1000</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![1000 identical to zero left parenthesis mod eight right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ587.png), a number is divisible by 8 if and only if the value made up of the final three digits is divisible by 8.
> 
> Moving on, there is a slightly different nice trick for checking whether a number is divisible by 3, which also works because of modular arithmetic. First observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>10</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![10 identical to one left parenthesis mod three right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ588.png)(and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>100</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![100 identical to one left parenthesis mod three right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ589.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1000</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![1000 identical to one left parenthesis mod three right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ590.png), and so on). Every digit in the usual decimal representation of a number represents a multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msup></math>![one times zero super i](images/c004_dequ591.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c004_dequ592.png)(for example, the number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>456</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![456 equals four multiplication one times zero squared plus five multiplication one times zero super one plus six multiplication one times zero super zero](images/c004_dequ593.png), where as always <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![one times zero super zero equals one](images/c004_dequ594.png). But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![one times zero super i identical to one left parenthesis mod three right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ595.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c004_dequ596.png). So, working modulo 10, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>456</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![456 identical to sum with 3 summands four plus five plus six left parenthesis mod three right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ597.png), and the same is true for any number; that is the sum of the digits of a number is congruent to the number itself modulo 3. So if the sum of the digits is divisible by 3, then so is the number. In the example I just mentioned, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands four plus five plus six equals 15](images/c004_dequ598.png), which is divisible by 3, so 456 is also divisible by 3.
> 
> Exactly the same trick works for checking divisibility by 9, since we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>10</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![10 identical to one left parenthesis mod nine right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ599.png). That is, if you sum all the digits of a number, then the sum will be divisible by 9 if and only if the original number is divisible by 9.
> 
> Finally, there is a slightly more complicated trick for checking divisibility by 11. This involves observing that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>11</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![11 identical to prefix plus of one left parenthesis mod 10 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ600.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>11</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>100</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![11 identical to negative one left parenthesis mod 100 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ601.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>11</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1000</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![11 identical to prefix plus of one left parenthesis mod 1000 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ602.png)and so on. So if we are given a number, for example 23456, to check for divisibility by 11, you add up the even digits <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis three plus five equals eight right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ603.png)and subtract the sum of the odd digits <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis sum with 3 summands two plus four plus six equals 12 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ604.png), and in this case get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>8</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![eight minus 12 equals negative four](images/c004_dequ605.png). Clearly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![negative four](images/c004_dequ606.png)is not divisible by 11 and so neither is 23456. However, for 93456 we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![left parenthesis three plus five right parenthesis minus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands nine plus four plus six right parenthesis equals negative 11](images/c004_dequ607.png), which *is* divisible by 11, and so 93456 is divisible by 11 (in fact <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>93456</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8496</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![93456 equals 8496 multiplication 11](images/c004_dequ608.png)).
> 
> To check divisibility by 6 we can simply check for divisibility by 2 and 3, and to check for divisibility by 12 we can check for divisibility by 3 and 4. Putting together all these methods, we have a simple way of checking for divisibility by every number less than 13 except for 7. As far as I know, there is no *very simple* way of checking for divisibility by 7, but there is a slightly more complex method (that works for 13 as well) based on the observation that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1001</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>13</mn></math>![1001 equals seven multiplication 11 multiplication 13](images/c004_dequ609.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>7</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1000</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![seven identical to one left parenthesis mod 1000 right parenthesis](images/c004_dequ610.png). I leave you to think about this.
>

I have presented you with an expression which apparently came out of thin air, and which helps prove the theorem, just like a rabbit appears out of a magician’s hat. It is a bit like cheating, since it took some work to find the rabbit, and I’m not showing you this work. However, it does keep the proof short! Of course, this use of the word rabbit is not to be confused with Fibonacci’s *rabbit breeding problem*, which leads to the definition of the celebrated *Fibonacci Sequence*: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …(see `https://oeis.org/A000045`), named after the 12th/13th-century Italian mathematician Fibonacci—see also `https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Fibonacci/`. # Chapter 5  
Groups

> It appears to me that if one wants to make progress in mathematics, one should study the masters and not the pupils.^()
> 
> ## 5.1 What Is a Group?
> 
> Groups are one of the most important, and also one of the simplest, structures in abstract algebra. A group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1.png)is defined to be a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ2.png)with an operation \* defined on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ3.png)which has the following three properties:
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ4.png)contains an *identity element* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c005_dequ5.png), i.e. an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c005_dequ6.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 g asterisk operator e equals part 2 e asterisk operator g equals part 3 g](images/c005_dequ7.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ8.png);
> *   every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ9.png)has an *inverse* in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ10.png), i.e. an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g super negative one element of cap g](images/c005_dequ11.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 g asterisk operator g super negative one equals part 2 g super negative one asterisk operator g equals part 3 e](images/c005_dequ12.png);
> *   the operation ∗ is *associative*, i.e. for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g comma h comma k element of cap g](images/c005_dequ14.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis g asterisk operator h right parenthesis asterisk operator k equals g asterisk operator left parenthesis h asterisk operator k right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ15.png).
> 
> These are, of course, the first three of the possible properties for an operation I introduced back in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012). Some authors would also add a requirement for *closure*, i.e. requiring that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g asterisk operator h element of cap g](images/c005_dequ16.png)for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g comma h element of cap g](images/c005_dequ17.png), but for the purposes of this book this is guaranteed by the definition of an operation.
> 
> It is worth pointing out at this point that the identity element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c005_dequ18.png)in a group is always unique (I proved this in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012)). In a group, it is also the case that inverse elements are unique. To show this suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c005_dequ19.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c005_dequ20.png)are both inverses of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ21.png)in the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ22.png). Consider the expression <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![h asterisk operator g asterisk operator k](images/c005_dequ23.png)(I can omit brackets since the associative law holds). First note that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 h asterisk operator g asterisk operator k equals part 2 left parenthesis h asterisk operator g right parenthesis asterisk operator k equals part 3 e asterisk operator k equals part 4 k](images/c005_dequ24.png). But it also follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 h asterisk operator g asterisk operator k equals part 2 h asterisk operator left parenthesis g asterisk operator k right parenthesis equals part 3 h asterisk operator e equals part 4 h](images/c005_dequ25.png), and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![h equals k](images/c005_dequ26.png). In fact, we only used the associative law to establish this result, so in any structure where there is an identity element and the associative law holds (i.e. in a *monoid*—see below), if an element has an inverse element, then it must be unique.
> 
> It seems that French mathematician Évariste Galois was the first to use the word group (actually ‘groupe’ in French) in this context in 1830. However, he used the term to mean what we would today call a particular example of a group of permutations. The term was next used in a more general context by British mathematician Arthur Cayley in 1854.^()
> 
> Mathematicians use the term *Group Theory* to describe the body of results covering the existence and properties of groups. Group Theory has become a major branch of mathematics, with a very wide range of applications not only in other areas of mathematics but in a wide range of sciences and the real world. A few of these applications are explored later in this chapter. It might seem surprising that such a simple object has such a deep and complex theory, but one might very well say the same about the integers—they seem deceptively simple creatures, but number theory is a very major part of mathematics and has been the subject of study for thousands of years.
> 
> One question that might spring to mind is: ‘Why this collection of properties, and not any other?’ I should first say that this is not because other possibilities have been ignored; many other possible structures have been studied—some of them also have a range of applications. Examples include the following:
> 
> *   A *magma* (or *groupoid*), is a set with a binary operation defined on that set. No additional properties are assumed of the operation. So, a group can be thought of as a magma with the three additional properties listed earlier. 
> *   A *semigroup* is a set with a binary operation that is associative, i.e. a semigroup is a magma with an associative operation. 
> *   A *monoid* is a set with a binary operation that is associative, and where the set contains an identity element. So a monoid is a semigroup with an identity element, and a group is a monoid where every element has an inverse. 
> *   Finally, I should mention *abelian groups.*^() 
>     
>     The only reason I can offer as to why groups have been so extensively studied—much more than other possibilities—is because the three defining properties give just the right amount of structure to make them interesting. Too little structure, and there are simply too many possibilities, many of which may be uninteresting (in a mathematical sense); too much structure, and there are not enough examples to study.
>     
>     Whilst on the subject of the defining properties of a group, you may have noticed that I required the identity element to be simultaneously right and left identities, and I also required inverse elements to be both right and left inverses. In fact, I could have made a slightly weaker assumption. That is, I could just have assumed that there is a right identity, i.e. an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c005_dequ29.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![g asterisk operator e equals g](images/c005_dequ30.png)for every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ31.png), and also that every element has a right inverse, so that for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ32.png)there is a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![g super negative one](images/c005_dequ33.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g asterisk operator g super negative one equals e](images/c005_dequ34.png). The left identity and left inverse properties can then be shown to be true. Please see if you can show this.^()
>     
>     If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ35.png)is a group and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ36.png)then, for any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ37.png), I write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![g super n](images/c005_dequ38.png)to mean
>     
>     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><munder><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo>,</mo></math>![asterisk operator asterisk operator asterisk operator asterisk operator asterisk operator ggg midline horizontal ellipsis g bottom curly bracket separator separator n times comma](images/c005_dequ39.png)
>     
>     i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ40.png)combined with itself a total of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ41.png)times. So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![g super one equals g](images/c005_dequ42.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![g squared equals g asterisk operator g](images/c005_dequ43.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![g cubed equals g asterisk operator g asterisk operator g](images/c005_dequ44.png), and so on. Note that this is well-defined since the operation ∗ is associative. I also define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![g super zero](images/c005_dequ46.png)to be the identity element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c005_dequ47.png).
>     
>     A key property of any element of a group is its *order*. The order of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ48.png)is the *smallest* positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ49.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g super n equals e](images/c005_dequ50.png), and I write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![ord left parenthesis g right parenthesis equals n](images/c005_dequ51.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![n equals ord left parenthesis g right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ52.png), then it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g super i times n equals e](images/c005_dequ53.png)for every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c005_dequ54.png). Of course, there may not exist such an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ55.png), in which case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ56.png)has *infinite order*.
>     
>     Finally, in the remainder of this book, I will be particularly interested in *finite groups*, that is groups <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ57.png)with the property that the set of elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ58.png)is finite. The number of elements in a finite group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c005_dequ59.png)is called its *order*, and I denote it by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![ord left parenthesis script cap g right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ60.png); if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ61.png)is infinite then the group is said to have *infinite* order. You will have noticed that I am using the term ‘order’ in connection with both an element of a group and the group itself, but I hope this will not cause confusion as the meaning should be clear from the context.
>     
> 
> ## 5.2 A First Example: The Integers
> 
> I suspect I am well past the point at which I should have provided you with an example of a group, so I’ll start by giving you perhaps the most obvious example of all, the integers with the addition operation.
> 
> You may have already realised that the integers with the operation +, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ62.png), form a group. Indeed, I already pointed out in [Section 2.8](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0012) that the integers under addition satisfy the three required properties of a group, namely that they possess an identity element (0), every integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ63.png)has an inverse (namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![negative a](images/c005_dequ64.png)), and the associative law holds. The fact that this last property holds is one of the properties of the integers we simply assume as a basic building block of mathematics (as discussed in [Section 3.1](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0001)).
> 
> The group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ65.png)is actually an abelian group, since, as I’m sure you know, addition over the integers is commutative, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![a plus b equals b plus a](images/c005_dequ66.png)for any integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ67.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c005_dequ68.png). Clearly the order of this group is infinite, as there are an infinite number of integers. The order of every element apart from zero is also infinite.
> 
> But what about the integers with other operations? Well, neither subtraction nor multiplication give a group, albeit for different reasons. The integers with the operation subtraction, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma minus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ69.png), fail to form a group because subtraction is not associative. Multiplication, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ70.png), also doesn’t work because, although there is an identity element (one), and multiplication *is* associative, there isn’t an inverse element except for the elements +1 and −1.
> 
> In order to make a multiplicative group, we need to expand the integers to the rationals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c005_dequ73.png). The rationals form an abelian group with addition, and also the non-zero rationals form an abelian group with multiplication. That is both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap q comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ74.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap q super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ75.png)are abelian groups, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap q super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ76.png)denoted the non-zero rationals.
> 
> ## 5.3 A Second Example: Modular Addition
> 
> Having said that I am particularly interested in finite groups, it may seem a little odd that the first examples I gave were of infinite groups. However, the integers are undeniably important so it seemed a good place to start. Anyway, I now want to give an example of a finite group.
> 
> In [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004), I introduced <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c005_dequ77.png), the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ78.png). I suspect it comes as no surprise to learn that the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ79.png)with addition, that is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ80.png), form a group for any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than one](images/c005_dequ81.png). The identity element is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket zero right curly bracket sub n](images/c005_dequ82.png)and the inverse of any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket a right curly bracket sub n](images/c005_dequ83.png)is simply <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![left curly bracket n minus a right curly bracket sub n](images/c005_dequ84.png). The fact that the addition operation + is associative follows immediately from the fact that + is associative over the integers.
> 
> As an example, [Table 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c05-tbl-1) gives a complete table^() 
> 
> [Table 5.1](#c005.xhtml#rc05-tbl-1) Addition modulo 5.
> 
> | + || 0 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 |
> | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | 0 || 0 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 |
> | 1 || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 || 0 |
> | 2 || 2 || 3 || 4 || 0 || 1 |
> | 3 || 3 || 4 || 0 || 1 || 2 |
> | 4 || 4 || 0 || 1 || 2 || 3 |
> 
> What can we learn by looking at this table? It should be immediately clear that 0 is an identity element; you can easily check that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 zero plus a equals part 2 a plus zero equals part 3 a](images/c005_dequ90.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ91.png), since the row for 0 and the column for 0 both contain 01234 in order. You can also check there is an inverse element for every element since 0 appears in every row and every column. Finally, you can see that + is commutative, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ92.png)is an abelian group, because the table is symmetric about the leading diagonal, i.e. the diagonal running from top left to bottom right.
> 
> However, as far as I know, there is no easy way of checking whether an operation is associative, just by looking at the table.^()
> 
> A further interesting property of this group is that it is *cyclic*. A group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ97.png)is said to be cyclic if there is an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/c005_dequ98.png)such that the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket e comma g comma g squared comma g cubed comma ellipsis right curly bracket](images/c005_dequ99.png)includes every element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c005_dequ100.png)(where, as previously, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ101.png)is a non-negative integer, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![g super n](images/c005_dequ102.png)is used as shorthand for
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><munder><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo>.</mo></math>![asterisk operator asterisk operator asterisk operator asterisk operator gg midline horizontal ellipsis g bottom curly bracket separator separator n times full stop](images/c005_dequ103.png)
> 
> If a group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ104.png)is cyclic, any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ105.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![left curly bracket e comma g comma g squared comma g cubed comma ellipsis right curly bracket equals cap g](images/c005_dequ106.png)is called a *generator* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c005_dequ107.png). Note that a cyclic group is always abelian; check this out for yourself—I have provided a brief proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section (see page 229).
> 
> So, for example, in the case of the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ108.png)with addition, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ109.png), the element 1 is a generator of the group for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ110.png), since the sequence 1, 1+1, 1+1+1, … will cover every element of the group. In the case of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n equals five](images/c005_dequ111.png), it should not be hard to check that every non-zero element is a generator. Does this means that this is always true for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ112.png)? The simple answer is ‘No’, but I leave it to you to think about for which values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ113.png)it *is* true that every non-zero element is a generator of the group under addition.
> 
> In fact, the same argument shows that the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ114.png), i.e. the integers with +, is also cyclic. In this case, only +1 and −1 are generators. So there are both finite and infinite cyclic groups.
> 
> ## 5.4 But What About Modular Multiplication?
> 
> As discussed immediately above, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ117.png)is an abelian cyclic group for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than one](images/c005_dequ118.png). But what about multiplication? Firstly, I need to remove zero from consideration, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![zero multiplication a equals zero](images/c005_dequ119.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ120.png), and so there is no hope of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ121.png)being a group. Instead I consider <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ122.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ123.png)consists of all the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c005_dequ124.png)apart from zero, and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator equals n minus one](images/c005_dequ125.png).
> 
> Even with this modification, the picture is much more complicated than for addition, and the situation depends on the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ126.png). Nonetheless, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ127.png)does possess two of the three defining properties of a group for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ128.png), namely:
> 
> *   there is an identity element, namely 1, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![a multiplication one equals a](images/c005_dequ129.png)for every non-zero element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ130.png); and
> *   multiplication is associative—this follows from the fact that integer multiplication is associative.
> 
> It is also true that multiplication in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ131.png)is commutative for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ132.png), again since integer multiplication is commutative.
> 
> The situation with regard to inverse elements is more complicated. First observe that, when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ133.png)is prime, everything is good—<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ134.png)is an abelian group. To show this, I need the following result, given as a lemma in [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004). I repeat it here for convenience.
> 
> How does this help? Well, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c005_dequ141.png)is prime, then every non-zero element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![a element of double-struck cap z](images/c005_dequ142.png)is coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ143.png).
