> 4.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1027.png)uses the value received from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1028.png)along with its stored value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c005_dequ1029.png)to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap k equals part 2 left parenthesis g super a right parenthesis super b equals part 3 g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1030.png).
> 
> That is, at the end of the process both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1031.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1032.png)have agreed on a group element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![cap k equals g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1033.png), which was never sent between them. Indeed, neither party actually chose this element.
> 
> The protocol is shown diagrammatically in [Figure 5.5](#c005.xhtml#c05-fig-5).
> 
> ![Figure 5.5 The Diffie–Hellman protocol.](images/c05f005.png)
> 
> [Figure 5.5](#c005.xhtml#rc05-fig-5) The Diffie–Hellman protocol.
> 
> The scheme is usable as long as computing an exponentiation in the group can be done efficiently. But what about security? Any party intercepting communications between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1034.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1035.png)will learn <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup></math>![g super a](images/c005_dequ1036.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![g super b](images/c005_dequ1037.png). The question is—can these two pieces of information be used to determine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1038.png)in a feasible way? Of course, if it’s possible to learn the discrete logarithm of a group element, then clearly the scheme is not secure, since it will be possible to learn <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c005_dequ1039.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup></math>![g super a](images/c005_dequ1040.png), and this can then be used to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1041.png)(from knowledge of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![g super b](images/c005_dequ1042.png)). However, we assumed that computing discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible. So the key question is: are there any other ways of determining <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1043.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup></math>![g super a](images/c005_dequ1044.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![g super b](images/c005_dequ1045.png).
> 
> The simple answer is that no-one knows. It is widely assumed that this problem, known as the *Diffie–Hellman Problem* or DHP, is about as hard as finding discrete logarithms, and for certain special cases it has been shown to be true. Using the language of computational complexity, a branch of computer science concerned with studying the difficulty of computational problems, we require that the *Computational Diffie–Hellman* (CDH) assumption holds for the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c005_dequ1046.png). The CDH assumption for a group simply asserts that determining <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></msup></math>![g super a times b](images/c005_dequ1047.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup></math>![g super a](images/c005_dequ1048.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![g super b](images/c005_dequ1049.png)is computationally difficult.
> 
> At this point, although not strictly relevant, I feel I must mention that the Diffie–Hellman key agreement scheme in some ways resembles an old idea for sending secret data between two parties that relies on padlocks. The idea goes as follows. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1050.png)wants to send <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1051.png)a secret message. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1052.png)writes it down and inserts it into an (impregnable) briefcase which is then secured using a padlock to which only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1053.png)has the key. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1054.png)sends the briefcase to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1055.png). <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1056.png)now adds a second padlock to which only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1057.png)has the key and sends it back to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1058.png). On receipt <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1059.png)removes their padlock and sends the case back to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1060.png). Finally, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1061.png)can remove their padlock, open the briefcase and read the message. At no time is the briefcase sent between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1062.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1063.png)without at least one padlock attached. This is a very neat idea—sadly I have no idea where it originated. It’s not terribly practical as I don’t believe anyone has yet invented an impregnable briefcase. Additionally, the scheme suffers from the same authentication problem as Diffie–Hellman, something we discuss below.
> 
> Anyway, back to the main topic. So what group might we use to implement Diffie–Hellman? In practice we need to choose both the nature of the group and the size of the group (typically, the larger the group, the harder the computational problem becomes).
> 
> For many years the group of choice was a subgroup of the multiplicative group of the integers modulo a large prime number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ1064.png), i.e. a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1065.png), discussed in [Section 5.4](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0004). Indeed, [Theorem 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0007) given there states that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1066.png)is cyclic, so we could, in principle, choose a generator of this group. However, there are good security reasons for wanting the cyclic group we use for Diffie–Hellman to have prime order, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1067.png)has order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p minus one](images/c005_dequ1068.png), which must be even and hence cannot be prime. So instead it is common practice to use a cyclic subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1069.png)with order a prime factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p minus one](images/c005_dequ1070.png).
> 
> One way of achieving this is to choose the prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ1071.png)to have the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p equals two times q plus one](images/c005_dequ1072.png)for another prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1073.png). Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1074.png)will have order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></math>![two times q](images/c005_dequ1075.png). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1076.png)is a divisor of the order of the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1077.png), by Cauchy’s theorem ([Theorem 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0014)) the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1078.png)contains an element of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1079.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ1080.png)say, and hence there is a cyclic subgroup of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1081.png). It has long been common practice to implement Diffie–Hellman schemes using a generator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ1082.png)of this form, i.e. within a subgroup of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1083.png)within the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two times q plus one super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1084.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two times q plus one](images/c005_dequ1085.png)is prime.
> 
> At this point I suspect a small worked example might help. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></math>![p equals 23](images/c005_dequ1086.png)(a prime), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>23</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![23 equals two multiplication 11 plus one](images/c005_dequ1087.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![q equals 11](images/c005_dequ1088.png)is also prime. We need to find an element of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>![q equals 11](images/c005_dequ1089.png)in the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub 23 super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1090.png). For the purposes of this example I will choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![g equals three](images/c005_dequ1091.png), which has order 11 in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub 23 super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1092.png)(you can check that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>11</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>177147</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![multirelation three super 11 equals 177147 identical to one](images/c005_dequ1093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times 23 right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1094.png)). We suppose that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1095.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1096.png)have previously agreed on the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ1097.png)and the generator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c005_dequ1098.png)—in practice these could be agreed amongst a large group of users, albeit the real life values would be very much larger than those in this toy example.
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1099.png)must now choose a random <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![a element of double-struck cap z sub 23 super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ1100.png). Suppose, to make life simple for this example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1101.png)chooses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![a equals two](images/c005_dequ1102.png). <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1103.png)now computes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 g super a equals part 2 three squared equals part 3 nine](images/c005_dequ1104.png), and sends it to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1105.png). Meanwhile <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1106.png)needs to choose a random <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>23</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![b element of double-struck cap z sub 23 super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ1107.png). Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1108.png)chooses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![b equals five](images/c005_dequ1109.png), computes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>243</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>13</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![multirelation g super b equals three super five equals 243 identical to 13 times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times 23 right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1110.png), and sends 13 to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1111.png).
> 
> To discover the shared secret key, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1112.png)uses the value 13 received from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1113.png)together with the secret value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis a equals two right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0031.png)to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>13</mn><mi>a</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>13</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>169</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>8</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![multirelation 13 super a equals 13 squared equals 169 identical to eight times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times 23 right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1115.png). Meanwhile <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1116.png)uses its secret value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis b equals five right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0032.png)along with the value 9 received from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1118.png)to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>9</mn><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>9</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>59049</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>8</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mn>23</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![multirelation nine super b equals nine super five equals 59049 identical to eight times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times 23 right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1119.png). That is, both parties can recover the shared secret as the value 8.
> 
> Of course, when using the scheme ‘for real’ we need to ensure that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ1120.png)(and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1121.png)) are large enough to ensure that the CDH assumption holds for the group generated by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c005_dequ1122.png). As briefly mentioned above, in practice this means choosing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c005_dequ1123.png)to be of the order of 1000 decimal digits long. Interestingly the recommended parameter sizes to ensure that the CDH assumption holds in the multiplicative group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator](images/c005_dequ1124.png)are the same as the recommended parameter sizes for RSA. Indeed, there are interesting relationships between the integer factorisation problem and finding discrete logarithms in the multiplicative group of integers.^()
> 
> Over the last 10–15 years, a major trend has been to switch to a completely different representation of a finite cyclic group in which the discrete logarithm problem is believed to be much more complex for a given size of group. This has the great attraction of enabling computations to be made simpler since the values in the computations are much smaller. The group in question consists of the points on an elliptic curve computed over a finite field. An elliptic curve in this context simply means the set of solutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1125.png)to an equation of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![y squared equals f of x](images/c005_dequ1126.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c005_dequ1127.png)is a cubic polynomial of a special type.
> 
> Since I have not yet defined what a field is, let alone a finite field, nor have I discussed polynomials, I will revisit these groups in [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008), after introducing fields in the next chapter.
> 
> Before moving on to look at other applications of discrete logarithms I need to mention one fundamental shortcoming of Diffie–Hellman key exchange—namely that is not *authenticated*. That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1128.png)does not have a means of determining whether the received value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![g super b](images/c005_dequ1129.png)really comes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1130.png), and similarly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1131.png)does not know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi></msup></math>![g super a](images/c005_dequ1132.png)really comes from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1133.png). As a result, although two parties agree on a secret key which is unavailable to any other party, neither <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1134.png)nor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1135.png)know who they have actually agreed a key with.
> 
> In practice this problem is solved by using another security scheme to protect the integrity and guarantee the origin of the messages exchanged. One possibility is for the two parties to create digital signatures on the exchanges of the Diffie–Hellman protocols, thereby enabling <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c005_dequ1136.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c005_dequ1137.png)to know who they are establishing a key with. However, this is getting into a level of detail beyond the scope of this book.
> 
> ## 5.12 Other Applications of Discrete Logarithms
> 
> The Diffie–Hellman protocol is by no means the only cryptographic scheme built on the Discrete Logarithm Problem. In 1985, the Egyptian cryptographer Taher Elgamal proposed two public key cryptographic schemes whose security rests on the discrete logarithm problem—a digital signature scheme and an encryption scheme.^()
> 
> Elgamal signatures have been very widely adopted. Of particular importance is a variant known as DSA (for *Digital Signature Algorithm*), which was adopted as a US Federal Standard in 1994.^()
> 
> However, the current version of the standard does not support the originally standardised scheme, and instead has adopted a closely related scheme known as EC-DSA (for *Elliptic Curve DSA*) in which the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c005_dequ1141.png)is replaced by a group of points on an elliptic curve (see [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008)).
> 
> ## 5.13 The Threat Posed by Quantum Computing
> 
> Over the last few years the impact of quantum computing on today’s cryptography has been widely discussed. Whilst there is still no general agreement that large-scale, general purpose, quantum computers will ever be built, huge efforts continue on developing them, and step by step progress is being made. Should such computers ever become available, the impact on the security of many of today’s cryptographic systems is considerable. In particular, a quantum algorithm, i.e. an algorithm which will run on a quantum computer, has been devised which seriously affects all of the public key cryptographic algorithms in wide use today, and in particular RSA and all schemes whose security is based on the difficulty of computing discrete logarithms.
> 
> This algorithm, devised by American mathematician Peter Shor and now known as Shor’s algorithm, was published in 1994. A key impact of this development is that, if a quantum computer becomes available capable of running this algorithm for appropriate parameter sizes, all public key cryptographic algorithms based on the difficulty of factoring large integers or computing discrete logarithms will be rendered insecure for currently used key lengths. Moreover, the (large) increase in key length needed to make currently used schemes secure would be so great as to render use of the algorithms infeasible in most cases.
> 
> Most commentators seem to agree that we are at least ten years away from the ‘quantum apocalypse’, when currently-used public key cryptography becomes vulnerable to attacks using quantum computers. However, the possibility means we need to think about the potential impact of cryptographic algorithms in current use being rendered insecure at some time in the future. For algorithms solely used for verifying the integrity of transmitted data, i.e. whose use has no long-term impact, there will no significant problems, as long as new ‘secure’ algorithms are introduced in time. However, the significance for encryption and key establishment algorithms in use today, years before this mooted apocalypse, is potentially catastrophic. Why is this?
> 
> Well, if ciphertext that is encrypted using an algorithm that becomes insecure at some future time is intercepted and stored, then it could be decrypted at the future point in time when the encryption algorithm is broken. That is, data whose secrecy has any kind of long-term significance is being made vulnerable right now through the use of algorithms which will become insecure if quantum computers are built.
> 
> Similarly, suppose a key establishment technique is employed which could be broken at some future time using data exchanged via an insecure link. If the key establishment exchanges are recorded, then any sensitive data encrypted generated using a key established using such a technique would be at risk of compromise as and when a quantum computer becomes available.
> 
> Given the potentially devastating consequences for the security of today’s cryptography, a number of agencies have been working for some years on developing new cryptography standards. The situation is very serious for public key cryptography, given that almost all current applications use algorithms which will become insecure. This has led to a number of standards organisations (including the US Federal Standards body the National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST), the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in partnership with the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), to work on developing a suite of asymmetric cryptographic algorithms which will remain secure in a future ‘post-quantum’ world.
> 
> At the time of writing, NIST has recently published three standards^()
> 
> That is not to say that abstract algebra will stop being relevant to cryptography! The replacement schemes use a variety of mathematical structures, some of which we touch on in [Chapters 8](#c008.xhtml#c008) and [9](#c009.xhtml#c009). The future of public key cryptography is still working itself out, although now that standards for replacement schemes are beginning to appear, at least from the US, the picture is starting to become clearer.
> 
> ## 5.14 Other Applications of Groups
> 
> The main focus of this book is on applications of abstract algebra in the field of computing and digital communications, and in particular on cryptography. However, there are many other applications of groups in a wide range of domains. I will briefly mention a few.
> 
> One area in which groups play an important role is that of *crystallography*. According to *Brittanica,*^()
> 
> One important aspect of this work is looking for, and working with, symmetries of the objects under study. The set of symmetries of any crystal or molecule will form a group, and understanding of this group enables us to learn more about the structure of the object. Indeed, if two objects have different symmetry groups then we immediately know that their internal structure is different. However, there is much more to it than this.
> 
> Another area where groups play a vital role is in quantum mechanics.^()
> 
> > During the earliest days of quantum mechanics, the mathematician Hermann Weyl quickly recognized that the mathematical structures being used were ones he was quite familiar with from his work in the field of representation theory.^()
> > 
> > I won’t even attempt to try to explain how group theory is actually used in quantum mechanics since, sadly, Richard Feynman’s quote applies to me.
> > 
> > This is by no means the end of the real world importance of groups. I should also add that groups crop up in many other areas of mathematics, making them an absolutely fundamental part of modern mathematical research. One obvious important application within mathematics is through automorphism groups. Although I only defined the notion of an automorphism for a group, an analogous notion can be defined for almost any conceivable mathematical structure, and the set of automorphisms of a structure will form a group. Studying these groups will not only reveal insights into the object having the group of automorphisms, but may also reveal interesting insights into group theory itself.
>

> 15.  [15](#c005.xhtml#rfn_15) These documents are called FIPS 203, FIPS 204 and FIPS 205, where FIPS is short for *Federal Information Processing Standard*. FIPS 203 contains an encryption method, more specifically a Key Encapsulation Method (KEM), and FIPS 204 and 205 standardise two quite different schemes for digital signatures. All three documents are available for free download at `https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/fips`.
> 16.  [16](#c005.xhtml#rfn_16) `https://www.britannica.com`.
> 17.  [17](#c005.xhtml#rfn_17) See, for example, the monograph by P Woit, ‘Quantum Theory, Groups and Representations: An Introduction’. Available from Peter Woit’s web page at `https://www.math.columbia.edu/∼woit/`.
> 18.  [18](#c005.xhtml#rfn_18) Hermann Weyl’s ‘The theory of groups and quantum mechanics’, which first put forward the links, was published in 1929.
>
