# Chapter 6  
Rings and Fields

> My methods are really methods of working and thinking; this is why they have crept in everywhere anonymously.^()
> 
> ## 6.1 Two Operations, Not Just One!
> 
> Having introduced groups in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005), I now want to describe a range of slightly more complex mathematical structures that build on the notion of a group. In particular, I will define what I mean by a ring and a field. I have to confess that this chapter is a little heavy on mathematical abstractions, and so I have tried to break up the formal expositions with examples. After all, it is hard to see the point of defining mathematical structures and proving theorems about them, if there are no known examples of these structures. It’s a bit like writing scientific volumes on the mating habits of unicorns, when there are actually no such things as unicorns.^()
> 
> The key property possessed by all the structures introduced in this chapter is that they involve two operations and not just one. Recall that a group is a set with a single operation defined on it. Here we are interested in structures which involve a set with two operations defined on it. More than this, we require the two operations to interact in a defined way.
> 
> Of course, I’m sure you can think of examples of sets with two defined operations, including the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ1.png), the rationals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c006_dequ2.png), the real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![double-struck cap r](images/c006_dequ3.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ4.png), the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ5.png). I will mention all of these examples at various points in this chapter, as they are all examples of the mathematical structures I am interested in.
> 
> Before going any further I want to explain the notation I will use for the pair of operations within the structures covered here. Throughout this chapter I will use the same two symbols for the two operations defined on a structure, namely + and × (sometimes referred to as addition and multiplication, respectively). An operation defined on a set can, of course, be represented by any symbol, but we already use these two symbols for operations in very familiar contexts, including the integers, rationals and reals. Whilst I am concerned here with structures other  than the more familiar ones, in all cases the two operations will have properties analogous to the properties we expect of the more familiar uses of these symbols.
> 
> Again in line with familiar examples, I will also use the symbol 0 for the identity element for the + operation, and if the identity element for the × operation exists, I will denote it by the symbol 1. The inverse of an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ9.png)under the + operation will always be written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![negative a](images/c006_dequ10.png), and the inverse of an element under the × operation will be written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![a super negative one](images/c006_dequ12.png)(if it exists). I will use two pieces of shorthand for an operation repeated multiple times on the same element:
> 
> *   I will write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi></math>![n times g](images/c006_dequ13.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c006_dequ14.png)added to itself <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ15.png)times, i.e.
>     
>     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><munder><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo>,</mo></math>![n times g equals plus plus plus plus gg midline horizontal ellipsis g bottom curly bracket separator separator n times comma](images/c006_dequ16.png)
>     
>     and
>     
> *   analogously, I will put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![g super n](images/c006_dequ17.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c006_dequ18.png)multiplied by itself <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ19.png)times, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><munder><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo>.</mo></math>![g super n equals multiplication multiplication multiplication multiplication gg midline horizontal ellipsis g bottom curly bracket separator separator n times full stop](images/c006_dequ20.png)
> 
> Finally, as is common practice, I will usually write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![a dot operator b](images/c006_dequ21.png)or even <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></math>![a times b](images/c006_dequ22.png)instead of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![a multiplication b](images/c006_dequ23.png).
> 
> ## 6.2 So What Is a Ring?
> 
> The simplest structure I will define is called a *ring*. Informally, a ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ24.png)is a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ25.png)with two operations + and × defined on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ28.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap r comma plus right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ29.png)is an abelian group, × is associative on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ31.png), and + and × obey the distributive law. This latter requirement governs how the two operations interact.
> 
> The roots of the theory of rings go back at least to the 19th century, where the work of Richard Dedekind and Leopold Kronecker can be seen as laying some of the foundations for the theory. Rings were only formally defined in the 1920s by Emmy Noether and Wolfgang Krull.
> 
> Some authors require a ring to possess an identity element 1 for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap r super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ34.png), where here, as throughout, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![cap r super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ35.png)denotes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ36.png)with zero omitted. However, for the purposes of this book I don’t make this requirement. Authors requiring a ring to contain a multiplicative identity would use the term ‘rng’ to describe what I call a ring (where, of course, ‘rng’ is ‘ring’ with the 1 removed).
> 
> More formally, a ring can be defined as follows. The triple <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ37.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ38.png)is a non-empty set, and + and × are operations defined on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ41.png), is said to be a ring if:
> 
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap r comma plus right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ42.png)is an abelian group;
> *   × is an associative operation on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ44.png);
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![a multiplication left parenthesis b plus c right parenthesis equals a multiplication b plus a multiplication c](images/c006_dequ45.png)for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![a comma b comma c element of cap r](images/c006_dequ46.png)(the *left distributive law*).
> *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![left parenthesis a plus b right parenthesis multiplication c equals a multiplication c plus b multiplication c](images/c006_dequ47.png)for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![a comma b comma c element of cap r](images/c006_dequ48.png)(the *right distributive law*).
> 
> The left and right distributive laws are referred to jointly as just the *distributive law*.
> 
> A motivating example is provided by the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ49.png)where, as I discussed previously, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ50.png)is an abelian group, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#215;</mo></math>![multiplication](images/c006_dequ51.png)is associative on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ52.png), and the distributive law holds for multiplication over addition. Another obvious example is provided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ53.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ54.png). For those of you familiar with matrices, the set of 2 by 2 matrices with real elements along with the usual addition and multiplication operations for matrices form a ring.
> 
> Some basic properties of rings are captured in the following trivial lemma. The lemma describes two important ways in which the two operations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo></math>![plus](images/c006_dequ57.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c006_dequ58.png)interact.
> 
> These results are so basic that I will use them without always referring back to this lemma. Finally, I need to introduce a very basic piece of terminology. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ87.png)is a ring, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ88.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ89.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c006_dequ90.png)are elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ91.png); then if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![a dot operator b equals c](images/c006_dequ92.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ93.png)is called a *divisor* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c006_dequ94.png). This clearly generalises the notion of a divisor for the integers, as introduced in [Section 3.7](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0010)—I use the term ‘generalises’ since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ95.png)is a ring, and so any definition applying to elements of a ring also applies to integers. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ96.png)is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c006_dequ97.png)then, just like for the integers, I will equivalently say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ98.png)divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c006_dequ99.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c006_dequ100.png)is a multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ101.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![a bar c](images/c006_dequ102.png).
> 
> There are many other examples of rings, including many not related to the integers, and rings play a very important role in various branches of mathematics.
> 
> ## 6.3 Types of Rings
> 
> There are a range of *types* of ring, i.e. rings with various additional properties. The algebraic structures I will examine in the remainder of this book, in particular the polynomials rings and the fields, are special types of ring. It is therefore important to review some of the key examples of types of ring, along with some of their most important properties.
> 
> *   A *ring with one* is simply a ring which possesses an identity element 1 for the multiplication operation (which must be both a right and a left identity), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![equation sequence part 1 a dot operator one equals part 2 one dot operator a equals part 3 a](images/c006_dequ103.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![a element of cap r](images/c006_dequ104.png). As I noted above, many authors would call a ring with one simply a ring. To avoid the trivial case where the ring contains just one element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![zero equals one](images/c006_dequ105.png), as is common practice I require that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![zero not equals one](images/c006_dequ106.png), and hence a ring with one contains at least two elements.^()
>     
>     If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ107.png)is a ring with one, then some of the elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![cap r super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ108.png)(where, as always, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![cap r super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ109.png)denotes the set of non-zero elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ110.png)) may have a multiplicative inverse. That is, for some elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo></math>![a element of cap r super asterisk operator comma](images/c006_dequ111.png)there exists an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![a super negative one element of cap r super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ112.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a dot operator a super negative one equals part 2 a super negative one dot operator a equals part 3 one](images/c006_dequ113.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ114.png)is such an element then it is known as a *unit*. Every ring with one will have at least one unit, namely 1 itself, which helps to explain the term unit. Another way of thinking about units is that an element is a unit if and only if it is a divisor of 1.
>     
>     As above, both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ115.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ116.png)(for any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ117.png)) are rings with one. But which elements of these rings are units? In the case of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ118.png), only <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![prefix plus of one](images/c006_dequ119.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![negative one](images/c006_dequ120.png)are units, the latter being a unit since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![left parenthesis negative one right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis negative one right parenthesis equals one](images/c006_dequ121.png). The situation for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ122.png)is a little more complicated. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ123.png)is prime then every element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ124.png)is a unit—this follows from [Lemma 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0014) stated in [Section 4.6](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0013). However, more generally, again from [Lemma 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0014), an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![a element of double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ125.png)is a unit if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis a comma n right parenthesis equals one](images/c006_dequ126.png), and as discussed in [Section 5.4](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0004), the set of units in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub n super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ127.png)form a group under multiplication called the reduced residue system. In fact, the collection of units form a multiplicative group in any ring with one, so, in particular, the product of two units is always a unit.
>     
> *   *Commutative rings* as their name suggests, are rings for which the multiplication operation is commutative. A commutative ring need not be a ring with one, and a ring with one need not be commutative. As I’m sure you will have observed, both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ128.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ129.png)are commutative rings with one. However, the ring of two by two matrices with real number entries has a one (namely the matrix with ones in the diagonal and zeros off the diagonal) but is not commutative. From here on I will mainly be discussing commutative rings with one.
> *   Finally, before defining a special type of ring known as an *integral domain*, I need to explain the notion of a zero divisor. A zero divisor in a ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ130.png)is an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![a element of cap r](images/c006_dequ131.png)for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a dot operator b equals zero](images/c006_dequ132.png)for some non-zero element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![b element of cap r super asterisk operator](images/c006_dequ133.png); i.e. as you might expect, it is an element which is a divisor of zero.
>     
>     Clearly, zero itself is a zero divisor in any ring. Other examples arise in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ134.png)if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ135.png)is not a prime. So, for example, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![n equals six](images/c006_dequ136.png), then, as is evident from [Table 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c05-tbl-3) in [Section 5.4](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0004), the values 2, 3 and 4 are all zero divisors. More generally, it holds that any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ137.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ138.png)that is not coprime to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ139.png), i.e. for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![gcd left parenthesis a comma n right parenthesis not equals one](images/c006_dequ140.png), is a zero divisor. That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ141.png)will possess non-zero zero divisors if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ142.png)is not a prime.
>     
>     Having explained what a zero divisor is, I can now give the definition: an *integral domain* is a commutative ring with one having no non-zero zero divisors. Interestingly, many key properties of the integers also hold for any integral domain, as we explore later in this chapter.
>     
>     So, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ143.png)contains non-zero zero divisors if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c006_dequ144.png)is not a prime, in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c006_dequ145.png)is a commutative ring with one, but is not an integral domain. However, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub p](images/c006_dequ146.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c006_dequ147.png)prime is an integral domain, as of course are the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c006_dequ148.png).
>     
> 
> There are many other special types of ring, but these are some of the most important. How some of the most significant types of rings relate to each other are shown in Venn Diagram form in [Figure 6.1](#c006.xhtml#c06-fig-1).
> 
> ![Figure 6.1 Key types of ring.](images/c06f001.png)
> 
> [Figure 6.1](#c006.xhtml#rc06-fig-1) Key types of ring.
> 
> ## 6.4 Combining Rings
> 
> Just as I showed in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005) for groups (in [Section 5.9](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0020)), it is possible to combine two rings to make a larger ring. Again, just as was the case for groups, I use the cartesian product of sets (see [Section 2.3](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0004)) to combine the sets of elements from the two rings.
> 
> Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ149.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap s equals left parenthesis cap s comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ150.png)are rings.^()
> 
> Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![r comma r super prime element of cap r](images/c006_dequ157.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![s comma s super prime element of cap s](images/c006_dequ158.png). Then let
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma s right parenthesis plus left parenthesis r super prime comma s super prime right parenthesis equals left parenthesis r plus r super prime comma s plus s super prime right parenthesis comma](images/c006_dequ159.png)
> 
> and similarly let
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma s right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis r super prime comma s super prime right parenthesis equals left parenthesis r dot operator r super prime comma s dot operator s super prime right parenthesis full stop](images/c006_dequ160.png)
> 
> That is, we simply combine the first elements from the two pairs using the appropriate ring operation for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ161.png), and the second elements from the pairs using the ring operation for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c006_dequ162.png). I need to establish that the operations are defined properly on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![cap r multiplication cap s](images/c006_dequ163.png), i.e. that for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![r comma r super prime element of cap r](images/c006_dequ164.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![s comma s super prime element of cap s](images/c006_dequ165.png), their combinations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma s right parenthesis plus left parenthesis r super prime comma s super prime right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ166.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma s right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis r super prime comma s super prime right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ167.png)are elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![cap r multiplication cap s](images/c006_dequ168.png). However, this follows immediately from the definitions since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![r plus r super prime element of cap r](images/c006_dequ169.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![r dot operator r super prime element of cap r](images/c006_dequ170.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![s plus s super prime element of cap s](images/c006_dequ171.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![s dot operator s super prime element of cap s](images/c006_dequ172.png).
> 
> The + operation forms a group on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![cap r multiplication cap s](images/c006_dequ173.png)with identity element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma zero right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ174.png)using precisely the same argument as employed in [Section 5.9](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0020). Finally, the distributive law holds trivially because it holds in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ175.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap s](images/c006_dequ176.png). Hence, the direct product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ177.png)is a ring.
> 
> Moreover, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ178.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap s](images/c006_dequ179.png)are commutative rings, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ180.png)is also commutative. Finally, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ181.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap s](images/c006_dequ182.png)are rings with one, then so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ183.png). However, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ184.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap s](images/c006_dequ185.png)are integral domains, then (apart from a trivial case) it is *not* true that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ186.png)is an integral domain.
> 
> This important point holds because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ187.png)will always contain non-zero zero divisors. That is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![r element of cap r](images/c006_dequ188.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>S</mi></math>![s element of cap s](images/c006_dequ189.png)are both non-zero, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma zero right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ190.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma s right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ191.png)are non-zero elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ192.png). However,
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis r comma zero right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis zero comma s right parenthesis equals part 2 left parenthesis r dot operator zero comma zero dot operator s right parenthesis equals part 3 left parenthesis zero comma zero right parenthesis full stop](images/c006_dequ193.png)
> 
> That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis r comma zero right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ194.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma s right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ195.png)are both non-zero zero divisors, and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></math>![script cap r multiplication script cap s](images/c006_dequ196.png)is not an integral domain.
> 
> To take a specific example, let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ197.png)(the ring of integers modulo 2) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap s equals left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub three comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ198.png)(the ring of integers modulo 3). Both of these rings are actually integral domains since 2 and 3 are prime. The Cayley Table for multiplication is given in [Table 6.1](#c006.xhtml#c06-tbl-1); as in previous Cayley Tables for multiplication, I have left out the row and column for the additive identity (i.e. in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma zero right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ199.png)), as it is not very interesting.

> ## 6.5 Integral Domains—Some Key Properties
> 
> In this rather abstract section I state and prove some key properties of integral domains. Whilst you may want to skip the proofs, I would encourage you to at least briefly look at the results I give, as they are important for ideas I develop later. These results trivially hold for the integers, and highlight how an integral domain has many of the properties of the integers.
> 
> I first need to give the following important result.
> 
> I could equally have defined an integral domain to be a commutative ring with one in which the cancellation law holds. That is, if the cancellation law holds then it can be shown that there are no non-zero zero divisors. I leave the proof as a small exercise for you. I provide a proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section (see page 235).
> 
> If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ221.png)divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ222.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ223.png)divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ224.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ225.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ226.png)are said to be *associates*. The following simple result characterises what it means for two elements to be associates.
> 
> However, integral domains do not possess all the properties that we take for granted in the integers. In particular, the ring-based analogue of the unique factorisation theorem does not necessarily hold. Nonetheless, we can get close. We need the following two definitions.
> 
> An *irreducible element* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c006_dequ260.png)of an integral domain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ261.png)is a non-unit with the property that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![p equals a dot operator b](images/c006_dequ262.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>R</mi></math>![a comma b element of cap r](images/c006_dequ263.png)then either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ264.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ265.png)is a unit. Note that exactly one of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ266.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ267.png)is a unit, since if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c006_dequ268.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c006_dequ269.png)are both units then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi></math>![a dot operator b equals p](images/c006_dequ270.png)must be a unit.
> 
> In an integral domain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ271.png), a non-unit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c006_dequ272.png)is said to be *prime* if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p bar left parenthesis a dot operator b right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ273.png)implies that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![p bar a](images/c006_dequ274.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![p bar b](images/c006_dequ275.png). This is, of course, a property that we know holds for integer primes ([Lemma 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0013)).
> 
> However, the converse does not necessarily hold. That is, there may be irreducible elements that are not prime. As a result, the unique factorisation property—i.e. that every element can be expressed uniquely as a product of irreducible elements (ignoring units)—does not necessarily hold in an integral domain.
> 
> There are no really simple examples of integral domains for which unique factorisation does not hold, at least as far as I am aware. That is, most examples in the textbooks involve a lot of mathematics I have not introduced here. The simplest example I can find is as follows.^()
> 
> Define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ299.png)to be the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c006_dequ300.png), where
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>:</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap r equals left curly bracket a plus b times Square root of five colon a comma b element of double-struck cap z right curly bracket](images/c006_dequ301.png)
> 
> and where addition and multiplication are the natural extension of integer addition and multiplication, i.e.
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>,</mo></math>![left parenthesis a plus b times Square root of five right parenthesis plus left parenthesis c plus d times Square root of five right parenthesis equals left parenthesis a plus c right parenthesis plus left parenthesis b plus d right parenthesis times Square root of five comma](images/c006_dequ302.png)
> 
> and
> 
> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>b</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis a plus b times Square root of five right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis c plus d times Square root of five right parenthesis equals left parenthesis a times c plus five times b times d right parenthesis plus left parenthesis b plus d right parenthesis times Square root of five full stop](images/c006_dequ303.png)
>

> It should be clear that addition and multiplication of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ310.png)always give an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c006_dequ311.png); 0 and 1 are additive and multiplicative identities; addition and multiplication is commutative; and every element has an additive inverse (the additive inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![a plus b times Square root of five](images/c006_dequ312.png)is simply <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi><msqrt><mrow><mn>5</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![negative a minus b times Square root of five](images/c006_dequ313.png)). So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c006_dequ314.png)is a commutative ring with one. Finally, to show it is an integral domain we need to show that there are no non-zero zero divisors. The usual argument says that this domain is simply a subring of the real numbers, and the reals have no non-zero divisors since they form a field,^()

Moreover, no two of them are associates of each other, i.e. none of these four values is equal to a unit times another of these values.^()
