> # Chapter 7  
> Polynomials and Polynomial Rings
> 
> > I, who do not profess to be a mathematician, but who, whenever there is leisure, delight in mathematical studies . . . .^()
> > 
> > ## 7.1 What Do I Mean by Polynomials?
> > 
> > I now want to introduce something you may already feel you are familiar with, namely *polynomials*. However, I will define and use them in a way that may not be so familiar.
> > 
> > The underlying idea here is to treat mathematical expressions, e.g. ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![three times x plus four](images/c007_dequ1.png)’ or ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 4 summands x cubed plus x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ2.png)’ as mathematical objects in themselves. I am interested here in expressions involving a single *unknown* or *indeterminate*, which I label <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ3.png). I suspect you are more used to handling these expressions as part of an equation, e.g. ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![three times x plus four equals seven](images/c007_dequ4.png)’ or ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x cubed plus x squared minus x minus one equals zero](images/c007_dequ5.png)’, which you are invited to solve. Assuming that arithmetic is done in the integers, in the former case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x equals one](images/c007_dequ6.png)is the unique solution, and in the latter case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x equals negative one](images/c007_dequ7.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x equals prefix plus of one](images/c007_dequ8.png)are two possible solutions. However, I am not interested here in polynomial equations, just the expressions involving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ9.png). I will treat these expressions as elements in an algebraic structure, and look at how expressions can be combined. That is, the expressions themselves are a kind of number, and it turns out they have many of the properties we expect from more ‘regular’ numbers, such as the integers.
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ10.png)is an expression involving elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ11.png), a commutative ring with one, and a single indeterminate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ12.png)(and possibly arbitrary powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ13.png)), then we call <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ14.png)a *polynomial in* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ15.png), and we refer to the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c007_dequ16.png)multiplying powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ17.png)in the polynomial as *coefficients*.
> > 
> > So, for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands three times x super four plus five times x squared plus seven](images/c007_dequ18.png)is a polynomial over the integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c007_dequ19.png), and the values 3, 5 and 7 are the coefficients of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>![x super four](images/c007_dequ20.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![x squared](images/c007_dequ21.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![x super zero](images/c007_dequ22.png)respectively. The zero polynomial is simply the ring element 0, i.e. the additive identity in the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ23.png).
> > 
> > In general, a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ24.png)will look like
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></math>![p of x equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero plus p sub one times x plus p sub two times x squared plus ellipsis plus p sub d times x super d](images/c007_dequ25.png)
> > 
> > where the values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![p sub zero comma p sub one comma ellipsis comma p sub d](images/c007_dequ26.png)are elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c007_dequ27.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![d greater than or equals zero](images/c007_dequ28.png). So, as well as polynomials like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![x squared plus five](images/c007_dequ29.png), individual ring elements are polynomials, i.e. the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ30.png)is contained in the set of polynomials with coefficients from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ31.png).
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ32.png)is a polynomial and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ33.png)is the largest power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ34.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ35.png)with a non-zero coefficient, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ36.png)is known as the *degree* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ37.png). Also, the term of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ38.png)involving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></math>![x super d](images/c007_dequ39.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ40.png)is the degree, is known as the *leading term* of the polynomial, and the coefficient of the leading term is known as the *leading coefficient*. So, for example, the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![six times x super five plus x super four minus seven times x squared minus four](images/c007_dequ41.png)has degree 5, the leading term is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup></math>![six times x super five](images/c007_dequ42.png), and the leading coefficient is 6; also, the polynomial 7 has degree zero (since the largest power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ43.png)appearing in the polynomial is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>![x super zero](images/c007_dequ44.png)), and the leading coefficient is 7. The polynomials with degree zero, which correspond to individual ring elements, are called *constant polynomials*; two constant polynomials of particular importance are 0 and 1 (the additive and multiplicative identities in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ45.png)).
> > 
> > Two polynomials are said to be equal if they have the same degree and their corresponding coefficients are equal. If the leading coefficient of a polynomial is equal to 1 (the multiplicative identity in the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ46.png)) then we call the polynomial *monic.*^()
> > 
> > I should at this point say that, although it is possible to define polynomials over an arbitrary number of indeterminates, we are only interested here in polynomials with a single indeterminate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ53.png)—so called *univariate* polynomials.
> > 
> > Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ54.png)is a commutative ring with one.^()
> > 
> > We put
> >

stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math>![multiline equation row 1 p of x dot operator q of x equals sum with variable number of summands left parenthesis p sub zero times q sub zero right parenthesis plus left parenthesis p sub zero times q sub one plus p sub one times q sub zero right parenthesis times x plus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands p sub zero times q sub two plus p sub one times q sub one plus p sub two times q sub zero right parenthesis times x squared plus ellipsis row 2 prefix plus of left parenthesis p sub d minus one times q sub d plus p sub d times q sub d minus one right parenthesis times x super two times d minus one plus left parenthesis p sub d times q sub d right parenthesis times x super two times d full stop](images/c007_dequ74.png)
> > 
> > That is, addition and multiplication of polynomials works in exactly the way you might expect. So, for example, if we take the two polynomials with integer coefficients: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![p of x equals three times x plus four](images/c007_dequ75.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![q of x equals sum with 4 summands x cubed plus x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ76.png), then
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 p of x plus q of x equals part 2 left parenthesis three times x plus four right parenthesis plus left parenthesis sum with 4 summands x cubed plus x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis equals part 3 sum with 4 summands x cubed plus x squared plus four times x plus five comma](images/c007_dequ77.png)
> > 
> > and
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 p of x dot operator q of x equals part 2 left parenthesis three times x plus four right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis sum with 4 summands x cubed plus x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis equals part 3 sum with 5 summands three times x super four plus seven times x cubed plus seven times x squared plus seven times x plus four full stop](images/c007_dequ78.png)
> > 
> > Now that we have defined two operations <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo></math>![plus](images/c007_dequ79.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c007_dequ80.png)on the set of polynomials, we can consider what sort of algebraic properties we get. We immediately have the following fundamental result.
> > 
> > The following lemma confirms what you expect to be true—but observe that for this to work we need to assume we are working in an integral domain and not just any commutative ring with one.
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > Observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>deg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>deg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>deg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![degree left parenthesis p of x plus q of x right parenthesis equals max of degree left parenthesis p of x right parenthesis comma degree left parenthesis q of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ144.png)unless <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ145.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ146.png)have the same degree and the leading terms of the two polynomials are additive inverses of each other. So if, for example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![p of x equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus x plus two](images/c007_dequ147.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![q of x equals negative x cubed plus two times x squared minus four](images/c007_dequ148.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![p of x plus q of x equals two times x squared plus x minus two](images/c007_dequ150.png), i.e. although <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ151.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ152.png)both have degree 3, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x plus q of x](images/c007_dequ153.png)has degree only 2.
> > 
> > We also have the following extension of [Theorem 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c007-secc-0002).
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > A similar result holds for unique factorisation domains (UFDs).
> > 
> > The proof of this result is highly non-trivial, and I include a short discussion in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section (see page 237).
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r of x equals left parenthesis cap r of x comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ180.png)is a UFD then we refer to the irreducible elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ181.png)as *irreducible polynomials*. These have properties analogous to those of the prime numbers in the integers. As we show in [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008), irreducible polynomials play a key role in building finite fields.
> > 
> > ## 7.2 Doing Arithmetic with Polynomials
> > 
> > I have already defined how addition and multiplication work for polynomials. I then showed that if the underlying ring is a commutative ring with one, then the set of polynomials with the defined addition and multiplication operations is also a commutative ring with one. Also, if the underlying ring is an integral domain, then so is the ring of polynomials.
> > 
> > In this section, I will further explore the arithmetic properties of polynomials over a ring, and in particular show how they have a key property of the integers. That is, we have an algebraic structure made up of objects very different from the whole numbers, that yet share many properties with them.
> > 
> > The main result of this section shows that when we can divide one polynomial by another we have a unique quotient and reminder, just like in the integers.
> > 
> > Before moving on I want to define an important concept for polynomials.
> > 
> > Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r of x comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ255.png)is a commutative ring, and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ256.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ257.png)be polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ258.png). Then if there is a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/c007_dequ259.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ260.png)with the property that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![p of x dot operator r of x equals q of x comma](images/c007_dequ261.png)
> > 
> > then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ262.png)is said to be a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ263.png).
> > 
> > This definition clearly corresponds directly to the notion of a divisor for integers, as introduced back in [Section 3.7](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0010). In fact, I already defined the notion of a divisor for a general ring back in [Section 6.2](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0002), and so, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap r of x](images/c007_dequ264.png)is a ring, arguably I did not need to give the definition again.
> > 
> > ## 7.3 Polynomials over a Field
> > 
> > I will next look at what happens when the coefficients for a polynomial are chosen from a field. That is, I am interested here in polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ265.png)when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c007_dequ266.png)is a field. Since a field is more ‘special’ than a commutative ring with one, notably all of its non-zero elements are units, the ring of polynomials <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ267.png)also has special properties.
> > 
> > First, observe that since a field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c007_dequ268.png)is an integral domain, as I observed at the beginning of [Section 6.8](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0013), it follows from [Corollary 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0005) that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ269.png)is an integral domain. I already defined the notion of *associates* for elements of an integral domain (see [Section 6.5](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0006)), but to make life simpler, I will repeat it here for the special case of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ270.png)for a field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap f equals left parenthesis cap f comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ271.png).
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ272.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ273.png)are polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ274.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ275.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ276.png)are associates if there exists a unit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![u of x](images/c007_dequ277.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ278.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x equals u of x dot operator q of x](images/c007_dequ279.png). So what do units in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ280.png)look like? Well, any element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup></math>![cap f super asterisk operator](images/c007_dequ281.png)is a unit (i.e. it has a multiplicative inverse), since, by definition of a field, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap f super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ282.png)is an abelian group. So the units of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ283.png)include all the elements with degree zero, i.e. the ‘constant polynomials’. I claim that no other elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ284.png)can be units, since the degree of the product of two non-zero polynomials is the sum of the degree of these polynomials (from [Lemma 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0003)), and hence no polynomial of degree greater than zero can be a unit. That is, the units in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap f of x](images/c007_dequ285.png)are precisely the elements with degree 0. That means we can rephrase the definition of associates in this special case to say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ286.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ287.png)are associates if there exists a non-zero <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>F</mi></math>![c element of cap f](images/c007_dequ288.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![c dot operator p of x equals q of x](images/c007_dequ289.png).
> > 
> > For example, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![script cap f equals double-struck cap q](images/c007_dequ290.png), the field of rationals, the following polynomials are associates:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mtext>&#8195;and&#8195;</mtext><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus one divided by two times x plus three and sum with 3 summands two times x squared plus x plus six comma](images/c007_dequ291.png)
> > 
> > since the second polynomial is twice the first. So for any polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ292.png), we can find an associate of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ293.png)with leading coefficient 1, i.e. that is monic. To see this observe that if the leading coefficient of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ294.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8467;</mi></math>![script l](images/c007_dequ295.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>&#8467;</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script l super negative one times p of x](images/c007_dequ296.png)will have leading coefficient 1.
> > 
> > Having made this observation, we can now give a simplified version of the division theorem, as it applies to polynomials over a field. The division theorem for polynomials over a commutative ring with one was given in [Theorem 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0007).
> > 
> > I defined the notion of a *greatest common divisor* for any pair of elements in a UFD back in [Section 6.6](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0010), and I also showed that every pair of elements in a UFD possesses a greatest common divisor. I also asserted (without proof) that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi></math>![cap r](images/c007_dequ327.png)is a UFD then so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ328.png)(see [Corollary 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0005)). So, since a field is trivially a UFD (there are no non-zero non-units), this means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ329.png)is a UFD for any field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c007_dequ330.png). For completeness, I give the definition of greatest common divisor for polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ331.png). A quick check should reveal it is exactly the same as the definition in [Section 6.6](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0010), except that I am dealing with polynomials rather than arbitrary elements of a UFD and I have added the requirement that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x](images/c007_dequ332.png)is monic.
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ333.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ334.png)are polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ335.png)for any field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c007_dequ336.png), then a monic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![d of x element of script cap f of x](images/c007_dequ337.png)is a greatest common divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ338.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ339.png)if
> > 
> > *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x bar p of x](images/c007_dequ340.png);
> > *   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x bar q of x](images/c007_dequ341.png); and
> > *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d super prime of x bar p of x](images/c007_dequ342.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d super prime of x bar q of x](images/c007_dequ343.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d super prime of x bar d of x](images/c007_dequ344.png).
> > 
> > Now we know that a greatest common divisor always exists since this holds for any UFD. [Lemma 6.5](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0011) says that any two greatest common divisors are associates, i.e. if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x](images/c007_dequ345.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d super prime of x](images/c007_dequ346.png)are both greatest common divisors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ347.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ348.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mover><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>&#729;</mo></mover><msup><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x equals c times d dot above prime super left parenthesis x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ349.png)for some non-zero field element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/c007_dequ350.png). But both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d of x](images/c007_dequ351.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>d</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d super prime of x](images/c007_dequ352.png)are monic, by definition, and hence the greatest common divisor of any two polynomials is unique. I will write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="normal">gcd</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![gcd of p of x comma q of x](images/c007_dequ353.png)for the unique greatest common divisor of polynomials <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ354.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ355.png). If the greatest common divisor of two polynomials is 1, then they are said to be *coprime*, just like two integers with greatest common divisor 1.
> > 
> > As an example, suppose we are working in the field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub three comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ356.png), i.e. where multiplication and addition work modulo 3. The following two polynomials are in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub three of x](images/c007_dequ357.png):
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![sum with 4 summands two times x super four plus two times x cubed plus x plus one and x cubed plus two comma](images/c007_dequ358.png)
> > 
> > but what is their greatest common divisor? It is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ359.png)since
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![sum with 4 summands two times x super four plus two times x cubed plus x plus one equals left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis two times x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ360.png)
> > 
> > and
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![x cubed plus two equals left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis x plus two right parenthesis comma](images/c007_dequ361.png)
> > 
> > and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two times x squared plus one](images/c007_dequ362.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![x plus two](images/c007_dequ363.png)are coprime.
> > 
> > So greatest common divisors exist and are unique, just as they are in the integers. But how can we find them? Well, fortunately, there are direct polynomial analogues of a number of important results for the integers, which can be used to easily find the greatest common divisor of any two polynomials.
> > 
> > I will start with a polynomial version of Bézout’s Identity (see [Lemma 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-secc-0011)).
> > 
> > The proof is essentially the same as the proof of [Lemma 3.2](#c003.xhtml#c003-secc-0011), so I won’t give it here. However, if you want to see the full proof I have given it in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ (see page 238).
> > 
> > There is also a version of the Euclidean Algorithm for polynomials over a field. As you will see if you compare it with [Algorithm 3.1](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0018), the algorithm below is identical to the integer version except that polynomials replace integers. This algorithm will compute the greatest common divisor for two polynomials. I invite you to use it to check what I claimed to be the greatest common divisor of the two polynomials:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8195;and&#8195;</mtext><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with 4 summands two times x super four plus two times x cubed plus x plus one and sum with 4 summands x cubed plus two times x squared plus two times x plus one full stop](images/c007_dequ372.png)
> > 
> > Again the proof is essentially the same as the proof for the integer version of the theorem (see [Theorem 3.4](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0019)), so I don’t give it here. As previously, if you want to see the full proof, I have given it in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ (see page 239).
> > 
> > Just as is the case for the integers, we can work backwards through the steps of the Euclidean algorithm to find solutions to Bézout’s Identity. This is known as the Extended Euclidean Algorithm.
> > 
> > ## 7.4 Shift Register Sequences
> > 
> > ### 7.4.1 What Do Shift Registers Do?
> > 
> > Polynomials have a very wide range of applications, both in other areas of mathematics and in uses of mathematics in communications and computing. The application domain I briefly introduce here, namely linear feedback shift registers (LFSRs), has links to cryptography, but also many other applications in engineering and computing.
> > 
> > However, before showing how polynomials are useful for analysing shift registers, I need to explain what a shift register is. I will explain the idea of a shift register as if it is something implemented in hardware (typically electronics), but a shift register can equally well be implemented in software.
> > 
> > The simplest example of a type of shift register is shown in [Figure 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-1). The ‘boxes’ represent *storage elements*, or *stages*, i.e. locations where a single symbol can be stored. The *state* of a shift register at any point in time is the sequence of symbols stored in the stages. For my purposes here, I am only interested in the case where the symbols are in a finite field, and of particular interest is the case where the field is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ392.png), where addition and multiplication work modulo 2, and there are only two symbols (0 and 1).
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.1 A shift register.](images/c07f001.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.1](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-1) A shift register.
> > 
> > The state of a shift register changes at regular intervals (or *time slots*), which involves the contents of a stage being moved into the stage to its left, as the arrows indicate. A new symbol is moved into the right-most stage (the *input* to the shift register) and the *output* of the register is whatever was in the leftmost stage. We number the time slots <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![t equals zero comma one comma two times ellipsis](images/c007_dequ393.png), so the *initial state* of the register is the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![t equals zero](images/c007_dequ394.png), the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t equals one](images/c007_dequ395.png)is the state for time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![t equals zero](images/c007_dequ396.png)moved left one place, and so on.
> > 
> > If you consider the register shown in [Figure 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-1), and suppose it has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ397.png)stages for some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ398.png), then the input at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ399.png)is the output at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![t plus n](images/c007_dequ400.png). Of course, whilst such shift registers may have applications in simple digital circuits, mathematically they are not very interesting.
> > 
> > A second simple type of shift register, namely a *feedback shift register*, is shown in [Figure 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-2). Here, the input is simply the same as the output. The contents of the register will simply rotate.
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.2 A feedback shift register.](images/c07f002.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.2](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-2) A feedback shift register.
> > 
> > Suppose there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ401.png)stages in the register. I label the stages <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub zero comma s sub one comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ402.png), as shown in the figure. Also, suppose that the contents of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![s sub i](images/c007_dequ403.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ404.png)is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub i of t](images/c007_dequ405.png). So at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![t equals zero](images/c007_dequ406.png), when the register is in its initial state, the contents of the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ407.png)stages of the shift register are
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub zero of zero comma s sub one of zero comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one of zero full stop](images/c007_dequ408.png)
> > 
> > So, because of the way the register shifts, we have
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mtext>&#160;and&#160;</mtext><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub zero of one equals s sub one of zero comma s sub one of one equals s sub two of zero comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus two of one equals s sub n minus one of zero and s sub n minus one of one equals s sub zero of zero full stop](images/c007_dequ409.png)
> > 
> > More generally, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub i times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals s sub i plus one of t](images/c007_dequ410.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![multirelation zero less than or equals i less than n minus one](images/c007_dequ411.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals s sub zero of t](images/c007_dequ412.png).
> > 
> > Now, since the feedback just recirculates, the state of the register at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ413.png)will be the same as the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![t plus n](images/c007_dequ414.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></math>![t plus two times n](images/c007_dequ415.png), and so on. Again, feedback registers as I’ve described them here are not very interesting mathematically, but they exhibit one important behaviour, namely *periodicity*, which is also true for the next and more important example. What do I mean by periodicity?
> > 
> > Well, the sequence output by a feedback shift register will repeat itself after <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ416.png)terms. That is, if the initial state of the register is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub zero of zero comma s sub one of zero comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one of zero](images/c007_dequ417.png), then the sequence output by the register will be
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub zero of zero comma s sub one of zero comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one of zero comma s sub zero of zero comma s sub one of zero comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one of zero comma s sub zero of zero comma s sub one of zero comma ellipsis full stop](images/c007_dequ418.png)
> > 
> > This is an example of a *periodic* sequence. More generally, a sequence
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![x sub zero comma x sub one comma x sub two comma ellipsis](images/c007_dequ419.png)
> > 
> > is said to be periodic if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub></math>![x sub i equals x sub i plus p](images/c007_dequ420.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![p greater than zero](images/c007_dequ421.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![i greater than or equals zero](images/c007_dequ422.png). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c007_dequ423.png)is the smallest positive integer for which the sequence has this property, then the sequence is said to have *period* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c007_dequ424.png). So, for example, the all-one sequence has period one, and the sequence 010101… has period two. I will refer to *a period* of such a sequence as being <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c007_dequ426.png)consecutive symbols, so a period of the sequence 010101… is simply \[01\].
> > 
> > So, going back to the feedback shift register case, what is the period of the sequence it outputs? It could be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ429.png), but it might be less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ430.png). If, for example, the initial state is all ones, then the sequence output will be 1111…, i.e. a sequence with period one. The only thing we can say for certain is that the period will be a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ432.png)—what the precise period is will depend on the initial state of the shift register.
> > 
> > ### 7.4.2 Linear Feedback Shift Registers
> > 
> > The next diagram, [Figure 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-3), shows the type of shift register I am particularly interested in here, namely the *linear feedback shift register*, or simply an LFSR.
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.3 A linear feedback shift register with bold-italic n stages.](images/c07f003.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.3](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-3) A linear feedback shift register with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic n](images/c007_dequ433.png)stages.
> > 
> > In this diagram, between every pair of stages there is a *tap*, with the output of the tap being added to the outputs of the other taps, after multiplication by a fixed value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/c007_dequ434.png)(which must be in the finite field). This means that the value fed back into stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ435.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ436.png)is equal to:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator s sub zero of t plus a sub one dot operator s sub one of t plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one dot operator s sub n minus one of t comma](images/c007_dequ437.png)
> > 
> > where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub zero of t comma s sub one of t comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one of t](images/c007_dequ438.png)represents the current state of the shift register. That is, the contents of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ439.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t plus one](images/c007_dequ440.png)is defined by:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator s sub zero of t plus a sub one dot operator s sub one of t plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one dot operator s sub n minus one of t full stop](images/c007_dequ441.png)
> > 
> > Using the terminology of [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006) (see [Section 6.9.2](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0020)), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ442.png)is a linear function of the state variables, which explains the term *linear* feedback shift register.
> > 
> > In the case of particular interest here, namely the binary case where we are working over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ443.png), every value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/c007_dequ444.png)is either zero or one, and so the value fed back is the sum of a selection of the values currently in the register. Normally, we always take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![a sub zero](images/c007_dequ445.png)to be non-zero, or else we can get exactly the same output sequence by deleting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![s sub zero](images/c007_dequ446.png)and working with a shorter register.
> > 
> > From now on, I will mainly focus on the binary case, i.e. where the field is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ447.png). However, pretty much everything I have to say can be generalised to the case where the symbols are drawn from an arbitrary finite field.
> > 
> > To make things clearer, I next give a simple example of a binary LFSR with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n equals five](images/c007_dequ448.png), as shown in [Figure 7.4](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-4).
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.4 A linear feedback shift register for bold-italic n equals five full stop](images/c07f004.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.4](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-4) A linear feedback shift register for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5.</mn></mstyle></math>![bold-italic n equals five full stop](images/c007_dequ449.png)
> > 
> > There are two taps, so the feedback is the sum of two of the stages. That is,
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![s sub four times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals s sub zero of t plus s sub two of t comma](images/c007_dequ450.png)
> > 
> > where the addition is computed in the field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ451.png).
> > 
> > Suppose the initial state is 00111, i.e.
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1.</mn></math>![s sub zero of one equals zero semicolon s sub one of zero equals zero semicolon s sub two of zero equals one semicolon s sub three of zero equals one semicolon and s sub four of zero equals one full stop](images/c007_dequ453.png)
> > 
> > Then, moving everything left one place, we have
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.5em"/></mstyle><mrow/><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1.</mn></math>![s sub zero of zero equals zero semicolon s sub one of one equals one semicolon s sub two of one equals one semicolon and s sub three of one equals one full stop](images/c007_dequ454.png)
> > 
> > It remains to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub four of one](images/c007_dequ455.png), the new value fed in at the right end of the register. Now, we know that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 s sub four of one equals part 2 s sub zero of zero plus s sub two of zero equals part 3 zero plus one equals part 4 one full stop](images/c007_dequ456.png)
> > 
> > Hence, the new state of the register (at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t equals one](images/c007_dequ457.png)) is 01111. By a similar argument, the state for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![t equals two](images/c007_dequ459.png)is 11111.
> > 
> > The successive states of the shift register for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></math>![t equals zero comma one comma ellipsis comma 32](images/c007_dequ461.png)are shown in [Table 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-1).
> > 
> >  ![Table 7.1 Successive states of the shift register in Figure 7.4.](images/c007_dequ462.png)
> > 
> > [Table 7.1](#c007.xhtml#rc07-tbl-1) Successive states of the shift register in [Figure 7.4](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-4).
> > 
> > I next want to make an important, albeit rather simple, observation. The state of an LFSR at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ468.png)depends only on the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t minus one](images/c007_dequ469.png). That is, if the state of an LFSR ever equals the state at some previous time, then the sequence of states thereafter will be exactly the same as the sequence of states after the previous occurrence of the repeated state. So the sequence of states of an LFSR will always, eventually, be periodic.
> > 
> > So what about the example I have just given? It is simple to see that the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>31</mn></math>![t equals 31](images/c007_dequ470.png)is the same as the state at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![t equals zero](images/c007_dequ471.png), and hence the sequence of states has period dividing 31. However, since 31 is prime, the period is exactly 31. You can check the table to see that no state recurs before <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>31</mn></math>![t equals 31](images/c007_dequ472.png).
> > 
> > So how long can the periodic sequence be? Well, this will clearly depend on the number of possible states of the shift register. That is, since if the same state recurs, the sequence will also recur from that point, then the period of any sequence of states must be at most the number of states.
