Thus, if the symbols that fill the stages of the register are taken from a set of size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c007_dequ473.png), then the maximum period for an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ474.png)\-stage shift register must be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![k super n](images/c007_dequ475.png). In fact, we can do slightly better than this.
> > 
> > Suppose the initial state of the register is all zeros. Then the feedback bit will be a linear function of all zeros, and hence will be zero. That is, if a shift register is ever in the all-zero state, then it will stay in this state for ever. So a maximum length sequence cannot contain the all-zero state, and so the maximum period of the sequence of states of an LFSR is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k super n minus one](images/c007_dequ476.png).
> > 
> > In the example above, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![k equals two](images/c007_dequ477.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n equals five](images/c007_dequ478.png), i.e. the maximum period is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>31</mn></math>![two super five minus one equals 31](images/c007_dequ479.png). So the period of the sequence of states in [Table 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-1) is the maximum possible. In such a case, the sequence output by the shift register is particularly important, and I discuss this further immediately below.
> > 
> > Before moving on, observe that the sum of the periods of the possible sequences of LFSR states always adds to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![k super n](images/c007_dequ480.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c007_dequ481.png)is the number of possible symbols and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ482.png)is the length of the register. I will leave you to think about why this is true. I have provided a brief explanation in the ‘Answer to Questions for the Reader’ section (see page 240).
> > 
> > Whilst I have so far focussed on the sequence of states, and the possible periods of these sequences, from now on I will be interested in the period of the *sequence output* by a LFSR, which will have the same period as the sequence of states of the LFSR. For example, the LFSR shown in [Figure 7.4](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-4) can output two possible sequences—the all-zero sequence (of period one), and the sequence
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>00111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11011</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10101</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00101</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>11000</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![00111 11000 11011 10101 00001 00101 one 00111 11000 times ellipsis comma](images/c007_dequ483.png)
> > 
> > which has period 31. I have actually shown 41 terms of the sequence, and I have left a large gap after the 31st term to show where it starts repeating (the small gaps after every five bits are simply there to improve readability). Of course, the sequence of symbols in any of the five stages of the LFSR will contain this sequence.
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > ### 7.4.3 LFSR Sequences and Polynomials
> > 
> > As I just mentioned, I am particularly interested here in the sequences output by a LFSR, and specifically the maximum period sequences, i.e. those with period <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k super n minus one](images/c007_dequ484.png). These are known as m-sequences (where the ‘m’ stands for *maximum* period), and they have a range of interesting properties which make them useful in a wide range of practical applications, which are explored a little further below.
> > 
> > Perhaps the key question is how to choose the feedback taps to ensure that the LFSR generates a maximum period sequence. This is where I need to use polynomials. However, before explaining the theory, I will give another example to illustrate that not all feedback tap settings generate maximum period sequences. The sequences generated by the LFSR shown in [Figure 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-5) do not have the maximum possible period.
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.5 A linear feedback shift register with four stages.](images/c07f005.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.5](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-5) A linear feedback shift register with four stages.
> > 
> > For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![n equals four](images/c007_dequ485.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![k equals two](images/c007_dequ486.png), the maximum period would be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>![two super four minus one equals 15](images/c007_dequ487.png). However, as shown in [Table 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-2), this LFSR actually generates four different sequences, of periods 6, 6, 3 and 1 (the last being the all-zero sequence, and so is not shown in the table).
> > 
> > ![Table 7.2 State sequences of the shift register in Figure 7.5.](images/c007_dequ488.png)
> > 
> > [Table 7.2](#c007.xhtml#rc07-tbl-2) State sequences of the shift register in [Figure 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-5).
> > 
> > If I make a small change to the tap positions in the four-stage register of [Figure 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-5) to get the LFSR shown in [Figure 7.6,](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-6) then we get a very different result. In this case, starting with any non-zero state results in a sequence of states of period 15, i.e. the maximum possible. The output sequence (of period 15) is:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>00110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00110</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![00110 10111 10001 00110 times ellipsis full stop](images/c007_dequ503.png)
> > 
> > I leave you to check this (the initial state to generate this sequence is simply 0011).
> > 
> > ![Figure 7.6 A second linear feedback shift register with four stages.](images/c07f006.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 7.6](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-6) A second linear feedback shift register with four stages.
> > 
> > So the positions of the taps is key to determining whether or not the state sequence is of maximum period. How this works is easiest explained in terms of polynomials over the relevant finite field, i.e. the field from which the symbols in the register are taken.
> > 
> > Suppose the feedback bit is equal to
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator s sub zero of t plus a sub one dot operator s sub one of t plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one dot operator s sub n minus one of t](images/c007_dequ504.png)
> > 
> > as is the case for the LFSR shown in [Figure 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-3). Then we define the *characteristic polynomial* (or *feedback polynomial*) for the LFSR to be the polynomial
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub zero plus a sub one times x plus a plus two times x squared plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one times x super n minus one plus x super n full stop](images/c007_dequ505.png)
> > 
> > of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ506.png).
> > 
> > In the example of a five-stage LFSR shown in [Figure 7.4](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-4), the characteristic polynomial is simply:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>5</mn></msup></math>![sum with 3 summands one plus x squared plus x super five](images/c007_dequ507.png)
> > 
> > since we are working over the field with two elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy='false'>(</mo><msub><mi>&#x2124;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy='false'>)</mo></mrow></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two right parenthesis](images/MathXIA4EQ_0038.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a sub zero equals part 2 a sub two equals part 3 one](images/c007_dequ509.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a sub one equals part 2 a sub three equals part 3 a sub four equals part 4 zero](images/c007_dequ510.png). In the examples of four-stage LFSRs shown in [Figures 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-5) and [7.6](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-6), the characteristic polynomials are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>![sum with 3 summands one plus x squared plus x super four](images/c007_dequ511.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>![sum with 3 summands one plus x plus x super four](images/c007_dequ512.png), respectively.
> > 
> > We can then state the following theorem which gives a precise characterisation of the sets of feedbacks that will generate maximum period sequences.
> > 
> > To make sense of this key result, I need to explain what I mean by a *primitive polynomial*. A primitive polynomial is a polynomial with degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ518.png)with the property that the smallest positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ519.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ520.png)is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x super n minus one](images/c007_dequ521.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>k</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k super d minus one](images/c007_dequ522.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c007_dequ523.png)is the number of elements in the finite field, i.e. the number of possible symbols in each stage of the register.
> > 
> > The proof of this theorem is non-trivial and involves concepts I have not yet introduced, so I leave the proof to the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of this book (see page 241).
> > 
> > Looking back to our examples, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>![sum with 3 summands one plus x plus x super four](images/c007_dequ524.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![sum with 4 summands one plus x squared plus x plus five](images/c007_dequ525.png)are primitive polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ526.png), whereas <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>![sum with 3 summands one plus x squared plus x super four](images/c007_dequ527.png)is not. Fortunately, there are primitive polynomials of every possible degree for any finite field, so it is possible to find sets of tap positions to generate an m-sequence of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super n minus one](images/c007_dequ528.png)for every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ529.png).
> > 
> > Before moving on, I want to define one more concept, namely that of a *linear recurrence relation.*^()
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator s sub zero of t plus a sub one dot operator s sub one of t plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one dot operator s sub n minus one of t full stop](images/c007_dequ532.png)
> > 
> > Now, because the values in the LFSR shift one place left at every time slot, the value in stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus two](images/c007_dequ533.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ534.png)(i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub n minus two of t](images/c007_dequ535.png)) is simply the value in stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ536.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t minus one](images/c007_dequ537.png)(i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t minus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ538.png). More generally, we have
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub i of t equals s sub n minus one times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands t minus n plus one plus i right parenthesis full stop](images/c007_dequ539.png)
> > 
> > So, we can substitute into the equation for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ540.png)to get
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t plus one right parenthesis equals sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t minus n plus one right parenthesis plus a sub one dot operator s sub n minus one times left parenthesis t minus n plus two right parenthesis plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus one dot operator s sub n minus one of t full stop](images/c007_dequ541.png)
> > 
> > This means that the contents of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ542.png)is a linear function of previous values in the same stage of the register. Now the successive contents of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ543.png)correspond to the sequence output by the LFSR.
> > 
> > This means that the output sequence itself satisfies the relationship in the above equation, i.e. any term in the sequence is equal to a linear combination of the previous <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ544.png)terms. So, if the sequence output by the LFSR is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![u sub zero comma u sub one comma u sub two comma ellipsis](images/c007_dequ545.png), then we know that, for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![i greater than or equals n](images/c007_dequ546.png):
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8901;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![u sub i plus one equals sum with variable number of summands a sub zero dot operator u sub i minus n plus one plus a sub one dot operator u sub i minus n plus two plus ellipsis plus a sub n minus two times u sub i minus one plus a sub n minus one times u sub i full stop](images/c007_dequ547.png)
> > 
> > This is an example of a linear recurrence relation.
> > 
> > Looking back to the example of an LFSR shown in [Figure 7.6](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-6), I already stated that this LFSR produces the output sequence
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>00110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![00110 10111 10001 ellipsis full stop](images/c007_dequ548.png)
> > 
> > If we call this sequence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![u sub zero comma u sub one comma u sub two comma ellipsis](images/c007_dequ549.png), then since in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a sub zero equals part 2 a sub one equals part 3 one](images/c007_dequ550.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 a sub two equals part 2 a sub three equals part 3 zero](images/c007_dequ551.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![n equals four](images/c007_dequ552.png), we know that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![u sub i plus one equals u sub i minus three plus u sub i minus two full stop](images/c007_dequ553.png)
> > 
> > This is simple to check.
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > ### 7.4.4 Properties of m-sequences
> > 
> > The m-sequences, i.e. the maximal period LFSR sequences, have a wide range of interesting properties. One obvious property, of course, is that a very simple circuit involving just a few storage elements can generate a sequence with a long period. For example, a 20-stage binary LFSR can generate a sequence with period over a million.
> > 
> > They also have the very nice property that if any two shifts of the same sequence are added together, then the result is another shift of the same sequence (or the all-zero sequence). Why is this? By a *shift* of a sequence, I simply mean starting in a different place. For example, if we consider the periodic sequence
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>00110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![00110 10111 10001 ellipsis comma](images/c007_dequ554.png)
> > 
> > then the shift of this sequence one place to the left is simply the periodic sequence
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>01101</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>01111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00010</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![01101 01111 00010 ellipsis full stop](images/c007_dequ555.png)
> > 
> > Why does this property hold? Well it is a consequence of the fact that both shifts of the sequence satisfy the same linear recurrence relation. The sum of two sequences satisfying a linear recurrence relation must satisfy the same recurrence, so this means that the sum of two shifts of the same m-sequence must be another shift of this sequence.
> > 
> > Apart from this, they exhibit a number of other properties which means the sequence looks rather like a random sequence (while, of course, it is very far from actually being random)! Sequences which are generated by a deterministic process, like m-sequences, and which, to some extent at least, resemble random sequences^()
> > 
> > The eminent American mathematician and engineer Solomon Wolf Golomb^()
> > 
> > *   **R1**: In any period of the sequence, the number of ones differs from the number of zeros by at most one.
> > *   **R2**: In any period of the sequence, approximately half the runs^()
> > *   **R3**: If the sequence is compared to a shift of itself, then over a period of the sequence the number of agreements minus the number of disagreements is a constant for all shifts (apart from the zero shift). Using more mathematical terminology, the out-of-phase autocorrelation of the sequence is a constant.
> > 
> > The m-sequences satisfy all of R1–R3. As an example, consider the m-sequence of period 15 generated by the LFSR shown in [Figure 7.6](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-6), namely the sequence:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>001101011110001</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![001101011110001 times ellipsis full stop](images/c007_dequ556.png)
> > 
> > I have given exactly one period of the sequence here. It is simply to verify that a period of the sequence contains eight ones and seven zeros, so R1 holds. There are four runs of zeros—a half of them (i.e. two of them) have length one, and a quarter (one) have length two. There are four runs of ones, and again half have length one and a quarter have length two. So R2 holds.
> > 
> > R3 holds as an immediate corollary of the property that the sum of two shifts of an m-sequence will yield another shift of the same sequence. When computing the sum of two bits, if the two bits being summed are the same then a zero will result, and if they are different then the outcome will be a one. But an m-sequence generated by an LFSR with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ557.png)stages will always contain exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![two super n minus one](images/c007_dequ558.png)ones and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super n minus one minus one](images/c007_dequ559.png)zeros, and so the number of agreements between any two shifts of an m-sequence with be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super n minus one minus one](images/c007_dequ560.png), and the number of disagreements will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![two super n minus one](images/c007_dequ561.png). Hence, the number of agreements minus the number of disagreements will always be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![negative one](images/c007_dequ562.png).
> > 
> > Of course, any sequence which satisfies R1–R3 will clearly not be random. Indeed, these properties mean that the sequence over a full period will be ‘too regular’, but if we are using just part of a m-sequence then it will be suitable for applications requiring random-looking properties.
> > 
> > ### 7.4.5 Applications of m-sequences
> > 
> > As I already mentioned, there are innumerable real-world applications of m-sequences. In particular, their pseudorandomness properties, large period and simplicity of generation make them useful for any case requiring large volumes of ‘random-like’ sequences of bits. Two examples of applications are as follows.
> > 
> > *   In *spread spectrum communications*, m-sequences are used to ‘spread’ radio signals across a broad band of frequencies as part of Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) systems. Each transmitting entity is assigned its own m-sequence code, enabling multiple signals to be transmitted simultaneously over the same set of frequencies, minimising interference. The m-sequences are important for spreading signals because of their autocorrelation properties, which minimises interference between two signals. Their balance and run properties also enable reliable synchronisation between transmitters and receivers. 
> > *   It is possible to derive codes for error detection and correction using m-sequences. The set of shifts of an m-sequence form what is the known as the Simplex Code, which is very closely related to first order Reed–Muller Codes.^() 
> >     
> >     There is one further application I will explore in a little more detail, namely their use as a component in a type of encryption technique called a *stream cipher*. The high level operation of stream cipher encryption is shown in [Figure 7.7](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-7).
> >     
> >     ![Figure 7.7 Stream cipher encryption.](images/c07f007.png)
> >     
> >     [Figure 7.7](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-7) Stream cipher encryption.
> >     
> >     Encryption works in a very simple way. The plaintext needs to be converted to a sequence of zeros and ones, although typically this is how data is stored anyway. The key component is the *sequence generator*. The sequence generator takes as input a secret key (which must be shared with the entity authorised to decrypt) and gives as output a sequence of zeros and ones, often referred to as the *keystream*. This keystream sequence is then combined bit by bit with the plaintext to give the ciphertext. This combination simply involves modulo 2 addition.^()
> >     
> >     The sequence generator needs to have a number of important properties if the stream cipher is to be secure. These include the following.
> >     
> >     *   The keystream sequence needs to have a large period (it must be periodic since like an LFSR it will have a finite number of possible internal states).
> >     *   The keystream sequence needs to have pseudorandomness properties, i.e. it must resemble a random sequence.
> >     *   Perhaps most importantly, it should not be computationally feasible to use knowledge of part of the keystream sequence to deduce other parts of the keystream sequence.
> >     
> >     Why these properties? First, if the period of the keystream sequence is not sufficiently large, then the same sequence of keystream bits may end up being used to encrypt two different pieces of plaintext. If this became known to a cryptanalyst, then this could be used to reveal information about some of the plaintext.
> >     
> >     If the keystream has non-random properties, e.g. if ones are much more likely to occur than zeros in the sequence, then statistical properties of the plaintext will ‘leak’ into the ciphertext, i.e. purely by doing statistical analysis of the ciphertext it might be possible to deduce information about the plaintext.
> >     
> >     The need for the final property is perhaps a little less obvious. The reason for requiring this is that it may be possible for the cryptanalyst who has access to the ciphertext to somehow know what part of the corresponding plaintext is. This could be for any number of reasons. It might simply be that the plaintext is highly formatted, and always starts in the same way. This is true for many popular file formats. The history of cryptography and cryptanalysis has many examples of where so called ‘known plaintext’ attacks have been possible.
> >     
> >     If a cryptanalyst knows a ciphertext bit and the corresponding plaintext bit, then their sum will be the keystream bit (this is just how modulo 2 addition works). So, knowledge of, say, a couple of hundred consecutive plaintext bits, and the corresponding ciphertext bits, will immediately yield 200 known keystream bits; it is therefore vital that this cannot be used to deduce more keystream bits (or, worst of all, work back to the secret key).
> >     
> >     So how does all this relate to LFSRs? I hope you will have already noticed that m-sequences satisfy the first two of the three desirable properties for a keystream sequence. Moreover, they are easy to generate at very high data rates with very simple electronics (or software). However, they dismally fail to meet the third requirement. Given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></math>![two times n](images/c007_dequ564.png)consecutive bits of an m-sequence, it is possible to easily work out any other bit of the sequence even if you don’t know the feedback tap positions. Indeed, it is hard to imagine a sequence which failed to meet the third property more disastrously!
> >     
> >     Nonetheless, LFSRs have a key role to play in many designs for stream cipher sequence generators. By combining two or more LFSRs using non-linear logic, pseudorandom sequences with large periods can be generated which, as far as we know, also possess the third property. The ease of implementation of LFSRs and their periodicity and pseudorandomness properties make them very attractive components in stream cipher designs.
> >     
> >     Before wrapping up this topic, I can’t resist mentioning a historically important family of stream ciphers, namely the Lorenz SZ40, SZ42a and SZ42b systems used by Germany during the latter part of the Second World War. They were used for high level traffic and were believed to be immune to cryptanalysis. However, thanks to the brilliance of British–Canadian mathematician William Thomas (Bill) Tutte^()
> >     
> >     Despite not knowing how the Lorenz sequence generator worked, he was able to deduce its operation given only a portion of keystream. This keystream was obtained from an accidental misuse of the system by its operators, where two versions of the same message were sent encrypted using the same keystream sequence. This allowed John Tiltman, a senior Bletchley Park cryptanalyst, to deduce that the encryption system in use was a stream cipher. Tiltman was then able to deduce the two messages and hence obtain a portion of the keystream sequence. This was then given to Bill Tutte to work on as a seemingly lost cause. To be able to deduce the operation of a complex sequence generator given only a portion of the output sequence was an incredible feat, one I still find hard to believe was possible, especially in the absence of any automated data processing.
> >     
> >     Once the operation of the Lorenz system was known, it became possible to work on methods of cryptanalysis. Eventually, it became clear that it was necessary to mechanise the process, which led to the design and construction of the *Colossus*, one of the world’s first digital computers. Colossus was designed by the Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers, and of course, as is well known, Alan Turing was also involved in the work. However, it should be made clear that, despite popular misconceptions, Colossus was built to help break the Lorenz stream cipher and not the Enigma machine.
> >     
> >     Colossus remained top secret for many years after the war, and, sadly, eventually all surviving instances of the device were securely destroyed. However, the good news is that enough information, and original creators, survived to enable a working replica to be built at Bletchley Park, and it can be viewed at the Bletchley Park Museum.^()
> >     
> >      
> >     
> >     ### 7.4.6 Non-linear Feedback Shift Registers
> >     
> >     So far, I have only looked at the case where the feedback function of the shift register is a linear function of the values stored in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ565.png)stages of the register. That is, as shown in [Figure 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-3), where the value of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ566.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t plus one](images/c007_dequ567.png)is a linear function of the contents of stages <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub zero comma s sub one comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ568.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ569.png). However, it is also of interest to consider the case where the feedback function is not restricted, i.e. where the value of stage <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ570.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![t plus one](images/c007_dequ571.png)is an arbitrary function of the contents of stages <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![s sub zero comma s sub one comma ellipsis comma s sub n minus one](images/c007_dequ572.png)at time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/c007_dequ573.png), as shown in [Figure 7.8](#c007.xhtml#c07-fig-8).
> >     
> >     ![Figure 7.8 A non-linear feedback shift register.](images/c07f008.png)
> >     
> >     [Figure 7.8](#c007.xhtml#rc07-fig-8) A non-linear feedback shift register.
> >     
> >     Shift registers with a non-linear feedback function are known as non-linear feedback shift registers (NFSRs). Such shift registers have been extensively studied and have a range of real-world applications, including in the design of stream cipher keystream sequence generators.
> >     
> > 
> > ## 7.5 Polynomial Arithmetic Modulo a Polynomial
> > 
> > I will conclude this chapter by introducing a way of doing modular arithmetic with polynomials; something that gives a close analogue to the ideas of [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004), except working with polynomials instead of integers. This is key to developing the theory of finite fields, as you will see in [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008).
> > 
> > Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ574.png)is a commutative ring. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ575.png)be a polynomial in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap r of x](images/c007_dequ576.png). I can define a new structure working modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ577.png), just as I defined the integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ578.png)for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c007_dequ579.png).
> > 
> > I will say that two polynomials <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x comma q of x](images/c007_dequ580.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ581.png)are *congruent modulo* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ582.png)if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ583.png)is a divisor of their difference. That is, I will say that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x identical to q of x times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times m of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ584.png)
> > 
> > if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x bar left parenthesis q of x minus p of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ585.png).
> > 
> > So, for example, if we are working in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z of x](images/c007_dequ586.png), the ring of polynomials with integer coefficients, we have
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x cubed identical to one times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands normal m times normal o times normal d times x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ587.png)
> > 
> > since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis x minus one right parenthesis equals left parenthesis x cubed minus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ588.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ589.png)is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x cubed minus one](images/c007_dequ590.png). Just as is the case with congruence over the integers, we have the following important result which is directly analogous to [Theorem 4.1](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0003).
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > The proof works in exactly the same way as the proof of [Theorem 4.1](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0003), and so I leave it as an exercise for you, the reader. I give a brief proof in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section at the end of the book (see page 243).
> > 
> > Because it defines an equivalence relation, the congruence relation modulo a polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ595.png)will divide the set of all polynomials into equivalence classes known as *residue classes* (*mod* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ596.png)). I will denote the residue class containing the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ597.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![of pp left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar](images/c007_dequ598.png). I also denote the set of equivalence classes by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap r of x solidus left parenthesis p of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ599.png).
> > 
> > Because of the following result, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ600.png)is monic and has degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ601.png), then there is a simple correspondence between all the polynomials of degree less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ602.png)and the set of equivalence classes.
> > 
> > So, when working modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ624.png), and given that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ625.png)is monic of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ626.png), I can represent any residue class (mod <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ627.png)) by a polynomial of degree less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c007_dequ628.png).
> > 
> > As an example, suppose we are working in the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ629.png)(which, of course, is actually a field). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ630.png)has only two elements (0 and 1), these are the only possible coefficients for a polynomial. Suppose also that we are working modulo the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![m of x equals sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ631.png). Then there are four equivalence classes, corresponding to the four possible polynomials of degree less than the degree of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ632.png), i.e. 2, namely:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover><mn>0</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#8195;</mtext><mover><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></math>![zero horizontal bar comma one horizontal bar comma x horizontal bar and plus plus x one horizontal bar full stop](images/c007_dequ633.png)
> > 
> > To determine which equivalence class a polynomial is in, we simply need to divide the polynomial by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![m of x equals sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ634.png). I demonstrate this by subtracting multiples of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ635.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ636.png), reducing the degree every time, until we get a result with degree less than 2. For those of you familiar with it, the process is a little like long division of integers.
> > 
> > So if, for example, I choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p of x equals sum with 3 summands x super four plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ637.png), we first multiply <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ638.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ639.png)raised to the power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>deg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mtext>deg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![degree left parenthesis p of x right parenthesis postfix minus degree left parenthesis m of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ640.png), i.e. two, and subtract it from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ641.png), as follows:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 p of x minus x squared times m of x equals part 2 sum with 3 summands x super four plus x plus one minus x squared times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis equals part 3 sum with 3 summands negative x cubed minus x squared plus x plus one full stop](images/c007_dequ642.png)
> > 
> > Note that all the arithmetic on coefficients is performed in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ643.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![one plus one equals zero](images/c007_dequ644.png). If we call the output of the first step <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p super prime of x](images/c007_dequ645.png), we now repeat this process, but this time multiplying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ646.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c007_dequ647.png)and adding instead of subtracting^()
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 p super prime of x plus x times m of x equals part 2 sum with 4 summands negative x cubed minus x squared plus x plus one plus x times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis equals part 3 one full stop](images/c007_dequ650.png)
> > 
> > That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![sum with 3 summands x super four plus x plus one identical to one times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands normal m times normal o times normal d times x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ651.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover accent="false"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![plus plus plus x four x one horizontal bar equals one horizontal bar](images/c007_dequ652.png).
> > 
> > Equivalently, we could simply observe that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 p of x minus one equals part 2 left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x super four plus x plus one right parenthesis minus one equals part 3 x super four plus x equals part 4 left parenthesis x squared plus x right parenthesis times left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis equals part 5 left parenthesis x squared plus x right parenthesis times m of x comma](images/c007_dequ653.png)
> > 
> > i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![m of x bar p of x minus one](images/c007_dequ654.png).
> > 
> > I can also define addition and multiplication on these equivalence classes, in exactly the same way as I defined addition and multiplication on the equivalence classes when working modulo an integer (as described in [Section 4.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0002)). That is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/c007_dequ655.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/c007_dequ656.png)are polynomials in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![cap r of x](images/c007_dequ657.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r equals left parenthesis cap r comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ658.png)is a commutative ring, I define:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![of pp left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar plus of qq left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar equals plus plus of pp left parenthesis right parenthesis x of qq left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar](images/c007_dequ659.png)
> > 
> > and
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>&#8901;</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></math>![of pp left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar dot operator of qq left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar equals dot operator dot operator of pp left parenthesis right parenthesis x of qq left parenthesis right parenthesis x horizontal bar full stop](images/c007_dequ660.png)
> > 
> > It follows from the definitions that these operations are well-defined, i.e. clearly the sum or product of any two equivalence classes will be an equivalence class.
> > 
> > As previously, I am cheating slightly and using the same symbols <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo></math>![plus](images/c007_dequ661.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c007_dequ662.png)for addition and multiplication of equivalence classes of polynomials as I am using for addition and multiplication of individual polynomials, but which operation I mean should, I hope, be clear from the context.
> > 
> > As an example of how these operations work, I have given Cayley Tables for addition and multiplication in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ663.png)in [Tables 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-3) and [7.4](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-4), i.e. the example I just looked at.
> > 
> > ![Table 7.3 Addition in double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands bold-italic x squared plus bold-italic x plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c007_dequ666.png)
> > 
> > [Table 7.3](#c007.xhtml#rc07-tbl-3) Addition in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands bold-italic x squared plus bold-italic x plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/MMit1EQ_0018.png)
> > 
> > ![Table 7.4 Multiplication in double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands bold-italic x squared plus bold-italic x plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c007_dequ691.png)
> > 
> > [Table 7.4](#c007.xhtml#rc07-tbl-4) Multiplication in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands bold-italic x squared plus bold-italic x plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/MMit1EQ_0019.png)
> > 
> > The addition table ([Table 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-3)) is very simple to check. However, the multiplication table involves first multiplying, and ‘reducing’ modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ664.png).
> > 
> > If you check the tables, you will see that both tables are the tables of a group. In fact, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ706.png)is actually a field. However, this will by no means always be the case for every polynomial ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap r of x](images/c007_dequ707.png)and every monic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ708.png). Nonetheless, we do have the following key result which states that the set of equivalence classes of polynomials modulo a monic polynomial, when combined with the addition and multiplication operations I just defined, forms a commutative ring. This result is particularly important as it forms the basis for defining the non-prime finite fields.
> > 
> > It is tempting to think that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ722.png)is an integral domain then, since we know that this means that the ring of polynomials <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap r of x](images/c007_dequ723.png)is an integral domain (from [Corollary 7.1](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0004)), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap r of x solidus left parenthesis m of x right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ724.png)will also be an integral domain for any monic polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ725.png). However, this is not true for all choices of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ726.png), as a simple example next shows.
> > 
> > The example uses the same ring as in the previous example, namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ727.png). However, instead of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c007_dequ728.png), we let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![m of x equals x squared plus one](images/c007_dequ729.png), which is (of course) monic. So [Theorem 7.7](#c007.xhtml#c007-secc-0024) still applies. However, the ring we get, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two solidus left parenthesis x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ730.png), is not an integral domain, even though <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub two comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ731.png)is not just an integral domain but actually a field.
> > 
> > Why is this? Well, just as previously, there are four elements in this ring, namely the equivalence classes
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover><mn>0</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></math>![zero horizontal bar comma one horizontal bar comma x horizontal bar and plus plus x one horizontal bar full stop](images/c007_dequ732.png)
> > 
> > Addition on these equivalence classes works exactly as it does in the previous example, i.e. for the case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two solidus left parenthesis sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ733.png), and so the Cayley Table for addition given in [Table 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-3) also applies in this case. However, multiplication is different. The Cayley Table in this case is given in [Table 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c07-tbl-5).
> > 
> > ![Table 7.5 Multiplication in double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c007_dequ735.png)
> > 
> > [Table 7.5](#c007.xhtml#rc07-tbl-5) Multiplication in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/MMit1EQ_0020.png)
> > 
> > The strangest behaviour happens for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![plus plus x one horizontal bar](images/c007_dequ750.png). First observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis times x equals x squared plus x](images/c007_dequ751.png).
