Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x squared plus x identical to x plus one times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ752.png)since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis x squared plus x right parenthesis minus left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis equals part 2 x squared minus one equals part 3 x squared plus one](images/c007_dequ753.png), since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![prefix plus of one equals negative one](images/c007_dequ754.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ755.png). That is, we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x squared plus one right parenthesis bar left parenthesis x squared plus x right parenthesis minus left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ756.png). So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x times left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis equals one times left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ757.png), and clearly the cancellation law doesn’t apply. Secondly, we have non-zero zero divisors, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![multirelation left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis squared equals x squared plus one identical to zero times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c007_dequ758.png). So clearly in this case we do not get an integral domain.
> > 
> > So, why the difference? I’ll leave you to think about this, and I discuss it further in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’ section (see page 244).
> > 
> > We return to this issue in [Chapter 8](#c008.xhtml#c008), where we show that, by using an appropriate polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ759.png)(and when the coefficients are from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub p](images/c007_dequ760.png)for a prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c007_dequ761.png)), the ring of polynomials modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![m of x](images/c007_dequ762.png)is actually a finite field.
> > 
> > ## Notes
> > 
> > 1.  [1](#c007.xhtml#rfn_1) François Viète, 1540–1603. He was a French amateur mathematician and astronomer who introduced the first systematic algebraic notation. His contributions are particularly relevant to this book, not only because of his contributions to algebra, but because he was also a cryptographer. For further details see, for example, `https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Viete/`.
> > 2.  [2](#c007.xhtml#rfn_2) Of course, a polynomial can only be monic if there exists a 1 in the ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi></math>![script cap r](images/c007_dequ763.png), so the definition only makes sense in a ring with one.
> > 3.  [3](#c007.xhtml#rfn_3) It is possible to generalise this definition to more general rings, but I am only interested in this case here.
> > 4.  [4](#c007.xhtml#rfn_4) A well-known example of an integer sequence that can be generated using a recurrence relation is the Fibonacci Sequence, mentioned in [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004).
> > 5.  [5](#c007.xhtml#rfn_5) I realise I haven’t actually defined what I mean by a random sequence. Indeed, this is a rather tricky thing to define, since a random process can generate any sequence. This is exemplified by the *Infinite Monkey Theorem*, which states that a monkey typing keys at random on a typewriter will eventually type the complete works of William Shakespeare. This notion apparently goes back at least to the French mathematician Émile Borel, writing in the early years of the 20th century. Anyway, that digression aside, for my purposes here, I mean a sequence generated by a process which selects each symbol with equal probability by some non-deterministic process, such as a fair coin toss.
> > 6.  [6](#c007.xhtml#rfn_6) Apparently his work on polyominoes inspired the game *Tetris*.
> > 7.  [7](#c007.xhtml#rfn_7) Here, a *run* is a sequence of zeros (or ones) preceded and followed by ones (or zeros).
> > 8.  [8](#c007.xhtml#rfn_8) As I mentioned in [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006), the Mariner space probe used a first order Reed–Muller Code to error-protect signals sent back from Mars.
> > 9.  [9](#c007.xhtml#rfn_9) I have described this cipher as if the plaintext and keystream must be binary sequences, and in practice, this is typically the case. However, the same idea works if the plaintext and keystream sequences are elements of an arbitrary finite field.
> > 10.  [10](#c007.xhtml#rfn_10) To link back to a theme briefly mentioned earlier in this book, the eventual proof of the four colour theorem built on Tutte’s work. A memorial to Bill Tutte can be found in Newmarket, Suffolk, his birthplace.
> > 11.  [11](#c007.xhtml#rfn_11) See `https://bletchleypark.org.uk/`.
> > 12.  [12](#c007.xhtml#rfn_12) In the special case of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub two](images/c007_dequ764.png), addition is the same as subtraction since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![negative one equals prefix plus of one](images/c007_dequ765.png), but more generally, this is what you would need to do.
> > 
> >  
> 
> # Chapter 8  
> Finite Fields
> 
> > An author never does more damage to his readers than when he hides a difficulty.^()
> > 
> > ## 8.1 The Core of the Book
> > 
> > It took me a while to get here, but I am now ready to describe the properties of finite fields, as well as a small selection of their many practical applications. As mentioned previously, the applications I have highlighted here reflect my interests; there are many that I don’t mention here. It turns out that finite fields are of key importance in modern information and communications technology, although I am sure that the mathematicians who developed the basic theory well over 100 years ago had no conception that this would be true.
> > 
> > The finite fields are known as Galois Fields after Évariste Galois, a quote from whom is given at the beginning of this chapter. Indeed, the Galois Fields form part of an area of mathematics known as Galois Theory. In his brief and turbulent life, Galois laid the foundations for a major branch of algebra, although, of course, the terminology we use today was developed a long time after he died in 1832. Although Galois is often credited with developing fundamental ideas underlying group theory and Galois Theory, the Italian mathematician Paolo Ruffini came up with many of the ideas first, although his work was ignored by the mathematical community at the time.
> > 
> > ## 8.2 The Prime Fields
> > 
> > I already introduced the notion of a field in [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006), where I observed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ1.png)is a field for every prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ2.png). Moreover, as I showed in [Lemma 6.7](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0015) every field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ3.png)elements is isomorphic to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ4.png).
> > 
> > These fields, known as the *prime fields*, are of key importance both to the rest of mathematics and in a wide range of practical applications, some of which I have already described. In particular, as [Theorem 6.1](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0016) shows, they are the foundation on which all fields with finite characteristic are built. That is, since finite fields must have finite characteristic, all finite fields must contain a copy of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ5.png)for some prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ6.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ7.png)is the characteristic of the field. As an example of a prime field, I gave Cayley tables for the field with five elements, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub five comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ8.png), in [Tables 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c05-tbl-1) and [5.2](#c005.xhtml#c05-tbl-2).
> > 
> > However, the prime fields are not the only finite fields; in [Section 8.3](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0003), I consider how many elements a finite field might have, and subsequently I show how to construct a ‘non-prime’ finite field for every possible number of elements. This then leads naturally to a consideration of applications for finite fields, in addition to those I have already mentioned.
> > 
> > ## 8.3 How Many Elements Might There Be?
> > 
> > Obviously the prime fields <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub p](images/c008_dequ9.png)have a prime number of elements, but how many elements can a finite field contain? [Theorem 8.1](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0004) says that the number must be a power of a prime.
> > 
> > In the next section, I give one way of constructing a field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ42.png)elements for any prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ43.png)and every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ44.png). So not only must a finite field have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ45.png)elements for some prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ46.png), there always exists a finite field with this number of elements.
> > 
> > ## 8.4 Prime Power Fields
> > 
> > I will now describe one way of constructing a finite field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ47.png)elements for any prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ48.png)and any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ49.png). In the mathematical literature, the construction is typically described in terms of concepts such as *ideals* that I have deliberately avoided introducing to try to keep the presentation as elementary as possible. So mathematicians reading this may be a little upset! However, I have nevertheless tried to be as rigorous as I can in the presentation.
> > 
> > The method of construction uses polynomials—indeed, elements of a finite field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ50.png)elements are defined as equivalence classes of polynomials with coefficients taken from the prime field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ51.png)elements. We build on [Theorem 7.7](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0024) to give the following general method for constructing a field using polynomials.
> > 
> > While [Theorem 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0006) holds for any field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c008_dequ93.png), finite or infinite, I am particularly interested in the case where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c008_dequ94.png)is a finite prime field. In such a case we have the following simple corollary.
> > 
> > So [Theorem 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0006) gives a general way of constructing a finite field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ117.png)elements for any prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ118.png)and any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ119.png). All you need is an irreducible polynomial over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub p](images/c008_dequ120.png)of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ121.png). Fortunately, irreducible polynomials exist with every possible degree over every prime field.
> > 
> > I already gave two simple examples of the operation of [Theorem 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0006):
> > 
> > *   At the end of [Section 7.5](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0021), I gave an example of how, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p of x equals x squared plus one](images/c008_dequ122.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x solidus left parenthesis p of x right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ123.png)has zero divisors, and this is because the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x squared plus one](images/c008_dequ124.png)is not irreducible when working in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x](images/c008_dequ125.png). In fact, we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![x squared plus one equals left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis squared](images/c008_dequ126.png).
> > *   I also gave an example where, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p of x equals sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c008_dequ127.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x solidus left parenthesis p of x right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ128.png)is a field, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands x squared plus x plus one](images/c008_dequ129.png)*is* irreducible when working in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub two of x](images/c008_dequ130.png).
> > 
> > I will next give a slightly more complicated example, which will be useful again later. I will show how construct a field with 9 = 3² elements, so we will need an irreducible polynomial of degree 2 over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub three](images/c008_dequ132.png).
> > 
> > I claim that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x squared plus one](images/c008_dequ133.png)is an irreducible polynomial in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub three of x](images/c008_dequ134.png). It is simple to check this, since it has degree only two—meaning that any non-trivial divisor must have degree one. Now, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ135.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x plus one](images/c008_dequ136.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![x plus two](images/c008_dequ137.png)are clearly not divisors of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x squared plus one](images/c008_dequ138.png), which is sufficient to show it is irreducible. (We only need to check possible divisors that are monic, since every polynomial over a field is equal to a constant times a monic polynomial).
> > 
> > The nine residue classes will correspond to the nine polynomials with degree less than two, namely:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover><mn>0</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover><mn>2</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></math>![zero horizontal bar comma one horizontal bar comma two horizontal bar comma x horizontal bar comma plus plus x one horizontal bar comma plus plus x two horizontal bar comma times times two x horizontal bar comma plus plus times times two x one horizontal bar comma plus plus times times two x two horizontal bar full stop](images/c008_dequ139.png)
> > 
> > The Cayley Table for addition in this field is simple to compute—see [Table 8.1](#c008.xhtml#c08-tbl-1).
> > 
> > ![Table 8.1 Addition in double-struck cap z sub three of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ141.png)
> > 
> > [Table 8.1](#c008.xhtml#rc08-tbl-1) Addition in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub three of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ140.png)
> > 
> > Computing the multiplication table is a little more complex, since we need to work modulo the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x squared plus one](images/c008_dequ241.png). For example:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![multirelation left parenthesis x plus one right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis two times x right parenthesis equals two times x squared plus two times x identical to left parenthesis negative two right parenthesis plus two times x identical to two times x plus one times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times x squared plus one right parenthesis comma](images/c008_dequ242.png)
> > 
> > since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>mod</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x squared identical to negative one times left parenthesis prefix mod of x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ243.png).
> > 
> > The full multiplication table for the non-zero elements of the field is given in [Table 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c08-tbl-2).
> > 
> > ![Table 8.2 Multiplication in double-struck cap z sub three of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ245.png)
> > 
> > [Table 8.2](#c008.xhtml#rc08-tbl-2) Multiplication in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mrow><mo>/</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub three of bold-italic x solidus left parenthesis bold-italic x squared plus one right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ140.png)
> > 
> > As usual, you can easily tell that every element has a multiplicative inverse since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![one horizontal bar](images/c008_dequ326.png)appears in every row (and column). Moreover, the table is symmetric so multiplication is commutative.
> > 
> > Observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![plus plus x one horizontal bar](images/c008_dequ327.png)is a generator of the multiplicative group, i.e. the multiplicative group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub three of x solidus left parenthesis x squared plus one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ328.png)is cyclic. This is simple to see as:
> > 
> > ![](images/c008_dequ329.png)
> > 
> > This is no coincidence, as we observe in [Section 8.5](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0008).
> > 
> > ## 8.5 Uniqueness and Representation of Finite Fields
> > 
> > A fundamental result in the study of finite fields is that, for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ338.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ339.png), the finite field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![p super n](images/c008_dequ340.png)elements, denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis p super n right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ341.png)where GF stands for *Galois Field*, is unique up to isomorphism. I regret to say that I haven’t managed to find a proof of this result that does not involve setting up quite a bit more mathematical machinery. So, unfortunately, you will need to look elsewhere for a proof, although any standard text on the subject will provide one. It is also the case that the multiplicative group of the non-zero elements of any finite field is cyclic.
> > 
> > From now on, I will assume this result and refer to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ350.png)as *the* finite field with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ343.png)elements, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![q equals p super n](images/c008_dequ344.png)for some prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ345.png)and positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ346.png). In particular, of course, we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![GF left parenthesis p right parenthesis equals double-struck cap z sub p](images/c008_dequ347.png)for every prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ348.png).
> > 
> > I suspect that if your instinct is to implement things, you may be wondering what the best way of handling the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ349.png)might be. In fact, performing computations with finite fields is more straightforward than you might think.
> > 
> > To remind you, the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ350.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![q equals p super n](images/c008_dequ351.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ352.png)prime) are residue classes of polynomials, where each class contains a unique polynomial of degree less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ353.png)that can be used to ‘represent’ that class. A polynomial of degree less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ354.png)can be represented as an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ355.png)\-tuple of coefficients, where each coefficient is from the prime field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![GF left parenthesis p right parenthesis equals double-struck cap z sub p](images/c008_dequ356.png). That is, if the residue class is
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover accent="false"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo></math>![plus plus plus plus plus times times r minus minus n one x minus minus n one times times r minus minus n two x minus minus n two midline horizontal ellipsis times times r one xr zero horizontal bar comma](images/c008_dequ357.png)
> > 
> > where the values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![r sub i](images/c008_dequ358.png)are from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub p](images/c008_dequ359.png), then we can represent the residue class by the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ360.png)\-tuple
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis r sub n minus one comma r sub n minus two comma ellipsis comma r sub one comma r sub zero right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ361.png)
> > 
> > For example, in the above example for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![q equals three squared](images/c008_dequ362.png), we can represent the nine residue classes by the nine 2-tuples:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma zero right parenthesis comma left parenthesis zero comma one right parenthesis comma left parenthesis zero comma two right parenthesis comma left parenthesis one comma zero right parenthesis comma left parenthesis one comma one right parenthesis comma left parenthesis one comma two right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma zero right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma one right parenthesis comma left parenthesis two comma two right parenthesis comma](images/c008_dequ363.png)
> > 
> > which correspond to
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mover><mn>0</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover><mn>2</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo></math>![zero horizontal bar comma one horizontal bar comma two horizontal bar comma x horizontal bar comma plus plus x one horizontal bar comma plus plus x two horizontal bar comma times times two x horizontal bar comma plus plus times times two x one horizontal bar comma plus plus times times two x two horizontal bar comma](images/c008_dequ364.png)
> > 
> > respectively. Thus, the field elements can be represented as elements from an array of dimension <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ365.png).
> > 
> > Moreover, addition is simply addition of the corresponding digits in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ366.png)\-tuple, e.g. for the above example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis zero comma one right parenthesis plus left parenthesis one comma two right parenthesis equals part 2 left parenthesis zero plus one comma one plus two right parenthesis equals part 3 left parenthesis one comma zero right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ367.png), corresponds to the polynomial addition <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mover><mn>1</mn><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover accent="false"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>x</mi><mo accent="true">&#8213;</mo></mover></math>![one horizontal bar plus plus plus x two horizontal bar equals x horizontal bar](images/c008_dequ368.png). So computing additions in the finite field is no more difficult than performing additions in the prime field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis p right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ369.png). In fact, addition works just like addition in the product ring <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub three multiplication double-struck cap z sub three](images/c008_dequ370.png), as defined in [Section 6.4](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0005). However, multiplication is not so simple.
> > 
> > If the finite field is small then probably the easiest way to implement multiplication is using a pre-computed table—much like the Cayley table shown in [Table 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c08-tbl-2). For larger fields, where a table would be prohibitively expensive in storage, a process akin to long division can be used to find the remainder when the product polynomial is divided by the irreducible polynomial defining the finite field. For computations involving large degree polynomials (i.e. when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ371.png)is large), other tricks are available to simplify computations.
> > 
> > ## 8.6 Elliptic Curve Cryptography
> > 
> > I now want to describe an important application of finite fields in cryptography. In [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005), I described the notion of *discrete logarithms*, which are defined for any finite cyclic group. As I described there, discrete logarithms are the basis of some very widely used cryptographic techniques. I also described how discrete logarithms work for one particular instance of a cyclic group, namely the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ372.png)for any prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ373.png). In fact, standard practice is to use a large cyclic subgroup of this group.
> > 
> > This particular instance of a cyclic group is used because:
> > 
> > *   computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![g super n](images/c008_dequ374.png)for any positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ375.png)is straightforward (where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c008_dequ376.png)is a generator of the cyclic group), even for large values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ377.png), whereas
> > *   if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c008_dequ378.png)is an arbitrary element of the group, then finding the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c008_dequ379.png)for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi></math>![g super i equals h](images/c008_dequ380.png)(i.e. computing the discrete logarithm of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c008_dequ381.png)) is believed to be computationally infeasible, at least as long as the group is large enough.
> > 
> > However, any instance of a cyclic group that has the aforementioned properties would work equally well in a wide range of cryptographic methods. In particular, it would be desirable to find instances of large cyclic groups where computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>![g super n](images/c008_dequ382.png)remains straightforward, but computing discrete logarithms is significantly more difficult than for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ383.png)for given sizes of group. In such a case, the desired level of security could be achieved using smaller groups, which would potentially make computations faster (and keys smaller). This is precisely the motivation for the development of *elliptic curve* cryptography.
> > 
> > In essence, using elliptic curves enables us to define cyclic groups for which solving the discrete logarithm problem is much more computationally demanding than the discrete logarithm problem for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ384.png)for a given size of group. As a result, over the last decade or more there has been a major switch from using cryptography based on discrete logarithms in a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ385.png)to cryptography using discrete logarithms in an elliptic curve group.
> > 
> > So what is an elliptic curve, and what is an elliptic curve group? I want to start by introducing the notion of a curve. For my purposes here, a curve is simply a set of solutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ386.png)to a particular equation defined over a field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c008_dequ387.png). So, for example, if the field is the real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![double-struck cap r](images/c008_dequ388.png), then the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y equals x](images/c008_dequ389.png)defines a very simple curve—in fact, if we plot all the solutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ390.png)on a graph we get a diagonal straight line that goes through the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis zero comma zero right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ391.png)and heads from south-west to north-east. A graph of the curve (kindly created by ChatGPT) is shown in [Figure 8.1](#c008.xhtml#c08-fig-1).
> > 
> > ![Figure 8.1 Graph of the curve bold-italic y equals bold-italic x.](images/c08f001.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 8.1](#c008.xhtml#rc08-fig-1) Graph of the curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic y equals bold-italic x](images/c008_dequ392.png).
> > 
> > A slightly more interesting curve, again for the field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></math>![double-struck cap r](images/c008_dequ393.png), is obtained if we consider the equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![y equals x squared](images/c008_dequ394.png). In this case we get the curve known as a *parabola* shown in [Figure 8.2](#c008.xhtml#c08-fig-2) (again provided courtesy of ChatGPT).
> > 
> >  ![Figure 8.2 Graph of the curve bold-italic y equals bold-italic x squared.](images/c08f002.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 8.2](#c008.xhtml#rc08-fig-2) Graph of the curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mstyle></math>![bold-italic y equals bold-italic x squared](images/c008_dequ395.png).
> > 
> > Although the two examples of curves that I have just given can be plotted as lines on a graph, as one might expect from the name *curve*, in general this will not be true. That is, for my purposes, a curve is simply the set of solutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ396.png)to an equation involving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ397.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ398.png), and does not necessarily have a nice geometric interpretation.
> > 
> > In general, an *elliptic curve* is simply a set of solutions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ399.png)to an equation of a particular form defined over a field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c008_dequ400.png). We will typically denote the set of points on the curve, i.e. the set of pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ401.png)that satisfy the defining equation, by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap e of script cap f](images/c008_dequ402.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/c008_dequ403.png)is the underlying field—or just by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ404.png)if the field is obvious from the context. A general elliptic curve equation looks like:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math>![sum with 3 summands y squared plus a sub one times x times y plus a sub three times y equals sum with 4 summands x cubed plus a sub two times x squared plus a sub four times x plus a sub six comma](images/c008_dequ405.png)
> > 
> > where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![a sub one comma a sub two comma a sub three comma a sub four comma and a sub six](images/c008_dequ406.png)are all elements^()
> > 
> > The reason they are called elliptic curves is that they originally arose as part of efforts to study the length of an arc in an ellipse. This in turn led to the study of certain functions called *elliptic integrals* over the real and complex numbers. So the relation to the term ellipse is not so straightforward—it certainly doesn’t mean that the curves are in the form of an ellipse, although they have ellipsoid features.
> > 
> > Fortunately it is possible to simplify the general equation defining an elliptic curve by changing the variables <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ408.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>;</mo></math>![y semicolon](images/c008_dequ409.png)this essentially involves choosing an elliptic curve with simple parameters from amongst a set of isomorphic curves, where curve isomorphism maps between two essentially equivalent curves, analogously to group or field isomorphisms. Unfortunately, the precise form of the simplified equations depends on the characteristic of the field, where, as discussed in [Section 6.8](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0013), the characteristic of a field is either infinite or equal to a prime number.
> > 
> > The following cases arise:
> > 
> > *   If the characteristic is not equal to 2 or 3, then the simplified equation for the curve is:
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b comma](images/c008_dequ410.png)
> >     
> >     where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi></math>![a and b](images/c008_dequ411.png)are field elements.
> >     
> > *   If the characteristic is 2 then there are two possible equations. 
> >     *   The *non-supersingular* equation^()
> >         
> >         <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared plus x times y equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x squared plus b comma](images/c008_dequ412.png)
> >         
> >         where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi></math>![a and b](images/c008_dequ413.png)are field elements**.**
> >         
> >     *   The *supersingular* equation is:
> >         
> >         <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared plus c times y equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b comma](images/c008_dequ414.png)
> >         
> >         where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>c</mi></math>![a comma b and c](images/c008_dequ415.png)are field elements.
> >         
> > *   If the characteristic is 3 then there are again two equations. 
> >     *   The *non-supersingular* equation is:
> >         
> >         <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x squared plus b comma](images/c008_dequ416.png)
> >         
> >         where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi></math>![a and b](images/c008_dequ417.png)are field elements**.**
> >         
> >     *   The *supersingular* equation is:
> >         
> >         <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b comma](images/c008_dequ418.png)
> >         
> >         where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mi>b</mi></math>![a and b](images/c008_dequ419.png)are field elements.
> >         
> > 
> > If you ever have reason to examine the implementation of an elliptic curve-based cryptosystem, then the aforementioned explains why the equations used vary slightly depending on the nature of the underlying field.
> > 
> > At some point, it was discovered that it is possible to define a group on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap e of script cap f](images/c008_dequ420.png), the points on an elliptic curve. In fact, if the field is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo mathvariant="double-struck">,</mo></mrow></math>![double-struck cap r double-struck comma](images/c008_dequ421.png)then the group operation has a nice visual geometric interpretation. Whilst this provides an underlying motivation for the definition of the operation, the visual geometric interpretation does not apply when the field is finite, although it is nevertheless possible to define concepts such as the tangent algebraically; moreover, I am only interested in the finite field case, and so I won’t go into details of this geometric motivation here.
> > 
> > Before giving details of how the group operation is defined, I should say that for the purposes of defining the group we actually add an extra element to the curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ422.png); this element is commonly referred to as the point at infinity. This name again derives from the geometric interpretation. It functions as a group identity, and following the usual convention I will simply call this added element ‘<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ423.png)’. Note that when I refer to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ424.png)hereafter, I mean the set of solutions to an elliptic curve equation together with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ425.png). If I simply refer to the curve or to solutions to the curve equation, I do *not* include <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ426.png).
> > 
> > The precise definition of the group operation depends on the characteristic of the field. I will only describe it for the case where the characteristic is greater than 3, i.e. where the equation defining the curve is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b](images/c008_dequ427.png).
> > 
> > *   Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ428.png)is not actually a point on the curve, we need to define how it interacts with a curve point separately from defining how two points are combined. By definition we put
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis dot operator infinity equals part 2 left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis equals part 3 infinity dot operator left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis comma](images/c008_dequ429.png)
> >     
> >     for any point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>E</mi></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis element of cap e](images/c008_dequ430.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ431.png)functions as the identity element for the operation.
> >     
> > *   Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ432.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap q equals left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ433.png)are two curve points, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![x sub one not equals x sub two](images/c008_dequ434.png). Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Q</mi></math>![cap p dot operator cap q](images/c008_dequ435.png)is defined to be the curve point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub three comma y sub three right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ436.png)where
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x sub three equals left parenthesis y sub two minus y sub one divided by x sub two minus x sub one right parenthesis squared minus left parenthesis x sub one plus x sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ437.png)
> >     
> >     and
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![y sub three equals left parenthesis y sub two minus y sub one divided by x sub two minus x sub one right parenthesis times left parenthesis x sub one minus x sub three right parenthesis minus y sub one full stop](images/c008_dequ438.png)
> >     
> >     It is not so easy to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub three comma y sub three right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ439.png)is indeed a point on the curve, i.e. that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![left parenthesis y sub three right parenthesis squared equals sum with 3 summands left parenthesis x sub three right parenthesis cubed plus a times x sub three plus b](images/c008_dequ440.png). I have included the details in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section (see page 244).
> >     
> > *   The inverse of a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ441.png)is defined to be
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![cap p super negative one equals left parenthesis x comma negative y right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ442.png)
> >     
> >     By definition we require that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![cap p dot operator cap p super negative one equals infinity](images/c008_dequ443.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c008_dequ444.png). It is simple to check that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ445.png)is a point on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ446.png)then so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma negative y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ447.png), since in the equation defining the curve, the only term involving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ448.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![y squared](images/c008_dequ449.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></math>![left parenthesis y right parenthesis squared equals left parenthesis negative y right parenthesis squared](images/c008_dequ450.png)in any field.
> >     
> > *   Finally, I need to define how to combine a point with itself. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ451.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![y sub one not equals zero](images/c008_dequ452.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap p dot operator cap p equals part 2 cap p squared equals part 3 left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ453.png), where
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![x sub two equals left parenthesis three times left parenthesis x sub one right parenthesis squared plus a divided by two times y sub one right parenthesis squared minus two times x sub one](images/c008_dequ454.png)
> >     
> >     and
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![y sub two equals left parenthesis three times left parenthesis x sub one right parenthesis squared plus a divided by two times y sub one right parenthesis times left parenthesis x sub one minus x sub two right parenthesis minus y sub one full stop](images/c008_dequ455.png)
> >     
> >     As previously, it is not so simple to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ456.png)is a point on the curve, and so I have again left discussing this to the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section (see page 244). If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![y sub one equals zero](images/c008_dequ457.png)then by definition <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![cap p equals cap p super negative one](images/c008_dequ458.png)and by the previous bulleted paragraph we have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![cap p squared equals infinity](images/c008_dequ459.png).
> >     
> > 
> > This completes the definition of the group operation. Four things about the definition merit a little more explanation.
> > 
> > *   To show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap e comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ460.png)is a group we need to show that the operation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c008_dequ461.png)is associative. Proving this is a rather laborious exercise that I won’t even suggest as an exercise, but I can assure you that it does work!
> > *   You may have spotted that I defined how to combine two points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ462.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ463.png)if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![x sub one not equals x sub two](images/c008_dequ464.png), and I also defined how to combine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ465.png)both with itself and with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma negative y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ466.png).
