However, I didn’t say how to combine <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ467.png)with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y super prime right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ468.png)when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>&#8242;</mi></msup></math>![y super prime](images/c008_dequ469.png)is not equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ470.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![negative y](images/c008_dequ471.png). Fortunately this isn’t necessary since this case cannot arise, because for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ472.png)there are at most two values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ473.png)such that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ474.png)is a point on the curve.
> > *   The group will always be abelian. This derives from the definition of the group operation. The equation for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![x sub three](images/c008_dequ475.png)would be the same if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ476.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ477.png)were interchanged, and so the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![x sub three](images/c008_dequ478.png)will be the same regardless of the order of the operands. Since, given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![x sub three](images/c008_dequ479.png), there are only two possibilities for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![y sub three](images/c008_dequ480.png), where one is the negative of the other, this shows that, for any two distinct points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c008_dequ481.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>Q</mi></math>![cap q](images/c008_dequ482.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#177;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p dot operator cap q equals prefix plus minus of cap q dot operator cap p](images/c008_dequ483.png). The fact that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p dot operator cap q equals prefix plus of cap q dot operator cap p](images/c008_dequ484.png)can be shown by a somewhat messy algebraic manipulation.
> > *   I have chosen to use the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c008_dequ485.png)symbol to represent the group operation. To put it a different way, I have described the group multiplicatively, i.e. using the terminology associated with multiplication. However, for historical reasons the group is usually described using additive notation. I have chosen to depart from the usual convention for consistency with the description of discrete logarithms in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005). Since the group operation is no more related to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>+</mo></math>![plus](images/c008_dequ486.png)than it is to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo>&#8901;</mo></math>![dot operator](images/c008_dequ487.png)in the underlying field, it is a completely arbitrary choice how to write it, and I have chosen the representation that fits better with the application I am interested in. This allows cryptosystems based on discrete logarithms to be presented in a way that is independent of the underlying group.
> > 
> > At this point an example may help. I have chosen to reuse an example given in a book by Darrel Hankerson, Alfred Menezes and Scott Vanstone.^()
> > 
> > The example is over the (prime) field GF(29) (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>29</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub 29](images/c008_dequ488.png)). The defining equation for the curve is:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus four times x plus 20 comma](images/c008_dequ489.png)
> > 
> > i.e., in the notation given, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![a equals four](images/c008_dequ490.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>![b equals 20](images/c008_dequ491.png). The set of 37 group elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ492.png)is shown in [Table 8.3](#c008.xhtml#c08-tbl-3), made up of the 36 points on the curve together with the special element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ493.png).
> > 
> > ![Table 8.3 Points left parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right parenthesis on an elliptic curve over GF(29).](images/c008_dequ495.png)
> > 
> > [Table 8.3](#c008.xhtml#rc08-tbl-3) Points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mstyle></math>![left parenthesis bold-italic x comma bold-italic y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ494.png)on an elliptic curve over GF(29).
> > 
> > First note that the equation defining the curve has no solutions for 11 values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ496.png), namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>21</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>23</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>26</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>28</mn></math>![x equals seven comma nine comma 11 comma 12 comma 18 comma 21 comma 22 comma 23 comma 25 comma 26 and 28](images/c008_dequ497.png), which explains why there are only 36 points in the curve and not <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>29</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>58</mn></math>![two multiplication 29 equals 58](images/c008_dequ498.png). Also observe that, as expected, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ499.png)is on the curve, then so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma negative y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ500.png), i.e. if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c008_dequ501.png)is on the curve, then so is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![cap p super negative one](images/c008_dequ502.png).
> > 
> > Two examples of the group operation are:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>27</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>;</mo><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.5em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mtext>and</mtext><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.5em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>22</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis five comma 22 right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis 16 comma 27 right parenthesis equals left parenthesis 13 comma six right parenthesis semicolon and equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis five comma 22 right parenthesis squared equals part 2 left parenthesis five comma 22 right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis five comma 22 right parenthesis equals part 3 left parenthesis 14 comma six right parenthesis full stop](images/c008_dequ503.png)
> > 
> > I leave you to check these!
> > 
> > So, how many points will there be on a curve over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ350.png)in general? Well, since there are at most two solutions to the equation for any value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ505.png), and there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ506.png)possible values for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ507.png), there will be at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></math>![two times q](images/c008_dequ508.png)solutions to the curve equation, i.e. there will be at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi></math>![two times q](images/c008_dequ509.png)points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ510.png)on the curve. Hence there will be at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two times q plus one](images/c008_dequ511.png)elements in the group (since we add the extra element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ512.png)). However, the actual number will always be significantly less than this. In fact, a result proved in 1931 by the German mathematician Helmut Hasse states that the number of points on an elliptic curve over a finite field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ513.png)is always in the range^()
> > 
> > The next result tells us that the group on a curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ517.png)is in most cases either cyclic or possesses a large cyclic subgroup.
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n sub two equals one](images/c008_dequ530.png)then clearly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap e comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ531.png)is cyclic. For the example of a curve given earlier  over GF(29), the order of the group is 37, which is prime, and hence in this case the group is cyclic. In fact, the point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis one comma five right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ532.png)is a generator of the group. The successive powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c008_dequ533.png)are shown in [Table 8.4](#c008.xhtml#c08-tbl-4).
> > 
> > ![Table 8.4 Successive powers of bold-italic cap p equals left parenthesis one comma five right parenthesis in an elliptic curve over GF(29).](images/c008_dequ534.png)
> > 
> > [Table 8.4](#c008.xhtml#rc08-tbl-4) Successive powers of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mstyle></math>![bold-italic cap p equals left parenthesis one comma five right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ532a.png)in an elliptic curve over GF(29).
> > 
> > So by choosing the curve appropriately, we can obtain a cyclic group. That is, given a generator of the cyclic group, we can define discrete logarithms with respect to this generator. It turns out that, as far as we know and as long as the parameters are chosen carefully, computing discrete logarithms in an appropriate elliptic curve group is much more computationally complex than computing discrete logarithms in the group of non-zero integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ572.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ573.png)(as discussed in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005)). As a result it is possible to use significantly smaller group sizes when implementing discrete logarithm-based cryptographic schemes, such as the Diffie–Hellman key establishment scheme described in [Section 5.11](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0022). This has significant practical advantages, and as a result elliptic curve-based schemes have become very widely used over the last 10–20 years.
> > 
> > As I just mentioned, the curve to be used needs to be chosen carefully to avoid certain cryptanalytic attacks, i.e. cases where computing discrete logarithms turns out to be much easier. Indeed there are widely recognised standards both for generating curves, such as ISO/IEC 15946-5^()
> > 
> > Individual curves have also been standardised, since there is no known risk in the same curve being used by multiple users.^()
> > 
> > Computations in an elliptic curve group are, on the face of it, rather more complex than in the group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ574.png). If you look at the equations given above for computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub three comma y sub three right parenthesis equals left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ575.png)when the curve is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b](images/c008_dequ576.png), you will see that:
> > 
> > *   computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![x sub three](images/c008_dequ577.png)involves four finite field additions (or subtractions), one division operation, and one squaring operation; and
> > *   computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![y sub three](images/c008_dequ578.png)involves four finite field additions (or subtractions), one division operation, and one multiplication operation.
> > 
> > Observing that division is simply multiplication by an inverse element, and the inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ579.png)is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x comma negative y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ580.png), this means that computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub three comma y sub three right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ581.png)involves three finite field multiplications, one squaring operation (which may be a little cheaper than a multiplication) and eight addition operations. While the addition operations will be much simpler than multiplication, this is still a considerable amount of computation if the field is large, as will be necessary to ensure that computing discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible.
> > 
> > Fortunately there are a number of well-documented optimisations which can reduce the computational load. For example, it is possible to choose the curve in such a way that the computations are less taxing.
> > 
> > Finally, as I have mentioned previously, what really makes use of the elliptic curve group in cryptography so attractive is that computing discrete logarithms is, as far as we know, significantly more complex in this group than in the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ582.png). The gains through the choice of significantly smaller parameters far outweigh the slightly increased computational cost of performing the group operation.
> > 
> > ## 8.7 Quantum Computing—What Comes Next?
> > 
> > Unfortunately, as was discussed in [Section 5.13](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0024), the security of discrete logarithm-based cryptosystems is threatened by the possible advent of large-scale general-purpose quantum computers. That is, a suitable quantum computer can make computing discrete logarithms feasible for large groups pretty much regardless of the representation of the cyclic group in which discrete logarithms are calculated. So, within the next few years we need to move away from all cryptosystems using discrete logarithms.
> > 
> > As I mentioned previously, a variety of new cryptographic methods have been proposed which are believed to be secure even in a world containing large-scale quantum computers. To date, the proposals taken most seriously are based on three mathematical problems, briefly summarised as follows, and all of which relate to themes already explored in this book. So just because there is a move away from (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) RSA and discrete logarithm-based cryptosystems does not mean that cryptography is moving away from abstract algebra. Far from it! Indeed, in recent years—mainly because of the threat posed by quantum computers—cryptographers have been ransacking much of abstract algebra looking for problems which could be used as the basis for new, and hopefully quantum-computing-resistant, methods for encryption and digital signature.
> > 
> > *   The first is the problem of decoding large block codes. In [Section 6.9](#c006.xhtml#c006-sec-0018), I introduced block codes and gave a simple example of a block code, namely the Hamming Code. I also introduced the idea of encoding and decoding for a block code, where encoding involves using data bits to compute the check bits, and decoding involves processing a received word to detect errors and/or correct errors in that word. More generally, encoding can be thought of as transforming a sequence of data bits into a codeword. Computing check bits and combining these with the data bits to obtain a codeword is just one type of transformation, but in general it may not be so simple. 
> >     
> >     I also mentioned that if the minimum distance between codewords is at least <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two times e plus one](images/c008_dequ583.png)then it is possible to correct up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c008_dequ584.png)errors in a received word. The purpose of a decoding algorithm in such a case is to work out the codeword with least Hamming Distance from the received word. In a general case, there may not be an efficient decoding algorithm, and so finding the ‘closest’ codeword to a received word may be computationally difficult, at least if the codeword is very long. One of the first ever proposed public key cryptosystems is built on this difficult computational problem. It was published by the distinguished American engineer Robert J McEliece way back in 1978.
> >     
> >     It has never been widely used, primarily because encryption and decryption are complex, and keys are very large. Nonetheless, in recent years it has gained significant interest because there are no known attacks, even using a quantum computer. Indeed, it is one of the ‘post-quantum’ encryption algorithms at an advanced stage of international standardisation (as a forthcoming amendment to ISO/IEC 18033-2^() 
> >     
> > *   The second, and most widely discussed, computational problem used as a basis for new cryptographic algorithms is the *learning with errors* (LWE) problem. It refers to the computational problem of inferring a linear function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ585.png)over a finite ring (typically <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub q comma plus comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ586.png), the ring of integers modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ587.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ588.png)) from given samples <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![y sub i equals f of x sub i](images/c008_dequ589.png), some of which may be erroneous. The LWE problem is believed to be hard to solve, even in the presence of a quantum computer. 
> >     
> >     More precisely, the unknown function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ590.png)maps from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ591.png)\-tuples of elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub q](images/c008_dequ592.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub q](images/c008_dequ593.png). The function is linear, so if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f of x sub one comma x sub two times ellipsis comma x sub n equals y](images/c008_dequ594.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></math>![y equals sum with variable number of summands a sub one times x sub one plus a sub two times x sub two plus ellipsis plus a sub n times x sub n comma](images/c008_dequ595.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![a sub one comma a sub two comma ellipsis comma a sub n](images/c008_dequ596.png)are the secret coefficients (from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub q](images/c008_dequ597.png)) and all the operations are computed in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub q](images/c008_dequ598.png). The input to the problem is a set of pairs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis left parenthesis x sub one comma x sub two times ellipsis comma x sub n right parenthesis comma y right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ599.png)where for each pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![f of x sub one comma x sub two times ellipsis comma x sub n equals y](images/c008_dequ600.png)with high probability. The problem is then to deduce <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ601.png). Of course, if all the inputs are correct, then finding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![a sub one comma a sub two comma ellipsis comma a sub n](images/c008_dequ602.png)is very simple given a sufficient number of pairs. However, if some of them are wrong, then the problem becomes much harder.
> >     
> >     The LWE problem, and variants of it, has been used as the basis for a wide variety of public key cryptosystems, including methods for encryption, digital signatures and secret key establishment. Techniques using LWE have been, and are being, formally standardised by a wide range of bodies.
> >     
> > *   The third problem relates to a special class of functions between groups known as *group isogenies*. More specifically, an isogeny is a special kind of function between elliptic curves that preserves the group structure. Recently proposed public key cryptosystems based on isogenies have been attractive because they offer significantly smaller key lengths than other methods. However, designing systems which are secure against subtle attacks has proved difficult. 
> >     
> >     Indeed, one very prominent scheme, known as SIDH or SIKE (for *Supersingular Isogeny Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange*) came quite close to adoption as a standardised scheme. SIDH is analogous to the Diffie–Hellman scheme described in [Section 5.11](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0022). However, it was shown to be completely insecure in 2022 by methods not involving a quantum computer.^()
> >     
> >     ## 8.8 Other Applications of Finite Fields
> >     
> >     Over the last 75 years or so, a wide variety of practical applications for finite fields have emerged. I have just described one, namely in elliptic curve cryptography. However, there are many others, and I will next briefly introduce just two, namely Reed–Solomon Codes, and bilinear pairings as used in cryptography.
> >     
> >     Indeed, such is the richness of the application domain for finite fields that there are academic journals devoted entirely to this topic, including *Finite Fields and their Applications*.^()
> >     
> >     ### 8.8.1 Reed–Solomon Codes
> >     
> >     The Reed–Solomon codes were invented by American mathematicians and engineers Irving S Reed and Gustave Solomon. Details were first published in 1960. They are block codes, where the individual codeword symbols are from a finite field. They are very widely used, for example, in protecting data stored in CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray media, as well as protecting transmitted data in many systems, including Digital Video Broadcast (DVB). Perhaps most famously, a Reed–Solomon code over the field GF(256) was used in conjunction with other coding techniques to protect data sent back to earth by the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes to the outer solar system.
> >     
> >     Like the Hamming Codes, they are systematic codes, i.e. where the data symbols are separate from the check symbols. Codewords contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ603.png)symbols, of which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c008_dequ604.png)are data symbols and the other <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![n minus k](images/c008_dequ605.png)are check symbols. If the symbols in a codeword are taken from the finite field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ606.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ607.png), the length of a codeword, must satisfy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>q</mi></math>![n less than or equals q](images/c008_dequ608.png). Whilst the codes exist for any finite field, in typical applications the symbols are drawn from a field of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis two super n right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ609.png)for some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ610.png), and so symbols consist of binary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ611.png)\-tuples (i.e. binary vectors of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ612.png)).
> >     
> >     The Reed–Solomon codes are examples of *Maximum Distance Separable* (MDS) codes. MDS codes have the highly desirable property that the distance between codewords is as large as possible for a given data rate. To explain this, I first need to introduce something known as the Singleton bound, named after American mathematical statistician Richard Collom Singleton, who published it in 1964. In fact, the bound had been published twice previously, by Indian statistician D D Joshi in 1958 and even earlier in 1953 by the Japanese mathematician Y Komiyama. So this is one of those cases where the bound is incorrectly named—perhaps it should be renamed the Komiyama–Joshi–Singleton bound, to reflect the fact that it was independently derived on at least three occasions. The bound is summarised in the following theorem.
> >     
> >     Since it is an MDS code, a Reed–Solomon code with minimum distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c008_dequ632.png)must contain precisely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![q super n minus d plus one](images/c008_dequ633.png)codewords. Alternatively, if the codewords have symbols from a set of size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ634.png), and there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c008_dequ635.png)data symbols, then there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math>![q super k](images/c008_dequ636.png)codewords, and the minimum distance is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![d equals n minus k plus one](images/c008_dequ637.png). But how do Reed–Solomon Codes work?
> >     
> >     There are various ways of describing these codes, and I will choose an approach that is a little different from that originally used by Reed and Solomon, but simpler. I assume that the data symbols are taken from a finite field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>GF</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![GF left parenthesis q right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ638.png)with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ639.png)elements, for some prime power <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c008_dequ640.png). A specially chosen polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of x](images/c008_dequ641.png), called the *generator polynomial*, is used to compute the check symbols from the data symbols. This polynomial has coefficients from the chosen finite field and has degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![n minus k](images/c008_dequ642.png). It is always possible to construct an appropriate polynomial, although I omit the details.
> >     
> >     Suppose that the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c008_dequ643.png)data symbols for a block are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![p sub zero comma p sub one comma ellipsis comma p sub k minus one](images/c008_dequ644.png). From this we define the data polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![p of x equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero plus p sub one times x plus ellipsis plus p sub k minus one times x super k minus one](images/c008_dequ645.png)of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k minus one](images/c008_dequ646.png). The codeword to be sent now corresponds to the coefficients of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x equals p of x dot operator g of x](images/c008_dequ647.png); that is, to ‘encode’ the data simply involves multiplying the data polynomial by the generator polynomial. Observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x](images/c008_dequ648.png)will have degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![left parenthesis n minus k right parenthesis plus left parenthesis k minus one right parenthesis equals n minus one](images/c008_dequ649.png), and so there will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c008_dequ650.png)coefficients. Because of the way in which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of x](images/c008_dequ651.png)is chosen, the resulting code is guaranteed to have minimum distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![d equals n minus k minus one](images/c008_dequ652.png).
> >     
> >     The procedure I have just described can be modified in a simple way to give a systematic encoding procedure, where each codeword contains the data symbols as the first <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/c008_dequ653.png)symbols and the check symbols as the last <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![n minus k](images/c008_dequ654.png)symbols. I leave you to think about this as an exercise; I have described how it works in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section—see page 247.
> >     
> >     Finally, there are also efficient decoding procedures, where a received word can be efficiently processed to correct up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![left parenthesis d minus one right parenthesis solidus two](images/c008_dequ655.png)errors, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c008_dequ656.png)is the minimum distance of the code.
> >     
> >     ### 8.8.2 Bilinear Pairings
> >     
> >     The final application of finite fields that I want to describe relates to cryptography (again)! It involves a special type of function between groups called a *bilinear pairing*. While the notion of a pairing is quite general, and can be defined over any commutative ring with one, I am interested in the following ‘special’ type of pairing.
> >     
> >     Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g sub one equals left parenthesis cap g sub one comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ657.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g sub cap t equals left parenthesis cap g sub cap t comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ658.png)be finite groups of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ659.png), for some prime <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ660.png)(and hence they are both abelian and cyclic—see [Theorem 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0007)). A *bilinear pairing* is a mapping <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ661.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one multiplication cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ662.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ663.png)that satisfies the following two properties.^()
> >     
> >     1.  *Bilinearity*: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of a dot operator b comma c equals f of a comma c dot operator f of b comma c](images/c008_dequ664.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![f of a comma b dot operator c equals f of a comma b dot operator f of a comma c](images/c008_dequ665.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></math>![a comma b comma c](images/c008_dequ666.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ667.png).
> >     2.  *Non-degeneracy*: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of a comma a not equals one](images/c008_dequ668.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ669.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ670.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a not equals one right parenthesis](images/c008_dequ671.png), where I write 1 for the identity element in both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ672.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ673.png).
> >     
> >     To be useful in a cryptographic application it is also necessary that the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ674.png)can be evaluated easily, and I assume this from here on. [Lemma 8.1](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0016) gives additional properties of a bilinear pairing.
> >     
> >     The proof of this lemma is elementary, and I leave it as an exercise for the reader. Full details are given on page 248 in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section.
> >     
> >     An interesting implication of the bilinearity property is that an instance of the discrete logarithm problem in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ686.png)can be reduced to an instance of the problem in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ687.png)in an efficient way. So that if a pairing exists between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ688.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ689.png), and there is an efficient means of computing discrete logarithms in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ690.png), then there will also be an efficient way of computing discrete logarithms in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ691.png)(since we assumed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ692.png)is easily computable).
> >     
> >     So, how does this reduction work? Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ693.png)is a generator of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ694.png), and suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![b equals a super x](images/c008_dequ695.png)for some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ696.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b element of cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ697.png). Computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c008_dequ698.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ699.png)(and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ700.png)) is straightforward (as long as we have an efficient method for computing products of elements), but computing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ701.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ702.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c008_dequ703.png)involves computing a discrete logarithm. From bilinearity (and [Lemma 8.1](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0016)) it follows that
> >     
> >     <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 f of a comma b equals part 2 f of a comma a super x equals part 3 f times left parenthesis a comma a right parenthesis super x full stop](images/c008_dequ704.png)
> >     
> >     So, if we put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f of a comma a equals g](images/c008_dequ705.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi></math>![f of a comma b equals h](images/c008_dequ706.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/c008_dequ707.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/c008_dequ708.png)are elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ709.png), then we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![h equals g super x](images/c008_dequ710.png). So, if computing discrete logarithms in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ711.png)is feasible, then we can compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ712.png). But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ713.png)is the discrete logarithm of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/c008_dequ714.png)with respect to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ715.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ716.png), i.e. we have a way of computing discrete logarithms in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ717.png).
> >     
> >     To be useful as the basis of a cryptographic algorithm we need to have an intractable computational problem. In the case of bilinear pairings the key problem is known as the *Bilinear Diffie–Hellman Problem* (BDHP), and is as follows. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ718.png)is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ719.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></math>![x comma y comma z](images/c008_dequ720.png)are positive integers. The BDHP requires you to compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></math>![f times left parenthesis a comma a right parenthesis super x times y times z](images/c008_dequ721.png)given four values: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ722.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![a super x](images/c008_dequ723.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi></msup></math>![a super y](images/c008_dequ724.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>z</mi></msup></math>![a super z](images/c008_dequ725.png).
> >     
> >     If solving the BDHP is computationally infeasible then this implies that the Diffie–Hellman Problem (DHP) (see [Section 5.11](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0022)) is hard in both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ726.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ727.png). Put another way, if we can solve the DHP in either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ728.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ729.png), then we can solve the BDHP for a pairing mapping <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ730.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ731.png). This is straightforward to check. However, no other ways have been found for solving the problem. Unfortunately, since a sufficiently capable quantum computer can find discrete logarithms in even very large groups, this means that the BDHP can also be solved by a quantum computer; thus, long term, all cryptographic schemes based on the difficulty of BDHP will need to be replaced.
> >     
> >     At this point you might reasonable ask why I am discussing bilinear pairings under the heading of applications of fields when only groups are involved. Well, the two most widely discussed bilinear pairings both involve finite fields; in fact, they involve elliptic curve groups defined over a finite field. These pairings are known as the Weil and Tate pairings after their respective inventors French mathematician André Abraham Weil^()
> >     
> >     Anyway, let’s suppose we have a bilinear pairing where the BDHP is hard to solve. A wide variety of cryptographic schemes have been devised based on the difficulty of the BDHP. I will briefly describe one that enables three parties to agree on a secret key; it is analogous to the Diffie–Hellman key agreement scheme I introduced in [Chapter 5](#c005.xhtml#c005) except that it involves three parties and not two. The scheme was published by French cryptographer Antoine Joux in 2000; the version I describe is the original scheme as modified in 2001 by Dutch cryptographer Eric Verheul.
> >     
> >     Suppose the three parties are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c008_dequ732.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c008_dequ733.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c008_dequ734.png), and that they have agreed on a suitable pair of groups <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ735.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></math>![cap g sub cap t](images/c008_dequ736.png)(of prime order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c008_dequ737.png)), a bilinear pairing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c008_dequ738.png)between them for which BDHP is hard, and a generator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ739.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ740.png). The main steps are as follows:
> >     
> >     1.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c008_dequ741.png)chooses a random integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ742.png)satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>p</mi></math>![one less than x less than p](images/c008_dequ743.png), computes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![a super x](images/c008_dequ744.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![cap g sub one](images/c008_dequ745.png), and sends (broadcasts) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![a super x](images/c008_dequ746.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c008_dequ747.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c008_dequ748.png).
> >     2.  Similarly, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c008_dequ749.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![cap c comma](images/c008_dequ750.png)respectively, choose random integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ751.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c008_dequ752.png), (respectively), and compute and broadcast <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi></msup></math>![a super y](images/c008_dequ753.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>z</mi></msup></math>![a super z](images/c008_dequ754.png).
> >     3.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c008_dequ755.png)can now compute the shared secret key as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>z</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></msup></math>![f times left parenthesis a super y comma a super z right parenthesis super x equals f times left parenthesis a comma a right parenthesis super x times y times z](images/c008_dequ756.png). <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c008_dequ758.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>C</mi></math>![cap c](images/c008_dequ759.png)can perform the corresponding calculations on the values they receive to obtain the same shared secret key.
> >     
> >     The Verheul protocol is shown diagrammatically in [Figure 8.3](#c008.xhtml#c08-fig-3).
> >     
> >     ![Figure 8.3 The Verheul protocol.](images/c08f003.png)
> >     
> >     [Figure 8.3](#c008.xhtml#rc08-fig-3) The Verheul protocol.
> >     
> >     Note that the three parties keep the values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c008_dequ760.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/c008_dequ761.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>z</mi></math>![z](images/c008_dequ762.png)secret, as knowledge of any one of them, together with the broadcast values, can be used to reveal the secret key. An eavesdropper who obtains the three broadcast values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></math>![a super x](images/c008_dequ763.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi></msup></math>![a super y](images/c008_dequ764.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>z</mi></msup></math>![a super z](images/c008_dequ765.png), and who can be assumed to know <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c008_dequ766.png), must solve an instance of the BDHP to obtain the secret key.
> >     
> >     There are many other cryptographic schemes that can be built on bilinear pairings, but the Joux scheme is particularly elegant in its simplicity (much like Diffie–Hellman key exchange). More generally, there are a host of other real-world applications of finite fields that I have not even touched on. Anyway, I hope I have convinced you in these few pages that the rather weird arithmetic of finite fields, where the ‘numbers’ are actually polynomials and multiplication involves working modulo a polynomial, is something that should be more generally known and thought about.
> >     
> >     ## Notes
> >     
> >     1.  [1](#c008.xhtml#rfn_1) Évariste Galois, 1811–1832.
> >     2.  [2](#c008.xhtml#rfn_2) The values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>and</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>6</mn></msub></math>![a sub one comma a sub two comma a sub three comma a sub four comma and a sub six](images/c008_dequ767.png)are required to satisfy a rather complex equation to ensure something called the *discriminant* is non-zero, but the details and rationale are way beyond the scope of this book.
> >     3.  [3](#c008.xhtml#rfn_3) The terms supersingular and non-supersingular are somewhat arbitrary and can simply be thought of as names for the two forms of the defining equation.
> >     4.  [4](#c008.xhtml#rfn_4) D Hankerson, A Menezes and S Vanstone, *Guide to elliptic curve cryptography*, Springer, New York (2004).
> >     5.  [5](#c008.xhtml#rfn_5) In most textbooks the range is given as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt><mo>&#8804;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mi>E</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt><mo>,</mo></math>![q plus one minus two times Square root of q less than or equals absolute value of cap e less than or equals sum with 3 summands q plus one plus two times Square root of q comma](images/c008_dequ768.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>E</mi></math>![cap e](images/c008_dequ769.png)includes the ‘added’ value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8734;</mi></math>![infinity](images/c008_dequ770.png); I have chosen to give the bound in terms of the number of solutions of the curve equation, which seems more logical to me, since a curve is normally defined as the set of points that satisfy the defining equation.
> >     6.  [6](#c008.xhtml#rfn_6) ISO/IEC 15946-5:2022, *Information security—Cryptographic techniques based on elliptic curves—Part 5: Elliptic curve generation*, 3rd edition, 2022.
> >     7.  [7](#c008.xhtml#rfn_7) Examples of recommended curves are given in Internet RFC 8032, S. Josefsson and I. Luisvaara, ‘Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)’, available at `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032`.
> >     8.  [8](#c008.xhtml#rfn_8) ISO/IEC 18033-2:2006, *Information technology—Security techniques—Encryption algorithms—Part 2: Asymmetric ciphers*, 1st edition, 2006.
> >     9.  [9](#c008.xhtml#rfn_9) For an excellent summary of the attack, see the blog by Steven Galbraith available at `ellipticnews.wordpress.com/2022/07/31/breaking-supersingular-isogeny-diffie-hellman-sidh/`.
> >     10.  [10](#c008.xhtml#rfn_10) From the point of view of users of cryptography, the advent of quantum computing is a huge pain in the arse. Since public key cryptography is embedded in much of the world of ICT, large-scale upgrades of systems will be required worldwide, at potentially huge cost and inconvenience. Moreover, the replacement cryptographic algorithms are simply not as easy to use as the schemes being replaced. If these costs are added to the huge costs of developing quantum computing, it is hard to imagine when—if ever—the potential advantages of quantum computing will pay off. I am tempted to wonder whether the world might have been better off if the notion of quantum computing had never seen the light of day; still, the genie is out of the bottle now! Of course, for cryptographers and quantum physicists this whole business has been a bonanza—so every cloud has a silver lining.
> >     11.  [11](#c008.xhtml#rfn_11) This journal is published by Elsevier—see `https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/finite-``fields-and-their-applications`.
> >     12.  [12](#c008.xhtml#rfn_12) The definition I give here is actually for a special case of a bilinear pairing known as a *symmetric* bilinear pairing—however it is sufficiently general for my purposes here.
> >     13.  [13](#c008.xhtml#rfn_13) Some of Weil’s greatest achievements were made when he was in prison in France in the early years of the Second World War. Whilst initially the conditions were hard, it seems that things improved for him over time. Indeed, he wrote the following to his wife from the prison: ‘My mathematics work is proceeding beyond my wildest hopes, and I am even a bit worried—if it’s only in prison that I work so well, will I have to arrange to spend 2 or 3 months locked up every year? In the meantime, I am contemplating writing a report to the proper authorities, as follows: “To the Director of Scientific Research: Having recently been in a position to discover through personal experience the considerable advantages afforded to pure and disinterested research by a stay in the establishments of the Penitentiary System, I take the liberty of, etc. etc.”’.
> >     
> >
