> # Chapter 9  
> Why Stop Now?
> 
> > If I have seen further than others, it is by standing upon the shoulders of giants.^()
> > 
> > ## 9.1 Some Edited Highlights
> > 
> > This is a sort of bonus chapter. My main goal in writing this book was to get as far as finite fields and their applications and, assuming you have read the previous chapters, you will have seen how I needed to build up to it in stages. This is how mathematics works—as mathematicians, major and minor (and I am very much in the latter category), we take the work that has been done by our predecessors and build on top of it. Unlike in the sciences where old theories or models eventually give way to new theories or better models, ‘old mathematics’ doesn’t fade away or become irrelevant. Instead it forms the foundations on which we build. This is captured by the very well-known Isaac Newton quote which starts this chapter.
> > 
> > So now we have reached the end of our quest, I would like to encourage you to continue to develop your knowledge of mathematics—so please don’t stop now! To encourage you I thought I would include brief introductions to a few topics which I find particularly interesting. This might be relating to applications or just because of the beauty of the results.
> > 
> > The topics I have chosen are quite a mixture, and I can’t claim there is any great logic to the selection I have made or any relationship between them. They are simply my personal edited highlights. I hope you like them.
> > 
> > ## 9.2 Sizes of Infinity
> > 
> > When I was introduced to this first topic as an undergraduate, I remember thinking it is both really surprising and rather wonderful. Certainly, in the 1870s when Georg Cantor first published the ideas I will briefly explore here, he got an extremely negative reaction from his contemporaries, including some of the leading mathematicians of the day. Leopold Kronecker accused him of being a ‘corrupter of youth’ by promoting his ideas, and also reportedly said that ‘I don’t know what predominates in Cantor’s theory—philosophy or theology, but I am sure that there is no mathematics there’. Pretty strong stuff, I think you’ll agree, but it goes to show that mathematicians care deeply about mathematics—perhaps Kronecker more than most.
> > 
> > So what are these radical ideas (which, by the way, are today an established part of mathematical thought)? Well, his really radical ideas^()
> > 
> > Cardinality for finite sets is something we discussed previously, and is simply the number of elements in the set. However, what does cardinality mean for sets where the number of elements is not finite? Well we can start by giving a simple way for deciding whether two sets have the same cardinality—this definition applies regardless of whether the two sets have finite or infinite cardinality.
> > 
> > If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ1.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>T</mi></math>![cap t](images/c009_dequ2.png)are sets, then we say that their cardinality is equal, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap s equals absolute value of cap t](images/c009_dequ3.png), if and only if there is a one-to-one and onto function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ4.png)mapping from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ5.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>T</mi></math>![cap t](images/c009_dequ6.png). In such a case we say that there is a *one-to-one correspondence* between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ7.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>T</mi></math>![cap t](images/c009_dequ8.png). This makes obvious sense for finite sets since if a set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ9.png)has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ10.png)elements then we can define a one-to-one correspondence between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ11.png)and the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma ellipsis comma n right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ12.png), and both sets clearly have cardinality <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ13.png). It is possible to show that this notion of cardinality-equality is an equivalence relation.
> > 
> > I next give our first infinite cardinal number. Define the cardinality of the natural numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ14.png)to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ15.png)(where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#8501;</mi></math>![normal alef](images/c009_dequ16.png), to be read as ‘aleph’, is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet). That is, any set which can be put into one-to-one correspondence with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ17.png)has cardinality <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ18.png). Also, any set which has cardinality <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ19.png)is said to be *countable*, that is the elements can be ‘counted’ through the correspondence with 1, 2, ….
> > 
> > Next observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c009_dequ21.png)is countable, i.e. it has cardinality <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ22.png). To establish this we need to define a one-to-one function that maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c009_dequ23.png)onto <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ24.png). There are many ways of doing this, one example of which is as follows. Define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![f colon double-struck cap z right arrow double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ25.png)as follows:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfenced separators="" open="{" close=""><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="left"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mspace width="1em"/></mtd><mtd columnalign="left"><mtext>if&#160;</mtext><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>![f of x equals case statement case 1column 1 plus plus times times two x one separator if greater than or equals greater than or equals x zero case 2column 1 minus minus times times two x separator if less than less than x zero](images/c009_dequ26.png)
> > 
> > so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![f of zero equals one](images/c009_dequ27.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![f of negative one equals two](images/c009_dequ28.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![f of one equals three](images/c009_dequ29.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![f of negative two equals four](images/c009_dequ30.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![f of two equals five](images/c009_dequ31.png)and so on. It is simple to check that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ32.png)is one-to-one and onto.
> > 
> > So <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c009_dequ33.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ34.png)have the same ‘size’, even though you might think that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![double-struck cap z](images/c009_dequ35.png)contains twice as many elements as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ36.png)! Infinite numbers behave a little strangely. But what about the rationals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ37.png)? Surely the cardinality of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ38.png)is larger than the cardinality of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ39.png)? Surprisingly the answer is no—that is, the rationals are countable.
> > 
> > Setting up the one-to-one correspondence is a little more tricky in this case. In fact, to make life simpler, I will first give a helpful lemma. Before giving the lemma I need to set up some notation. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ40.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>T</mi></math>![cap t](images/c009_dequ41.png)are sets, and suppose there is a one-to-one function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ42.png)from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c009_dequ43.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>B</mi></math>![cap b](images/c009_dequ44.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ45.png)is not necessarily onto). Then we say that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap a less than or equals absolute value of cap b](images/c009_dequ46.png).
> > 
> > Because of the above result, I simply need to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q less than or equals absolute value of double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ66.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap n less than or equals absolute value of double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ67.png). The latter is trivially easy to establish as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap n subset of or equals double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ68.png). It remains to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q less than or equals absolute value of double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ69.png). By definition I need to find a one-to-one function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ70.png)mapping <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ71.png)into <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ72.png). I will start by exhibiting a simple function which maps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></math>![double-struck cap q super plus](images/c009_dequ73.png), the positive rationals, into <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ74.png).
> > 
> > Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/c009_dequ75.png)is a fraction, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a greater than or equals zero](images/c009_dequ76.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![b greater than zero](images/c009_dequ77.png). Then define <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></msup><msup><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![f of a divided by b equals two super a times three super b](images/c009_dequ78.png). Clearly, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a greater than or equals zero](images/c009_dequ79.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![b greater than zero](images/c009_dequ80.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></msup><msup><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi></msup></math>![two super a times three super b](images/c009_dequ81.png)is a positive whole number. Moreover, every distinct pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a comma b right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ82.png)will give a distinct element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ83.png), by the unique factorisation of the integers (see [Theorem 3.3](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0016)). So it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q super plus less than or equals absolute value of double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ84.png). To generalise this result to all of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></math>![double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ85.png), I can simply extend <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/c009_dequ86.png)so that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a divided by b less than zero](images/c009_dequ87.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi></msup><msup><mn>3</mn><mi>b</mi></msup><mn>5</mn></math>![f of a divided by b equals two super a times three super b times five](images/c009_dequ88.png), and we are done.
> > 
> > However, unlike the rationals, the real numbers are not countable, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![multirelation absolute value of double-struck cap r greater than absolute value of double-struck cap n equals absolute value of double-struck cap q](images/c009_dequ89.png). The proof of this result is extremely elegant and simple, and is due to Cantor; it is known as Cantor’s diagonal argument.
> > 
> > The proof actually shows that the real numbers between 0 and 1 (including 0 but excluding 1) are uncountable, and goes as follows. The proof is by contradiction, so we start by supposing that the real numbers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ90.png)satisfying <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![multirelation zero less than or equals x less than one](images/c009_dequ91.png)*are* countable, and hence can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the positive integers 1, 2, 3, ….
> > 
> > The real numbers in this range can all be represented as infinite decimal expansions of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![zero full stop a times b times c times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ93.png), e.g. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.333</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![one solidus three equals 0.333 times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ94.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.500</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![one solidus two equals 0.500 times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ95.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.14159</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![pi minus three equals 0.14159 times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ96.png), and so on. So suppose we use the one-to-one correspondence to put all the real numbers in the range in a numbered list, e.g. something like:
> > 
> > | Integer || Real number |
> > | --- | --- |
> > | 1 || `0.0148934844``…` |
> > | 2 || `0.1258934885``…` |
> > | 3 || `0.2387834832``…` |
> > | 4 || `0.8059021346``…` |
> > | 5 || `0.6789059021``…` |
> > | `…` ||  |
> > 
> > Every real number in the range will appear somewhere in this list, although depending on how the list is put together they won’t necessarily be in ascending order.^()
> > 
> > I will now construct a number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ105.png)which isn’t in the list but yet is in the range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![multirelation zero less than or equals x less than one](images/c009_dequ106.png). The decimal representation of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ107.png)is defined to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![zero full stop a sub one times a sub two times a sub three times a sub four times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ108.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/c009_dequ109.png)is set equal to one more than the digit appearing in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c009_dequ110.png)th position of integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/c009_dequ111.png)in the list (working modulo 10), except if the integer is 8 then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/c009_dequ112.png)is set to 0. So if we use the example list I have just given, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ113.png)will look like:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>0.13001</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![0.13001 times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ114.png)
> > 
> > Why is this? Well <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![a sub one equals one](images/c009_dequ115.png)since the first number in the list has a 0 in the first position in its decimal expansion, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![a sub two equals three](images/c009_dequ116.png)since the second number in the list has a 2 in the second position in its decimal expansion, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![a sub three equals zero](images/c009_dequ117.png)since the third number in the list has an 8 in the third position in its decimal expansion (and 8 is the special case mentioned above) and so on.
> > 
> > It should be clear that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ118.png)is not in the list, since it differs in at least one digit from every number in the list. It is also clearly in the right range, and does not end with nine recurring (since it does not have any nines in its decimal expansion). But the list includes every possible number in the range and hence we have a contradiction. So the real numbers in the range zero to one are uncountable, and so clearly all the real numbers are uncountable.
> > 
> > There is much more that can be said about infinite cardinals, and I mention just two more things. The *algebraic numbers* are all the real numbers that are solutions to equations with rational coefficients. So numbers like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></math>![Square root of two](images/c009_dequ119.png)are algebraic, although they are not rational. However, clearly all rational numbers are algebraic. So if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/c009_dequ120.png)denotes the set of algebraic numbers then
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q less than or equals absolute value of cap a less than or equals absolute value of double-struck cap r full stop](images/c009_dequ121.png)
> > 
> > Clearly we can’t have equality in both cases since we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mo>&#60;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q less than absolute value of double-struck cap r](images/c009_dequ122.png).
> > 
> > It turns out that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap q equals absolute value of cap a](images/c009_dequ123.png), i.e. even the algebraic numbers are countable. So all the weird and wonderful real numbers like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi></math>![pi](images/c009_dequ124.png)(which is not algebraic) are really much more numerous than all the algebraic numbers. That is, the *transcendental* numbers, i.e. all the real numbers that are not algebraic, are uncountable. If you find this hard to get your head around, don’t worry; when the results were first published they caused a major shift in thinking about sets and the nature of infinity.
> > 
> > Finally, you might wonder whether there are even ‘larger’ infinities than the cardinality of the real numbers. Well, this is not immediately obvious, since it is fairly straightforward to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap c equals absolute value of double-struck cap r](images/c009_dequ125.png). So there are ‘the same number’ of complex numbers as there are real numbers.
> > 
> > However, for any set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ126.png), we can define the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi></msup></math>![two super cap s](images/c009_dequ127.png), which consists of all subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ128.png). So if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap s equals left curly bracket one comma two comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ129.png), then
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8709;</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![two super cap s equals left curly bracket normal empty set comma left curly bracket one right curly bracket comma left curly bracket two right curly bracket comma left curly bracket three right curly bracket comma left curly bracket one comma two right curly bracket comma left curly bracket one comma three right curly bracket comma left curly bracket two comma three right curly bracket comma left curly bracket one comma two comma three right curly bracket right curly bracket full stop](images/c009_dequ130.png)
> > 
> > For a finite set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ131.png), it is simple to see that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msup></math>![absolute value of two super cap s equals two super absolute value of cap s](images/c009_dequ132.png)
> > 
> > which explains the notation. To see why this holds simply go through every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ133.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ134.png)in turn, and observe that there are two possibilities for any subset—it either contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/c009_dequ135.png)or it doesn’t. So the number of subsets is simply
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><munder><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo>.</mo></math>![multiplication multiplication multiplication multiplication 22 midline horizontal ellipsis two bottom curly bracket separator separator vertical line vertical line cap s times full stop](images/c009_dequ136.png)
> > 
> > As an example observe that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![absolute value of cap s equals three](images/c009_dequ137.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 absolute value of two super cap s equals part 2 two cubed equals part 3 eight](images/c009_dequ138.png), and I showed that there are eight subsets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ139.png)in the example above.
> > 
> > So for finite non-empty sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ140.png)we clearly have
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>S</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![absolute value of cap s less than absolute value of two super cap s full stop](images/c009_dequ141.png)
> > 
> > It turns out that this inequality also holds for infinite sets, so, for example
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap r less than absolute value of two super double-struck cap r full stop](images/c009_dequ142.png)
> > 
> > The process can be repeated indefinitely, so there is no ‘largest’ infinity.
> > 
> > There is a ‘smallest’ infinity, however, and that is the cardinality of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![double-struck cap n](images/c009_dequ143.png)—which we write as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ144.png). You might also reasonably ask whether there is an infinity larger than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ145.png)but smaller than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap r](images/c009_dequ146.png). The simple answer is that no one knows! It is one of the great unsolved problems of mathematics. The *Continuum Hypothesis* due to Georg Cantor, states that there is no set with cardinality greater than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>&#8501;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>![normal alef sub zero](images/c009_dequ147.png)but less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of double-struck cap r](images/c009_dequ148.png). It turns out that the question of the truth or falsehood of the Continuum Hypothesis cannot be decided with ‘standard’ set theory, and it is possible to build two versions of mathematics—one with the hypothesis true and one with it false; this was established by American mathematician Paul Joseph Cohen, and the result was published in 1965. Intuitively this is beyond weird, but so much for intuition! I should conclude by saying that this is an ongoing area for work by logicians and set theorists, so there is still a lot to be said on this subject, although it’s way beyond my pay grade.
> > 
> > ## 9.3 How Many Prime Numbers Are There?
> > 
> > I now want to revisit integers and prime numbers. I hope you are all familiar with primes, and the series of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …. One obvious question about the primes is whether they ever ‘run out’, i.e. is there a largest prime, or are there more primes no matter how large you get? This problem was resolved in antiquity, and a proof was provided by Euclid in his ‘Elements’.
> > 
> > This proof is very simple and elegant and is one of many beautiful proofs included in the volume *Proofs from the Book* by Austrian mathematician Martin Aigner and German mathematician Günter M Ziegler.^()
> > 
> > The study of prime numbers and their distribution has fascinated mathematicians for millennia, and remains a key part of mathematics today. There are, it seems, endless questions that can be asked, many of which are hard to resolve. One of the most famous results concerns the approximate number of prime numbers less than any given positive integer. Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![pi of n](images/c009_dequ162.png)be the number of primes less than or equal to the positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ163.png). The values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![pi of n](images/c009_dequ164.png)for small <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ165.png)are given in [Table 9.1](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-1).
> > 
> > ![Table 9.1 Values of bold-italic pi of bold-italic n for small bold-italic n.](images/c009_dequ163a.png)
> > 
> > [Table 9.1](#c009.xhtml#rc09-tbl-1) Values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mstyle></math>![bold-italic pi of bold-italic n](images/c009_dequ166.png)for small <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mstyle></math>![bold-italic n](images/c009_dequ163a.png).
> > 
> > By the end of the 18th century mathematicians were already looking at the behaviour of the function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![pi of n](images/c009_dequ173.png)for increasing values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ174.png), and conjecturing how it might behave. In 1798, French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre was the first to conjecture what became known as the Prime Number Theorem (when it was eventually proved a 100 years later).
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > I suspect the statement of this theorem needs some explanation! First, what is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![natural log of n](images/c009_dequ177.png)? This simply means the *natural logarithm* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ178.png), i.e. the logarithm of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ179.png)to the base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c009_dequ180.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8771;</mo><mn>2.71828</mn></math>![e asymptotically equals 2.71828](images/c009_dequ181.png)(<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c009_dequ182.png)is irrational). That is, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![x equals natural log of n](images/c009_dequ183.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![e super x equals n](images/c009_dequ184.png). Second, what do I mean by ∼? This symbol denotes ‘is asymptotic to’, where asymptotic means that the ratio of the expressions on the right and left sides of the symbol gets ever closer to 1 as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ186.png)gets larger and larger. So I could equally have written
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mstyle></math>![pi of n times natural log of n divided by n](images/c009_dequ187.png)
> > 
> > gets ever closer to 1 as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ188.png)gets ever larger.
> > 
> > Building on work by many mathematicians, notably including the renowned German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, in 1896 two French mathematicians independently arrived at a proof for this theorem: Jacques-Salomon Hadamard and Charles de la Valée Poussin. The proofs they came up with involve the theory of complex numbers and are long and difficult. Other proofs have been devised since, but none can be described as simple. A proof which avoids using complex numbers was devised by Norwegian mathematician Atle Selberg and Paul Erdős in 1949; this is referred to as an ‘elementary’ proof since it avoids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></math>![double-struck cap c](images/c009_dequ189.png), but it is far from elementary in the normal sense of the word.
> > 
> > ## 9.4 Difference Sets, Sequences and Finite Geometry
> > 
> > The next ‘extra’ topic I want to introduce is not as famous as the previous two, but is a subject close to my own mathematical interests, and one which relates to many of the themes introduced in this book. The topic is difference sets.
> > 
> > I will start with a simple example. Consider the subset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero comma one comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ190.png)of the integers modulo 7 (i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>7</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub seven](images/c009_dequ191.png)). I am interested here in all the possible differences between pairs of elements of this subset. It is not hard to see that this subset has a rather special property—as summarised in [Table 9.2](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-2), every possible difference occurs exactly once. Note that in the table and throughout this discussion, instead of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![a plus left parenthesis negative b right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ192.png)I have simply written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![a minus b](images/c009_dequ193.png).
> > 
> > [Table 9.2](#c009.xhtml#rc09-tbl-2) The difference set {0, 1, 3} in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>7</mn></msub></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub seven](images/c009_dequ195.png).
> > 
> > | Pair of elements || Difference |
> > | --- | --- |
> > | 1 − 0 || 1 |
> > | --- | --- |
> > | 3 − 0 || 3 |
> > | 0 − 1 || 6 |
> > | 3 − 1 || 2 |
> > | 0 − 3 || 4 |
> > | 1 − 3 || 5 |
> > 
> > This subset is called a (7,3,1)-difference set because the overall set is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>7</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub seven](images/c009_dequ202.png), the subset is of size 3, and every possible difference occurs exactly once. More generally, if the set from which elements are drawn contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math>![v](images/c009_dequ203.png)elements, the subset has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c009_dequ204.png)elements, and every possible difference occurs exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ205.png)times, then it is called it a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis v comma k comma lamda right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ206.png)\-difference set.
> > 
> > Another example of a difference set is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![cap d equals left curly bracket zero comma two comma three comma four comma eight right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ207.png), which is an (11,5,2)-difference set for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub 11 comma plus right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ208.png). The 20 possible differences, giving each of the non-zero elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ209.png)twice, are summarised in [Table 9.3](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-3). I leave you to check it works!
> > 
> > ![Table 9.3 The difference set {0, 2, 3, 4, 8} in double-struck cap z sub 11.](images/c009_dequ211.png)
> > 
> > [Table 9.3](#c009.xhtml#rc09-tbl-3) The difference set {0, 2, 3, 4, 8} in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></mstyle></math>![double-struck cap z sub 11](images/c009_dequ210.png).
> > 
> > In fact the idea of a difference set can be defined for a subset of any finite group, and not just the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub v comma plus right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ235.png). That is, a *difference set* <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ236.png)is a subset of the elements of a finite group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ237.png)with the following very special property. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi></math>![absolute value of cap g equals v](images/c009_dequ238.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![absolute value of cap d equals k](images/c009_dequ239.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ240.png)is said to be a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis v comma k comma lamda right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ241.png)\-difference set if every element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ242.png)(apart from the identity element) can be expressed as a product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![d asterisk operator e super negative one](images/c009_dequ243.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/c009_dequ244.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c009_dequ245.png)are distinct elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ246.png), in exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ247.png)ways.
> > 
> > If the group operation is written additively, as would be the case if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub v comma plus right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ248.png)for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math>![v](images/c009_dequ249.png), then the definition can be equivalently stated as follows. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ250.png)is said to be a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis v comma k comma lamda right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ251.png)\-difference set if every element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ252.png)(apart from the identity element) can be expressed as a sum <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d plus left parenthesis negative e right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ253.png), where <math
