display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c009_dequ255.png)are distinct elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ256.png), in exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ257.png)ways. In such a case it is normal to simply write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![d minus e](images/c009_dequ258.png)instead of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d plus left parenthesis negative e right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ259.png), as I have in the examples, and so this means every element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ260.png)occurs as a *difference* between two elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ261.png)in exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ262.png)ways. This, I hope, explains why they are called *difference sets*.
> > 
> > The following simple result constrains the possible values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math>![v](images/c009_dequ263.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/c009_dequ264.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ265.png).
> > 
> >  
> > 
> > There are a number of reasons why difference sets are of interest. I will briefly describe two of them. The first relates to finite geometry. I should first explain what I mean by the term. For my purposes here, a finite geometry is simply a pair of finite sets called *points* and *lines* and a relation between them called *incidence*. That is, a point is either incident with a line or it isn’t. So a finite geometry <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi></math>![script cap p](images/c009_dequ280.png)can be defined as a triple <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap p comma cap l comma cap i right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ281.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c009_dequ282.png)is the set of points, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>L</mi></math>![cap l](images/c009_dequ283.png)is the set of lines and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>I</mi></math>![cap i](images/c009_dequ284.png)is the incidence relation between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/c009_dequ285.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>L</mi></math>![cap l](images/c009_dequ286.png). I will use the common geometric terminology and refer to a point being on a line or a line going through a point if the point and line are incident.
> > 
> > Perhaps surprisingly, such a simple definition gives rise to a wealth of possibilities. A particularly important class of finite geometries consists of what are known as the *finite projective planes*. A finite projective plane is a finite geometry with the following three key properties:
> > 
> > *   the number of lines is the same as the number of points (and the sets have cardinality at least two);
> > *   every line has the same number of points incident with it;
> > *   for every pair of points there is a unique line that is incident with them both.
> > 
> > The following simple result follows without difficulty.
> > 
> > A simple example with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![n equals two](images/c009_dequ368.png), i.e. where there are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![sum with 3 summands two squared plus two plus one equals seven](images/c009_dequ369.png)points and lines and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![two squared plus one equals three](images/c009_dequ370.png)points on a line and lines on a point, is given in [Table 9.4](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-4).
> > 
> > ![Table 9.4 A projective plane for bold-italic n equals two full stop](images/c009_dequ372.png)
> > 
> > [Table 9.4](#c009.xhtml#rc09-tbl-4) A projective plane for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mstyle mathvariant="bold"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2.</mn></mstyle></math>![bold-italic n equals two full stop](images/c009_dequ371.png)
> > 
> > This very simple projective plane is known as the Fano Plane after the Italian mathematician Gino Fano,^() ![Figure 9.1 The Fano plane.](images/c09f001.png)
> > 
> > [Figure 9.1](#c009.xhtml#rc09-fig-1) The Fano plane.
> > 
> > The study of finite projective planes is an area of mathematics in its own right. Before moving on I will just mention that there are plenty of examples of projective planes with order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c009_dequ379.png), whenever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/c009_dequ380.png)is a power of a prime. However, there are no known projective planes with order not equal to a power of a prime; whether there might exist such a projective plane is not known. The non-existence of a projective plane of order 6 (the smallest case) is a simple corollary of the fact that the 36 officers problem^()
> > 
> > So why have I suddenly introduced projective planes when I was talking about difference sets? Perhaps you have guessed already. Difference sets with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![lamda equals one](images/c009_dequ382.png)can be used to construct projective planes (but not always the other way round). Indeed, the difference set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero comma one comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ383.png)summarised in [Table 9.2](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-2) was used to construct the Fano Plane. In [Table 9.4](#c009.xhtml#c09-tbl-4), seven sets of points are all derived from this difference set by adding a constant to each element, i.e. the sets of points are simply
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero plus i comma one plus i comma three plus i right curly bracket comma](images/c009_dequ384.png)
> > 
> > for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![i equals zero comma one comma ellipsis comma six](images/c009_dequ385.png).
> > 
> > This method of going from a difference set to a projective plane always works, as I now show.
> > 
> > The notion of a projective plane can be generalised to something known as a symmetric <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![two minus left parenthesis v comma k comma lamda right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ412.png)design. The definition is identical to that of a projective plane except that every pair of points is incident with exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/c009_dequ413.png)lines^()
> > 
> > Symmetric designs are interesting in their own right as combinatorial structures; however, they are also of practical importance in statistics, and in particular in the design of experiments. Indeed, this application motivated their study in the first place.
> > 
> > The second reason that difference sets are interesting relates to the construction of binary sequences with interesting and useful properties. A difference set over the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/c009_dequ418.png)can be used to construct a binary sequence in a very simple way.
> > 
> > As an example, take the difference set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket zero comma one comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ519.png)over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>7</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub seven](images/c009_dequ520.png). This will yield the following binary sequence of period 7:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>1101000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1101000</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>1101</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![1101000 1101000 1101 times ellipsis](images/c009_dequ521.png)
> > 
> > Suppose we compare one period of this sequence with itself shifted one place to the left, as shown immediately below:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtable columnalign="center center center center center center center" columnspacing="1em"><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo>+</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>&#8722;</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>&#8722;</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>&#8722;</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>+</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>+</mo></mtd><mtd><mo>&#8722;</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></math>![matrix row 1column 1 1101000 row 2column 1 1010001 row 3column 1 plus minus minus minus plus plus minus full stop](images/c009_dequ522.png)
> > 
> > For each position I have put a ‘+’ underneath if the two digits agree and a ‘–’ if they disagree. The autocorrelation is equal to the numbers of agreements minus the number of disagreements, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![three minus four equals negative one](images/c009_dequ523.png). The lemma states that this should be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![v minus four times left parenthesis k minus lamda right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ524.png), and since in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![v equals seven](images/c009_dequ525.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![k equals three](images/c009_dequ526.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![lamda equals one](images/c009_dequ527.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 v minus four times left parenthesis k minus lamda right parenthesis equals part 2 seven minus four multiplication left parenthesis three minus one right parenthesis equals part 3 negative one](images/c009_dequ528.png), so we get the expected result. You can check that the same occurs for every possible shift.
> > 
> > Sequences with the R3 property have a range of applications in digital communications, meaning that difference sets are not only interesting from a mathematical point of view, but are also highly relevant to real world communications engineering.
> > 
> > In [Lemma 9.4](#c009.xhtml#c009-sec-0011), I showed that a difference set over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub v](images/c009_dequ529.png)can be used to construct a binary sequence of period <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math>![v](images/c009_dequ530.png)with constant out-of-phase autocorrelation. However, this is only half the story. The reverse is also true—that is, the following result holds.
> > 
> > Note that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>D</mi></math>![cap d](images/c009_dequ543.png)contains the bit positions of the ones in the sequence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/c009_dequ544.png). The proof is straightforward and I leave this as an exercise. The full proof is given in the ‘[Answers to Questions for the Reader](#b01.xhtml)’—see page 249.
> > 
> > To show how this works consider the following example of a binary sequence of period 15, taken from [Section 7.4.3](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0016).
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mn>00110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10001</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>00110</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>10111</mn><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8230;</mo></math>![00110 10111 10001 00110 10111 ellipsis](images/c009_dequ545.png)
> > 
> > It is simple to see that ones appear in bit positions 2,3,5,7,8,9,10 and 14. So it follows immediately that {2,3,5,7,8,9,10,14} is a difference set. The parameters are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis 15 comma eight comma four right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ546.png), that is, every number in the range 1 up to 14 occurs four times as a difference. Just to take an arbitrary example, 3 occurs as a difference four times, namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>14</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 three equals part 2 five minus two equals part 3 eight minus five equals part 4 10 minus seven equals part 5 two minus 14](images/c009_dequ547.png)(working modulo 15, of course). I leave you to check the other cases!
> > 
> > The reason this works is that this sequence is an m-sequence, and all m-sequences satisfy Golomb’s randomness postulate R3 (see [Section 7.4.4](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0018)). That means that all binary m-sequences can be used to create a difference set by [Lemma 9.5](#c009.xhtml#c009-sec-0012).
> > 
> > Now binary m-sequences of period <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super n minus one](images/c009_dequ548.png)exist for every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ549.png), they contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![two super n minus one](images/c009_dequ550.png)ones in a period, and out-of-phase autocorrelation^()
> > 
> > This is by no means the only way of constructing difference sets. Indeed, there are a wide range of methods, and finding new difference sets remains an area of active research. However, exploring this further would be well beyond the scope of this book, and so regrettably I must stop here.
> > 
> > ## 9.5 Finite Simple Groups
> > 
> > The very final topic I want to briefly explore relates to finite groups, and is one of the greatest mathematical achievements of the second half of the 20th century. This achievement is the classification of all finite simple groups.
> > 
> > To explain what this means I first need to tell you want a simple group is, although to get there I first need to introduce some other ideas. As I explained in [Section 5.5](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0008), if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ554.png)is a group, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap h equals left parenthesis cap h comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ555.png)is a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ556.png)if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![cap h subset of or equals cap g](images/c009_dequ557.png)and the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ558.png)form a group under the operation \*. I also defined the notion of a *coset*, where if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap h equals left parenthesis cap h comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ559.png)is a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ560.png), then the coset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![cap h asterisk operator a](images/c009_dequ561.png)is the set of all elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ562.png)of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![h asterisk operator a](images/c009_dequ563.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![h element of cap h](images/c009_dequ564.png). I need to go a little further here and introduce the notion of right and left cosets. What I have just defined is a *right coset* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ565.png). A *left coset*, written <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![a asterisk operator cap h](images/c009_dequ566.png)is simply the set of all elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ567.png)of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>h</mi></math>![a asterisk operator h](images/c009_dequ568.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![h element of cap h](images/c009_dequ569.png).
> > 
> > Of course, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ570.png)is abelian, i.e. a group for which the operation is commutative, then a left coset is exactly the same as a right coset, but in general this won’t be true.
> > 
> > I can now make a key definition. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap h equals left parenthesis cap h comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ571.png)is a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ572.png); <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></math>![script cap h](images/c009_dequ573.png)is said to be a *normal subgroup* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ574.png)if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![a asterisk operator cap h equals cap h asterisk operator a](images/c009_dequ575.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![a element of cap g](images/c009_dequ576.png). That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></math>![script cap h](images/c009_dequ577.png)is a normal subgroup if all the left cosets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ578.png)are the same as the right cosets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ579.png). It is common to write <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8884;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow></math>![script cap h normal subgroup of or equals script cap g](images/c009_dequ580.png)to indicate that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></math>![script cap h](images/c009_dequ581.png)is a normal subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ582.png).
> > 
> > Of course, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ583.png)is abelian then, as I just noted, left cosets and right cosets are automatically the same, so all subgroups of an abelian group are normal. However, the definition becomes more interesting for non-abelian groups.
> > 
> > A simple example is provided by the group of permutations of the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma three right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ584.png), described back in [Section 5.7.2](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0017). This group, usually referred to as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ585.png), has six elements and is non-abelian. The six elements are

comma](images/c009_dequ586.png)
> > 
> > where the first element in the list is the identity element in the group (it maps 1 to 1, 2 to 2 and 3 to 3). Three of the elements, namely
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math>![matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 123 comma matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 231 comma matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 312 comma](images/c009_dequ587.png)
> > 
> > form a subgroup known as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ588.png), which is a normal subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ589.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8884;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three normal subgroup of or equals cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ590.png). It is simple to check it forms a subgroup since the two non-identity elements are inverses of each other. One way of showing it is a normal subgroup is to observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ591.png)is half the size of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ592.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 absolute value of cap s sub three solidus absolute value of cap a sub three equals part 2 six solidus three equals part 3 two](images/c009_dequ593.png). Now, since a (left or right) coset of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ594.png)will always have the same number of elements as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ595.png)(see [Section 5.5](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0008)), there are only two possible right cosets and two possible left cosets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ596.png). One of the two will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ597.png)itself, and so the other left coset and the other right coset must be the same, consisting of all the elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ598.png)not in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ599.png)! This argument immediately gives us the more general result that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap h equals left parenthesis cap h comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ600.png)is a subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ601.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![absolute value of cap g solidus absolute value of cap h equals two](images/c009_dequ602.png), it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></math>![script cap h](images/c009_dequ603.png)will always be a normal subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ604.png).
> > 
> > The subgroup <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub three](images/c009_dequ605.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ606.png)consists of all the *even permutations* in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ607.png). Odd and even permutations can be defined in the following way. First define the identity permutation to be an even permutation. Next, consider the ‘simplest’ possible permutations, namely those that interchange two elements but otherwise leave everything unchanged—these are known as *transpositions*. For example, in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math>![cap s sub three](images/c009_dequ608.png)the following three permutations are transpositions:
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mtable align="axis" style="" equalrows="false" columnlines="none none none none none none none none none" equalcolumns="false" rowlines="none none none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>2</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mn>3</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math>![matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 132 comma matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 321 comma matrix row 1column 1 123 row 2column 1 213 full stop](images/c009_dequ609.png)
> > 
> > All transpositions are defined to be ‘odd’ permutations.
> > 
> > Working on from there, the product of two transpositions is, as you might expect, an even permutation; the product of three transpositions is an odd permutation; and so on. We can define when every permutation is odd or even in this way, since every permutation can be expressed as a product of transpositions. When expressing a permutation in terms of transpositions, oddness and evenness is preserved, no matter how you might express it.
> > 
> > As I described in [Section 5.7.2](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0017), the set of all permutations on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma ellipsis comma n right curly bracket](images/c009_dequ610.png)is known as the symmetric group and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub n](images/c009_dequ611.png); the order of this group is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n factorial equals n multiplication n minus one multiplication ellipsis multiplication two multiplication one](images/c009_dequ612.png). The set of all even permutations in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub n](images/c009_dequ613.png)always forms a subgroup known as the alternating group, and is denoted by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ614.png). There are always the same number of odd and even permutations, and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 absolute value of cap a sub n equals part 2 absolute value of cap s sub n solidus two equals part 3 n factorial prefix solidus of two](images/c009_dequ615.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ616.png). Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap s sub n equals two times absolute value of cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ617.png), this means that, as above, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ618.png)is always a normal subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap s sub n](images/c009_dequ619.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8884;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n normal subgroup of or equals cap s sub n](images/c009_dequ620.png).
> > 
> > I can now define the key term for this discussion. A group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ621.png)is said to be *simple* if the only normal subgroups are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/c009_dequ622.png)itself and the trivial subgroup containing just the identity element. It turns out that simple groups are fundamental to understanding the possible structure of finite groups.
> > 
> > So which groups are simple? Well, any group which has no non-trivial subgroups must be simple, and hence the cyclic groups of prime order (often written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></math>![cap c sub p](images/c009_dequ623.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/c009_dequ624.png)prime) must be simple. This follows since the order of a subgroup divides the order of a group (see [Theorem 5.2](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0010)), and if the order is prime then a subgroup can only have order the prime itself or one.
> > 
> > A more interesting family of simple groups is provided by the alternating groups <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ625.png). It can be shown (although the details are well beyond the scope of this book) that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ626.png)is simple for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n greater than or equals five](images/c009_dequ627.png). The fact that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></math>![cap a sub five](images/c009_dequ628.png)is simple was first shown by Évariste Galois, although the full importance of simple groups in the understanding of finite groups only emerged in the 20th century.
> > 
> > I need one further definition before I can give the key results establishing the fundamental role of simple groups, namely that of a quotient group. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap h equals left parenthesis cap h comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ629.png)is a normal subgroup of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ630.png). Then we define the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![cap g solidus cap h](images/c009_dequ631.png)to consist of all the right cosets of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ632.png)(which will be the same as the set of left cosets, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></mrow><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo>&#8884;</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></mrow></math>![script cap h normal subgroup of or equals script cap g](images/c009_dequ633.png)). The set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![cap g solidus cap h](images/c009_dequ634.png)will contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>/</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap g solidus absolute value of cap h](images/c009_dequ635.png)elements, since every coset will contain <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap h](images/c009_dequ636.png)elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ637.png). We can now define an operation ⋅ on the set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![cap g solidus cap h](images/c009_dequ639.png)in the following way.
> > 
> > Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![cap h asterisk operator a](images/c009_dequ640.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![cap h asterisk operator b](images/c009_dequ641.png)are two elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![cap g solidus cap h](images/c009_dequ642.png). Then define
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator b right parenthesis equals cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator b right parenthesis full stop](images/c009_dequ643.png)
> > 
> > I claim that this operation on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi></math>![cap g solidus cap h](images/c009_dequ644.png)satisfies the axioms of a group, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap g solidus cap h comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ645.png)is a group.^()
> > 
> > First observe that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator b right parenthesis asterisk operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator c right parenthesis right parenthesis equals part 2 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis b asterisk operator c right parenthesis right parenthesis equals part 3 cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator left parenthesis b asterisk operator c right parenthesis right parenthesis comma](images/c009_dequ646.png)
> > 
> > by the definition of ⋅. Similarly
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator b right parenthesis right parenthesis asterisk operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator c right parenthesis equals part 2 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator b right parenthesis right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator c right parenthesis equals part 3 cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis left parenthesis a asterisk operator b right parenthesis asterisk operator c right parenthesis right parenthesis full stop](images/c009_dequ648.png)
> > 
> > But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ649.png)is a group, and hence \* satisfies the associative law. Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator left parenthesis b asterisk operator c right parenthesis right parenthesis equals cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis left parenthesis a asterisk operator b right parenthesis asterisk operator c right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ650.png)and so ⋅ is associative.
> > 
> > The identity element is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi></math>![cap h](images/c009_dequ652.png), since
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator cap h equals part 2 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator e right parenthesis equals part 3 cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator e right parenthesis equals part 4 cap h asterisk operator a comma](images/c009_dequ653.png)
> > 
> > where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/c009_dequ654.png)is the identity element in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ655.png).
> > 
> > Finally, the inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi></math>![cap h asterisk operator a](images/c009_dequ656.png)is simply <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a super negative one right parenthesis](images/c009_dequ657.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![a super negative one](images/c009_dequ658.png)is the inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/c009_dequ659.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/c009_dequ660.png). To see this, observe that
> > 
> > <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 left parenthesis cap h asterisk operator a right parenthesis dot operator cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a super negative one right parenthesis equals part 2 cap h asterisk operator left parenthesis a asterisk operator a super negative one right parenthesis equals part 3 cap h asterisk operator e equals part 4 cap h full stop](images/c009_dequ661.png)
> > 
> > I can now explain why simple groups play such a central role in the study of groups. The key facts that make simple groups so important are encapsulated in the following two theorems, which I give without proof.^()
> > 
> > This is complemented by the following fundamentally important theorem due to French mathematician Marie Ennemond Camille Jordan and German mathematician Ludwig Otto Hölder.
> > 
> > It is important to observe that although a group can have two different composition series, and two different groups can have the same composition series, the Jordan–Hölder Theorem means that any two composition series are equivalent up to the ordering of the composition factors.
> > 
> > The above results mean that the finite simple groups are in a sense the ‘atoms’ or building blocks of all finite groups, a little like prime numbers for the integers or irreducible polynomials for polynomials. So, if you understand all the possible finite simple groups, you have a handle on understanding *all* the finite groups. As a result, during much of the 20th century the most high profile problem in finite group theory has been to classify all the finite simple groups. The problem was finally solved only in the last few decades of the 20th century. So what are the finite simple groups?
> > 
> > I already mentioned two infinite families of simple groups which have long been known, namely the cyclic groups of prime order and the alternating groups <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![cap a sub n](images/c009_dequ668.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![n greater than or equals five](images/c009_dequ669.png). There are two further infinite classes of finite simple groups. These are the ‘classical groups’, i.e. matrix groups over a range of fields, and the exceptional groups of Lie type (terminology I won’t even try to explain)! These were all known by the early 1960s, together with a small number of so-called *sporadic* finite simple groups, notably including the five Mathieu groups, named after their discoverer 19th-century French mathematician Émile Léonard Mathieu. These are called sporadic as they are not obviously part of any of the infinite families.
> > 
> > At the turn of the 20th century, British mathematician William Burnside conjectured that all the non-abelian finite simple groups must have even order. It was only proved true in 1962–1963, by Austrian-American mathematician Walter Feit and American mathematician John Griggs Thompson. Their proof, which covers over 250 pages, helped give impetus to the project to classify all the finite simple groups.
> > 
> > American mathematician Daniel Gorenstein was the organiser of the coordinated effort. During the 1960s and 1970s, as work proceeded, further sporadic simple groups were discovered, bringing the total of such groups to 26 (apart from the five Mathieu groups, they were all discovered after 1965). Perhaps the most remarkable of these sporadic groups, and the last to be found, is that known as the ‘Monster’, discovered by American mathematician Robert Griess and announced in 1980. It is enormous having order
> > 
> > > 808,017,424,794,512,875,886,459,904,961,710,757,005,754,368,000,000,000≃ 8 × 10^(53).
> > 
> > The monster group contains 20 sporadic groups (including itself) as sub-quotients.
> > 
> > The classification theorem of finite simple groups (or simply *CFSG*) states that there are no more. That is, the only finite simple groups are the known infinite families and the 26 sporadic groups. It is difficult to give a single date as to when this theorem was proved. The proof involves tens of thousands of pages in several hundred different research papers written by many tens of authors, where these papers were mostly published between 1955 and 2004. Indeed, in his book (mentioned above), Robert Wilson makes the following statement.
> > 
> > > There has been much debate about whether CFSG deserves to be called a theorem, and this debate has contributed to the philosophical arguments about what a theorem is, what a proof is, what mathematics is (or are) and how we recognise them when we see them.
> > > 
> > > …
> > > 
> > > So what of the CFSG? Has it indeed been proved? Certainly the process of collating the various parts of the proof, filling in the gaps and correcting errors, has taken longer than anyone expected when the imminent completion of the proof was announced around 1980. The project by Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon to write down the whole \[the so-called *second generation*\] proof is still in progress; six of a projected eleven volumes have been published so far.^()
> > > 
> > > I’m afraid I will have to leave the final topic of this book there. This brief account only just scratches the surface of what is a huge topic, with many implications for other parts of group theory. However, before finishing I must just mention one other book, namely the Atlas of Finite Groups, by John Horton Conway, Robert Turner Curtis, Simon Phillips Norton, Richard Alan Parker and Robert Arnott Wilson.^()
> > >

This book is intended to collect ‘brilliant ideas, clever insights and wonderful observations’. It derives from an idea of the great Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős. To quote the preface from the book ‘Paul Erdős liked to talk about The Book, in which God maintains the perfect proofs for mathematical theorems, following the dictum of G H Hardy that there is no permanent place for ugly mathematics. Erdős also said that you need not believe in God but, as a mathematician, you should believe in the book.’ I think almost every mathematician believes in The Book, at least to some extent, in that there is something wonderful about certain proofs.

I am pleased to report that I have an Erdős number of three, thanks to having co-authored papers with Don Coppersmith and Jonathan Jedwab (who both have an Erdős number of two). In fact, arguably I have an Erdős number of two via a brief editorial co-authored with Canadian mathematician Ronald Cleveland Mullin who has an Erdős number of one, but I think this is cheating as it’s not a research paper.

[6](#c009.xhtml#rfn_6) The 36 officers problem involves trying to arrange 36 army officers from six regiments and with six different ranks in a six by six square such that no two officers from the same regiment and with the same rank appear in any row or column. In 1782, Leonhard Euler wrote ‘After we have put a lot of thought into finding a solution, we have to admit that such an arrangement is impossible, though we can’t give a rigorous demonstration of this’. The corresponding problem for an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ685.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ686.png)grid *does* have a solution for all positive integers <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ687.png)except for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![n equals two](images/c009_dequ688.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![n equals six](images/c009_dequ689.png). As a first step towards showing this, the Cayley Table for any group of odd order can be used to construct a solution for any odd <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ690.png). However, the situation is not so simple for even <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ691.png). Euler conjectured that the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ692.png)squared officers problem was insoluble whenever <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ693.png)is congruent to 2 modulo 4. It wasn’t until 1959 that the two great Indian mathematicians and statisticians Raj Chandra Bose and Sharadchandra Shankar Shrikhande disproved Euler’s conjecture by finding a solution for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn></math>![n equals 22](images/c009_dequ694.png). Shortly afterwards, they (along with American mathematician Ernest Tilden Parker) published a paper showing the existence of a solution to the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/c009_dequ695.png)squared officers problem for all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![n greater than or equals seven](images/c009_dequ696.png).
> > > 7.  [7](#c009.xhtml#rfn_7) In fact, the word *block* is used instead of line in the literature for symmetric designs, but we need not worry about that here.
> > > 8.  [8](#c009.xhtml#rfn_8) I never previously stated that the out-of-phase autocorrelation of an m-sequence is −1. However, I did observe that the modulo 2 sum of an m-sequence with a shift of itself yields another shift of the same sequence. When adding a sequence to a shift of itself, a zero results if the two bits agree and a one results if they disagree. Now the autocorrelation of an m-sequence is equal to the number of agreements minus the number of disagreements, which must equal the number of zeros minus the number of ones in a period of the m-sequence, which equals −1.

# Answers to Questions for the Reader

## Sets and Relations

### Balls in the Bag Probabilities

In [Section 2.2](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0002), I made a claim about a ‘balls in the bag’ probability question. This is closely related to something known as Bertrand’s box paradox, after the 19th-century French mathematician Joseph Louis François Bertrand. Suppose the two balls are labelled <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ1.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ2.png). We supposed that the probability that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ3.png)is white and the probability that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ4.png)is white are both equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by two](images/b01_dequ5.png)(i.e. 0.5 or 50%, whichever you prefer).

So there are four cases to consider, each with probability 1/4:

*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ6.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ7.png)are both black;
*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ8.png)is black and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ9.png)is white;
*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ10.png)is white and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ11.png)is black;
*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ12.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ13.png)are both white.

When you draw out a ball I assume that it is equally likely to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ14.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ15.png). That is, there are eight possible events that could occur when you draw out a ball, each with probability 1/8:

1.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ16.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ17.png)are both black, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ18.png);
2.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ19.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ20.png)are both black, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ21.png);
3.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ22.png)is black and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ23.png)is white, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ24.png);
4.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ25.png)is black and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ26.png)is white, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ27.png);
5.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ28.png)is white and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ29.png)is black, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ30.png);
6.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ31.png)is white and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ32.png)is black, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ33.png);
7.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ34.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ35.png)are both white, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ36.png);
8.  <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![b sub one](images/b01_dequ37.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ38.png)are both white, and you draw out <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![b sub two](images/b01_dequ39.png).

Since the ball you draw out is actually black, clearly what has occurred is one of events 1, 2, 3 and 6 from the above list, all of which are equally probable (probability 1/4). But what about the other ball? Well, if events 1 or 2 have occurred (total probability 1/2), then the remaining ball is black. If events 3 or 6 have occurred (total probability 1/2) then the remaining ball is white, i.e. I have proved the required result.

There are many other examples of simple probability calculations which give non-obvious results. Perhaps the most well-known is the so-called Monty Hall problem, which has been very widely discussed.^()

### The Definition of an Equivalence Relation

In [Section 2.5](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0006), I gave an argument suggesting that we can simplify the definition of an equivalence relation to be one which just satisfies symmetry and transitivity, since reflexivity can be deduced from the other two properties. Why is this argument wrong?

In the argument I gave, I started by saying ‘Choose any element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ40.png), and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/b01_dequ41.png)be any other element in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>S</mi></math>![cap s](images/b01_dequ42.png)for which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>y</mi></math>![x times cap r times y](images/b01_dequ43.png)’. However, it’s incorrect to say this, since there may not be such an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/b01_dequ44.png). That is, the element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ45.png)may not be related to any other element of the set, in which case a suitable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi></math>![y](images/b01_dequ46.png)wouldn’t exist. In this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>R</mi><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>x</mi></math>![x times cap r times x](images/b01_dequ47.png)will not be true, and so reflexivity does not hold. That is, even if we assume symmetry and transitivity we also need to assume the reflexive property.

### Composing Functions

[Section 2.7](#c002.xhtml#c002-sec-0009) contains the following lemma, for which I now provide a proof.

I also claimed that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/b01_dequ80.png)is one-to-one then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ81.png)need not be, and if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/b01_dequ82.png)is onto then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/b01_dequ83.png)need not be. Consider the following pair of functions:

*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi></math>![f colon double-struck cap n right arrow double-struck cap z](images/b01_dequ84.png)defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![f of x equals x](images/b01_dequ85.png);
*   <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></math>![g colon double-struck cap z right arrow double-struck cap n](images/b01_dequ86.png)defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![g of x equals absolute value of x](images/b01_dequ87.png)(where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of x](images/b01_dequ88.png)is the absolute value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ89.png)).

Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/b01_dequ90.png)is not onto, since negative integers and zero do not have a pre-image under <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math>![f](images/b01_dequ91.png). Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ92.png)is not one-to-one since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of negative x equals g of x](images/b01_dequ93.png)for any integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ94.png). However, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/b01_dequ95.png)is both one-to-one and onto. In fact, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![f ring operator g](images/b01_dequ96.png)is the identity function, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![left parenthesis f ring operator g right parenthesis times left parenthesis x right parenthesis equals x](images/b01_dequ97.png)for every positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ98.png).

## Numbers as We Know and Love Them

### Least Elements

In [Chapter 3](#c003.xhtml#c003), I claimed that it is simple to prove that the set
