<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>y</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo>:</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>}</mo></mrow></math>![cap a equals left curly bracket one divided by y colon y element of double-struck cap z super plus right curly bracket](images/b01_dequ99.png)

does not have a least element, using a reductio ad absurdum argument. One possible argument of this type goes as follows.

> Suppose that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/b01_dequ100.png)*does* have a least element. By definition of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/b01_dequ101.png)this must equal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by x](images/b01_dequ102.png)for some positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ103.png). But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/b01_dequ104.png)also contains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by x plus one](images/b01_dequ105.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by x plus one less than one divided by x](images/b01_dequ106.png), contradicting our assumption that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![one divided by x](images/b01_dequ107.png)is the least element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/b01_dequ108.png). This is the desired contradiction, so we have shown that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>A</mi></math>![cap a](images/b01_dequ109.png)does not have a least element.

### A Flawed Induction Argument

Later in the same chapter (in [Section 3.5](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0006)), I gave the following induction argument.

> Suppose the statement <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/b01_dequ110.png)is ‘Every group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ111.png)people have the same name’. To prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of n](images/b01_dequ112.png)is true for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n greater than or equals one](images/b01_dequ113.png)we need to show that (a) <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/b01_dequ114.png)is true, and (b) if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/b01_dequ115.png)is true then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p times left parenthesis k plus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ116.png)is true. Now <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of one](images/b01_dequ117.png)is clearly true since one person clearly has the same name as themselves. Now suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/b01_dequ118.png)is true, i.e. we know that any group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/b01_dequ119.png)people always have the same name. Now consider any group of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k plus one](images/b01_dequ120.png)people, and suppose they line up in order. We know that the first <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/b01_dequ121.png)people have the same name (since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap p of k](images/b01_dequ122.png)is true), and also that the last <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/b01_dequ123.png)people have the same name. Thus all <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k plus one](images/b01_dequ124.png)people must have the same name.

So where is the mistake? The problem comes in moving from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k equals one](images/b01_dequ125.png)to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![k plus one equals two](images/b01_dequ126.png). There won’t be any overlap between the set of the first <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/b01_dequ127.png)people and the set of the last <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi></math>![k](images/b01_dequ128.png)people. So we can’t conclude that any set of two people will have the same name (not surprisingly, perhaps)!

### Prime Divisors

In [Section 3.7](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0010), I stated the following lemma.

### Defining the Rationals

[Section 3.10](#c003.xhtml#c003-sec-0020) contains the claim that the relation ∼, defined on the fractions, is an equivalence relation. Recall that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b](images/b01_dequ155.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![c divided by d](images/b01_dequ156.png)are two fractions, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator c divided by d](images/b01_dequ157.png)if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times d equals b times c](images/b01_dequ158.png). The three properties of an equivalence relation (reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity) hold for ∼ for the following reasons.

*   Reflexivity holds, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator a divided by b](images/b01_dequ160.png), since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>a</mi></math>![a times b equals b times a](images/b01_dequ161.png).
*   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator c divided by d](images/b01_dequ162.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times d equals b times c](images/b01_dequ163.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></math>![c times b equals d times a](images/b01_dequ164.png)and thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![c divided by d tilde operator a divided by b](images/b01_dequ165.png)(showing symmetry).
*   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator c divided by d](images/b01_dequ166.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![c divided by d tilde operator e divided by f](images/b01_dequ167.png)then, by definition, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></math>![a times d equals b times c](images/b01_dequ168.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></math>![c times f equals d times e](images/b01_dequ169.png). Multiplying the two equations together we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></math>![a times d times c times f equals b times c times d times e](images/b01_dequ170.png). Rearranging and cancelling <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></math>![c times d](images/b01_dequ171.png)from both sides we arrive at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>e</mi></math>![a times f equals b times e](images/b01_dequ172.png). But this implies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8764;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>![a divided by b tilde operator e divided by f](images/b01_dequ173.png), showing that transitivity holds.

 

## Modular Arithmetic on the Integers

### Properties of the MOD 11-2 Check Digit

In [Section 4.4](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0005), I stated that the MOD 11-2 method means that any single numerical error, as well as any transposition of adjacent digits (as well as transposition of digits separated by one other digit) will be detected by the check digit. That is, if any of these types of error occur then the check digit calculation will give the wrong result, and hence the error will be detected.

There are two claims here.

*   The first is that any single numerical error will be detected, as is the case for the binary check digit.
*   The second is that ‘localised’ transpositions will be detected.

To justify these claims I need to look a little more at the definition of the MOD 11-2 check digit. As stated in [Chapter 4](#c004.xhtml#c004), if the sequence of digits to be protected against error is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a sub n comma a sub n minus one comma ellipsis comma a sub two right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ176.png)then the check digit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![a sub one](images/b01_dequ177.png)is computed so that the following equation holds:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![sum with variable number of summands a sub one plus two times a sub two plus two squared times a sub three plus ellipsis plus two super n minus one times a sub n identical to one times left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis full stop](images/b01_dequ178.png)

The number 2 was not chosen at random. If we look at the values of successive powers of 2 (working modulo 11), we see that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![two super one identical to two](images/b01_dequ179.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![two squared identical to four](images/b01_dequ180.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>8</mn></math>![two cubed identical to eight](images/b01_dequ181.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![two super four identical to five](images/b01_dequ182.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>10</mn></math>![two super five identical to 10](images/b01_dequ183.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>9</mn></math>![two super six identical to nine](images/b01_dequ184.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>7</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>7</mn></math>![two super seven identical to seven](images/b01_dequ185.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>8</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![two super eight identical to three](images/b01_dequ186.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>9</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>6</mn></math>![two super nine identical to six](images/b01_dequ187.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>10</mn></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![two super 10 identical to one](images/b01_dequ188.png). That is, successive powers of 2 range across all the non-zero integers less than 11. This shows that 2 is a generator of the group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub 11 super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ189.png), which must therefore be cyclic. We say that 2 is a *primitive element* in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>11</mn><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub 11 super asterisk operator](images/b01_dequ190.png).

As far as the first claim is concerned, if there is a single numerical error at position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/b01_dequ191.png), say the digit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![a sub i equals x](images/b01_dequ192.png)is changed to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>![a sub i equals y](images/b01_dequ193.png), then the sum will be changed by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![two super i minus one times left parenthesis y minus x right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ194.png). Now, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>x</mi></math>![y not equals x](images/b01_dequ195.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8802;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![y minus x not identical to zero left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ196.png), and we also know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8802;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![two super i minus one not identical to zero left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ197.png). That is, the sum will be different to 1, and the error will be detected.

Next suppose that the values for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/b01_dequ198.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![a sub i minus one](images/b01_dequ199.png)are interchanged. In contributing to the sum, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![a sub i minus one](images/b01_dequ200.png)is multiplied by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></math>![two super i minus two](images/b01_dequ201.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/b01_dequ202.png)by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![two super i minus one](images/b01_dequ203.png). That is, the contribution to the sum (modulo 11) is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![a sub i minus one times two super i minus two plus a sub i times two super i minus one](images/b01_dequ204.png). If their order is reversed then the contribution to the sum will be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![a sub i times two super i minus two plus a sub i minus one times two super i minus one](images/b01_dequ205.png). That is, the difference in the sum will be

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![left parenthesis a sub i minus a sub i minus one right parenthesis times two super i minus two plus left parenthesis a sub i minus one minus a sub i right parenthesis times two super i minus one equals left parenthesis a sub i minus a sub i minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis two super i minus two minus two super i minus one right parenthesis full stop](images/b01_dequ206.png)

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>![a sub i](images/b01_dequ207.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![a sub i minus one](images/b01_dequ208.png)are distinct, and we don’t need to worry if they are the same, then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8802;</mo><mn>0</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis a sub i minus a sub i minus one right parenthesis not identical to zero left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ209.png). Similarly, we already observed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8802;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mn>11</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![two super i minus two not identical to two super i minus one left parenthesis mod 11 right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ210.png)for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>i</mi></math>![i](images/b01_dequ211.png), and hence the modulo 11 sum will be different after the interchange of two digits, and the error will be detected. Indeed, if digits are interchanged that are separated by less than 10 positions, an error will be detected.

 

### The Euler phi function

In [Section 4.5](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0006), I claimed that the Euler phi function, otherwise known as the Euler totient function, is *multiplicative*; i.e. the following result holds.

A simple example may help. In [Section, 4.5.2](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0009) I gave the example of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn></math>![equation sequence part 1 n equals part 2 15 equals part 3 three multiplication five](images/b01_dequ344.png). First observe that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![phi of three equals two](images/b01_dequ345.png), where the set of positive integers less than 3 and coprime to 3 is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two right curly bracket](images/b01_dequ346.png). Also, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>![phi of five equals four](images/b01_dequ347.png), and the set of coprime integers in this case is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></math>![left curly bracket one comma two comma three comma four right curly bracket](images/b01_dequ348.png). Then the set of values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math>![a multiplication five plus b multiplication three](images/b01_dequ349.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/b01_dequ350.png)is coprime to 3 and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/b01_dequ351.png)is coprime to 5, is:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mtable columnalign="left" rowlines="none none none"><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>19</mn><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="right"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></math>![multiline equation line 1 left curly bracket one multiplication five plus one multiplication three equals eight comma two multiplication five plus one multiplication three equals 13 comma line 2 one multiplication five plus two multiplication three equals 11 comma two multiplication five plus two multiplication three equals 16 comma line 3 one multiplication five plus three multiplication three equals 14 comma two multiplication five plus three multiplication three equals 19 comma line 4 one multiplication five plus four multiplication three equals 17 comma two multiplication five plus four multiplication three equals 22 right curly bracket full stop](images/b01_dequ352.png)

After reducing modulo 15 this gives the set of eight values

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![left curly bracket eight comma 13 comma 11 comma one comma 14 comma four comma two comma seven right curly bracket comma](images/b01_dequ353.png)

which are precisely the values coprime to 15.

### Proving Fermat’s Little Theorem

I gave Fermat’s Little Theorem at the end of [Section 4.5](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0006), and left the proof as an exercise. The theorem itself is as follows.

### Factorising Large Numbers

In [Section 4.8](#c004.xhtml#c004-sec-0016), I asserted that it is not hard to show that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></math>![cap n equals p times q](images/b01_dequ381.png)and you can find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ382.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ383.png)such that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>mod</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![d multiplication e identical to one times left parenthesis prefix mod of left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis right parenthesis comma](images/b01_dequ384.png)

then it is possible to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ385.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ386.png), i.e. to factorise <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi></math>![cap n](images/b01_dequ387.png).

Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d multiplication e identical to one left parenthesis mod left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ388.png), we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d times e minus one equals s times left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis q minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ389.png)for some integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/b01_dequ390.png). Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>![c equals left parenthesis d times e minus one right parenthesis solidus two](images/b01_dequ391.png); we can do this since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![d times e minus one](images/b01_dequ392.png)is even; this follows since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ393.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ394.png)are both odd. Choose a random value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g left parenthesis one less than g less than cap n right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ396.png)and compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi mathvariant="normal">mod</mi><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mtext>&#8201;</mtext><mi>N</mi></math>![h equals g super c mod cap n](images/b01_dequ397.png). There is a reasonable probability that either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ398.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ399.png)is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h minus one](images/b01_dequ400.png); this follows since

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>1</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![multirelation h squared equals left parenthesis g super c right parenthesis squared equals g super two times c equals g super d times e minus one identical to one times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times cap n right parenthesis full stop](images/b01_dequ401.png)

Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap n bar left parenthesis h squared minus one right parenthesis equals left parenthesis h plus one right parenthesis times left parenthesis h minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ402.png), and so either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ403.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ404.png)both divide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h plus one](images/b01_dequ405.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h minus one](images/b01_dequ406.png), or one divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h minus one](images/b01_dequ407.png)and the other divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h plus one](images/b01_dequ408.png)(the latter being the desired case we want).

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ409.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ410.png)is a factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![h minus one](images/b01_dequ411.png), then either <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ412.png)or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ413.png)will equal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![gcd left parenthesis h minus one comma cap n right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ414.png), which is straightforward to compute using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm. If the gcd is 1, then one can simply try another value <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ415.png)until <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi></math>![p](images/b01_dequ416.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi></math>![q](images/b01_dequ417.png)are found.

 

## Groups

### Identities and Inverses

When I gave the definition of group in [Section 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0001), I required the identity element to be a right and left identity and also for inverses to be simultaneously right and left inverses. However, I then claimed that it was only necessary to require there to be (a) a right identity, and (b) a right inverse for every element, and the rest followed. I will now show why this is true.

Suppose that for every element in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis cap g comma asterisk operator right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ418.png)there is a right identity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ419.png)(i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi></math>![g asterisk operator e equals g](images/b01_dequ420.png)for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/b01_dequ421.png)) and that every element has a right inverse, i.e. for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/b01_dequ422.png)there is an element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g super negative one element of cap g](images/b01_dequ423.png)with the property that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g asterisk operator g super negative one equals e](images/b01_dequ424.png).

Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![g element of cap g](images/b01_dequ425.png), and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![g super negative one](images/b01_dequ426.png)is its right inverse, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g asterisk operator g super negative one equals e](images/b01_dequ427.png).

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 g super negative one equals part 2 g super negative one asterisk operator e equals part 3 g super negative one asterisk operator g asterisk operator g super negative one full stop](images/b01_dequ428.png)

The first equality holds because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ429.png)is a right identity, and the second equality holds since I assumed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></math>![g asterisk operator g super negative one equals e](images/b01_dequ430.png). But since every element has a right inverse, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![g super negative one](images/b01_dequ431.png)must have a right inverse—call it <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![left parenthesis g super negative one right parenthesis super negative one](images/b01_dequ432.png). Multiplying both sides of the above equation by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![left parenthesis g super negative one right parenthesis super negative one](images/b01_dequ433.png), I get:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></math>![g super negative one asterisk operator left parenthesis g super negative one right parenthesis super negative one equals g super negative one asterisk operator g asterisk operator g super negative one asterisk operator left parenthesis g super negative one right parenthesis super negative one comma](images/b01_dequ434.png)

i.e.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 e equals part 2 g super negative one asterisk operator g asterisk operator e equals part 3 g super negative one asterisk operator g full stop](images/b01_dequ435.png)

So if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![g super negative one](images/b01_dequ436.png)is the right inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ437.png)then it is also the left inverse of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ438.png).

I now need to prove that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ439.png)is a left identity as well as a right identity. I assumed that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![e equals g asterisk operator g super negative one](images/b01_dequ440.png)for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ441.png), and so, post multiplying both sides of this equation by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ442.png)it follows that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo><msup><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>&#8727;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 e asterisk operator g equals part 2 g asterisk operator g super negative one asterisk operator g equals part 3 g full stop](images/b01_dequ443.png)

That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>e</mi></math>![e](images/b01_dequ444.png)is a left identity, and the result follows.

### Cyclic Groups Are Abelian

In [Section 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0003), I made the claim that every cyclic group is abelian, and I asked you to see if you could prove it.

### Generating the Group of Integers Modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>m</mi></math>![m](images/b01_dequ462.png)Under Addition

I posed a simple question about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub n](images/b01_dequ463.png)in [Section 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0003). I observed that every non-zero element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub five](images/b01_dequ464.png)is a generator of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub five comma plus right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ465.png). I said that a similar result does not hold for every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ466.png), and asked you to find out exactly which <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ467.png)it *does* hold for. The simple answer is that it is true if and only if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ468.png)is prime.

First suppose that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ469.png)is prime, and let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ470.png)satisfy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![one less than or equals x less than or equals n minus one](images/b01_dequ471.png). Then clearly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mi>x</mi><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>mod</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![n times x identical to zero times left parenthesis prefix mod of n right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ472.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![ord left parenthesis x right parenthesis bar n](images/b01_dequ473.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![ord left parenthesis x right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ474.png)is the smallest positive integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math>![s](images/b01_dequ475.png)such that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><munder><munder><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&#9183;</mo></munder><mrow><mi>s</mi><mtext>&#160;</mtext><mtext>times</mtext></mrow></munder><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="1em"/></mstyle><mrow/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi></mrow><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mstyle scriptlevel="0"><mspace width="0.167em"/></mstyle><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![plus plus plus xx times times midline horizontal ellipsis x bottom curly bracket separator separator s times identical to zero times left parenthesis normal m times normal o times normal d times n right parenthesis full stop](images/b01_dequ476.png)

But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x not equals zero](images/b01_dequ477.png)and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![s equals ord left parenthesis x right parenthesis greater than one](images/b01_dequ478.png). Thus, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ479.png)is prime, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![ord left parenthesis x right parenthesis equals n](images/b01_dequ480.png).

Now suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ481.png)is not prime, and hence suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/b01_dequ482.png)is a divisor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math>![n](images/b01_dequ483.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![one less than a less than n](images/b01_dequ484.png). Hence there is a integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi></math>![b](images/b01_dequ485.png)that satisfies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![a times b equals n](images/b01_dequ486.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mn>1</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![one less than b less than n](images/b01_dequ487.png). So we know that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![ord left parenthesis a right parenthesis bar b](images/b01_dequ488.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>b</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>n</mi></math>![b less than n](images/b01_dequ489.png). Hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>a</mi></math>![a](images/b01_dequ490.png)is not a generator of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub n comma plus right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ491.png).

### The Group <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma multiplication right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ492.png)Is Cyclic

[Section 5.4](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0004) concludes with [Theorem 5.1](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0007). I stated there that the proof of this result is non-trivial and promised to provide more information here. In fact, to establish this result I will use some key results and terminology from [Chapter 6](#c006.xhtml#c006), so it makes sense to relegate this to the end of the book.

To make life simpler for you the reader, I will start by repeating the result I want to prove.

I also need to introduce the notion of roots of polynomials. Suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/b01_dequ555.png)is a polynomial in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![script cap f of x](images/b01_dequ556.png)for a field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/b01_dequ557.png). If we suppose

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></math>![p of x equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero plus p sub one times x plus p sub two times x squared plus ellipsis plus p sub d times x super d comma](images/b01_dequ558.png)

and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/b01_dequ559.png)is an element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></math>![script cap f](images/b01_dequ560.png), then the *evaluation* of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/b01_dequ561.png)at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/b01_dequ562.png), written as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of c](images/b01_dequ563.png), is simply the field element obtained by substituting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/b01_dequ564.png)for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi></math>![x](images/b01_dequ565.png), i.e.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>c</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![p of c equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero plus p sub one times c plus p sub two times c squared plus ellipsis plus p sub d times c super d full stop](images/b01_dequ566.png)

If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![p of c equals zero](images/b01_dequ567.png)for some field element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/b01_dequ568.png), then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>![c](images/b01_dequ569.png)is called a *root* of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/b01_dequ570.png).

Suppose, for example, the field is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mn>7</mn></msub></math>![double-struck cap z sub seven](images/b01_dequ571.png), the integers working modulo 7, and

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![p of x equals sum with 4 summands x cubed plus five times x squared plus x plus five full stop](images/b01_dequ572.png)

Then 2 is a root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![p of x](images/b01_dequ574.png)since

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>&#8901;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo class="stixwiley" rspace="0" lspace="0">&#8801;</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>mod</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></math>![multirelation p of two equals sum with 4 summands two cubed plus five dot operator two squared plus two plus five equals sum with 4 summands eight plus 20 plus two plus five equals 35 identical to zero times left parenthesis prefix mod of seven right parenthesis full stop](images/b01_dequ575.png)

I can now state the following important result.

This gives the following valuable corollary.

I am now ready to prove the theorem.

*Proof of the main theorem.* If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ629.png)is any element of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator](images/b01_dequ630.png)then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![ord left parenthesis g right parenthesis bar left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ631.png)(since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ632.png)is a group of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p minus one](images/b01_dequ633.png), this follows by [Lemma 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0012)). So the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![p minus one](images/b01_dequ634.png)elements of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator](images/b01_dequ635.png)can be partitioned into sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ636.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![g element of cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ637.png)if it has order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ638.png)(and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ639.png)is only defined if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d bar left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ640.png)). Then

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 n ary summation over d bar left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis over absolute value of cap x sub d equals part 2 absolute value of double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator equals part 3 p minus one full stop](images/b01_dequ641.png)

I next introduce a related family of sets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ642.png), where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ643.png)consists of all elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ644.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup></math>![double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator](images/b01_dequ645.png)which satisfy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![g super d equals one](images/b01_dequ646.png). So clearly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8838;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d subset of or equals cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ647.png)and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap x sub d less than or equals absolute value of cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ648.png).

I next claim that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi></math>![absolute value of cap y sub d less than or equals d](images/b01_dequ649.png). Why is this? Well, every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ650.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ651.png)is a solution of the polynomial equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![x super d minus one equals zero](images/b01_dequ652.png), i.e. every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ653.png)in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ654.png)is a root of the polynomial <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x super d minus one](images/b01_dequ655.png). Hence, by the Factor Theorem (Corollary 1) it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x minus g right parenthesis bar left parenthesis x super d minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ656.png).

Now from [Corollary 7.2](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0005) it follows that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></math>![double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator of x](images/b01_dequ657.png)is a Unique Factorisation Domain, and hence there can be at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ658.png)factors <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x minus g right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ659.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![x super d minus one](images/b01_dequ660.png), and so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi></math>![absolute value of cap y sub d less than or equals d](images/b01_dequ661.png).

Next suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![d bar left parenthesis p minus one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ662.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ663.png)is non-empty (I want to show that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ664.png)is non-empty for every such <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ665.png), but I’m not there yet). Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![g element of cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ666.png); then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ667.png)generates a cyclic subgroup <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![script cap g equals left parenthesis cap g comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ668.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">Z</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>&#8727;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis double-struck cap z sub p super asterisk operator comma dot operator right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ669.png)of order <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ670.png)(see the proof of [Lemma 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0012)). By [Lemma 5.3](#c005.xhtml#c005-sec-0012) this means that every element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>h</mi></math>![h](images/b01_dequ671.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/b01_dequ672.png)satisfies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>ord</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>d</mi></math>![ord left parenthesis h right parenthesis bar d](images/b01_dequ673.png), and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap g subset of or equals cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ674.png), i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap g less than or equals absolute value of cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ675.png). But <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></math>![absolute value of cap g equals d](images/b01_dequ676.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi></math>![absolute value of cap y sub d less than or equals d](images/b01_dequ677.png)and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math>![absolute value of cap g equals absolute value of cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ678.png)and thus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap g equals cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ679.png)(since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap g subset of or equals cap y sub d](images/b01_dequ680.png)).

So, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>&#8838;</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi></math>![cap x sub d subset of or equals cap y sub d equals cap g](images/b01_dequ681.png), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ682.png)is equal to those elements in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/b01_dequ683.png)which have order precisely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>d</mi></math>![d](images/b01_dequ684.png). Recalling that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi></math>![g](images/b01_dequ685.png)is a generator of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi></math>![script cap g](images/b01_dequ686.png), this means that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>![cap x sub d](images/b01_dequ687.png)is equal to the elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msup></math>![g super t](images/b01_dequ688.png)of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>![cap g](images/b01_dequ689.png)where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mtext>gcd</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![gcd left parenthesis t comma d right parenthesis equals one times left parenthesis one less than or equals t less than or equals d right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ691.png).
