However, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1266.png)is monic and has degree three, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>![x minus x sub one](images/b01_dequ1267.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>![x minus x sub two](images/b01_dequ1268.png)are also monic. Then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x](images/b01_dequ1269.png)must be monic and have degree one, i.e. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>t</mi></math>![s of x equals x minus t](images/b01_dequ1270.png)for some <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/b01_dequ1271.png). So there is a third root (namely <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>t</mi></math>![t](images/b01_dequ1272.png)) of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1273.png), and so we are OK after all.

In [Section 8.6](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0009), I also promised to show why the formula for combining a point with itself results in a point on the curve. Recall that if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ1274.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>![y sub one not equals zero](images/b01_dequ1275.png), then I defined <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 cap p dot operator cap p equals part 2 cap p squared equals part 3 left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ1276.png), where

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo></math>![x sub two equals left parenthesis three times left parenthesis x sub one right parenthesis squared plus a divided by two times y sub one right parenthesis squared minus two times x sub one comma](images/b01_dequ1277.png)

and

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced separators="" open="(" close=")"><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![y sub two equals left parenthesis three times left parenthesis x sub one right parenthesis squared plus a divided by two times y sub one right parenthesis times left parenthesis x sub one minus x sub two right parenthesis minus y sub one full stop](images/b01_dequ1278.png)

Showing that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ1279.png)is on the curve defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>![y squared equals sum with 3 summands x cubed plus a times x plus b](images/b01_dequ1280.png)uses a similar argument to the previous case. That is, the argument involves showing that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p equals left parenthesis x sub one comma y sub one right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ1281.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>P</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![cap p squared equals left parenthesis x sub two comma y sub two right parenthesis](images/b01_dequ1282.png)both lie on the curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>L</mi></math>![cap l](images/b01_dequ1283.png)defined by

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>,</mo></math>![y equals lamda times x plus nu comma](images/b01_dequ1284.png)

for two field elements <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/b01_dequ1285.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#957;</mi></math>![nu](images/b01_dequ1286.png)(as well as all lying on the elliptic curve). However, in this case <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#955;</mi></math>![lamda](images/b01_dequ1287.png)is different; the two field elements are defined to satisfy:

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></math>![lamda equals three times left parenthesis x sub one right parenthesis squared plus a divided by two times y sub one comma](images/b01_dequ1288.png)

and (as previously)

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>.</mo></math>![nu equals y sub one minus lamda times x sub one full stop](images/b01_dequ1289.png)

Again, the fact that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>P</mi></math>![cap p](images/b01_dequ1290.png)lies on the curve <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>L</mi></math>![cap l](images/b01_dequ1291.png)follows immediately from the definition of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>&#957;</mi></math>![nu](images/b01_dequ1292.png). The remainder of the argument is analogous to that given above.

### Making Reed–Solomon Encoding Systematic

In [Section 8.8.1](#c008.xhtml#c008-sec-0013), I left it as an exercise to discover how to make Reed–Solomon encoding systematic. The key point to note is that the codewords correspond to polynomials of degree at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n minus one](images/b01_dequ1293.png)that are multiples of the generator polynomial.

Recall that the data polynomial (of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![k minus one](images/b01_dequ1294.png)) is

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></math>![p of x equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero plus p sub one times x plus p sub two times x squared plus ellipsis plus p sub k minus one times x super k minus one comma](images/b01_dequ1295.png)

where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![p sub zero comma p sub one comma ellipsis comma p sub k minus one](images/b01_dequ1296.png)are the data symbols, i.e. elements from the chosen finite field. The generator polynomial (of degree <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n minus k minus one](images/b01_dequ1297.png)) is

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></math>![g of x equals sum with variable number of summands g sub zero plus g sub one times x plus g sub two times x squared plus ellipsis plus g sub n minus k minus one times x super n minus k minus one comma](images/b01_dequ1298.png)

where again <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>![g sub zero comma g sub one comma ellipsis comma g sub k minus one](images/b01_dequ1299.png)are elements from the chosen finite field.

To generate a codeword <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x](images/b01_dequ1300.png)which includes the data symbols, proceed as follows. First compute

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>.</mo></math>![p of x times x super n minus k equals sum with variable number of summands p sub zero times x super n minus k plus p sub one times x super n minus k plus one plus p sub two times x super n minus k plus two plus ellipsis plus p sub k minus one times x super n minus one full stop](images/b01_dequ1301.png)

That is, this is a polynomial for which the coefficients of the ‘most significant’ terms are the data symbols. I now simply need to choose the coefficients for the ‘least significant’ terms so that the resulting polynomial is a multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of x](images/b01_dequ1302.png). To do this I first use the Division Theorem for polynomials over a finite field ([Theorem 7.3](#c007.xhtml#c007-sec-0009)) to find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/b01_dequ1303.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1304.png)such that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![p of x times x super n minus k equals q of x dot operator g of x plus r of x comma](images/b01_dequ1305.png)

where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1306.png)has degree less than the degree of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of x](images/b01_dequ1307.png), i.e. less than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></math>![n minus k](images/b01_dequ1308.png). That is, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1309.png)has degree at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n minus k minus one](images/b01_dequ1310.png).

Now put <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x equals p of x times x super n minus k minus r of x](images/b01_dequ1311.png). I claim that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x](images/b01_dequ1312.png)is a multiple of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![g of x](images/b01_dequ1313.png)and is hence a codeword. To see this observe that

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="block"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8901;</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></math>![equation sequence part 1 s of x equals part 2 p of x times x super n minus k minus r of x equals part 3 q of x dot operator g of x comma](images/b01_dequ1314.png)

by definition of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![q of x](images/b01_dequ1315.png)and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1316.png). Finally, since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![r of x](images/b01_dequ1317.png)has degree at most <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math>![n minus k minus one](images/b01_dequ1318.png), subtracting it from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></math>![p of x times x super n minus k](images/b01_dequ1319.png)will leave the coefficients of the terms <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>![x super n minus k comma x super n minus k plus one comma ellipsis comma x super n minus k minus one](images/b01_dequ1320.png)unchanged, and hence <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll" display="inline"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>![s of x](images/b01_dequ1321.png)incorporates the data symbols as the coefficients of its ‘most significant’ terms, and I am done.

I also claimed the converse holds, in the form of the following lemma, but I left the proof as an exercise.

# Further Reading

The main problem I had in putting together this final part of the book was in deciding what to leave out—there are so many excellent books to recommend. Indeed, looking through these books reminded me that this small effort rather pales into insignificance by comparison. Nonetheless, I still feel that this volume attempts to do something that no other book I am aware of achieves. In any event, I hope you have found it helpful—and perhaps even enjoyable! I have certainly had fun writing it; after all, as author I get to include all the material I enjoy and leave out the bits I don’t.

I have divided my suggestions for further reading into four main categories, the first three of which list recommended books covering mathematics itself (and mathematicians), abstract algebra and applications. The final category is online resources—there are some really excellent online resources for mathematics, and I list some of those I found most useful.

## Mathematics and Mathematicians

These books give personal views on the nature of mathematics, and also descriptions of some of the more famous mathematicians.

*   A D Aczel, ‘*Fermat’s Last Theorem*’, Viking (1996), describes the history and influence of a ‘theorem’ that the 17th-century mathematician Pierre de Fermat claimed to have a proof for, but did not write down. Attempts to prove this theorem, that forms part of number theory, have had huge impacts in the development of mathematics across a wide range of fields. In 1993, Andrew Wiles gave a proof, which—after some repair work—is now generally accepted as having resolved the problem, i.e. it is now a theorem without the quotation marks!
*   M Aigner and G M Ziegler, ‘*Proofs from the Book*’, Springer (2001), 2nd edition. This book contains a collection of particularly beautiful proofs of theorems, and was inspired by the late, great Paul Erdős, who talked about ‘The Book’ as something maintained by God for perfect proofs.
*   E T Bell, ‘*Men of Mathematics*’, Touchstone Books (1986), contains a series of short biographies of major mathematicians, originally published in 1937. The accounts are not always 100% reliable, but are eminently readable and bring the people to life. Of course, the title is somewhat sexist in that it suggests, deliberately or accidentally, that mathematics is for men only. One woman is mentioned, however, namely Sonja Kowalewski.
*   D Debakcsy, ‘*A History of Women in Mathematics*’, Pen & Sword Books (2023), provides brief portraits of major women mathematicians from antiquity to the present. It is something of a counterpoint to E T Bell’s ‘*Men of Mathematics*’, and shows the breadth of mathematical results achieved by women over the centuries despite the many obstacles placed in their way.
*   G H Hardy, ‘*A Mathematician’s Apology*’, Lector House (1940), is a personal view of mathematics, written by one of the greats of the first half of the 20th century and originally published in 1940. He defends the idea that mathematics is something beautiful and worth pursuing for its own sake, and not just for its potential applications. I think he would be surprised to learn how much mathematics viewed as useless but beautiful in 1940 has turned out to be useful!
*   R Kanigel, ‘*The Man Who Knew Infinity*’, Scribners (1992), is an immensely readable life of the mathematical genius Srinivasa Ramanujan and his friendship with G H Hardy. Indeed, you may be more familiar with the 2016 film adaptation, but I would encourage you to explore the book.
*   M Kline, ‘*Mathematics: The Loss of Certainty*’, Oxford University Press (1980), is vast in its scope, covering the development of rigorous mathematics over almost 3000 years. It culminates in a review of the state of mathematical foundations, which suffered what seemed then a major disaster in the early 20th century. A gross simplification might say that efforts to prove the consistency of mathematics using mathematics itself was shown to be impossible.
*   L M Osen, ‘*Women in Mathematics*’, MIT Press (1974), is further evidence of the rich, but often ignored, contributions made by women to mathematics. The book contains eight biographies of women, along with summaries of their mathematical contributions.
*   B Wardaugh, ‘*The Book of Wonders*’, William Collins (2020), is an entertaining and illuminating history of Euclid’s Elements, one of the first (if not the first) treatises to attempt to give a rigorous treatment to mathematics, involving theorems and proofs. Euclid’s Elements have had a profound influence on the development of mathematics since it was first written some 2300 years ago.

 

## Abstract Algebra

The books listed here all cover much of the ground I cover in this book, although typically with a much broader and deeper scope, and in a more textbook-like fashion.

*   G Birkhoff and S Mac Lane, ‘*A Survey of Modern Algebra*’, A K Peters (1997), 4th edition, is a classic text on abstract algebra, and remains an excellent introduction, albeit one that is not to be taken lightly. It served as the default textbook on abstract algebra for a generation or more, as exemplified by its unlikely appearance in a 1964 short story, ‘The Mathenauts’ by Norman Kagan.^()
*   A Meijer, ‘*Algebra for Cryptologists*’, Springer (2016), is perhaps the book that is closest to this one in scope. It aims to provide a rigorous introduction to the mathematics necessary to understand modern cryptography. However, it is a ‘proper’ mathematics textbook aimed at readers already happy with the theorem–proof style, and is much more comprehensive in its scope than this book.
*   C W Norman, ‘*Undergraduate Algebra: A First Course*’, Oxford University Press (1986) is a textbook aimed at introducing abstract algebra to undergraduates. It is rather more gentle in its approach than Birkhoff and Mac Lane.
*   R A Wilson, ‘*The Finite Simple Groups*’, Springer (2009), provides an introduction to the finite simple groups. Written in the wake of the classification of all finite simple groups, it provides very detailed information about all these groups. It is a mathematically sophisticated text, but excellent if you want to learn much more about these groups.

## Applications

Throughout this book, interspersed with my introductions to groups, rings and fields, I have described some key applications, focussing mainly on those relating to computing and digital communications. There are so many relevant books—the following are my personal favourites:

*   T Beth, D Jungnickel and H Lenz, ‘*Design Theory*’, Bibliographisches Institut Mannheim (1985), provides a comprehensive account of the theory of combinatorial designs, including difference sets. An updated 2nd edition in two volumes was published in 1999.
*   R Hill, ‘*A First Course in Coding Theory*’, Oxford University Press (1986), does what it says on the tin. This is an easy to read and thorough introduction to mathematical coding theory, a subject built on abstract algebra that only emerged in the mid-20th century but has grown to be vitally important in today’s world of ubiquitous digital communications.
*   K M Martin, ‘*Everyday Cryptography: Fundamental Principles and Applications*’, Oxford University Press (2017), provides a first introduction to the uses and abuses of cryptography. It is not so much concerned with the underlying mathematics, although this is not ignored, but the main focus is on what cryptography can be used for.
*   S Golomb, ‘*Shift Register Sequences*’, Holden-Day (1967), is the original classic text on shift register sequences, written by the man who played a major role in developing the theory. The presentation now seems rather dated, but it is a very readable and entertaining book.
*   M Goresky and A Klapper, ‘*Algebraic Shift Register Sequences*’, Cambridge University Press (2012), is a comprehensive and modern account of the subject. It includes a detailed appendix providing the necessary mathematical background.
*   D R Hughes and F C Piper, ‘*Design Theory*’, Cambridge University Press (1985), gives a highly accessible introduction to block designs, including difference sets. Whilst it is much less comprehensive than Beth, Jungnickel and Lenz, it nevertheless covers the fundamentals of the subject.
*   D Knuth, ‘*The Art of Computer Programming*, Volumes 1, 2, 3, 4A and 4B’, Addison-Wesley, 1997–2023, is a monumental work, covering a vast range of computer algorithms. It is both comprehensive and rigorous from a mathematical perspective; indeed, it covers much of the material in this book, albeit in a much more condensed form. The books are wonderful, albeit not always an easy read.
*   A Pott, P V Kumar, T Helleseth and D Jungnickel (eds), ‘*Difference Sets, Sequences and their Correlation Properties*’, Kluwer Academic (1999), contains a series of chapters by leading experts in their field. The topics addressed relate closely to several of the applications introduced in this book.
*   E S Selmer, ‘*Linear Recurrence Relations Over Finite Fields*’, Department of Mathematics, University of Bergen (1966), covers much of the same ground as Golomb’s book, but from a mathematical rather than an engineering perspective. Despite never being published in the normal way, it served as a key reference for many years, and remains an excellent resource. It is rather a shame that the University of Bergen has not made an electronic version available.
*   T M Thompson, ‘*From Error-correcting Codes Through Sphere Packings to Simple Groups*’, Mathematical Association of America (1983), is an immensely readable account of a range of topics which also relate closely to subjects introduced in this book.
*   D Welsh, ‘*Codes and Cryptography*’, Oxford University Press (1988), now looks a little dated, but it is an excellent and very accessible introduction to coding theory and cryptography, focussing on areas of interest from a mathematical perspective.

## Online Resources

Finally, I would like to mention a few online resources that I found especially useful when writing this book. There are, of course, many more.

*   A personal favourite is the Combinatorial Objects Server (`http://combos.org/`). This site enables you to play with combinatorial objects, such as permutations with particular properties.
*   MacTutor (`https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/`) is an excellent free online resource containing biographies of more than 3000 mathematicians, and much else besides. I have used this resource extensively in providing much of the biographical information in this book.
*   The Mathematics Stack Exchange (`https://math.stackexchange.com`) is one of 183 online ‘question and answer’ communities, and enables anyone to ask a mathematical question and receive detailed and informative answers from the mathematical community. I thoroughly recommend it—often the question you want to ask has been asked and answered already.
*   I already mentioned the splendid Online Encyclopaedia of Integer Sequences (the OEIS)—available at `https://oeis.org/`. It is difficult not to get sucked into endless rabbit holes when exploring this terrific resource.
*   ProofWiki (`https://proofwiki.org`) is a freely accessible repository of proofs of a very wide range of mathematical results, as well as containing a huge collection of definitions of mathematical concepts.
